This is one of those times I wish there was a "meh" rating. I love this game, I do, but I believe that feeling is heavily influenced by the fact that I'm obsessed with all things LEGO, and the fact that the game was gifted to me by my SO.
Pros
- Explore whole worlds made out of LEGO
- Drive around in cool LEGO vehicles, or ride on adorable LEGO animals
- You can build pretty much any structure you can think of
- The sense of progression in the game now that it's out of alpha has kept me playing a lot longer than when I first
experimented with it
- The graphics are whimsical and fun
- Interacting with various minifigures before being able to 'discover' them is fun.
- I like the narrator that pops up from time to time
Cons
- This game is no longer in alpha, WHY is it still SO DARN BUGGY!
- You will clip through layers of the world (ie get rocketed back to the surface) if you walk too hard at the wall or ceiling in
a cave
- Sometimes completeing a quest will not register with the NPC minifig and you have to abandon it without your reward.
- The building tool is so inconvinient to use! You will accidentally take out the wrong terrain/ too much terrain/ place
bricks in a place you did not at all intend to. This can make the main draw of the game (ie building cool stuff with LEGO)
more frustrating than fun if you're doing something big.
- The controls are not intuitive. I cannot tell you how many times I've accidentally gone to the universe map when trying
to close a menu or put a tool away.
- You can't make custom drivable vehicles (as far as I know/ have encountered in the game)
Overall, at this price point, I just can't recommend it. The main issue for me is that this is being sold at a full release price but has so many bugs that you feel like you're playing a beta. Either the bugs need to get fixed, or it needs to be on half price sale for this game to be worth it.

I really love ARPGs and the way they play, that said I absolutely despise this game.
I'm reccomending it because despite its major flaws it's still playable and has a great atmosphere, although you're very likely to get fed up with it and uninstall.
I'll start this off by saying that all of its problems are caused by too many enemies at once, this game goes completely overboard in that department.
Area of effect damage is a requirement, anything that does single target is next to useless here. The further you go into the game the larger the mob of enemies it constantly throws at you becomes, you can't even pick them off from a distance because chances are that the entire mob is going to react and come after you, and another thing to note is that your ranged attacks do not go over enemies which means all those high damage ranged enemies are safe behind the giant wall in your face. And on top of that some of them can heal other enemies, so you HAVE to kill them first.
There is a perk that makes you atheral when your health runs out, you're going to find yourself getting a lot of useage out of that one. Along with that you're going to find yourself needing to heal constantly, so cooldown reduction is an absolute must so you can use heal often.
I cannot even fathom playing the game class due the fact that there are enemies who drain your mana beyond faster than you can regenerate it even with mana potions, and this doesn't stop being a pain if with other classes, because all of your skills cost mana to use except your default skills.

As an introduction, I am a veteran player of Guility Gear and Blazblue series. I've won numerous tournaments in all versions of Blazblue and held the rank #1 spot for several characters on Xbox live. As i write this review I will be as neutral as possible.
Blazbue is a very unique fighting game franchise, many call it the sister of Guility Gear. Blazblue is an air dasher, high speed,  combo heavy fighting game. The game is very visually satisfying and has one hell of a soundtrack. People who have a history in Street figher, SoulCaibur, DOA, Tekken, etc. Tend to somewhat stray away from Blazblue. The game sets itself apart by its core engine mechanics and unforgivable mistakes.
But fray not, the game is very newcomer friendly. Unlike many other fighting games, Blazblue Extend has an ingame voice over tutorial that guides you step by step on EVERY single game mechanic while teaching you combos at the sametime. After you go through the tutorial, you are encouraged to try "challenge mode." But don't get the challenge mode in this game twisted like the one in Street fighter or Street Fighter x Tekken.
90% Challenge mode combos in this game actually teach you Basic "Bread and butter" combos that you will be using during live play. Even high level pros use some of the bread and butter combos you will see in challenge mode. They are very practical and meter efficient. Once you feel comfortable training and getting your challenge mode combos down you can take the fight online.
Online BB extend has a few differences from the console. You CANNOT turn off your ingame mic and you CANNOT see your opponents ping levels before the fight. The only way to estimate the lag is by actually engaging into the battle. With that being said, there are players from all over the world playing online. If you wish to play in player matches simply name your lobby in the general area of where you live. For example, I live in South Carolina so I name my lobby "Southeast USA", that way people can get a better estimate of the ping to be expected.
But for the sake of keeping the wall of text down, Blazblue is a great fighting game franchise for newcomers and experienced fighters. You will enjoy the incredibly unique and flashy combos by all of the characters. The game also has an interesting and yet paradoxal story which you will have fun trying to figure out on your own! Also check out the blazblue anime online if you have a hulu subscription.
If you have an specific questions regarding the game, you can reply to my review or send me a message on steam.
EDIT: Mics can be muted or turned off ingame now.

EDIT: I changed this review to negative. The building is lovely, the biomes and items are nice, but without proper multiplayer, there's just no real point to it. You can only play in 2-player (and even it is a bit broken). I'd love this game if you could share it with your friends, build huge castles together and have battles.
____________________________________________________________________________
Love the exploration and all the little things to find and unlock, and it has been MASSIVELY improved since the Early Access days (I get a stable >60 FPS on my laptop with no dips now***). The building tools are beyond incredible.
However, the gameplay is a bit floaty, similar to other Lego titles. Combat feels impresise and there's no penalty to dying. There's also just support for two players at the time - Would love to be able to play it with many more.
Also noteworthy: Because of the insane amount of brick types and many complex tools for building, it doesn't really invite bulding as much as for example Minecraft. If you take the time though, you can create literally anything. Your creations (or just random things you find) can be copied, pasted and exported too.
Still no Steam Workshop integration, but it certainly must come soon. I can't imagine why it wouldn't. This game is perfect for content creation and sharing.
Another nuiscance is the lack of mappable hotkeys. When you have a billion tools and items at your disposal, it's really annoying to have to open a selection wheel and scroll through huge lists every time you want to change equipment.
***UPDATE: I Take it back! Having now unlocked the "massive worlds" it's not uncommon for me to see sub-50FPS now, and in some areas with lots of glowing things (lava, crystals, etc.) I even dip below 30 - Which is really bad!

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful game. That is the very first thing that stands out when you start the game.
The first 5 minutes of the game are probably the best introduction to a game that I've ever played. Period. Wonderful bit of story telling.
Unfortunately after the first 5 minutes the platformer starts and while it is very well done - smooth animations, well designed combat and just generally fun - it doesn't really carry the feeling created at the start of the game which I think is a pity.
The first game comparable to this one that comes to mind is Bastion but where Bastion managed to keep a magical feeling going for me for a good few hours while playing this one has gone from being a great game to being a good game. So far at least. Having just started the game and only reached the barest beginnings of the storyline my opinion may well change.
So, do I think the game is worth buying? Yes.
Even if the game had only its first few minutes I would recommend it but the fact is that the game after those few minutes is also very good and although it doesn't manage to fully carry the feeling of those first few minutes, that introduction does make you far more invested in the main character than you would normally be in a platformer.

This review is for both Trine and Trine 2. Still haven't gotten to play Trine 3 yet.
Trine is platformer puzzle game with some action combat to destroy walls, enemies and terrains. There are 3 characters that can be played and will be free to switch around when playing in single player. While in co-op, each control a character up to a max of 3 players and are free to switch character if both party agree. Each character has their own special abilities and are required to change character to cross the level.
I've played the game in co-op for both Trine and Trine 2. Co-op is really fun with the psyhics and there will be alot of laughter when playing it with friends. There are some very minor glitch but nothing really gameplay affecting.
Trine in co-op is about 6 hours of gameplay time, without rushing anything and getting all the exp.
Trine 2 in co-op is about 6-8 hours of gameplay time, depending on how many times you died fighting the boss or getting out of the body of the monster that ate you.
All played in hard difficulty.
It's a really fun game to play with friends and really helps to build your teamwork in co-op. I would recommend waiting for the game to be on sale before buying it unless you really can't wait. While it's on sale, it will be around a dollars so it's worth getting it when's it's really cheap. Otherwise, the price is still abit high.

This game is a story and atmosphere heavy walking simulator mixed up with puzzle and combat segments. Besides tackling mental health as a subject matter the game tries (and as far as I can tell succedes) to imitate symptomes of psychosis through audio and visuals - and hits a homerun on all borders.
However, besides an intriguing, likeable and well written lead and a interesting world, the game stumbles on some of it's basic mechanics. Combat is simple but functional, repeats itself due to a lack of enemies. The last two hours are just a boring wave survival that is hampered by the soulslike lock on camera and the heavy zoom on the character model.
Puzzles get the job done but never manage to amaze and in the end kinda bore your way through the game since it is always just walking to point A, do B and then C opens - over and over again.
Overall I still recommend this game, if the theme and one story heavy character can carry a game for you. If you are a purely/mostls mechanicly driven player, this won't make you happy as it has zero replay value and mechanics are not in depth enough to spent time learning anything.
Still, I applaud the devs for their vision, the fantastic audio and motion capture work as well as the very atmosphereic music. I do hope to see more unique projects from them - but please put more work in the core mechanics and the  enemy design/number.

I really enjoyed this game. After playing the previous Wolfenstein game and realizing how damn good it was I couldnt wait to check this out. The game was pretty wonderful overall aside from it going by way to fast. I put in 20 hours so far and its left me wanting more!
There are a few hickups in the game that get annoying like getting stuck on things or behind things in the environment and not being able to get out but overall the game is pretty polished and lot of fun.
My only complaint is that ive finished the game and I want more and thats not really a complaint :D

- Graphics & Processing :
The game process nicely, but at some points the game started to freeze on me and I had to reset it (very rare occasion).
(and my drivers were up to date this time)
Nonetheless : it looks good and run at a smooth 60FPS
- Sound & Musics :
Mick Gordon saved it. 11/10
- Gameplay :
It's the same thing as in The New Order so there's not much more to say ; I said the gameplay was excellent in my review of Last Order, so it's still excellent here. There are the "body upgrade" at some point which are more situationnal than anything, and don't really contribute to anything.
The one flaw I see is that a lot of the areas where the shootings happen are mostly enclosed and don't have the same kind of "playground" feel as DOOM had last year. It's not a straight up corridor a la CoD either, so this is not too much of an issue.
- Storytelling :
Aïe.
I really didn't want to believe this would be this bad, but...
Spoiler free of what I had to say :
I can appreciate them trying to rewrite history & try to fit in historical characters, what I don't appreciate is them clearly not doing research and limiting the writing to "he's crazy & EVIL >:(", and trying to shove in an agenda which limits to "nazis are bad people yo" which I believe everyone here agrees on (even tho some people tend to think the opposite by calling other people disagreeing with them nazis)
Note : I wouldn't mind the clichés if there weren't as obnoxious as they are here. Again, The New Order's main villain was a cliché nazi mad scientist ; but he wasn't as obnoxious as the plot of this game is, and as the main villain which turned out to be a giant letdown...
- Length :
... and speaking of letdown, let's talk about the length now.
I don't know if there are as much cutscenes as there are gameplay segments, but I can tell you that they artificially boosted the length of the game by making enemies gang up on you really fast (which is a death sentence if you're low on armor). I don't mind the difficulty (Because I don't work at Polygon... YET :>), but when it's so obviously put to increase the length of your game because you didn't think to add some other levels or bossfights... I'm gonna call BS on that.
Note that this isn't HORRIBLE per say, the difficulty doesn't spike that much, but it's pretty obvious at some time that the devs wanted you to die multiple times so the game would feel longer.... and there's no better moment to see that as the final boss
All of this tells me one thing : this game is going to have some big story DLC, isn't it ? we're going to have to pay to have a more complete game, right ? and it'll be filled with some more cringy storytelling that insists on telling us that nazi are bad, right ?
CONCLUSION :
My problems with the story aren't why I'm not recommending it, or rather, they are not the only thing.
As I said : gameplay is very very good & the game performs fairly well ; so if you're just here for the gameplay & performances, you're safe.
Thing is, Steam doesn't allow for anything else than "Yes" or "No" as far as recommendations are concerned. And this is another case where I would say "no, but..."
I'd say "Not recommended YET". Wait for a sale (maybe a patch ?), also maybe wait for a "complete edition"...
I'm sad to say I can't really recommend the game at this time. Oh sure it's fun, it's not like a generic CoD clone FPS.... but guess what :
- DOOM is like that too
- Wolfenstein The New Order is like that too
- in fact... now that DOOM was considered a really good game, every dev is trying to make a FPS that would meet the same success, thus the same criteria... so you may be safer playing any other "new" "old" FPS than this one...

TL:DR No man's sky had a very bad case of overhype. But with the release of 1.3 bringing a lot of the content promised at launch and some amazing new features. The ARG brought back new old players and enticed new people to buy this game so I feel that the community will only grow from here. Definitely, a must buy.
The lack of content before 1.3 was an issue but Atlas Rises added not only quests(procedurally generated so you will never run out) but also makes planets more enjoyable to explore with its new biome system adding hours of enjoyment.
Atlas Uprising also added much more story to the game and overhauled many old flawed systems. Adding the ability to low fly is great as you no longer need a mod for it. Flying in and out of canyons and valleys is an amazing experience.
With this update, they laid the ground work for more multiplayer updates in the future. Exploring systems with friends is sure to be a blast and I can only see Hello Games adding on to this system in the future.
The Terrain Manipulator lets you add and remove ground as you see fit letting you build bigger and better than before!
For those who like exploring you can now find crashed freighters around planets. You can search them to find lost cargo. Using the new terrain manipulator you can find and excavate buried resources.
My verdict is that this update breathed a new life into this game that will keep it moving forward for quite a long time.
-Full patch notes-
Update 1.3, Atlas Rises, brings a brand new and overhauled central storyline, portals, a new procedural mission system, trade improvements, system economies, joint exploration and more.
This update marks the one year anniversary of No Man’s Sky, and a lot has changed. Please see Pathfinder and Foundation for previous major updates. This is the next step on our journey.
Full Update Article
Atlas Rises Trailer
Come chat about the Atlas Rises with us on our Discord Server!:
A NEW STORY
In the Atlas Rises story, the fabric of existence is starting to falter. A mysterious new interdimensional race have appeared. Glitches are causing ancient portals to activate. Our story brings a new context, quest system and branching narrative to No Man’s Sky. 30 hours of new story content. Double the lore and interactions of the existing game. Discover the truth behind the Abandoned Building logs, the World of Glass, the Sentinels, the redemption of the Gek, and the meaning of sixteen… After Waking Titan, Atlas Rises.
NEW WORLDS
The variety and visual quality of planetary biomes has been improved. Explore rare new exotic planet types as you journey toward the galactic core.
CRASHED FREIGHTERS
Discover and scavenge lost cargo from gigantic crashed Freighters on planetary surfaces.
Use the terrain manipulator to excavate buried resources in the region.
Complete Salvage missions for Guild rewards.
MISSION SYSTEM
Visit the new Mission Agent in Space Stations to pick up unique and rewarding new tasks.
Missions are constantly generated, and cater to all play styles (scanning, trading, combat and exploration).
New NPC guilds have been introduced, each with standing and objectives.
Build your standing with numerous NPC guilds and unlock more difficult, more rewarding missions.
INTERSTELLAR TRADING
New economic variables bring new depth to trading between star systems.
Star systems are now classed based on their economic strengths and weaknesses.
New trade goods have been added. Meet supply and demand by purchasing goods at a low price, and hauling them to economically favourable systems.
A tiered crafting system allows increasingly valuable products to be crafted by combining harvestable materials.
Gas harvesters have been introduced, allowing explorers to extract valuable elements from a planet’s atmosphere to use in crafting.
Combine crafted products to create increasingly valuable items that can be sold on the Galactic Marketplace.
New maintenance interactions have been introduced for all harvesting equipment, bringing more depth to farming, mining and harvesting.
ANALYSIS VISOR
Analysis Visors have been re-calibrated to show more information and offer better rewards for scanning.
Analyse resources before harvesting for to gain alternative resources from mining.
See more information about each discovery.
Scanning Flora and Fauna now yields increased rewards.
Specialised analysis visor upgrades can be equipped to further improve effectiveness.
TERRAIN EDITING
Transform the ground beneath your feet using the new terrain editing Multi-Tool enhancement.
Add or remove terrain to mould the landscape as you see fit, anywhere on any planet.
Choose from a number of materials, shapes and sizes to sculpt your unique creations.
Form terrain around your base to make it feel like part of the environment.
PORTALS
Ancient portals can now be activated. Revisit previous planets, others bases or jump randomly to new worlds.
Learn the language of portals by unlocking mysterious glyphs as you journey through the universe.
Interact with a portal and input a specific combination of glyphs to quick travel to a specific planet.
Share glyph combinations with the community to help others travel quickly to specific planets and points of interest.
SPACE COMBAT
A number of improvements have been made to space flight and combat.
Enemy artificial intelligence has been overhauled, and new difficulties have been added.
Ship manoeuvrability has been improved, bringing more skill to dog-fighting.
Devastating rockets can be equipped to ships and upgraded for even greater firepower.
A new HUD has been introduced to improve the experience of space combat. This includes a communicator, which can be used to advance mission steps, or even to hail pirates before they attack.
LOW FLIGHT
Atmospheric low flight assist now allows players to cruise above the terrain.
Low flight and improved flight control make in-atmosphere dog fighting more likely and exciting.
Warning: crashing into obstacles will cause damage to your ship. If your ship is destroyed, you’ll need to repair it before leaving the planet.
JOINT EXPLORATION
Glitches in the simulation have begun to appear.
Visualised by strange floating orbs, up to 16 players can see and communicate with one another, and explore the universe together.
While interaction with others is currently very limited, this is an important first step into the world of synchronous co-op in No Man’s Sky.
While interaction is very limited, VOIP (Voice over IP) allows proximity based voice chat with other nearby explorers.
Use portals to quickly travel to more populated planets, or to meet up with friends.
NEW SHIPS
New Class S ship designs have been introduced, and can be found roaming the galaxy. Interact with their owners to view, and offer to buy their ship.
Wealthier systems have more expensive, higher class ships.
QUALITY OF LIFE
Temperature measurement has been converted from Celsius to Fahrenheit based on locale.
Summon your ship from anywhere on a planet’s surface using your quick menu.
Specific Technology and Cargo inventories have been added to improve inventory management.
Playstation 4 players can now adjust their field of view via the options menu.
Jump between systems from the comfort of your Freighter. Just interact with the hologram on your bridge, and select a location to travel to.
Landing your ship no longer auto-ejects you from the cockpit. Take time to survey the planet before exiting.
GENERATION
A regenerated system adds wealth, economy and conflict levels to star systems.
To control this the Galaxy Map has been overhauled, improving navigation and providing access to key information.
Install galactic technology to be able to filter the map by lifeform, wealth and economy.
Improved waypointing, and navigation allows you to see your journey so far, from beginning to end.

Sine Mora Review.
A hit and miss... but still well done.
This game is sort of a mix bag for me at the beginning but it went well at the end... kinda... its quite a bumpy ride at the beginning... but it was worth every second of it.
Gameplay : Now... I have three major issue with this game and we'll start off with the elephant in the room... this game when you first play it has so many instant death situations that at some point, it started to make me feel that they added them there to make the game feel longer than what it is on the outset like it needed any extending I mean hell... the game is One and a Half Hours long... that's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing long for a SHMUP already. The game has multiple mechanics which includes Time Slowing(and many more outside the story missions), having a timer as your health that replenishes when you kill enemies and degenerates when you get hit and, Multiple Characters and Ship combination for the types of Bombs and Vulcan you'll be using... its quite robust outside of the Story mode... that is if you can chew up how hard it is.
Difficulty: Okay, so let me step back for a second... Sine Mora is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play but not because of the bullets even though they are bullet hell like, they are still manageable since they are slow although confusing for the most part since there are so many types of them, some are even one hit wonders which adds to the whole bumpy ride at the beginning that I was talking about... Anyways... the game is hard for three reasons... The "Stage Specific Mechanics", The Confusing Hitbox and The Flying Power Ups... Let us start with Stage Specific Mechanics... I'm talking specifically about Stage III really... The Stealth part of that stage plus the wrecking ball made me go down from Challenging to Normal difficulty. Later on, there would be other stage specific mechanics that will one hit you... you'll see. Now the confusing hitbox is quite the thing because it reminds me of ♥♥♥♥ing DonPachi. Apparently, its the Ship's class(where the pilot is) is the hitbox, which is different on each ship... Lastly, it's the Flying Power ups... now this game has four difficulty. Normal and Challenging for Story and, Hard and Insane for Arcade. Normal is easy as hell, Challenging adds more Health to enemies, bullets, health penalties and so much more that is quite a damn gap... and it just gets crazy from there...
The Power Up Annoyance: So here is how it works... You get hit, you loose time and all of your Power ups fly off at random directions, if you play on a harder difficulty, you have less invulnerability period in between hits and health penalties are bigger. So either risk dying trying to pick them all up again or just use your tiny Vulcan, so that means now you can't deal that much damage and in harder difficulties... enemies have more health... so in summary... Don't... Get... Hit... like ever... it's pretty damn strict.
Story: The Reason why this game is M rated is because of its storyline... It's Grim... grim as all hell. I don't really need since the whole story like is really interesting(although why is it only on Hungarian Language confuses me) to spoil anything but let's just say that Blackmailing a girl that suffered both♥♥♥♥♥♥and cancer(not to mention the extinction of her race with the survivors being put into forced labor and experimentation) is just not cool bro.
Art: The characters are furries... Did that turn you off? ♥♥♥♥ off then. Either way... it adds to the creative side of the game... It has amazing graphical fidelity and it runs really well... on my Titan anyways... Also... the boss design are really interesting and very imaginative like the rest of the game... Now I'm not a fan of the whole 2.5D perspective even if its an eye candy... I just want to see♥♥♥♥♥♥clearly like in Akai Katana and Progear Storm... this reminds me of Enhander... a little too much in fact. Now... In my screen... this game actually has some graphical issues however which sadly lets down the experience a little bit...
Music: The Last problem that I have with this game is the music... it doesn't... fit... it sounds ambient and... strangely cheerful(especially the boss theme), which for a grim storyline and a strange world that is shown to the player... this... is a contrast... I just cant tell if its meant to be though...
Verdict: Its still a thumbs up meanly because of how challenging it is while still being operational(just keep a lot of things in mind that is). The story itself is intriguing enough to keep me playing and the modes that it offers gives it a lot of replay value and top it off with a rich scoring system. Sine Mora is quite a treat for shoot em up fans out there... just... toss most of what you think of other shmups and just keep your mind on this one... before you can disappointed or frustrated by your own standards and by the things you are used to. Am talking to you Touhou and Cave fans. ;)

In that way, all victories feel so much more rewarding in contrast to most newer games that just hand them to you on a silver plate. This is an oldschool game in that sense. Frustratingly difficult.
I've played a solid 3 hours and managed 30%, as I had it minimised a bit while I tried to work out where the f*ck to go. It's so hard you spend a lot of the game feeling like you are sequence breaking.
-Your weapon has a range of about two arms lengths
-No diagonal firing so it can be awkwardly challenging hitting enemies
-Enemies tend to circle you, do a lot of damage, move very fast and come out of nowhere (remember you can only fire about two blocks in front of you)
-Forced exploration where you try to recollect where all of THOSE COLOURED BLOCKS you can now destroy were. Which leads to a hell of a lot of dead ends "hey i can get through here now.. into a dead end"
-Bosses are just insane, you can try like 5 times to kill a boss only to finally get there to find that was only phase one of three
-Weapon upgrades, in three hours I have found just a charge shot, and it just keeps getting harder with some enemies jumping around all over the place taking about six charged shots to kill
-Platforming, frustrating as hell, I was stuck on one segment for about 15 minutes solid. If I hadn't already explored literally everywhere else I would have though (not for the first time) that I was sequence breaking and meant to go elsewhere. I swear some of the jumps and hookshot moves require literal pixel perfection.
-No health pickups from killing enemies, so even the most basic ones that are just a pain in the balls to hit will just slowly grind you down in between save stations.
After multiple occasions where I had to use cheatengine to slow the game down to 50% on some bosses and platforming sections, I got to one boss, died three times, realised I didn't have a hope in hell and just quit. Which sucks to be honest as the story is genuinely quite compelling and I wanted to continue and find all the upgrades. Although that story.. "go here, might be researchers that survived, OH NO JUST KIDDING GIANT MECHA-SNAKE".. doesn't always make sense
There were a lot of times when the game was fun sure, but it mostly made me want to stab somebody in the throat. The story is good, and it has it's moments, but I have personally given up and am instead choosing to watch some other mug that is much better than me die over and over and over again on youtube whilst I watch, eat all the nearby food and laugh at their pain. At least I know they eventually do it.
A lot of potential, interesting story, could be fun but is instead ridiculously difficult not only in terms of the limited health and hard as balls bosses, but the pixel perfect platforming too. Edit: Nominated for the “I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award” award

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: This is one of those games that I would've had absolutely no interest in whatsoever if it hadn't been for a friend of mine recommending this game quite a lot. It's a Metroid-inspired platformer with retro graphics, so from premise alone it doesn't really have that "wow" factor that really compels me to play some games. After having played through it, I'll say that it wasn't the most inspired of games out there, but what it did, it did pretty well.
Of course, one of the most important parts of any Metroid-derivative game is the sense of exploration. At first, I was worried that the world seemed really small, given that the map at the time didn't seem exactly large. However, there's a lot within this map, and even by screen count alone, there's over 800 screens in the game. Even though it is a pretty big map, the map is very dense; there's a lot to do in this world, and even though it did get tiresome having to backtrack all the time when exploring the western side of the map, at least the rest of the map is very easy to explore. After a while in game you also unlock teleporters, which as mentioned in the previous sentence are pretty evenly placed with the exception of the desert and water areas.
Another big part of any Metroid style game is to have really cool powerups. I found 14 throughout my playthrough (although I've heard rumors of a soopur sekrit 15th), and while a few were either completely unnecessary (the rough map, for example really shouldn't be a powerup) or just served as an arbitrary gating mechanism (the keycard that unlocks golden blocks), there are a lot of really fun powerups as well. You've got standard things for a Metroid-esque game like the Heat-Resistant Suit and the Charge Beam, but there's also powerups that let you dash around all over the place, as well as a grapple hook which is easily the most fun powerup in the game.
This game also has bosses, and these sure are some bosses. While some of these bosses could do with either not having as many phases or having one health bar so that you know how many phases the boss has, almost all of these bosses are very fun to fight. There's only two bosses in the game that I would consider bad, and those are one boss where the only way you can damage the boss is to kite its projectiles back at the boss (a lot less fun than it sounds TBH) and a boss where it's impossible to defeat it without a certain powerup and stupidly easy to defeat with the powerup. However, for these missteps there are more than a few bosses which definitely make up for it.
Finishing the game for the first time took me about seven hours, but that's far from when the game is over. You can either choose to leave the game there or go on and play the post-game which can easily take you as long to beat as the main game does. While the mystery of unlocking pillars which are hitherto unknown to you is very cool, after a while the postgame turns into an insane amount of tedious backtracking and puzzles which are almost certainly way too obscure for their own good. I've played La-Mulana; I'm used to obscure puzzles, and while the now infamous Clock puzzle is cleverly structured, actually executing what has to be done to finish the puzzle just isn't worth it to me. As such, that's where I stopped playing.
Even though the post-game does get incredibly long-winded after a while, the main game is still a whole lot of fun, but one thing that concerns me is that, much like La-Mulana, all the magic is gone after the first playthrough once you know how to do everything and where to go. While the bosses are a load of fun, that's really all any subsequent playthroughs of this game are gonna be about. While unfortunately this game may be a "one-and-done" for me, at least it was a pretty solid one-and-done. 8/10.
Story: While I never got the third ending for completing the post-game (yes, this game has multiple endings), I did quite enjoy the writing of this game. It's written in a very sparse way, with some humor from time to time, but mostly detailing the crew attempting to survive from whatever the hell happened here on the station. While it does get a little overdone with its 2spooky-ness from time to time, it's still pretty well presented, and it leaves just enough for you to start filling in the gaps yourself. Not bad. 7/10.
Graphics: Well, you can tell from the store screenshots that this game is an 8-Bit pixel style game, and while that's far from anything terribly original, much like the gameplay it is at least done pretty well. The spriters made good use of their palette and screen royalty to give you some pretty damn awesome looking areas and enemies. Also, given that this game makes use of pixel art, you wouldn't expect any lag. Thankfully, I never had any lag throughout the entirety of the game. Resolution is a bit of a tricky spot, though; the game fullscreens by default, but renders as a square, leaving some pretty unsightly black bars on the sides. While this is something of a nitpick, I kinda wish they had done something like what La-Mulana did and have some graphics to the sides to at least make the screen feel a bit more full. Still though, the area, monster and boss designs are more than enough to hold your attention. Great job for the visual artists here. 5/5.
Sound: This game does have a tendency to feel a bit confused as far as the sound direction goes. Even though the game was "8-Bit," the OST feels like it would be more at home on an SNES. The sound effects feel pretty out of place from time to time as well; some of the sounds are realistic and some of the sounds are chippy. Even though this is pretty weird given the game's staunch insistence on looking like Metroid, at least the OST gets one thing right: ambience. While a couple of the songs get tired due to having to backtrack through a couple of areas (*cough* desert and water areas *cough*), each of the songs make the area feel like its own. It may not be the catchiest of OSTs, but it does its job well for providing atmosphere. Again, while the sound direction does kinda clash against the graphical direction from time to time, at least it works. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 8/7/5/4; cumulative score of 8.0/10. I'd definitely say there's enough to this game to easily warrant a full price purchase irrespective of supporting indie devs; there's just a lot of meat to this game. You may feel like throwing up after eating all that meat, but at least it was good before you threw it all up.

I'd heard very mixed things about The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, but I do enjoy a good ARPG and this one had a unique setting and some interesting mechanics to recommend it, so I gave it a go. I'm surely glad I did, because Van Helsing is one of my favorite ARPGs to date. Now, I know a lot of people go into these games looking primarily at theorycrafting builds and chasing loot. If you're one of those people, take my opinions with a grain of salt because that isn't what I get out of them at all. Oh, sure, making my numbers go up is a hook in any RPG and I get a basic pleasure out of that sort of thing, but I need something more than that to make loot genuinely compelling - unique modifiers like Diablo 3's legendaries or Marvel Heroes' uniques and artifacts, that sort of thing. And I'm not going to replay the game enough to really tweak a build into optimal form. I just want a variety of classes with cool powers that give visceral feedback when I use them.
Van Helsing's loot is capable enough - a spread of rarities including epic and set gear (and, though I didn't see any, legendaries), an enchantment system, a separate "essence" system, a forge where you can feed unwanted gear to roll new items (and later get some control over what you're crafting), a gambling vendor, etc. Fairly standard Diablo-type fare, no notable lack but none of the unique effect hooks that really get my motor running. Classes are definitely fun - I played an Arcane Mechanic and chucked around grenades while spawning turrets and mechanical spiders, but I could have gone a bunch of other ways or tried the base game Hunter (a traditional monster hunter with sword and gun) or the other DLC class, the Thaumaturge (an occult specialist). And the skill system seems robust and innovative, with various temporary powerups to pump rage into on your primary skills and expertise bonuses you can buy into to further improve your favored abilities, as well as a stacking bonus to everything whenever you spend skill points in your main tree and bonuses at certain thresholds. Beyond that, there's a "reputation" track to level by killing champions and bosses that lets you select perks to further customize your build, unlocked by achieving various criteria during the game. And once you've hit the level cap there's even a "glory" system for further tweaking your character in post-story modes.
So all that's well and good. But really, what sold me on the game is the story mode itself. Oh, it's not a tremendously deep or nuanced story, although it's a bit more creative and interesting than the typical ARPG story. But it takes you through dozens of handmade, beautiful, atmospheric levels that are densely packed with monsters, quests, and secrets. And treasure, of course. The game really rewards you for digging into every last nook and cranny of every map and talking to all the NPCs, triggering special bosses, rare loot drops, stat rewards and more. As someone who really enjoys exploration in videogames, this is exactly the sort of thing I am clamoring for.

Name of Game: Fallout 3 GOTY
Initial release date: 28 October 2008
Genre: Action role-playing game
Awards: VGX Award for Best RPG, MORE
Rating (Steam): 9/10
Platforms: Xbox One, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Microsoft Windows
Developers: Bethesda Softworks, Bethesda Game Studios
As a game that holds dearly to my heart and one of my first PS3 games, Fallout 3 is one of the first in the Fallout franchise I played and massively enjoyed. Like Skyrim, I played it for days and days, enjoying everything there was to do, every quest to complete, every DLC to do, every town to explore and every mutant to try and kill. I still to this day play it and enjoy it a lot, and therefore decided I would review it. Despite it being a good game in my eyes, there are still things that I wish to discuss and wish were improved.
Fallout 3 is an action roleplaying game, as well as open world. It's set in a post apocalyptic world that follows on in the same setting as Interplay entertainment and Black Isle Studio's Fallout 1 and 2. Rougly, it takes place 36 years after the old game Fallout 2 and is set in the region of Washington D.C. now known as the Capital Wasteland. The game's lore is the same, going all the way back to a great war against America and China, eventually leading to Nuclear devastation. Most people were lucky enough to seek shelter in large underground Vaults and that brings me on to the plot.
The game takes place in a Vault, Vault 101. Your character is a resident here, a vault dweller along with your father. You get to see glimpses of your character growing up, and his rough childhood. But you don't stay in the Vault for long, as you find out that your father escapes the Vault, and you have to escape as well if you want to find him. After taking caring of some Radroaches and the guards trying to take you in to the Overseer for your father's crimes, you will eventually find yourself out in the Wasteland, which was previously known as Washington D.C.
You have to travel to various places to find people who may know your dad and where he went, but of course it is dangerous and a long journey. On the way, you can do various different side quests to help people and other various deeds. There are also the DLCs, which are great fun and good to do. Apart from that, I won't spoil the rest of the plot, since there are a few turns and twists which should only be uncovered by your own experience. At the end however, you get a choice which can effect your ending and also your karma, which i'll explain later. Once you complete the main quest though, I should warn you that the game will end unless you have the DLC "Broken Steel" (Which is why I recommend the GOTY edition or even just Broken Steel).
I think the story is rather good, but nothing massively amazing. It's pretty simple and suprising at some parts, which is rather good. The ending was great personally, without the Broken Steel DLC a rather good wrap up. The beginning of the plot is clear and also quite touching from time to time, but it's halfway through the main plot that really is emotional. Of course, i'll leave it to you to uncover.
Gameplay wise, this game is far different to the previous Fallout games by Black Isle Studios and Interplay Entertainment back in 1997 and 1998. The combat is much more fast paced and not turn based combat, which means more smooth and action packed combat. Fallout 3 takes elements from the older games aswell however, such as VATS, the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system and karma.
The first big thing that effects the gameplay greatly is the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system. Aka, your Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility and Luck. These can all alter your major attributes one way or another. For example, if you have 10 Charisma, chances are you will succeed much more in persuading, bribing and any other speech skill. However, Strength effects your initial strength and carry weight. This can be very important and always has been in the Fallout games. One thing i've always liked is the little touch the developers added where with 1 intelligence, your character will be very dumb and won't even be able to talk to people without them not understanding.
The VATS system is also good, allowing you to slow down time completely and pick a limb to hit on an enemy. Sometimes this can lead to a lot of gore in that body part, such as shooting the head can sometimes make it explode into little bits. Very gruesome and very cool. Like the previous games, your AP (Action Points) is the limit of VAT hits you can do, but unlike the previous games your AP doesn't effect all of the combat, just VATS.
Karma is very neatly polished in this game, which can develop your character to be good or evil. Depending on what you do at the ending, it can make a different ending (e.g. a bad karma ending or a good karma ending). It's even used when you do simple things such as kill an innocent, steal something or even blow up a town. Yes I said blow up a town. You can blow up a town, but it will greatly reduce your karma level. Worth it though if your evil like that...
Another element of the gameplay is you can once again have companions, another returning feature of the previous Fallout games. The companions range from a dog, to a friendly mutant, a mercenary and more. They all are very useful and quite fun to have around as your faithful companions or hired guns.
The DLCs are very good, and that's why I would recommend getting the Game of the Year Edition, which is currently only £14.99. The DLCs include Broken Steel, which extends the game and doesn't make it end after completing the main quest. Point Lookout which is a whole new island to explore full of new monsters and lots of terrifying hillbillies. Mothership Zeta which takes you on a bizzarre journey into space and on a quest of killing aliens. Operation Anchorage which takes you into a simulation where you become a soldier of the great war and finally the Pitt, where you fight your way through an old Steel mill, fighting Raider Slavers and horribly mutated slaves.
All the DLCs are very well done, and worth all the money. All of them are interesting, keep you on your toes and can be very challenging to new level people. It even brings new amazing armours and weapons and also new lands. I definately recommend you get them to complete the Fallout 3 experience.
Despite all the good things I've spoken about, we must also talk about the flaws. My first one being the levelling system. In one of my run throughs, I got to the maximum level easy (Which was 30 due to me having GOTY) and it was so quick to achieve. I didn't even complete the main questline and i'd become the OP level, which seemed cheaply achieved and too quick. There was nothing to be proud about, no bigger threats and nothing majorly good about this. Another complaint I have is with the colour and somewhat graphics. Usually I don't talk about anything to do with graphics, since I don't really care and don't really see why an outdated game with bad graphics is a problem. No, I mean the actual colour. The textures weren't an issue. It was the colour on everything. It had a strange tint on the world, green mucky like. If Bethesda wanted to make it look all "radioactive" and "dead", then in some ways they did accomplish that. But it made the game feel really dull at times, there was nothing new to the sky, or the colour. It felt so bland and boring which was very sad since the game wasn't at all boring. It just looked rather dull and never changed.
Of course, there are mods for those complaints to fix them, and I recommend getting a couple of mods to change those things. But apart from that it was a rather good game and I had nothing to complain about.
In conclusion, Fallout 3 is a great game, and a great start if your a new player. Therefore, I give it what Steam also rated it. 9/10.

When comparing the content in this game to that of the previous entry, it's no wonder Calamity Trigger was recently on sale for only a few bucks. There's a lot to do in Continuum Shift, and you'll find the hours slipping away as you get sucked in.
Such as the extensive storylines with full voice acting. There's barely a time when you will be reading text without somebody speaking it. Not to mention the Japanese voice pack. Never before has a fighting game got me so invested in the characters with the story.
I actually want to learn the details behind Carl's slow decent into madness and the story behind his puppet. I want to learn the story of Hellsing's past and where he got his werewolf powers. I want to know why Taokaka is so familiar with Litchi that she refers to her as "Boobie Lady".  To learn all this, you play their stories. And as you play their stories, you start to get good with the characters. This all translates into hours and hours spent playing the game. That alone makes the game a worthy purchase at full price.
There are only a few minor problems with the game. There is no option to turn off voice chat when playing online, which leads to hearing feedback from speakers because people don't realize their mic is on. Also, you'll be hearing "counter counter counter counter counter" so much that it seems like a gross oversight by the developers to leave that in the game. As far as I know, it's not exactly vital information and can be done without. Yet, you'll still have to put up with it.
I've never been very good at fighting games, but I attribute that to never getting invested in them because of a lackluster story or characters that I couldn't grow to like. Blazblue is the first fighting game that I've put the effort into learning how to play, and it's actually showing! Because I love the characters, the story, the voice acting, the music, and all the extra features put into the game. Not to mention, the extensive tutorial that was missing for the previous game has been a life saver.
Man, I just love this game.

I really enjoyed this game. After playing the previous Wolfenstein game and realizing how damn good it was I couldnt wait to check this out. The game was pretty wonderful overall aside from it going by way to fast. I put in 20 hours so far and its left me wanting more!
There are a few hickups in the game that get annoying like getting stuck on things or behind things in the environment and not being able to get out but overall the game is pretty polished and lot of fun.
My only complaint is that ive finished the game and I want more and thats not really a complaint :D

- Graphics & Processing :
The game process nicely, but at some points the game started to freeze on me and I had to reset it (very rare occasion).
(and my drivers were up to date this time)
Nonetheless : it looks good and run at a smooth 60FPS
- Sound & Musics :
Mick Gordon saved it. 11/10
- Gameplay :
It's the same thing as in The New Order so there's not much more to say ; I said the gameplay was excellent in my review of Last Order, so it's still excellent here. There are the "body upgrade" at some point which are more situationnal than anything, and don't really contribute to anything.
The one flaw I see is that a lot of the areas where the shootings happen are mostly enclosed and don't have the same kind of "playground" feel as DOOM had last year. It's not a straight up corridor a la CoD either, so this is not too much of an issue.
- Storytelling :
Aïe.
I really didn't want to believe this would be this bad, but...
Spoiler free of what I had to say :
I can appreciate them trying to rewrite history & try to fit in historical characters, what I don't appreciate is them clearly not doing research and limiting the writing to "he's crazy & EVIL >:(", and trying to shove in an agenda which limits to "nazis are bad people yo" which I believe everyone here agrees on (even tho some people tend to think the opposite by calling other people disagreeing with them nazis)
Note : I wouldn't mind the clichés if there weren't as obnoxious as they are here. Again, The New Order's main villain was a cliché nazi mad scientist ; but he wasn't as obnoxious as the plot of this game is, and as the main villain which turned out to be a giant letdown...
- Length :
... and speaking of letdown, let's talk about the length now.
I don't know if there are as much cutscenes as there are gameplay segments, but I can tell you that they artificially boosted the length of the game by making enemies gang up on you really fast (which is a death sentence if you're low on armor). I don't mind the difficulty (Because I don't work at Polygon... YET :>), but when it's so obviously put to increase the length of your game because you didn't think to add some other levels or bossfights... I'm gonna call BS on that.
Note that this isn't HORRIBLE per say, the difficulty doesn't spike that much, but it's pretty obvious at some time that the devs wanted you to die multiple times so the game would feel longer.... and there's no better moment to see that as the final boss
All of this tells me one thing : this game is going to have some big story DLC, isn't it ? we're going to have to pay to have a more complete game, right ? and it'll be filled with some more cringy storytelling that insists on telling us that nazi are bad, right ?
CONCLUSION :
My problems with the story aren't why I'm not recommending it, or rather, they are not the only thing.
As I said : gameplay is very very good & the game performs fairly well ; so if you're just here for the gameplay & performances, you're safe.
Thing is, Steam doesn't allow for anything else than "Yes" or "No" as far as recommendations are concerned. And this is another case where I would say "no, but..."
I'd say "Not recommended YET". Wait for a sale (maybe a patch ?), also maybe wait for a "complete edition"...
I'm sad to say I can't really recommend the game at this time. Oh sure it's fun, it's not like a generic CoD clone FPS.... but guess what :
- DOOM is like that too
- Wolfenstein The New Order is like that too
- in fact... now that DOOM was considered a really good game, every dev is trying to make a FPS that would meet the same success, thus the same criteria... so you may be safer playing any other "new" "old" FPS than this one...

For four dollars, Sine Mora is a game list inflating impulse buy. Given the choice, I would remove this game from my collection and write off the money as an experience worth paying for. If Steam had a 'rent' option, this game would be good for one to two nights of play, based on my experiences.
Positive aspects:
+ Graphical style
+ Interesting character/ship/weapon combination grid
+ Standard schmup gameplay
+ Responsive controls
Negative aspects:
- Buggy graphics cause distracting glitches
- Buggy gameplay causes unfair deaths
- Fast forward feature slows framerate and stops sound, but doesn't fast forward, making the necessary replays to perfect this sort of game unnecessarily tedious, especially with the many scripted scenes players are forced to sit through
- Awkward pacing between gameplay and scripted scenes
- Not much information about selectable weapons and ships
If these bugs weren't present, Sine Mora would be an excellent game at the price asked. As it is now, it was worth a couple hours of my time before I couldn't ignore how inconvenient it is to play, and I was hoping to spend hours mastering a new schmup. I do not recommend buying this game without downloading the demo to test for bugs. If things function as expected, or you can ignore the pacing & technical issues, then it's worth the price.
However, I do not recommend this game to anybody who doesn't have the time or dedication to try inexpensive games before buying, and who doesn't have the time or patience to deal with the problematic aspects of the game. The cost of purchase is not worth the risk of experiencing the game breaking bugs that I experienced.

The gameplay is a mix between puzzle, video editing and beat-em-up.
The fighting sequences are fairly simplistic at first, you have a few "combos" that are punches and kicks that you assign attributes to, being extra damage, self-heal, or cooldown. There's a been a trend of late where classic genres of games have been coming back via the indie scene.  One can imagine, with the passage of time, these game genres have evolved.  To me, Environmental Station Alpha is just that.
Environmental Station Alpha lives much in the spirit of Super Metroid, with a dash of Bionic Commando.  Traveling through the decrepit station is a mostly enjoyable experience, with the occasional difficulty spike.  There's a fair amount of content here, or at least there was for myself and my subpar platforming skills.  My final file complete time was around 10 hours, but due to bad process management and numerous deaths/reset, I likely completed the game in around 20.  That is all the content of the game, including the fairly meaty end-game, which proves a real challenge in both skill and, to a lesser degree, intellect.   One of the devs has been very active in the Steam forum, and has released several patches based directly off of feedback.
Ultimately, if you're looking for a decent, challenging metroidvania, I would recommend this game.  Some of the mechanics take some practice, and some of the bosses require a bit of trial-and-error, but the overall package feels polished, and the minimalist pixel-art remains consistently eye-catching.  If you're on the fence there's a demo, which does feature one of the more skill-based mechanics.

A shockingly good metroidvania despite the visual presentation of the game.   After playing the game for about 10 minutes I realized that under those old graphics is a monster of a game.   Heavily influenced by Super Metroid in terms of world and level designs, as well as power-ups, this game really recaptures the magic.   The game also has multiple endings, which may not be obvious when you play through it.   There is a massive amount of content that is optional in order to find the alternative endings.   You will need to solve many puzzle and riddles, and decipher another language akin to what was seen in FEZ if you want find out how deep the rabbit hole goes. Overall the game is well worth the asking price, and if you decide to chase after the bonus content, you will be driven to madness.   The only real beef with the game is a lack of achievements.

Environmental Station Alpha is a love letter to the original Metroid games, with a style and execution that is unique to the developer.  The game is the definition of a "metroidvania."  You are given a large, maze-like station to navigate, filled with puzzles, monsters, and bosses.  You expand your ability to reach areas by obtaining powerups, which primarily change the way you move through the game, although there are also weapon upgrades and the like.
In terms of gameplay, this game does it right.  You are given the right amount of control over your character, and the movement and abilities feel good and work the way you expect them to.  The bosses have a great variety, and each fight feels and plays out differently.  Each new boss is an interesting and satisfying new experience.  The station is very well constructed, with a pretty good mix of dungeon and maze.  The station is also solid; there are no empty rooms or spaces inside the station itself, so there is lots to explore, and tons of hidden rooms to find.
Graphics and Audio really shine in this game.  The graphics are charmingly done pixels.  Most of the environments are interesting to explore, and many are downright pretty.  At many points I was struck by the direct visual influences taken from Super Metroid, and they are done wonderfully.  The soundtrack is also fantastic, giving the right mix of mystery, hostility, creepiness, and alien strangeness.
The main story premise is simple:  You are a robot sent to find out why the station went dead.  The story is advanced in small ways throughout the course of the game, given through some dialogue but mostly through computer terminals and logs.  The story is heavily one of mystery, however, so don't expect answers to all of your questions.  The game boasts multiple endings, and they are fun to unlock and see.
The game has a couple unique features to be mentioned.  First of all, once the game is completed, new objects and events appear in the station.  You are then able to undertake a new mystery (one that might take you beyond the station itself.)  This is done very well, aside from a couple frustrating moments, and it is absolutely worth completing.  Once this is done, you get an interesting little spin on the New Game + system, which you'll have to see for yourself.
It should be noted that this game is challenging.  I personally think it got the challenge level about right for most of the rooms, monsters and bosses.  However, players who are not experienced in some of the older and more challenging metroidvanias might find it a step up in difficulty from what they're used to.  Its a good kind of challenge, though, and anyone who enjoyed the original Metroids, Castlevanias, or more recent games like Cave Story should find the challenge level reasonable.  The mystery and extended end-game is tougher, but worth your time (and the forum is full of helpful posts by those who managed to puzzle most of it out first to help get you through.)
This review got long, but only because the game deserves to have its virtues extolled.  It was a pleasure to play through this game, particularly as a lover of Metroidvanias (real ones, at that.)  Its also not very expensive, which is always a plus.
This is a genuinely great metroidvania.  It might be the best Metroid since Super Metroid.  The creator has produced a love letter to the genre that firmly deserves a place in it.  Its just that good.  For the price of admission, you honestly can't go wrong.

(This review may contain minor spoilers, warnings are written before passages that may spoil the story, mechanics, boss fights, progression, or other gameplay elements)
As of writing this review I have less than an hour of play time, but I am already in love with this game. I will come through and edit this review as needed when I finish the game, but off the bat there were so many good things that I liked.
Environmental Station Alpha was introduced to me through a Metroid community, by someone who claimed that it had a very much Metroid feel to it. It becomes very aparent that this is incredibly true. The isolation and exploration are two huge giveaways, and the boss fights just add to it. As a massive Metroid fan, and someone who plays games that try to replicate the Metroid-feel, I can say for sure that this is one of the games that manages to pull it off exceptionally well.
ESA, at least the very very early game (Pre-second boss) is a lot like the classic Metroid in that it is very unforgiving. Health is pretty sparce (as far as I know, only save stations replenish), which made each encouter much more tense because I could only afford a few hits before I was killed.
The game tells a lot through the use of color, but some parts are missing a bit of color. I found myself constantly falling in the green water (acid?) and not realizing it until my character exploded. The acid is only showing as a collection of green pixel waves at the top of the liquid. I think possibly filling in the pools with even a light, almost completely transparent green, would make them a bit more visable to the player. So far I've seen a lot of use of cool colors for the backgrounds. Dark blues, greys, purples, and blacks dominate the colors, with a bit of red accents. Most interactable machines are easy to pick out because they generally use brighter cool colors, and machines such as the save station feature a lot of contrasting red to really pop out. Walking in to an environment with a new color palette than before really adds to that exploration factor because you feel like you're finding new things, new places.
The bosses are the right amount of hard from what I found. Without doing any sort of walkthrough I could easily see myself taking no more than two tries on the bosses that I faced. You just need to take time to learn their patterns and find a way to hit them without hurting yourself.
When I first saw the store page for this game, I noticed multiple developer announcements, many regarding patches. So I came in expecting a bit of a buggy game, but not in a bad way because it seems the developers are hard at work fixing everything they can. Great job guys. I personally only had issues with enemies being stuck in vertical 'doorways' to another level, which really just made them an easy target, and I also had some framerate issues (Intel i5 4200H, GTX 860m) occasionally, but both issues were nothing to really get upset about. I should also add that my Xbox 360 controller didn't seem to be picked up by the game, launched through Big Picture and regular mode, nothing on either. It was set to controller mode in the settings, on Windows, but again, nothing to really fuss about.
I'm excited to spend a day going through this game and seeing what it has to offer, and I hope that others take the time to enjoy the mood and atmosphere that the game has to offer. As I said before, I will edit this review as needed when I complete the game.
UPDATE 1 (Minor boss fight spoilers, although no specific bosses mentioned, just mechanics): I still have yet to complete the game currently I have just unlocked the teleporters. The bosses get very tough, very fast. The boss fights are all about learning the boss' paterns, but some bosses require attacking parts of the environment and even their own projectiles to defeat them, but the game does nothing really to help the player (generally environmental things turned on if they were computers, but it wasn't something pointed out). Now you could attribute this to the game's exploration factor, where you keep trying until you find the right way, but it does get a bit frustrating after a while. I have already found myself playing just until I beat the next boss, then stopping to cool down for a while, but the "just one more boss..." mentality does start to set in.
I can't help but feel that I have completely missed some crucial health tanks though, because I have fought three or four bosses now, but have only found one health upgrade, which increased my health by a measly (yet suprisingly life-saving) four points. I cannot tell if I am completely missing them, or if the game just doesn't have very many very often, but it's been interesting fighting bosses who take almost a quarter of my health with every hit.
My review still stands though. If you enjoyed Metroid and Metroid-style games, if you enjoy exploring a world and learning through the environment, then you will enjoy ESA.
I should also add that for my entire time spent in-game, controller input doesn't seem to be recognized. I use a USB wireless Xbox 360 controller reciever. I'd love to try the game out with a controller, but I am unable to.
UPDATE 2: (A boss fight spoiler, and story spoiler in the last sentence, you have been warned)
The Serpent fight really needs to be looked at. It is incredibly inconsistant and has become quite a frustrating fight. I discovered that I missed at least one health upgrade back in the hookshot area, so fighting the boss with only 14 health is pretty rediculous, especially when I believe that I would have defeated the boss if I had had the extra four units of health. So why don't I just go back and get it? I can't. The charge shot room has all exits that don't lead to the boss completely blocked by currents. I am stuck fighting a boss that I cannot beat with the amount of health I have.
The fight has some pretty rediculous parts. The hitbox of the wave attack is very misleading near the back, and I seemed to notice that I took damage even after I was one block from the back of the wave, but this damage only happened sometimes, making it pretty hard to judge when it would and wouldn't happen. In some fights the serpent very nicely hops out of the water sprays a rediculous amount of shots, and then drops back into the water. Other fights the boss hits me once so that I take no damage temporarily, moves into the center of my character, and begins very quickly spinning, damaging me until I die. This is completely unavoidable, and seems to happen about sixty percent of the time. In a game where you learn to beat the bosses by learning their attacks and patterns through constant fight attempts, this sort of inconsistancy just doesn't belong and only ends with a frustrated player.
The boss also has multiple phases. I'm all for bosses with phases, but, as the writer of 'Wot I Think' said in his ESA review, having no way to regenerate your health mid-fight makes the game much more frustrating. ESA could really benefit from small health packs that maybe restore two or four points of health, instead of relying on save stations and health stations (which there are very few of in the water area). I hate having to run back through my last five to ten minutes of progress just to recharge at a save station.
Right now I'm in a bit of a love/hate relationship with this game. I love Metroid, and this game reminds me so much of it. But the constant frustration from so many factors (the biggest being a constant feeling that I'm going the wrong way) limits me to around half-hour sessions that generally end with me angrilly mashing alt-f4 on the "Continue?" screen. I want to play this game, I really do, but I can't help but think about how frustrated I will be very soon.
The difficulty and frustration now makes me fear the sudden difficulty spike that so many players have ranted about once the AI is reactivated.

The Jackbox Party Pack and its sequels have formed a unique collection of casual multiplayer games.
The games are quirky, irreverent fun whether you win or lose. They're built to be used with smartphones or other devices around a screen all the players can see, but some of the slower games can also be streamed over the internet at a distance. This is how I play.
The game presents you with a title or caption. You draw a picture that hopefully captures the tagline given.
Other people see your picture and write down a title they think fits it. All the titles are presented, and everyone except the artist tries to guess what the "real" title was. Points for those who succeed, and to the artist when they do. Points to those who make up fake answers that trick other players. It's basically Draw My Thing, but with the classic You Don't Know Jack sense of humour, and password-locked game hosting for you and your friends. The time limits are reasonably lax, making it a good one for streaming.
Get a word or syllable prompt. Combine it with something else to form a compound word, phrase or joke. All other players vote your answer up or down. If you got at least as many upvotes as downvotes, what you typed (or the last word if it's a phrase) becomes the new prompt for the next person. At the end, try having one of your friends read aloud the huge run-on word salad as smoothly as possible. This game is a more casual, unstructured experience, and it's essentially up to the group who are playing to decide what the rules really are, since upvotes or downvotes can be based on anything, including grammar and spelling, giving the next person a reasonable prompt or not, jokes being clever or overused, etc.
Players are presented with a fill-in-the-blank crazy fact. Each player writes something funny or believable to fill in the blank. All the answers given are shown, with the true one mixed in. Each player guesses which answer was true, and get points if they succeed, or if someone else guesses their false answer. This game works a lot like Drawful, except that incredulous factoids take the place of drawings and captions. It can be a lot of fun, and teach you some interesting trivia, but the question bank is unfortunately rather limited, and lacks a feature to prevent repeats, so they can become a problem after a few games have been played, due to players already knowing the answers.
See a piece of trivia. Hit true if you think it's true, or false if you don't. Get points for guessing correctly and for being the first person to do so. This one is extremely simple, but can be played with dozens of people at once if desired, so it can be good for populous streams if you like trivia.
Another edition of the classic irreverent gameshow. In this version, the game is lumped into "episodes", games which always have the same questions in the same order, and are capable of ongoing themes. Once per episode, getting a wrong answer can get you more money than the right one, based on a hint "sponsor" given at the very beginning of the game. A variety of silly gimmicks give the questions variety including DisorDat; Who's the Dummy?; Foggy Facts with Old Man; and Kangaroo, Peanut, Albert Einstein, or Uranus.
Points scored (or lost if you get an answer wrong) are based on how fast you buzz in, so this one suffers horribly from the internet lag if it happens.
I've also encountered a bunch of glitches in this game. Most are cosmetic, preventing the question number cinematic clips from displaying properly, but at one point, the game locked up after someone used a "screw" at the same time as their target was attempting to buzz in and answer the question.

Party Pack has its fair shares of winners and losers, but is a must for anyone who regularly throws parties. Where most local multiplayer games have the hassle of controller or player limitations, each of the Party Pack games are more inclusive and easy to understand. All who owns or can get a cellphone can easily join the game.  Most importantly, the games are just plain fun to play, offering a series of unique experiences that will have players thinking hard and laughing even harder.
The weakest game in this pack would be Word Spud. A form of word association, it gives you a word to start off with and sees you chaining together answers, with other players awarding points based on how good they thought it was. While fun in theory, the other players have no reason to up-vote your word, as unlike the other games they don’t get points themselves for doing so, and relying on good sportsmanship after playing the more competitive games doesn’t really work.
The Jackbox Party Pack is a party game that truly can be played by anyone. Its excellent presentation combined with its variety means that this is a must have for anyone who regularly has friends over.

Fallout 3 is praised for being super amazing, amazing graphics, amazing story, amazing everything you can think of.
It has a 91/100 on Metacritic and was developed and published by Bethesda Software & Bethesda Gameworks. Is it really all that good though..?
Obviously one of the main problems with this game is that it does NOT play well with new computers. Running this game on Windows 10 with a 6 core GTX 1080 may seem like you'll get 120 FPS, but in reality you're going to crash a lot. Like, unplayable a lot.
There is mods and fixes and .ini changes that you can do to improve the games stability but you'll still often find yourself crashing. I'm not going to dwell too much deeper since the rest of the game will run realitively smooth (unless you try to make the game lag/crash).
Born in a Vault, Vault is tutorial. Dad leaves, go find him. The rest is story spoilers so if your interested, keep reading/
It's a very mundane story only powered by a few notable characters and a bunch of sidequests. In earlier Fallouts you'd run into many notable characters, and you'd get sidequests with plenty of reading. There's a few notable sidequests in Fallout 3, but some of them a little less boring.
The main problem with this is that your allies are the Brotherhood of Steel, and if you've never played the original Fallouts, the BoS in this game look like the good guys. But they never really were, sure they might've been good but they weren't super friendly to random outsiders, and you could never really truly join them. Now they're tincans that are all about being the good guys.
Fallouts 1 and 2 had turn-based combat, where you had a limited amount of action points to do whatever is needed. Fallout 3 radically changes the combat from a "take your time, plan ahead" combat style to an action game where your Pip-Boy is a magical watch that stops time. It became a shooter. It works alright, it's a bit of fun. V.A.T.S is still in the game, and instead of getting 10 ways to shoot your target, you can shoot 6 different limbs with a chance to hit. It's a little less fun than in FO1 and FO2, but it's alright. Shoot bad guys, yay!
Fallout 3 comes with the 5 DLCs that came out with it, Point Lookout, Mothership Zeta, Operation Anchorage, The Pitt, and Broken Steel. I'd say these are more than likely some of the best parts of FO3. The first 4 DLC listed are completly new areas to explore with new characters, new enemies, new perks, and new weapons and armor. Broken Steel is a continuation of the main story, and it's really just about finishing off the 'bad guys'. I think it's slightly better than the main story because there was a bit more choices on what you could do, especially the ending.
I honestly don't think there is any reason to play FO3. It doesn't work well on modern day systems (without mods and changes to .ini files), the story is a bit bland, you are VERY limited on what you can do for an RPG (not counting Broken Steel).
I'd say if you want to play FO3 for the DLC or if in general you want to play it, I would get this game, install it, then get Fallout: New Vegas Ultimate Edition, and then for that game, install the "Tale of Two Wastelands" mod.
Edit: If you want a more in-depth review on why Fallout 3 isn't too good, look up "Fallout 3 is Garbage, and heres why" on Youtube.

Faster fins, a better camera, more accurate spear gun etc. Nothing too “deep” here, but it still adds to the gameplay. There are several fish types and other hazards to avoid. Lastly, I really enjoyed the ambient music. It gave me a relaxing escape from the usual shooter games I play. You could call this game a snorkeling simulator because that’s essentially what it is (and I’m perfectly fine with that).
