The Blazblue franchise is a delightful 2D fighting game series presenting 2D characters fighting in 3D backgrounds. Although the background textures aren't amazing, a lot of crazy stuff can go on in dem backgrounds. The resolution settings don't present you with a lot of options, which may be disappointing for some of you. The online network mode also has some flaws, as the settings are very basic, not really allowing you to fight other players in specific regions, and no option to turn off chat within matches (which could potentially get very annoying). I should also mention that the player pool for online play isn't really expansive, as few rooms with specific match settings accepting other players show up, and the the whole "player skill matchup" feature is either hit-or-miss. Even if set to "same strength as me" or "stronger than me," chances are you may run into unknowledgable players or god-tier masters, because the player pool is small. Even though this is isn't the latest in the series, it's still enjoyable and comes with a lot of content, being both friendly to both people who know zilch about 2D fighting games and those who are veterans, as they have a tutorial for you fledglings as well as a lot of content and changable difficulty settings for the hardcore audience. The story is extremely complicated, which is something me and my fellow players never really bring up. Even so, the gameplay is more than enough for make up for it, as investing your time in playing allows you to unlock a lot of content that's just waiting for you, with an entire gallery of artwork, alternate announcer voices, alternate character colors (which may or may not make references to other characters), unlimited forms of said characters (cuz everyone likes utterly destroying your foes) and more items for you to buy (with in-game currency, not real-world money) to change up your chances of faring in the game's Abyss mode. The one thing that Blazblue has that most fighting games lack is the fact that you can rebind both keyboard controls and gamepad controls, which is really helpful.

I really have mixed feelings about the New Colossus. On one hand, when it's Wolfenstein, it's great. On the other hand, in 11 hours of play, there was about 3 or so hours, where the game was really Wolfenstein and not some generic cover shooter with stealth elements or a mediocre movie. There are just far too many of the cutscenes.
In terms of gameplay, it's a step-back in almost all aspects from the New Order and the Old Blood. You die far too easily and I'm not talking about the difficulty. I was playing on "Bring 'Em On" but also tried on "Call Me Terror-Billy" and "Can I Play, Daddy" just to see what changes and I have to say, in all difficulties, you die way too quickly from enemy bulletfire. Again, this is not a problem in difficulty, it just forces you into a playstyle, that for me, is not Wolfenstein. I'm fine with a little bit of sneaking around but practically forcing you to do it is really annoying in the long-term. The weapons also seem less imaginative than in its predecessors.
In terms of story, it's okay I guess, but nowhere as good to warrant this many cutscenes and this much exposition. All in all, I felt like I was an inactive observer for hours in the game, which is, again, a really big letdown from a Wolfenstein game.
All in all, it's not a bad game. This was the first I've preordered in ages and I'd be lying if I'd say I feel ripped off, but I feel a bit unsatisfyed nevertheless. Awesome side-scroll shooter.  Would definitely argue against it being hard core. The levels are hard core, but the amount of replays is very forgiving vs older types of this genre.  To spell it out for those unfamiliar, similar games of this type would only allow a set amount of replays, similar to what you would encounter in a coin-op arcade game.  This one give you something like 11 replays per level, and once you use them up and restart a level you can restart the level with all the replays again.  Makes getting to the end of the game so much more possible.

While I love the genre and I love aspects of ESA, I found it too frustrating to play as some key pieces of the game are counter-productive to the game itself. Judging by how it is designed, ESA borrows heavily from Metroid Fusion/Zero Mission in style, two games which I enjoy and own. However, ESA plays more like a puzzle mixed with a "Souls" game when pertaining to the memorable sections like the boss fights and punishing deaths.
This is compounded by the initial weapons given to the player and after the third or so boss dealing any significant damage to bosses falls short. In addition, weapon upgrades are hard to come by, but things like the Charge Shot come in too late and feel more like keys rather than an upgrade. The Triple Shot and Supercharge module are optional, but again come in too late and, with the Supercharge module specifically, aren't worth the effort put forth to obtain them. They really should be obtained from the bosses themselves, rather than in some out of the way zone on the map. However, both are optional and aren't needed to complete the game proper, but it hurts the player to not obtain these items as boss fights are punishing without the proper equipment.
In lieu of that and a few other hiccups, like some bosses being able to hit the player during a room transition, I finished the game. In the end, I don't hate or have cause to bad mouth ESA. It's fun and enjoyable up to a point, but it falls flat and only serves to shoot itself in places where it counts. If you like the overall style and aren't bugged by the shortcomings I found, then it's a worthwhile buy.

Certainly repetitive but overall not a terrible game if you can will your way through the repetitiveness. It is important to remember that this game is nowhere near completion. Whether or not you have fun is almost entirely based on whether you can handle doing a couple of the same quests over and over without getting bored. I, for one, didn't get that bored and managed to have quite a bit of fun with the other stuff you get or find later on, but I have seen many people buy this game just to refund it after an hour for this reason.
It's worthwhile to mention that some people will downright HATE the camera angles and controls for this game, and it's safer to have both a keyboard AND controller at hand, in case you end up heavily disliking one of the two and can just rely on the other instead. Make sure to change camera settings as well. I prefer having it manually adjusted, rather than the poorly-implemented following mechanism it starts off with.
Everything else about the game is pretty much classic Lego-ism with a touch of freedom. Fight stuff, build stuff, enjoy some cutscenes and narrator dialogue, etc. There isn't a story, though, so if you're not a big fan of doing things like that, chances are you WILL get bored.
At the time of writing, there is a decent selection of things that may keep the kind of person who WILL like this game interested in playing:
- Different biomes and worlds: The variety of things you can explore is one of the greatest motivators to play this game. There's tons of different character types, animals, buildings, etc. You can also find cities/towns. However, that also means that AFTER you've discovered all the types of worlds there are to discover (which isn't an incredibly lengthy list at all), it begins to get a fair amount more boring. I really wish that this game had procedurally generated worlds with different biomes as well, instead of having to travel to different worlds just to see maybe one or two major biomes featured there. It's like loading a world in Minecraft just to see the ENTIRE world is a ONLY a jungle biome, or ONLY a desert biome, and having to load another one if you want something else.
- Customization: Dress up like a cowboy and shoot your friends. Lots of customization, and every time you find a different world, you will also find new characters to
borrow looks from. This will, of course, require you to complete a boring quest for them first, though.
- Vehicles: New worlds, new vehicles. Fly a helicopter. Fly a plane. Fly a plane with guns and shoot your friends.
- Weapons: New worlds, new weapons. Shoot your friends.
Not much else to say. The soundtrack, or at least the floaty-space theme, is great.

- nice atmosphere and art
- interesting character builds
- decent story and voice acting
- the game looks great and runs pretty well - no sudden slowdowns or anything like that
Cons:
- frequent crashing/locking up when doing scene transitions, to the point where we were lucky to play 2h at a time
- frequent bugs that interrupt the gameplay (ie you are dead and can't respawn, or you respawn in your home-base but are dead and need resurrecting *in the base*)
- bugs that break missions (had en entire level bug out with no enemies spawning over multiple visits/session, broke the final boss quest 3 or 4 times)
- ridiculous difficulty. maybe we were playing it wrong after Diablo but dying constantly on Casual difficulty was not fun
- as a spellcaster, I had frequent lock-ups where a spell would remain stuck casting, so I couldn't cast any other spells and could not move - had to just wait to die and respawn
Not sure how that stacks up in single-player since I was not interested in that aspect, so if you're never intending to play multiplayer read some other reviews. However, if you want to play multiplayer, I hope you have endless patience.

The first thing to say about Remember Me is that the French development really does impact the game. Throughout the game there is French graffiti and with antagonists like Madame, it's hard to miss. This is by no means a bad thing; it adds to the character of the game, and the references to the French Revolution (La Bastille) are a nice, albeit overt, touch. However, it may have had a negative effect on the game - I don't know if it was lost in translation or if it was just the way it was written, but the game's attempts to have shocking and reality-altering revelations fell a little short. That being said, the story is captivating and made me want to play if only to find out what happens next. In addition to a solid plot, the game is quite stunning. The level design is original and the cinematics are beautiful. Playing through a level is a mix of Assassin's Creed parkour, Arkham-Asylum-like combat, and a Bioshock kind of atmosphere, all with a soundtrack that complements the fast-paced feel. There's even the occasional puzzle. Clearly, this game has a mix of everything, which kept it refreshing and entertaining. I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a solid game they can play through numerous times and always have fun.

Remember Me feels like a breath of fresh air in this day and age of videogaming. It might not be a masterpiece, but it certainly is a unique title, blending combat a-la-God Hand with a classic cyberpunk setting (evil megacorps ruling, class warfare, hacking!).
The plot begins as your standard cyberpunk story: evil corporation running the place and doing evil stuff, main character is a talented hacker working for the revolutionaries, ROW ROW FIGHT THE POWER! Or is it? Nillin, the main protagonist, often questions herself between missions about the morality of her actions, while trying to forge a new identity for herself having lost her memories before the game starts. And in the end even some of the villains end up being somewhat sympathetic, normal people having to deal constantly with the heavy burdens of their past.
The game world manages to fascinate thanks to the stunning art design of Neo-Paris and a soundtrack that fits the cyberpunk overall theme of the game. Even when moving through the linear structure of the levels, one can admire the cure and dedication put into the world. Sadly, as written above, the game is set on a sequence of linear paths, with little to none exploration to be had.
Gameplay-wise, the combat unfortunately becomes quite repetitive quite fast due to the lack of variety in both combos and enemies, with certain encounters entirely based on a "use special move, wait for CD, repeat" pattern (some boss battles, while entertaining and varied, fall into this category).
The really juicy and unique mechanic is the remixing of memories: by witnessing some key moments in the lives of the target, Nillin can change subtle but important details in order to change those memories completely, therefore manipulating the actions of the "remixed". While finding the correct solution is an easy task overall, it leaves open the possibility to mess around  for a while and explore all the possible outcomes. Sadly, this mechanic is only used 4 times in the game. A pity, really.
Overall, I would recommend this game for the world building, the memory-related mechanics and the story (an advice: play it in French with English subtitles, the voice acting is really on point), though the fairly monotone combat could prove too boring for someone.

Not so memorable as the title begs. Nevertheless it has its own style, great graphics,  music and the world which seems interesting enough. However much information about the world is gained through large ingame codex texts instead of actual gameplay and ingame world presentation. Some characters seems underused and/or underdeveloped - especially Olga Sedova, the bounty hunter, whose potential has been almost completely killed. She was somewhat interesting, but honestly... after a few months I cannot remember much of other characters (mainly due to their cliched personalities). As I am not much skilled in console-style fighting games the combat and combo system were standart for me - not outstanding, not poorly done. Gameplay is linear, never even trying to seem nonlinear or giving you bigger open area to explore. Platforming is weak, always holding your hand and not allowing you to choose another path (because there is none).
To be fair the game had one unexpected and very fresh idea which piqued my interest and was the initial impulse to buy the game - the memory remixes, which were great but too rarely used to my taste (4 total) and thus left me disappointed in the end. All in all it was a fun game. Gameplay lenght is actually (and paradoxically) one of the pluses (10 or so hours for an experienced player who is trying to find all collectibles), otherwise it would be so damn repetitive.
I would recommend it mainly for those who want to try the remixes.

Before I kick off, let me just say this: I do not play shoot-em-ups or bullet hell games on a regular basis. Saying that I represent the target audience would be optimistic at best, and I appreciate that some of the features in Sine Mora that annoy me are probably what the target audience likes. I only bought the game because it was on heavy discount and I figured I might be in for a pleasant surprise.
Let's start with the biggest plus: Sine Mora looks great, with cartoonish 3D graphics and wonderful backgrounds and awesome boss enemies. The world is vibrant with all manners of details, which makes it nice to look at, but unfortunately I often encountered severe problems with perceiving depth: it was difficult to tell when an enemy was within line of fire or just off to the side depth-wise, a situation made more confusing by some enemies you can engage even though they are far in the background. The edges of certain levels are ridiculously difficult to identify because of their depth curvature, which is exacerbated by the fact that colliding with a wall kills you. What is this, Silver Surfer on the NES? Avoiding walls and projectiles is particularly difficult on the awfully twitchy keyboard controls, so much so that I would never have beaten the game without a controller. Other than these issues, the game is fairly challenging but far from impossible on normal difficulty, although it thinks nothing of throwing a couple of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t deaths your way whenever it thinks it can get away with it.
Apart from the wonky perspectives and useless keyboard controls, which are frustrating enough for me not to recommend the game, I suppose Sine Mora is solid enough. There is no health bar; instead you have a set time in which to reach the next checkpoint, and getting hit reduces that time whilst dispatching enemies increases it, which I thought was actually quite a fine and innovative mechanism. I only wish it had been stuck to a better game.
The story is a bit difficult to keep track of, and it seems to me that it sets off to tell too much in too complex a manner in too little time, but this is the kind of game that people are probably going to play and replay in hopes of high scores, so they should be able to soak up the plot well enough, I suppose.
Incredibly mediocre experience, if you're hankering for bullet dodgy fun time on Steam, try Jamestown instead.

Depth Hunter 2 is a decent little indie game about snorkeling under the water. Its a ok game for being a underway swimming game and some nice touches here and there. The graphics in the game are nice and like the little details they do here and there. There’s plenty of fish swimming around ranging from so reef fish all the way up to sharks and a Blue Whale on one mission. Mission wise the game is kinda short on that. Most of the missions, including the DLC's, are basicly all the same. You either hunt for a certain fish or spear as many as you can, look for treasure, or take pictures. On all the 3 base maps and the 2 DLC's that’s basicly what you do. There will be a 2-4 missions that will have you stump for a bit on what you need to find but once you get it done, its a cake walk after that. If you do all the missions and don't do free dives, you'll have the game done in hour and a half to two hours. You can upgrade your character, which is a balded head man with no option to change your character, and have him swim better, spear better, and take a lot of pics. Once you done all the missions you can tackle the achievements and with the recent update, makes one of the achievements, Sharpshooter, basicly easy to get since you can hardly miss now. The maps are really detailed with you able to swim around a downed plane, a couple of ships, a sunken city, and a underwater trench. You can swim around as long as your oxygen holds out, which doubles as your health. You can swim right up to any fish and sharks and don't have to worry about getting attacked by any of them. So in short the game is fun and relaxing but gets very tedious and repetitive with the missions.

I'll get the obvious out of the way first - the art direction and music scoring for Ori is great.
Unfortunately, the actual gameplay could have used just as much attention.
--For starters with this game's problems, it falls into the same trap as many other games with gorgeous art - the scenery that won't kill you is nigh indistinguishable from the scenery that will. This is a big no-no.
--Secondly, while I appreciate the devs taking some risks and giving the player some unusual skill combinations, the Stomp skill is by far the WORST implementation of controls in any platformer. Accidentally hitting 'down' will send your character plummeting usually into a spike pit to their death.
--Another problem that games with lots of beautiful effects have is sometimes the screen gets too mulled by craziness to tell what is going on. Ori suffers from this, as well, when the spirit flame attack pretty much obstructs any enemy wind-ups; and there is a dodge/reflect mechanic that hinges on this ability to see incoming attacks.
--The temple escape scenes are all WRETCHED. Often times, the player will die a good few dozen times because it's unclear what is killing them or there are just tons of instant death elements that will ambigously kill the player. If you're really lucky, things that will hurt/kill you one moment you will need to use the dodge-bash mechanic on seconds later - BEST SCENARIO PLANNING EVAR (sarcasm). Especially in the case of the first dungeon, beat the rising water...except the water auto-rises in certain parts. So, no matter how well you are doing, the water is just going to raise to a certain mark once you reach a particular area and likely screw up any platforming you may have gotten a leg-up on by doing well. Why punish the player for excelling in your game?
All in all, I feel you'd have to be a special sort of masochist to play through and enjoy Ori for what it is. I feel like they wanted to make a Lilo and Stitch meets Fern Gully animation, but decided to milk the gaming realm for cash instead. It has a pretty style, but also is a pretty bad game.
Final edit - made it through to the end. It was not fun, mostly sloppy controls (can't exclusively use the D-pad due to the bash skill requiring the precision of the joystick during many jumping puzzles), and intentionally frustrating in the liberal use of instant death scenery that is ambiguously harmful to the player. I wish this team had hired a veteran game designer so these glaring errors wouldn't have made it into the final product. I'm glad my initial impressions were correct. Don't buy this garbage, although it is very pretty garbage.

I recently heard about Spooky's House of Jump Scares and was incredibly excited to sit down with a friend and take on the challenge of the cursed castle. Did we beat it? Yes. Was it worth it? Well... That's not entirely a straight-forward answer...
Spooky's starts out with a charming atmosphere that slowly becomes more and more twisted and demented as you travel deeper into the castle. The game is based around an adventure style where you choose doors to travel to new locations, however "adventure" is used in the loosest sense possible. 98% of the time, having to choose a door at a fork in the road doesn't matter, which makes the fact of even having multiple doors seemingly pointless... At the start of the game, coming to a split with two doors felt exciting and nerve-wracking, however soon after you realize your decision means nothing, which is really sad.
The current build goes up to about 750 rooms before reaching the technical end point of the game, however even that is too much. Although the main shtick of the game is the "1000 rooms", it's definitely an artificially stretched limit, since the vast majority of rooms you go through are randomly chosen ones you been through 60 times already. To be honest, if every section had about 40-50 less recycled rooms, I feel like this would have been a much better game. A longer game is definitely not equal to a better game.
Another saddening issue with the game is the hollow, emptiness to it. Although there are very short sections in each level of 100 rooms with great, new content, the vast majority of the game is spent in corridors and rooms with absolutely nothing in them except an occasional pumpkin or stump popping out of the wall and making a loud noise. Sure, they were pretty hilarious at the beginning, but once you go past them over a hundred times, the initial charms wears off.
I genuinely hope that the last "mechanic" where Spooky makes you unable to run anymore was simply a joke that'll be scrapped in later versions, because if the ending message hadn't come up shortly after that point, I would have flat-out quit the game from irritation. Being forced to slowly walk through rooms you've already seen a million times is not remotely enjoyable, but instead feels like a punishment to the players themselves for no discernible reason.
Although a bit of a nitpick rather than an actual complaint, there's currently a pretty bad bug where, the longer you play the game, the farther off sound effects get from when they actually occurred. For example, in the beginning, the sound only seems a tiny bit off, but after about 2 hours of playing, all the sounds of monsters, pop-up scares, and swinging your axe occur about 6-7 seconds after it actually happened, which pretty much defeats the entire purpose of the redundant jump scares.
Reading this so far, you probably think I'm just some angry reviewer that despises everything about this, however that's far from the truth. The sections which introduce a new monster (usually between 10-30 doors in on a new floor) are brilliant. It temporarily ditches the recycled, randomized rooms and puts you in an incredible, new area with its own unique theme. In one section, you're tossed into an old, abandoned school building with nothing but a flashlight to find your way, to winding up in what appears to be a forest outside filled with seemingly friendly deer. Trying to find a key to open that mysterious locked door while ominous sounds emanate through the air is absolutely the best blend of atmosphere. Also, these sections always add lore to either the new monster, or the actual castle itself, making it exciting to anxiously wait to find out what you'll learn next... Because trust me, there's a lot of in-between waiting...
I won't go too much into the monsters themselves to avoid spoiling anything for people who haven't tried it yet, but they're all great. Each one has their own personal style and attributes, such as having hallucinogenic effects, making all the doors entirely vanish requiring you to find your way by memory, or making it so you can't simply run for the door without using some tact. Monsters you've previously encountered randomly come back later, meaning you could see some lovely, familiar faces come back to chase you at any time. However, the only time you encounter new monsters is by completing 100 more rooms, making it feel like a chore to have to travel through 90 rooms of the same crap you've been through before to see 10 rooms of new content. Then, repeat ad infinitum...
All in all, Spooky's is a game with a lot of great potential and several memorable moments, however having to trudge through excessive monotony to reach the "good parts" simply isn't worth it. I would advise people to wait for a later update before giving this a whirl.

ESA gives a great exploration experience: you're a robot, a large abandoned space station lies before you and you've only got your wits and a trusty gun to rely on. Very liberating experience, nothing unnecessary, so it's very easy to immerse yourself in it.
The difficulty is a subjective topic, I guess, but to give an example it's more like a Cave Story than Meat Boy.
Highly recommended.

Van Helsing is an aRPG set in the mythical land of Borgovia. If you've played Grim Dawn, Diablo or Torchlight you'll be familiar with the gameplay. The game does have a unique ability system though, as you fight you gain rage which can be spent to powerup your abilities. For example lets say you're using a lightning spell, powering it up may cause enemies to be shocked, or it may increase the number of enemies hit. A powered up spell only has one charge and can be activated with the spacebar, although this becomes tedious very fast and I'd wager 99.9% of people have this set to auto cast whenever available. The game allows you to set up powerup presets so you can very much set it and forget it and the game will automatically boost the chosen ability(s) whenever you have sufficient rage. Apart from that it's your usual aRPG fare, you have a standard talent tree with forks and paths, passive abilities and stat points which allow you to customise your character further.
When you create your character you have the choice of three classes, the Arcane Mechanic who is an engineer archetype, the Thaumaturge who is a mage and finally the Hunter who is the iconic poster child for the series. All classes can have two different weapon sets which can be swapped on the fly, and the Hunter can also specialise in either melee or range attacks.
Throughout the game you're accompanied by your ghostly companion, Katarina. She works very much like the Torchlight pet, she can pick up items, fight for you and even be sent back to town to sell and buy which saves you the bother! She also has her own stats and talent tree, you can either build her to become stronger herself, or build her as a complete buff bot which will give you lots of powerful auras. Usefulness aside she's actually a big part of the game, and the banter between you and her is often really enjoyable, the voice acting for both Van Helsing and Katarina is top notch (the same can't be said for all the characters though!).
The story will take around 15 hours to complete which is decent, but beyond that there's not much reason to continuing playing at max level. You do unlock scenarios which are basically dungeons with over levelled mobs which makes for a stiffer challenge and supposed higher rewards (I didn't get anything of worth) but there's no real point as the loot is lacking, which is a pretty big deal in an aRPG and why I didn't score the game higher. During my playthrough I saw a total of three legendary items and barely upgraded my gear at all, plus the items are all very generic and frankly boring. There was no excitement when an item dropped. You're also able to gamble for items with gold, but once again I never got anything of worth. I will say that this has been improved in the second game, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II which I started after finishing the first game so I'm sure I wasn't the only one who noticed this massive flaw.
Technically the game is fine, most quests have voice acting which isn't always a given for this genre, especially from the smaller studios, and while not perfect it is pretty funny at times and there are plenty of references to other games and TV shows which I enjoyed. Graphically the game is OK, it's a couple of years old and wouldn't have been anything to rave about back then, but it's fine, and it performs well, I was able to maintain 60fps on ultra without dips (as you'd expect from an older game on a GTX 970). The audio is decent and the voice acting is good for the main characters and acceptable for the supporting cast, the game doesn't take itself too seriously in this department and you will find yourself smiling throughout the game at the silly things that are said.
Overall it's a decent aRPG with some major flaws that prevent it from being more than decent but if you can grab it at 75% off in a Steam sale I would say go ahead and buy it, you'll get your monies worth at that price and while it's not perfect, it is an enjoyable experience. The devs are also still supporting the game two years later, and plan to bring out a "Final Cut" of all three games with new features and a more streamlined experience, this will be free if you own all three games already. If you're interested in the series it may be smart to wait until September to play it as the Final Cut will be released then.

I adore this style of gaming and the fantasy theme calls to something within me. So when the game on sale I quickly clicked 'buy' and began my quest as a Van Helsing. So, what did I think (and still do as I have by no means completed it)?
I FREAKING LOVE this game! The theme and back-drop to the game is spot on as you wade through hordes of all varieties of mythical monstrosities.  Graphically, the game delivers well and is pleasing to the eye. The voice acting for Van Helsing and Katarina (DLC) is superb. Really well done! The banter between them adds depth to their characters and is a real treat to hear. The musical score/sound effects are brilliant too and again adds to the immersion.
Character customisation is varied and gives much choice to the three classes to choose from. Each gives a different way of combating the horrors that await.
Loot... oh the loot. Much is to be gathered and acquired as one would expect from a game such as this. The game is fun to play, even more so with friends (or my dad in my case) but beware, the game (for me) can get addictive. I always feel I need to keep playing just to get that next item that will boost my DPS or to see what new enemies are lurking around the corner.
For all its pros there are unfortunately some cons. Certain shrines cannot be activated, instead once clicked causes your character to wander trying to find it even though it's right in front of them, denying you an XP/DMG boost. With the Arcane Mechanic class (which I play and love burning monsters with) when I click over an enemy to attack, he wonders off, not knowing where it is. A pathing issue with this and the shrines I'm thinking.
The worst issue (for me) is no matter how long I play for, be it five minutes or five hours, upon exiting the game my PC shows a CPU temperature warning. My PC is not old and boasts some high-end hardware so I was quite surprised when the message popped up. Never before have I seen such a message other than playing Skyrim (with mods and graphical enhancements) for almost an entire day straight, which is justified. These issues I have are not enough for me to stop playing, but it would be nice if they were resolved.
9/10

I started playing this game because I didn't really feel like playing Diablo 3, and all in all I'm pretty happy with my choice.
Story:
I was expecting the game to be a Diablo-clone in most ways, so having the big bad be a
instead of a
was a pretty nice surprise. Fighting robots(?) in a steampunk-ish world also felt a bit fresh compared to fighting the same old demons and mythological creatures (some of which
appear in this game as well). The basic story is of course the good old "hack your way through a bunch of enemies to defeat the big bad trying to take over the world (or country?)", but there's nothing wrong with that.
Gameplay:
If you have played Diablo or any other ARPG you will probably recognize the play style right away. You use your mouse and a couple of buttons to dash out various spells while keeping an eye on your health and mana. The addition of rage, which refills when you kill a creature and can be used to power up your spells, was a nice  touch. It gives you an extra thing to do during fights, as well as more ways to personalize your skill tree, so an extra plus there.
Graphics:
The graphics were fine. Not great, not bad. Some creatures looked pretty good, some looked pretty bland. The same can be said for the environment. Personally I enjoyed the city zones more than the nature zones. The (few and short) cut scenes were pretty meh, especially compared to the Diablo cut scenes, but that's acceptable.
Music:
While playing the game I thought that the music fit the mood pretty well, but as soon as I stopped playing I forgot the soundtrack right away.
The voice acting in this game... At first I thought that the voice acting was just really, really bad, and almost lol'ed a couple of times during the first few hours of the game. But then I realized that that was what they were going for (probably?). Sort of cheesy, over-the-top voice acting, that when you get used to it fit the game really well, and was sometimes just really funny (in a good way!). Some of the comments from both Van Helsing and Lady Katarina were just hilarious, although by the end of the game Katarina was becoming quite annoying.
Overall:
Overall I enjoyed this game, even my second playthrough, which was a little unexpected. I don't really want to call Van Helsing a Diablo-clone, since there were a couple of things that set it apart from Diablo, so let's just call it a decent option if you like ARPGs. I recommend this game, even at full price if you don't want to wait for a sale, however I do have a couple of warnings:
1. There are some bugs in the game, the most common being corpses stuck in walls or terrain that can't be looted. I also found a couple of chests that I couldn't open for whatever reason. The biggest bug I faced was a door leading to the next zone being closed, forcing me to start over with a new character. (Luckily this didn't happen with my hardcore heroic character.) There was a fix posted on the developer's forum to fix this, but that fix didn't work for me. On July 2nd 2015 they added the "Mantis Bug Tracker" to the game, which should help fix more bugs, but I wasn't able to test this out myself.
2. If you care about achievements you can get
of the achievements by playing through the game twice. None of them are really that hard to get, as my first playthrough was on hardcore heroic difficulty (=perma-death), and I only died four times, so the game is fairly easy. However, there is
achievement that is just plain stupid. It requires you to get 500,000 kills, which is a lot, seeing as you only get about 10,000-15,000 kills per playthrough. Luckily there is a way to make Lady Katarina afk farm kills for you, which she is doing for me as I am typing this, but just be aware that there is this one really annoying achievement if you (like me) want to clear the game 100%.
But all in all, a really good game.

A fairly simple example of it genre, yes, but Remember Me is a rarity on the PC, as most adventure games of its type are console-only.  It may have its flaws; some hackneyed dialog, plot holes, linear level designs, but as a whole Remember Me offers a competant play experience.
The environments are gorgeous. Neo-Paris is incredibly detailed to the point of being cluttered. There's just so much to look at -- even someplace as sterile as a prison.  Sadly, the linear nature of the levels makes exploring limited. Character designs are just as beautiful though. 3D models unlock with achievements for you oogling pleasure. This high detail makes cutscene trasitions near seamless. Combat is easy to grasp; one button to dodge and a variation of two other buttons to combo attacks.  A simple leveling mechanic allows to later customize and extend combos, adding a little strategy and depth.
The most unique feature of Remember Me is the memory remixes -- changing a person's (victim's?) memory of a specific event to manipulate them. Remixes themselves are basically cutscenes which can be edited to change little details in the person's memory which compound into completely changing the outcome of the event.  This leads to the person's outlook or personality to completly change. Remixes also add some experimentation and replayability to the game, as there can be multiple outcomes in these manipulations. (only the 'right' way will progress the story though)
Overall I recommend Remember Me. Its short length (about 8 hours) benefits the pacing of the game, as no chapter (level) feels slow or trodding, nor do the linear levels and combat feel too shallow.

In every facet of its design Sine Mora exudes excellence. Considerably well polished from presentation to gameplay, it tells a surprisingly engaging tale of a father's unremitting resolve to take revenge for the death of his son, and takes itself very seriously with mass genocide, physical abuse, and suicide all sharing a place in the unflinching narrative. Even if the plot occasionally becomes convoluted, there is so much conviction in every line of script that it almost didn't matter what was being said. I found it fascinating, and though it is entirely possible to skip straight to the action, those wanting for something more substantial should find plenty to keep them occupied.
A side-scrolling shooter is only as good as its gameplay though, and once again Grasshopper Manufacture outdoes itself. Contrary to my expectations of Ikaruga like color swapping, Sine Mora is an entirely new breed of bullet-hell centered around time. Your life is literally dictated as seconds on the clock, and with each enemy you kill that time is extended. Inversely getting hit reduces it, and thus the frenzied back and forth between racing through levels and sending as many enemies to their grave as possible is born.
I've never pretended to be good at this style of game, but Sine Mora strikes a perfect balance between the constant insanity of bullets and giving you the control needed to survive them. In contrast to just about everything similar I have played, there was never a point that I felt overwhelmed or unable to continue, and it is for that very reason that I would whole wholeheartedly recommend those interested in bullet-hell games start here. It isn't an easy game by any stretch, but completing it is certainly achievable for both veterans and novices alike (the former will find plenty of challenge in the higher difficulty level, score challenges, and multiple ranks to shoot for).
It only takes one look at Sine Mora in motion to see it is a downright gorgeous game, but more impressive than even the great texture, lighting and particle effects is the fantastically creative steampunk art direction. Each level is taken up in large part by incredible boss battles the design of which only become more involved and more impressive in scale as they go on, reminding me of everything from The Matrix to Porco Rosso. I rarely bother with concept or unlockable artwork, but I was actually disappointed there was none to be found here. I do wish they had done away with the letterbox framing, but otherwise I was simply awestruck at the visuals and have no doubt that other games will be compared to them for a long time to come.
Grasshopper Games diverse and bizarre catalog is more often than not know for offering quirky yet ultimately shallow experiences, but Sine Mora isn't one of them.  This is a full package of outstanding quality, hands down one of the best side-scrolling shooters I have played in years, and one that can be enjoyed regardless of skill level. If you're a fan of bullet-hell shooters or ever wanted to be, then this is something you should definitely be checking out!

Wow.. oh.. Wow.. OH WOW..!! From halfway through the opening in the log canoe I began to realise I was in for unique and original experience.. Little did I realise the true nature of the journey I was about to undertake and how intense, mind shatteringly awesome, distressing and magnificent was the tale that I was about to become a tiny part of.. I had a few concerns as aspects of the subject matter had been so incredibly poorly represented in the past.. But those concerns quickly melted away as I became more and more engrossed in the gorgeous and deeply disturbed world. THIS IS NOT A GAME FOR EVERYONE..!! THIS IS NOT A GAME FOR 'POPCORN' GAMERS - Looking for a more hand-holding and safe, escapist, ego massaging, positivity boosting, re-assuring re-enforcement of the self delusional media products that we all consume to 'wind down after a hard day' and restore our sense of peace, reliability, predictability and assurance in the world we come to know and try to create for ourselves. THIS IS NOT A GAME FOR THE EMOTIONALLY IMMATURE..!! If you are the type of person who finds the world to be a little too vast, scary and over-whelming at times and to survive and stay ‘sane’ enough to function, have to retreat to ‘safe’ chemically, electronically or ‘spiritually’ induced fantasies, illusions , delusions or realities to allow our minds to catch up with ourselves and make sense of our experiences. Or the type of person who has yet to experience enough of the ‘real’ world to properly contextualise what this game has to say to you and to give to you. Or the type of person who as their coping method and strategy is to deny, vilify, attack and turn your back on anything that may challenge your conception of your reality. Or people whose life is consumed, ruled and crippled by fear. Or people who are helplessly addicted to their favourite junk food and will only eat the same thing again and again and again and again and again and again..!! That said.. MAYBE.. this is EXACLTY THE GAME YOU SHOULD PLAY..!! THIS IS A GAME FOR.. people who care, who love, who explore , who genuinely wish to gain a greater understanding of the varieties of our existences. People who want to relish their time in their existence, taste new tastes, hear new sounds, see new sights, feel new feelings and think new thoughts..!! THIS IS A GAME FOR.. people who ADORE a challenge, THIS IS A SUBLIME GAME of stunning design, artwork, sound, music, performance, pacing, story and intent. This is a game which may very well ‘rock your world’. This is a game that WILL F##K WITH YOUR MIND..!! This is a game that will whimper, then cry, then shriek, then SCREAM, THEN ROAR in your face and ears.. as it tries to convey it’s simple subtleties and depths. Its conceptions and understandings.. THIS IS NOT A GAME THAT EVEYONE CAN HANDLE..!! For my third and final session of play I chose to play without headphones as the ‘furies’ whispering in my ears continued to gnaw at my own sanity..!!  I did learn to better ignore the negative and unhelpful furies and welcome and appreciate the positive and helpful ones and bizarrely, once I had finished the game, I began to miss the furies..!! But.. THIS IS NOT A ‘NICE’ GAME..!! This game is Unsettling, frustrating, disturbing, chilling, freaky, soothing, beautiful, reassuring, infuriating, terrifying, awful, upsetting and terrible in the best ways. THIS GAME IS A TRIUMPH in the way that, to me, Ninja Theory has accomplished its goals with this product and the limitations and liberations of the technology it utilises. But ultimately it is just a game. A game that may open insights, understanding, empathy, compassion and appreciation of the issues its players will play through and thusly it may hopefully bring a little more empathy, understanding and compassion into the world. But still, it is, just a game.. A powerful, terrifying, inspirational and provocative, But just a game.. imperfect, sometimes, thankfully, only very occasionally, a little buggy, laggy and glitchy but somehow perfected and strengthened by its imperfections, mostly.. However, it is just a game.. a game that, through the epic, relentless and exhausting battles. Through the epic, tragic and invigorating story, that may serve to change the conceptions, prejudices and assumptions of its players and hopefully, subtly, in its humble way, change the world for the better, giving it the gentlest of nudges towards a wiser and enriched state of existence and for that I applaud all at Ninja Theory and all that helped with and contributed to the creation of this game, no matter how small or subtle, with every fibre, atom and electron of my being.. This game is a challenge. This game is challenging, This game is great.. But just a game.. and these are the thoughts, rants and ramblings of just a person, just one person,  who, in Senua has found a fellow traveller through the battles, darknesses and furies of this world, just one person who, is left asking a question. As Senua, hopefully, continues her journey through her existence, as she, like us all, strives to find love, acceptance, build a home and find their place in their world, will we get to witness and play our part in Senua’s vengeance, revenge and/or justice..?? I truly hope so, but that said.. I am still yearning for Half Life 3..!!!

I think those that call this "not a game but an experience" in fact do it a disservice. Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one of my favourite games in recent memory.
The world is fascinating and a very grim and satisfying portrayal of norse mythology and lore. It is at times stunningly beautiful and other times deeply disturbing.
Senua is a very compelling protagonist and made even more interesting by her psychosis and how It is expertly weaved into both the narrative and the gameplay. The few supporting characters do a wonderful job of getting you into the mindset of Senua and her view of the world.
The rest of the gamplay is made up mostly of puzzles and combat. The puzzles usually revolve around trying to find a path or some runes that are present in the scenary, They are fine and a fitting way of progressing but they can be repetitive, although some of the ways of hiding the runes in the world are very fun.
Some people have called the combat medicore and again repetitive but I think its actually really fun and at times quite intense, Its based on timing your attacks, blocks and dodges in a cirucular arena against numerous enemis of different types, although there are only about 5 different variations they each provide their own challenge. I hope to see this combat expanded on in future games by Ninja theory,
Overall I would definetly recommend Hellblade if you want a slower more thought provactive game and definetly think supporting these developers will go a long way.

I just bought this game while it was on sale for $2 and I must say that am 100% addicted!
Initially, I bought it because, well, I'm not one to pass up on deals but also I enjoy good platformers.
Before I dive right into my personal feelings towards this game, here's a quick rundown of what I felt were the major pros and cons of this game:
PROS:
-- Artwork (Need I say more?)
-- Storyline
-- Soundtrack
-- Game mechanics such as what the characters can do individually
-- Ability to switch between characters with other players
CONS:
-- Far too repetitive
-- Characters are fairly generic
-- Game is very short
-- Early levels are extremely simple
MIXED:
-- While the characters can do some really neat things individually, it feels very limited
-- Storyline of this game is good, but there is an element of suspension of disbelief that is simply missing that could serve to suck you into the story a little more.
The ambiance of Trine is about as beautiful as they come. I cannot even find the words to describe truly how gorgeous the artwork is. The lighting scheme is what completely sets the mood and the soundtrack is well composed as well. But it is the multiplayer game mechanics that really set this game apart as you and your friends switch characters back and forth while trying to cooperatively build your through each level.
This game isn't perfect however, it does have a few issues that weren't huge deal breakers but are still rather annoying. For what you pay at full price, it sure is a short game and even though it does have some replay-ability value, I would recommend waiting to get this game until you can find it on sale due to how short it is. The story line is actually pretty good for what it is but it just doesn't seem to really draw you in all the way and make you forget it's not real, which also isn't that big of a deal considering it is a platformer. I also would have personally liked a few more options when it comes to what each of the three characters can do.
I conclusion, this is one heck of a game that will mesmerize your eyes and ears and will quickly grab ahold of you and not let go until it's over. Great fun on solo and REALLY fun with a few friends. I highly recommend adding Trine to your game library.

I'll get the obvious out of the way first - the art direction and music scoring for Ori is great.
Unfortunately, the actual gameplay could have used just as much attention.
--For starters with this game's problems, it falls into the same trap as many other games with gorgeous art - the scenery that won't kill you is nigh indistinguishable from the scenery that will. This is a big no-no.
--Secondly, while I appreciate the devs taking some risks and giving the player some unusual skill combinations, the Stomp skill is by far the WORST implementation of controls in any platformer. Accidentally hitting 'down' will send your character plummeting usually into a spike pit to their death.
--Another problem that games with lots of beautiful effects have is sometimes the screen gets too mulled by craziness to tell what is going on. Ori suffers from this, as well, when the spirit flame attack pretty much obstructs any enemy wind-ups; and there is a dodge/reflect mechanic that hinges on this ability to see incoming attacks.
--The temple escape scenes are all WRETCHED. Often times, the player will die a good few dozen times because it's unclear what is killing them or there are just tons of instant death elements that will ambigously kill the player. If you're really lucky, things that will hurt/kill you one moment you will need to use the dodge-bash mechanic on seconds later - BEST SCENARIO PLANNING EVAR (sarcasm). Especially in the case of the first dungeon, beat the rising water...except the water auto-rises in certain parts. So, no matter how well you are doing, the water is just going to raise to a certain mark once you reach a particular area and likely screw up any platforming you may have gotten a leg-up on by doing well. Why punish the player for excelling in your game?
All in all, I feel you'd have to be a special sort of masochist to play through and enjoy Ori for what it is. I feel like they wanted to make a Lilo and Stitch meets Fern Gully animation, but decided to milk the gaming realm for cash instead. It has a pretty style, but also is a pretty bad game.
Final edit - made it through to the end. It was not fun, mostly sloppy controls (can't exclusively use the D-pad due to the bash skill requiring the precision of the joystick during many jumping puzzles), and intentionally frustrating in the liberal use of instant death scenery that is ambiguously harmful to the player. I wish this team had hired a veteran game designer so these glaring errors wouldn't have made it into the final product. I'm glad my initial impressions were correct. Don't buy this garbage, although it is very pretty garbage.

I like to call this the poor-mans Torchlight or the indie Diablo since they lie in the same genre, play much the same and have similar mechanics, but don't have the well crafted and unique style and persona that Van Helsing has, which make it different enough to overcome many of the small issues and problems that many smaller titles such as this come with. The atmosphere and style, coupled with the lengthy playtime and interesting world make for good value for money for fans of the genre.
* The game never shies away from its gloomy old-world Victorian science & magic era, and layers on nods to Dracula, Frankenstein, Dr Jekyl and Mr Hyde and more
* The Ghost of Katarina is a wonderfully designed character and listening to the seemingly random dialogue between the two main characters is endearing
The variety of small but annoying problems that this game has all tend to stem from the same vein of poor optimization and lack of polish/production value. There are a ton of jiggly little problems in everything from enemy AI and pathing to graphical and UI options. Even insignificant things like achievements have bugs, and it's often very jarring and takes away from the persona and impressiveness of the well designed world.
* Poor AI often makes hunting down mobs a tiresome chore, especially when they're tied to quests, pathing is also occasionally poor and annoying. There is a strong lack of enemy variety, despite them having unique and interesting designs, they all have similar boring melee or ranged attacks and the only notable difference is the number of hits it takes to ware them down
* The loading screens take far too long and the games file sizes are huge and poorly optimized. There is also awful use of RAM, and you can consistently see 2GB+ of your memory sunk into this game
* There are only two or three boss fights in the 12 hours of game time, and they're badly designed, buggy, boring, and completely forgettable
* Gem slots and gems are very boring and unvaried, add nothing to the gameplay and make a barely noticeable difference to your stats
Van Helsing has a ton of content and offers a hefty gameplay time of 13-16 hours, more for completionists. It's available at £11.99/14.99€/$14.99 and it feels fairly priced if you're likely to play it through on even one character. When on sale, it's a great buy.
Personally I feel the DLC has been sold separately purely to force people to pay the extra few bucks for the Complete Pack, which is a shady tactic, especially considering all of the DLCs add content (2 extra classes, some combat fixes & companion improvements) which you'd naturally expect to be included in the game anyway. With that said, the DLC isn't especially expensive, and the Complete Pack is still fairly priced at £14.99/19.99€/$19.99, just a few bucks more. So if you expect to play more than once and even if you don't, it's probably a better idea to grab the Complete Pack.

I heard of this game by accident and, after playing Torchlight I & II, I decided to give it a try since it seemed so dark and atmospheric.
And it seams I wasn't wrong.
The first thing I noticed was that, unlike other similar games, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is a game with a distinct "personality" (assuming this can be said about a video game).
The action takes place in the dark and mysterious world of Borgovia, a world where magic and science(and of course mad scientists) can coexist.
The world is beautifully designed and it seems the designers paid a lot of attention to details. The atmosphere somehow reminded me of London as imagined by Conan Doyle as well as Transylvania as portrayed by Bram Stocker in "Dracula".
The soundtrack is great and it fits perfectly with the dark foggy streets full of strange creatures hiding in the shadows. It's really hard to tell how much it adds to the game feeling but it's obviously, once you start playing, that the game wouldn't be the same with a different soundtrack.
The game features 3 classes, The Hunter, The Thaumaturge and The Arcane Mechanic, the last 2 being sold separately as 2 DLCs.
Each class has a very complex skill system, with multiple skill trees as well as many abilities that can be both, passive or active. While this can be frustrating for those who don't like to replay the game, due to the fact that it's quite impossible to complete a skill tree in a single playthrough, unless you wonder around and kill monsters just for fun, this makes more sense if you plan on playing the sequel, since you can import everything and continue from where you left.
The main character, Van Helsing, also has his own companion, Lady Katerina, the ghost of a noble lady. Just like Van Helsing, Lady Katarina has her own skill system with a few active and passive skills as well as different combat modes (melee, ranged). You can also set her to attack those who attack you, those you are attacking or anyone around or you can tell her to stay out of battle. She can be very useful when you're overwhelmed and she can also go grab loot for you and sell/buy items.
Voice acting and dialog is great and you can actually see the chemistry between Van Helsing and Lady Katarina.
The game also has a lot of pop culture references to movies/games like The Witcher and Lord Of The Rings.
Unfortunately, for those who are used to games like Diablo and Torchlight, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, is a hard game and sometimes it can be very frustrating and cheap.
There are moments when you will be overwhelmed by creatures 2+ levels ahead of you, in confined spaces and if their huge health given by the higher level won't be a problem for you, the huge number will eventually make it impossible for you to move so you'll just have to wait for your inevitable death and respawn.
Overall, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is a great game that will please many Diablo/Torchlight fans.

The amount of loot that drops in this game borders on trolling. There's too damn much loot, and the stats compare is a pain, not only because you have to do it for two characters, but because it's confusing and unreliable. A lot of the gametime tends to be about sorting out items.
I think I'm only managing to keep playing it because of the achievements.
(The game has a demo, so the rest you can derive from that.)
- Terrain scrolling is far from being smooth. Considering the visual quality and my system, it's a bit sad. Fog even causes extreme framerate drops. This engine seems unoptimized.
- Fakenook, Twitter and Youtube links on the main screen, hurting immersion. This is about as annoying as Youtubers saying "like, comment, favorite and subscribe" all the time.
- And now the big issue right at the beginning:
Rarely does a game bombard a personal firewall as much as this. It tries to connect to
and
and oftentimes every half a second to
(even after startup - it basically bombards your firewall permanently) and if you don't allow this stuff, then the game will freeze for several minutes before you even see the main menu.
This is with a set block rule, mind you. And turning off my network is not an option since it's a Steam game. Unless you are willing to not care about the motivational factor of achievements. (Not sure whether they register in offline mode though. The game does have its own achievement UI.)
First time it didn't switch to the resolution I selected, and since it can't switch it in-game, I had to wait yet another couple of minutes. I thought that would fix the ugly text, but it seems the game uses a web font without hinting, so even in native resolution text in the menus still looked ugly.
Oh and if I alt-tab out of the game while it pauses with futile connection attempts, it might default to 640x480, requiring me to launch it yet again.
And don't say "Just let it connect.". I pay attention to what the software on my PC tries to do, since it's necessary these days.
Most games with internet connectivity get the message and don't spam firewall logs like that and stop doing anything. Especially since I already have set a block rule.
(Another game that has this kind of issue (even worse) is Super Meat Boy, although there the problem might have resolved itself somehow.)
P.S.: The game is a real space waster. Its videos (intro, cutscene, outro) are present in ten different languages, and the difference is really just the audio track and the subtitles. Extremely clumsy way to do that. 149 MB English videos and 912 MB other-language versions. They could have used that space to provide lossless sounds instead of OGG for example.
And the map files are present as separate huge versions for low, medium and high detail. Model files too. And both sometimes are of exactly the same size. (Otherwise it would probably be necessary data.)
Then again, since this game has all files separately, if you need the space and only play on high detail, you can delete 6.42 GB of terrain data alone. This plus the video thing taken care of and the game has now 11.8 GB instead of 19.1 GB.
This is basically the poor man's Bloodborne.

I think those that call this "not a game but an experience" in fact do it a disservice. Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one of my favourite games in recent memory.
The world is fascinating and a very grim and satisfying portrayal of norse mythology and lore. It is at times stunningly beautiful and other times deeply disturbing.
Senua is a very compelling protagonist and made even more interesting by her psychosis and how It is expertly weaved into both the narrative and the gameplay. The few supporting characters do a wonderful job of getting you into the mindset of Senua and her view of the world.
The rest of the gamplay is made up mostly of puzzles and combat. The puzzles usually revolve around trying to find a path or some runes that are present in the scenary, They are fine and a fitting way of progressing but they can be repetitive, although some of the ways of hiding the runes in the world are very fun.
Some people have called the combat medicore and again repetitive but I think its actually really fun and at times quite intense, Its based on timing your attacks, blocks and dodges in a cirucular arena against numerous enemis of different types, although there are only about 5 different variations they each provide their own challenge. I hope to see this combat expanded on in future games by Ninja theory,
Overall I would definetly recommend Hellblade if you want a slower more thought provactive game and definetly think supporting these developers will go a long way.

Again, I was pleasantly suprised by Depth Hunter 2. I got it cheap in the newest FPS bundle from Bundle Stars so can't complain about the price.

That all said, I give the game a 7/10 and recommend it in a bundle or when on sale for about $5, as that is the price point for games of similar ability to keep me interested like this one.

Depth Hunter 2 is a relaxing game where you explore the fishy depths.  Its like a walking simulator only for diving. Taking pictures is very rewarding there is an excellent feature of being able to make them your desktop as well.  There are multiple places to visit for diving that have many attractions under water from ships, to planes, all kinds of things that make exploring fun.
The dev is active in the steam community, if encountering a bug or making a suggestion the dev is quick to respond.  The music is perfect for the game, gives it a feeling of isolation like being on a real dive.  Missions are as short or long except a couple timed objectives to mix it up.  Great summer game to spend time swimming around exploring the oceans.
*This is a snorkel game so be sure to go to the surface when air is low.
Rating:  10/10  Value:  $9.99

The only other downside of this game are a few of the boss battles, some of which becoming very tedious and drawn-out. This game oozes style and is confident in its lore and environmental design. The story is very Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥ The technologies in the game explore the ramifications of artificial reality, memory modification, and how our memories shape our reality.
The majority of the gameplay isn't bad, nor is it anything memorable nor annoying, but just a mechanic for engaging the player in the story and environment. Hacking someone's memory is the coolest thing to do in the game, I'll just say that.
I love how it portrays memories, which I think it does a wonderful job visualizing.
I think the success of this game suffers from the same thing games with premises hard to describe in one sentence. Psychonauts suffered from the same problem; it and this game are too non-mainstream to be massively profitable. Therefore, we probably won't see a sequel because this is, afterall, a game made by a large publisher who only measures sucess by the millions. I'm just glad a game like this actually got made.

An interesting story in the futuristic setting of Neo-Paris. You are Nilin who has lost her memory and tries to regain it while fighting against Memorize Corporation, a company virtually in control of the whole society due to their brain implantats.
Why I recommend this game:
- The graphics are quite innovative: An interesting mix of a "conventional" Paris upgraded with high-tech appliances.
- CYBERPUNK setting!
- A classical single player game. I love that.
- The story takes unexpected twists.
- Innovative combo-system: You must adapt your tactics to win your combats.
- The boss-fights are quite challenging.
- There are (too few) situations where you must manipulate the memories of other persons. Quite interesting approach.
It took me about 18 hours to finish the game. A fair value at its price!
So, if you are into cyberpunk, futuristic settings and single player games, gives this game a chance!

Despite a negative review, overall I don't think Wolfenstein II is a bad game. It's got plenty of great parts and is a fairly solid sequel overall, however I expected more after the first game in the series.
Its over the top characters and exaggerated stereotypes are still there, but I guess this time they offended people because they're american stereotypes this go around.  The new characters are enjoyable enough, though we don't really get to learn much about them. Unlike the first game where you'll have plenty of time to learn about each of the cast members, the resistance has gotten so large and you don't really get to work with any of the characters closely.  It's kind of a shame too, even fergus/wyatt don't really get much screentime. The only new character who gets a lot of exposure is grace, but she's kind of annoying and one-dimensional.
Let's talk a bit about
.   It's definitely not as varied as the first game, where almost every stage is a new location. There's only a handful of locations in the second game. Airship, Manhatten, Roswell,  New orleans, Venus.  There are also a few of very small stages, courthouse, Roswell (town) and a Texas farm.  The manhatten levels suck. It's the ruins of a nuked city, filled with grey everywhere, and a subway section. New orleans suffers from almost the same problem, it's dark and run down, or you're in the sewers. It's a bland level with little that says louisana or new orleans. The roswell levels are pretty solid, it feels like the most work went into them. There are usually multiple angles of approach and you get to sneak through a nazi base.  None of the levels are memorable as the broken bridge, prison camp, moonbase, or even the london museum raid from the first game.
The different kinds of enemies are almost unchanged from the first game, and they're all pretty bland. The new supersoldiers are no longer absurd bullet sponges, in exchange for being able to thrust across the map. There's a new kind of laser dog thing, and the Super Nazi Robot, that you fight as a boss in the first game comes back as a recurring enemy with different weapons. That's about it.  The kampfhunds are more annoying than ever, and I'll bring that up later.
To compound the problem with the low number of enemies, the number of weapons is virtually unchanged from the first game. There's an SMG now, and a sort of pistol grenade launcher I never bothered with.  For some reason the heavy MG was removed, and there are instead 4 heavy weapons instead. One doesn't appear until almost the end of the game, and the others are kind of useless on the harder difficulties. The heavy shotgun weapon is terrible. There's already only a few weapons in the game, so they're all different and useful, right?
No.  If you're sneaking you'll use the pistol.
If you aren't you'll dual wield the assault rifle.
Fully upgraded it will fire single shots fairly accurately and be able to kill pretty every kind of enemy with ease, aside from the large panzerhunds. Even then, it will only take a single reload if you aren't hitting any weakpoints. The assault rifle reloads quickly, is ammo efficient, is effective at every range, and ammunition for it is plentiful.
About halfway through the game you get access to gadgets which can offer new ways to get through a level. Each gadget also gives you a few passive bonus skills. Unfortunately aside from 1 of them (the extendo boots) they're mostly useless outside of acting like glorified keycards.
With the game set int 1950/60's america, I thought it would have at least a few time relevant comtemporary hits, but I guess this is kind of subverted with the whole being conquered by germany situation. The music that is left is kind of bland, but nothing offensive.  What's really offensive is that just like the first game it's often hard to hear what the characters are saying, it being BJ's monologues during the levels or even characters speaking at the home base. Enemies are abnormally quiet. Despite them all wearing boots and armor, only the supersoldiers and giant robots will make any sort of noise while moving, no matter how close, no matter the surface. For a game with stealth aspects, this is kind of unexcusable. The biggest insult are the stealth (aka all of them) kampfhunds; They don't bark, they don't growl, you can't hear them running. Your only audio notice to them is that they make a wimpy growl noise as they lunge at you. A fast enemy that can knock you over, and is small enough to be hidden even when running because of chest high cover everywhere that gives no warning of its presence is just bad game design. The only thing from keeping it getting out of hand is that they're a pretty rare enemy.
I beat the game on the highest difficulty available at the start.  I wouldn't reccomend it. It's kind of a crapshoot as an enemy firing at you might miss, or it might take about 80% of your life in a short window.   The difficulty right below that probably offers the best balance between challenge and fun.
The ending is 100% buy the sequel. It wasn't particularly offensive to me, but I say the same thing about Mankind Divided's ending.
The game's length is inflated with [optional] asssination missions, which have you return to stages you've already cleared to fight enemies again and explore usually a single new room in the level and kill a generic commander.
Despite all these bad things said about the game, it's still a fairly competant FPS game, but it's definitely carried more along by it's style, setting, and characters, not its gameplay.

Blazblue features a great sci-fi story told via visual novel sections interspersed with the best 2D fighter gameplay I've ever experienced.
Continuum Shift Extend contains a condensed version of Calamity Trigger's story complete with most of the memorable fights as well as minor beneficial tweaks, the entirety of Continuum Shift, and a few extra story routes not found elsewhere. Because of this, it makes a great entry point into the series for newcomers.
The story takes place in a post-apocalyptic world in which society has already been rebuilt and futuristic tech that runs off magic has been developed. The lore is quite complicated, but most of it is explained in the non-canon "Teach Me, Miss Litchi" segments, which consist of light-hearted skits performed by super-deformed versions of the game's main characters. Having the lore explanations separate from the main game allows for the main storylines to move at a decent pace. As for tone, there is a serious story in the game that is told in a serious manner, but there is also an abundance of humour and gag routes in the series.
The actual gameplay seems to cater to both hardcore competitive fighter fans and unskilled casual players (like me). Combos are easy to pull off and flow together well and the easy difficulty is rather easy. The game also features some more complex mechanics for the more hardcore fans and there is a ranked online mode so such individuals can really put their skills to the test.
The PC version seems to play just as well as the console versions. The 16 song soundtrack features the songs of the new characters and the opening to Continuum Shift 2. The opening to Extend, "Sōkyū no Hikari," and a special Ranga vs. µ-12 song, "Pandora Tears," are missing while an instrumental version of "Blue Bloom" titled "Spiral" is included. The music mostly focuses on a mix of orchestral metal and a bit of pop. The bonus art is all highly compressed into one PDF file and I recognize most of it from the in-game gallery.
Highly recommended to all but those who already own it on other platforms.

Admittedly, during my playthrough, I may have gotten a little overzealous trying to access areas early before getting a new ability - as it turns out, the solution to getting up onto a ledge WASN'T to bring over two frog enemies so you could bounce from one to the other while bouncing off a third that would hop down to reach the upper ledge in a terribly convoluted manner... you were really just supposed to wait for the charge jump ability, which is the only way to fully access the area anyway :P I'm probably a minority in putting that much effort towards this, though.
Each ability is quite well thought out. Many are similar to other platformer abilities, so it's not necessarily innovative in that sense. However, despite that, it all has a nicely polished feel. It's not glitchy or rough in any way. Everything is smooth and works how you'd expect it to - every death, you can see where you went wrong.
My only complaint is that I would have liked the game to be a little longer - as it was, there wasn't really enough time to fully max out the skill tree during normal gameplay. I know that's not *necessary*, but I enjoy that small bit of completionism. I didn't really want to grind a bunch for it needlessly, either. This may be resolved in the new content release coming up, however. :)
Overall, I greatly enjoyed this game. I had a great time with it. Easily one of the best modern platformers I've gone through!

In this game, Phoenix Wright attempts to defend in court a being intending to consume the earth like an oversized grape.
10/10
Being real though, when it comes to fighting games, I think it's difficult to measure exactly what makes one "good" or "bad". Enjoyment of fighters is based heavily in preference and what one personally wants out of a game, so I'm going to tell you what I got out of it and try and break it down as best I can.
First off, the character roster is diverse and interesting, and I think most people could find a team of three to have fun with. I'm not a sizable fan of Marvel characters, but there's enough of a variety of them and they play differently enough that they may grow on you. The Capcom characters are where I personally believe most of the fun mains are to be had, however. A lot of them have very interesting and unique mechanics and tend to be very true representations of their source games.
Additionally, if you're the sort to play arguably bad characters (like me) you'll be pleased to note that the ability to switch and to craft a team to support your questionable decisions in mains, and generally if you play well enough you'll not be left wanting. That's the real strength of this game, I feel; the ability to make anything and anyone work reliably through clever team play and combo-crafting.
There's also a very real ability to retaliate and do crazy comebacks, even at a massive disadvantage. This trait may sell people who enjoy high-octane, anyone's-game style of fighters like Melty Blood, Blazblue and Guilty Gear, and scare people away who prefer methodical, more advantage-pressing games like Soul Calibur or arguably Tekken.
The game has a great soundtrack and a nice visual style that's aged well; it hasn't lost much in the years since its release. The modes are interesting and you start out with all the characters which is always a plus in my book, since plenty of people have no interest in the story mode and simply want to play with their friends.
TL;DR
Pros: Good design, diverse cast, possible to make anything/anyone work, technically complex but not impossibly daunting to learn for newbies, good soundtrack, good voice acting, start with every character unlocked.
Cons: Repetitive and basically nonexistant "story" mode. Very complicated and difficult to get into if you're not experienced in other 2d fighters.
Pro/Con: Fast, Lots of Capcom/Marvel characters, comebacks are always possible, high-octane and aggressive.
Overall Rating: 9.1/10
