This game is an adventure game/action RPG set in ancient Greece in which you play the role of Jason, king and warden of Iolcus under the protection of Zeus himself. That sets the tone for the story. It's definitely a setting in which being a hero actually means something. The game itself is served by serviceable combat mechanics which are pretty common when it comes to hack and slash games at best it will remind you of a game like Kingdoms of Amalur but most of the time you can get by with simply mashing buttons (apart from the boss fights which will require you to study your foe to understand the pattern used by the boss to defeat him or her which is pretty standard gaming practice anyway). Some finishing moves are nice to behold and give a heroic feel to the fights.
The game may not look incredibly good for 2017 and some of the textures can be a bit blurry but considering it was released in 2008 it's definitely not terrible and more importantly the art direction is rather solid with some nice touches in the background and a consistent use of assets in environments. Some faces seem to be recycled a bit too much but others really stand out in a good way. Animations are fine but they probably won't keep you up at night either. Foes usually look good and if you're into sandals you will probably like the way the main character looks (before playing this game I had no idea they made bikini armours for guys and Jason clearly likes showing his six pack abs so that may be a plus for the ladies).
Voice acting is mostly good and sometimes excellent and the music is simply incredible. It sets the tone and give an epic vibe to the game (which doesn't come as a surprise considering that the composer was responsible for the music for the movie 300 and arguably the music wasn't the worst or the most controversial part). A great soundtrack is an important feature and that's an area in which this game shines.
Considering the lack of games set in ancient mythic Greece especially when it comes to games that actually try to tell a story (I've enjoyed Titan Quest but it wasn't for the story) Rise of the Argonauts is an interesting title. It gets even better when it becomes obvious that despite its linearity (the game opens up a bit just like Bioware games in which you can explore several areas in a different sequence) it's actually a pretty good story for any fan of Greek mythology and computer RPGs. Of course the game takes some liberties with the myths and that can be irksome if you're a purist some of these changes annoyed me at first until I came to accept that the game was trying to keep things fresh and after a while I came to terms with that. The name dropping may annoy you and the fact that Achilles was supposed to be a baby at the time when Jason set off for his quest may annoy you just like the fact that some characters have slightly different roles like for instance Medea or even Perseus.
In any case the writing is really good and there is plenty of dialogue (probably too much for some players) so it's a game that will require some patience and that may explain why it didn't do so well.
What sets the game apart is the way experience is handled. After completing a quest or an achievement you get a deed that you can dedicate to a particular deity which allows you to get some points to buy skills in that god's skill tree. Each skill tree is focused on a different weapon type the mace, the spear, the sword and the shield so there is an incentive in focusing on a particular god. During dialogues you usually have four choices which are symbolized by a different icon so you can pick your lines by following a god's attitude for a particular situation. You have Ares (violent and brutal but straightforward and honest), Athena (mostly the just and sensible one but also the one who goes by the book), Apollo (compassionate, fair and dignified but also sometimes a bit proud) and Hermes (full of guile, mischief but also clever and manipulative). It gives some great flavour to the game. Quests make you feel like your choices actually matter which is good but in the end you're still moving along the main quest so it may be more of an illusion. Still the game offers enough leeway to actually feel less linear than it is and that's something that is really nice.
Bottom line it's a good title for CRPG players who thirst for a mythological setting, it's not perfect (some backtracking is involved at times and there isn't much in the way of exploration) but it's much better than what the critics gave it credit for especially if you value the story above the rest.
There is a caveat though and that's the fact that the game tends to crash a lot simply because it has to be run on a single core on modern computers. I used to have some pretty regular crashes but the game has been running very smoothly ever since I switched to a single core.

This is a game that had great potential. Despite some of the technical faults it manages to deliver an amazing experience.
If you like Jade Empire then you will love this game. It is a real Role Playing game, without having Level or XP. You play the role of an Ancient Hero, Figter and King. You find companions, make friends and enemies. Gods offer you powers. You don't simply become 10 times stronger because you killed 100 rats. The improvements are incremental, you can see them and enjoy them.  There are no heal potions or inventory.
The combat is really satisfying, focused on melee combos and the strengths and trade-offs of your 3 weapons. The Mace, Spear and Sword. Your shield is always at your side.
The other aspect of the game is the dialog. The choices you make affect part of the storyline and is just an opportunity to pick your style without having to overthink the consequences. Just enjoy them. The story is good and the characters develop in a very interesting way. It took me 20 hours to finish the game (one playtrough on Legend), and now that I finished it I want more. I could play easily another 20 hours, another 3-4 cities, another campaign. Unfortunately there is little replay value once you finish it once, but just the fact that I mention this means it was worth the first one.
The end-game is simply amazing. When you meet the Oracle of Depli for the second time, make sure you have a free evening because you won't be putting the controller down until the credits roll. Simply not happening. The epilogue is simply incredible.
When the game starts the combat feels a bit awkward. That's because of the tutorial and some of the combos being disabled until about the first 40 minutes of gameplay. The game really only starts after you leave the palace. Make sure to keep playing passed this initial phase and not judge the game based on the first 5 minutes of gameplay. Trust me a fantastic experience awaits.
The greatest enemy in the game is alas the crashes. The game crashed for me no matter what I tried to do. However I did finish it. Use the checkpoint system to your advantage, a crash can only set you back a few minutes if you make sure to change area after every major cutscene, before you engage in more dialog.
One design complain is about the map. The map should be accessible from a single button, and some form of minimap should let you go to your next objective.
Finally a special mention to the music of the game composed by Tyler Bates, simply incredible. Check for it online.
Do I recommend this game? **** YEAH!

A fun fantasy RPG set in Ancient Greece and follows a quest of King Jason and the Argo crew in search of the Golden Fleece. I was surprised to find out that the game was released back in 2008, considering how good it looks for its time.
The story takes you to a number of locations, in which you acquire some new party members and other allies to help you on your quest. 3 of the major locations in the middle part of the game can be done in any order of preference. The gameplay consists of combat sections, exploration sections, and dialogue/role-playing sections.
Combat is really well done. You are able to swap between using a mace, a sword, and a spear, and each one has their own combos and special abilities. The special abilities and various passive bonuses are learned from skill progression trees attributed to 4 different Greek deities: Ares, Hermes, Apollo, and Athena. Overall the feel of combat is very fluid and visceral. Enemies get their heads popped by mace swings or get sliced in half by a sword, and so on. Only thing I wasn't too fond of were the boss fights. They weren't terrible, but most of them were somewhat frustrating and at times even cheap. A few required you to do something very unique and unintuitive, and hence a solution would be unclear.
The rest of the game you'd spend exploring the locations and completing quests, some of which are optional, but completing them gains you additional weapon choices or pieces of armour. There are a lot of the dialogue sections in the game where you get to make decisions and choose how you respond. Even if a dialogue choice doesn't have any consequences, it still has an alignment with one of the four deities, and acquiring a certain number of deity-aligned choices nets you a skill point to spend in their skill tree.
Overall it's a pretty fun adventure RPG and anyone who likes Greek mythology should give it a try. It does change some of the stories and characters from the myths slightly, but it's still done in a fresh and engaging manner to keep things interesting. I'll recommend this game. It's quite underrated.

My opinion: Repetitive, immersion breaking, with great elements (visual, sound, and art design) that the bad elements (everything else) overshadow. This game is short but manages to wear out its welcome well before the end. If you are looking for a great game with great visuals, good story, fun combat and a female protagonist, play Horzion Zero Dawn.
In my opinion, you might like this game if you really love Assassins Creed-style combat and/or you like to look at good-looking games with dark themes.
Attempts at objective remarks about the game:
Combat: Very much like Assassins Creed, particularly AC2, AC3, AC Brotherhood era. You attack, dodge, parry, repeat. There is a mirror that builds "focus" which when activated functions like slow motion for enemies. Difficulty increase as the game goes on is accomplished effectively by increasing the number of enemies, serially and in parellel. There is no evolution of combat in the game. Different enemies are added to the mix through the game. You do the same exact actions in battles, they just get longer as the game goes on.
Graphics:
Better than recent Far Cry games (FC4  and FC Primal), a lot better than Mass Effect Andromeda, but not as good as Horizon Zero Dawn.
Puzzles:
Look at a door, then wander around a level and look at other things until you see the runes on the door. Then open the door. Repeat.
The good, in my opinion:
Looks good with interesting art style.
Some levels have interesting surroundings, like the chapter filled with flaming corpses, who writhe and grasp.
The mini-stories provided by the lorestones are interesting.
The premise of the story is somewhat different and compelling.
No HUD or button/keyboard prompts.
In spite of the uninteresting description of the puzzles above, they were still interesting through most of the game.
The bad, in my opinion:
Combat. Period. The combat is a repetitive grind. To make the whole thing worse, due to the threat of "permadeath" you are disuaded from really experimenting which makes the whole thing a chore.
The voices in your head start of interesting but eventually become tedious. Who would have thought that psychosis is not actually cool and fun?
Permadeath, which means if you fail (i.e., die) enoguh times you must start the game over from the beginning. This would be a great feature but makes attempts at making the combat fun seem too risky a proposal.
The "immersion" wears off quickly. I played the entire game with (good) headphones. Unlike the voices in the original Dead Space game, which were often creepy, these voices become annoying. It may take a couple of hours, but they wear out their welcome.
Nothing about the game, from start to finish, is actually creepy or scary.
The game was enjoyable for a couple of hours but after that I pushed to the end just to see what would happen. I first heard of the game through the developer diaries and and It seemed like a game I would love. I really wanted to like it, but did not. A much better use of time would have been to read a book on Norse mythology. The combat, voices, and story all wore out their welcome by the end, and before then end I was just looking forward to it ending, like I am sure you are with this review if you are still reading.

I know this game is a little on the older side but I finally got a chance to play it and I feel like it could have been one of the most underrated games in recent history.  A lot of the features of this game are absolutely fantastic and judging my articles about the game the one gripe most people had was the combat (which honestly wasn't that bad).  To get right into what this game is about, Remember Me is a 3rd person action game with combo based fighting mechanics and a parkour style level progression design. Essentially it is like many other climb, jump, crawl games like Tomb Raider, Uncharted and Enslaved but the main character instead of using projectile weapons only uses her fists and her power arm.  Now the Combo system runs a little differently from other combo fighting games in that there are 4 primary "pressens" with 4 separate, and each more complicated, combos . However with these combos you can set any presser to each combo. The longer the combo the more xp you can get the more pressens you can unlock. There are 4 separate Pressens; Power which hits hard, Regen which heals you some each time you use it in a combo,  Chain which increases a combo multiplier making it do more damage and get more xp (these are best used at the end of the a combo) and cool down which lowers the time required to use a S-Pressen.

S-Pressens are powerful, specialized pressens that you can only use once per certain time period and must have enough focus to use it. There are 5 S-Pressens which include Fury which lets Nilin (the main character) attack with each hit being more powerful than the last, Sensen Dos which stuns enemies and is very useful versus specific enemies, Rust in Pieces is a bomb that is effective versus robots, Camo which cloaks Nilin allowing her to move around regaining health and being able to perform a takedown on powerful enemies and logic bomb which can break shields and heavily damage enemies. Now the Specials and the basic combat system albeit are unique in their names and how they look, deep down it is just a generic combo based system and can get repetitive over time and can be prone to problems with connecting hits.
My biggest problem with the game however is the buggy parkour system. As it is a lot of times the camera control can be all over the place and Nilin could miss a jump that she should have been able to make. At times the parkour makes sense but other times it feels like it was just put there to have something for the time between fights and memory syncs.

One of the coolest features of this game however is the memory stealing/manipulating and as far as I'm concerned is not used enough in this game. Nilin's main ability (one of the main reasons she is such a sought after person) is that she can manipulate a characters memories of an event and completely change their personality of what happened during that event. During this mechanic you can go forward and backwards during a memory and slightly alter things in the room to make the characters do things including killing each other or remembering something to not be as tragic. It was used 3 or 4 times throughout the game but just the process of going into someone's mind and changing a memory to get a different outcome was absolutely facinating.

Enough about the gameplay, on to the story.  The year is 2084 in Neo-Paris and Memorize corporation has invented a new implant called the Sensen which enables others to share memories with others, remove memories or even sell memories to earn money. During this time due to an infection and corruption of the implant, a new race of humans developed called Leapers. These Leapers are very basic in their mental capacity and are very aggressive towards non-Leapears. Enter our character Nilin who is a memory manipulator but in the beginning she has had almost all of her memories wiped because she had been captured by memorized and been punished.  However thanks to someone called Edge, she is able to escape and work to find her memories and try to take down Memorize. Throughout the game Nilin has to manipulate the memories of many in order to get to the bottom of the whole situation of Memorize and the Sensen.  The story is very unique and it is wonderful to have a main female protagonist that is the strongest character in the game.

The graphics of this game are absolutely beautiful and to top it all off, Dontnod Entertainment really did a top notch job of creating a very beautiful and realistic future Paris. The whole game is very aesthetically pleasing with the variations locations being so different showing the true difference between the impoverished  and the wealthy in Neo-Paris.  On top of that Olivier Deriviere did an absolutely fantastic job bringing the soundtrack to life to match the game beautifully. The music is much like the works done by Daft Punk in Tron Legacy in that Deriviere mixed a bit of electronic with orchestral sound. The end result is a soundtrack that I have ended up listening to repeatedly at work while I have been programming. The voice actors also do a fantastic job bringing their characters to life and make the dialogue all that much better.

Overall this game is absolutely fantastic, from the story, characters, music, graphics etc.  The only downside is the generic gameplay and flawed camera angles during the parkour/climbing mechanics. I would highly recommend this game and I look forward to see if Capcon would bring us a sequel at some time in the future.

"Remember Me" - Review
Highly recommended.
Gameplay:  9/10
When i bought Remember Me (for PC) i couldn't help but have only one expectation in mind; Oni version 2.0. My expectations weren't just met, but blown out of the water. While there are many aspects of this game that closely resemble Oni, it has been created with all the gusto and complexity one can expect from a modern game. The gameplay was overall intuitive and straight forward. The combat was lots of fun. It felt just as nice and flows just as smoothly as Oni did, but with more.... everything. More moves, more dynamics, more customization, more varying gameplay, more challenges, just... more!! It is a brilliant mix up of action and adventure.
The only reason i give it a 9 and not a 10 is because of the limitations set. I wish there was a greater ability to go exploring. In a game that's as well finished as this one i don't want to be stopped.
...And i wish i could zoom in and out with the mouse wheel.
Game ambiance: 9/10
The sound ambiance initially seems somewhat minimalist, but play a little longer, and you'll find it's just right for where you are at any given time. Great use of post production effects, subtle noises, and dynamic music helped to create a convincing reality that is easy to be immersed into. The visual ambiance was fantastic. People, birds, rain, sunshine, fog, day, night, wind, water, flies, bugs, i could go on.
Reliability/Stability: 10/10
This game was created with the Unreal Engine and i had no issues with stability or CTD.
Story/Plot: 10/10
A good action/adventure game needs a strong plot and Remember Me leaves nothing to be desired. An emotional roller-coaster; It's deep, touching and enthralling. The story is well written with all the twists and turns needed for an epic tail. Just when you think you have it figured out something new is thrown into the mix to keep your attention and maintain enthusiasm. It encourages you to want to know more, and it's not until after hours of gameplay you finally blink, take a breath, realize it's 4am and that you probable should get some sleep.
Not a game for kids though. Violence, suicide themes, language and alcohol use warnings apply here.
Concept: 10/10
While the idea for the gameplay isn't original, the concept on which the game is based is very creative. I can't say much about it without giving anything away, suffice to say there's nothing more it needs. Well conceived, extremely well finished, exceptionally well done.
Concept execution: 10/10
This game was created so beautifully that i wanted to explore places that weren't plot related nor necessary.
The way this game takes you on a journey is truly awe-inspiring. Evey where the plot takes you, every emotion it conjures, every environment explored and every skill it calls upon is a reflection of the high quality, high standards and an extraordinary ability to convey an idea through a game. The Capcom/Dontnod team has really delivered what might be called a master piece; change little, continue the story and bring on Remember Me 2!!!!! This is possibly the best action/adventure game in the last 10 years.
Textures: 10/10
Very, very nice. The textures add exactly what is needed in this complex 'Remember Me' world. Not once did i think "that could have been done better". Variations, lighting, subtleties, randomness, bump maps, ray-tracing. So much eye-candy it's breathtaking. Enough said.
Modelling: 10/10
One word, spectacular. So much work has been put into the modeling in this game it's unbelievable. It's been a long time since I've played a game that has left me smiling at every turn while I gasp in astonishment. It is so well constructed i was only too happy to walk through the game rather than run. I felt compelled to really take in the whole picture, detail and scale of what has been created. I feel privileged to be able to witness game creation on this level.
The use of motion capture adds a fantastic element of realism and fluid movement to the people and adds to the game's overall charm.
Graphics: 10/10
The execution of the graphics as a whole is just awesome. HDR lighting was just right. Volumetric effects were spot on. In a word: Seamless.
Sound: 10/10
Exceptional production quality in Dolby with lots of different sounds throughout the game. I can't think of a place where a sound was needed or out of place. Dynamic, big and precise.
Music: 10/10
Excellent production quality and dynamically changing the music adds just what is needed. Very well written and creative compositions by Olivier Deriviere and the Philharmonia Orchestra. It gets the blood pumping and the heart beating. What more could you want? ...Possibly the soundtrack.
Adjustable shadow mapping: No
Bonus/Extras: unlockable in-game concept art.

Did not think in a million years I would be into a game such as this. I picked this game up on extreme sale (under $3) and for the first time ever, picked up a DLC within a few days. Do not let the hand drawn animations fool you, this is one exciting game.
Skullgirls is about a mystical skull that appears every 7 years. It's power can be held by a soul but the soul can easily be manipulated and cursed if not careful. Here's the issue though, as soon as the skull re-appears, the whole city goes nuts. Skullgirls by it's game play definition is a fighting game. Upon playing the game, I noticed a few similarities between Street Fighter IV and this game. The move schemes are slightly similar but I feel they are lot more effective and simpler. Meaning, more moves that seem extremely challenging to do in SF IV, can be done with a bit less intensity and damage to your controller. The combos are insanely ridiculous though. Unlike SF IV, you're not stuck with one fighter.
You can have up to three in your party. This means when doing special moves, you may have another character come jumping in randomly. Although this is a really cool feature and an awesome offense, you'll have to be double careful as if they miss they can get damaged as well. 1 character vs 3 should be strong enough as they seemed to have gone to great lengths to balance it all out. The moves are pretty smooth and combos up to 30 or more hits can be executed. I feel this game is a lot more "free" in the sense that you're not scripted to press this button after you've pressed this button. Okay, maybe there is a little button mashing involved but it seems like control chaos. I feel a lot more immersed in this game than I do in SF IV as I feel I can string more successful combos together. There is your basic light, medium and hard punch and kick but there are also buttons to call in for support (if available). There are a few modes available in game such as career, versus and extras (where you can view the gallery or even fight the main boss but at 300%). The campaign was actually well done. It follows a comic strip sort of dialogue where characters expressions and backgrounds will change accordingly.
Obviously, there will be breaks in between where you have to fight another character. I really like how the campaign was done as you only have to fight each person once. Some may argue (and have) that it's made the game slightly short. With all the characters available though, you should have at least 4-5 hours geared towards this particular mode. Each character has a different story that is being told. Some characters will need you to beat the campaign before you can move on and use them. The DLC characters even have stories but I found one or two sort of are gimmicky.
The visuals in this game are absolutely fantastic. It's hard to believe that it was hand drawn. I personally don't find any lack in this sort of animation style but some have brought to my attention it seems to "jumpy" for them. This shouldn't be an issue for you as the game play will certainly pull you in. The animations done for certain moves are absolutely insane. Big Band for example or Double have some crazy animations regarding their attacks or when they get hit. The sounds are actually really good and you'll hear characters chime in before and after matches with a quick insult.
Overall, this is a great game. I would highly highly recommend buying it on sale but if your a fighting fan, you may want to get it full price.
RATING : 7.35/10

Skullgirls is the fighting game aimed towards people who don't like fighting games, and it finally gave fighting games to the masses. Known far and wide for its EASE OF USE, and SUPER GREAT TUTORIALS THAT WILL TEACH YOU HOW TO WIN, the game revolutionized the genre. Featuring an array of new, inventive mechanics, such as the ubiquitous 10 minute combos, the burst that's not actually controlled by the player, and 3v3 battles that allow you to see almost the entire cast in a single match, skullgirls was a roaring success, and over the course of one week, it edged out past titans like SNK, Capcom, and ARCSYS, their games now considered truly inferior compared to the new emperor of fighting games.
And then you play the game, and what do you know? It's not that good.
It also turns out that all those old companies, with their established formulas, casts of characters, stables of voice actors, and decades of experience making fighting games actually know what they're doing. Who would have guessed that making fighting games is hard? Not only do you have to create a good system, but you have to balance it, and make appealing characters that look great, play great, and sound great, and ideally, they should all be viable.
Skullgirls isn't like that, and while this version is MUCH better than the one they initially released, they still refuse to address the most common complaints and annoyances. Combos drag on forever, and the lead developer doesn't understand why this is a problem. After all, these long combos, that sometimes last so long you have time to put the controller down and chug a soda, aren't infinites, and if they're not for real infinite, it's totally not a problem.
Originally, once you were trapped in the long, long combos, you were essentially done for. It's true that they weren't infinite, but 20-60 seconds of getting looped in the corner to a certain reset and death is only marginally better than 60-80 seconds of a 'true' infinite touch of death combo. To counter this problem, they introduced a burst system. In a normal game, you press the burst button to burst. It will have different properties depending on if you use it as a combo breaker, as a counter, as an offensive tool, you might need to resource manage it, it can be used to shift the momentum of the match, and so on, but in skullgirls, the burst is only ever used as a combo breaker, because it's only ever available to you when you're trapped in a long combo. Who designed this system, and why was this decision not challenged?
Thanks to this, the game is VERY centered around touch of death combos, resets, and what the developer perceived to be hype moments. A hype moment is hype because someone had to work very hard to set it up, and it usually happened unexpectedly. When every moment is a hype 200 hit reset combo, it's not really hype anymore, but routine. You stop thinking of how cool everything is, and just consider the button presses you're doing to the other guy. Meanwhile, he puts down his controller and reaches for his soda.
In the olden days, this was pitched as a good game for casuals, because apparently, tutorials will teach you all you need to know for taking on stone cold killers in real matches. Now, let's think about this. You have essentially a MvC2 clone - a hyper fighting game - and you're saying that casuals should play this, because your tutorials will totally make them good at fighting games. I'll let you guess how this worked out in the long term.
As an experiment, skullgirls was a success. Thanks to it, we now know for a fact that tutorials don't make you good at fighting games. We have conclusive evidence that hard mode singleplayer boss fights don't prepare you for actual human opponents, no matter how many times you fight them. It's been proven that in order to get good at fighting games, you have to play a lot, and if you play a lot, you're gonna lose a lot. To attain the most git guds, you have to fight players who are far above you skillwise, and it'll take many sessions before you adjust to such veterans' abilities, and finally take a match off them. Because of operation: skullgirls, there's now hard evidence that casuals are casuals because they're casual, and if there's one thing casual people hate more than losing, it's going into a match knowing you're gonna lose, because the other guy practiced his 86 hit Ms. Fortune reset combo for 860 hours, while the casual in question has a total playtime of 8.6 hours, 86 minutes of which were spent fighting human opponents.
Obviously, this isn't a game for casuals. Obviously, the game did much better with the hardcore audience, right? Wrong. Other than resets, touch of death combos, and the occasional zoning war, there's just not a lot to it. It's as if they believed they could for real make a game for casuals, so they didn't bother putting any depth into the game, and it suffers a lot because of it.
Once you've got your fat combos down, that's it. I want to say that there's more, but there isn't.
Many people played this game with their online community of choice, and most of them have the same story. They bought the game, it had some pretty cool characters, they picked their waifu, played a couple hours, then one guy developed a fat combo, and it ceased to be fun, because they had to develop their own fat combo as a response, at which point matches were all about landing that fat combo. Their one waifu wasn't really viable, because assists and health regen are MUCH stronger than a moderate increase in life and damage, thus forcing them to add two more characters to support the one character they wanted to play.

Did not think in a million years I would be into a game such as this. I picked this game up on extreme sale (under $3) and for the first time ever, picked up a DLC within a few days. Do not let the hand drawn animations fool you, this is one exciting game.
Skullgirls is about a mystical skull that appears every 7 years. It's power can be held by a soul but the soul can easily be manipulated and cursed if not careful. Here's the issue though, as soon as the skull re-appears, the whole city goes nuts. Skullgirls by it's game play definition is a fighting game. Upon playing the game, I noticed a few similarities between Street Fighter IV and this game. The move schemes are slightly similar but I feel they are lot more effective and simpler. Meaning, more moves that seem extremely challenging to do in SF IV, can be done with a bit less intensity and damage to your controller. The combos are insanely ridiculous though. Unlike SF IV, you're not stuck with one fighter.
You can have up to three in your party. This means when doing special moves, you may have another character come jumping in randomly. Although this is a really cool feature and an awesome offense, you'll have to be double careful as if they miss they can get damaged as well. 1 character vs 3 should be strong enough as they seemed to have gone to great lengths to balance it all out. The moves are pretty smooth and combos up to 30 or more hits can be executed. I feel this game is a lot more "free" in the sense that you're not scripted to press this button after you've pressed this button. Okay, maybe there is a little button mashing involved but it seems like control chaos. I feel a lot more immersed in this game than I do in SF IV as I feel I can string more successful combos together. There is your basic light, medium and hard punch and kick but there are also buttons to call in for support (if available). There are a few modes available in game such as career, versus and extras (where you can view the gallery or even fight the main boss but at 300%). The campaign was actually well done. It follows a comic strip sort of dialogue where characters expressions and backgrounds will change accordingly.
Obviously, there will be breaks in between where you have to fight another character. I really like how the campaign was done as you only have to fight each person once. Some may argue (and have) that it's made the game slightly short. With all the characters available though, you should have at least 4-5 hours geared towards this particular mode. Each character has a different story that is being told. Some characters will need you to beat the campaign before you can move on and use them. The DLC characters even have stories but I found one or two sort of are gimmicky.
The visuals in this game are absolutely fantastic. It's hard to believe that it was hand drawn. I personally don't find any lack in this sort of animation style but some have brought to my attention it seems to "jumpy" for them. This shouldn't be an issue for you as the game play will certainly pull you in. The animations done for certain moves are absolutely insane. Big Band for example or Double have some crazy animations regarding their attacks or when they get hit. The sounds are actually really good and you'll hear characters chime in before and after matches with a quick insult.
Overall, this is a great game. I would highly highly recommend buying it on sale but if your a fighting fan, you may want to get it full price.

Skullgirls is the fighting game aimed towards people who don't like fighting games, and it finally gave fighting games to the masses. Known far and wide for its EASE OF USE, and SUPER GREAT TUTORIALS THAT WILL TEACH YOU HOW TO WIN, the game revolutionized the genre. Featuring an array of new, inventive mechanics, such as the ubiquitous 10 minute combos, the burst that's not actually controlled by the player, and 3v3 battles that allow you to see almost the entire cast in a single match, skullgirls was a roaring success, and over the course of one week, it edged out past titans like SNK, Capcom, and ARCSYS, their games now considered truly inferior compared to the new emperor of fighting games.
And then you play the game, and what do you know? It's not that good.
It also turns out that all those old companies, with their established formulas, casts of characters, stables of voice actors, and decades of experience making fighting games actually know what they're doing. Who would have guessed that making fighting games is hard? Not only do you have to create a good system, but you have to balance it, and make appealing characters that look great, play great, and sound great, and ideally, they should all be viable.
Skullgirls isn't like that, and while this version is MUCH better than the one they initially released, they still refuse to address the most common complaints and annoyances. Combos drag on forever, and the lead developer doesn't understand why this is a problem. After all, these long combos, that sometimes last so long you have time to put the controller down and chug a soda, aren't infinites, and if they're not for real infinite, it's totally not a problem.
Originally, once you were trapped in the long, long combos, you were essentially done for. It's true that they weren't infinite, but 20-60 seconds of getting looped in the corner to a certain reset and death is only marginally better than 60-80 seconds of a 'true' infinite touch of death combo. To counter this problem, they introduced a burst system. In a normal game, you press the burst button to burst. It will have different properties depending on if you use it as a combo breaker, as a counter, as an offensive tool, you might need to resource manage it, it can be used to shift the momentum of the match, and so on, but in skullgirls, the burst is only ever used as a combo breaker, because it's only ever available to you when you're trapped in a long combo. Who designed this system, and why was this decision not challenged?
Thanks to this, the game is VERY centered around touch of death combos, resets, and what the developer perceived to be hype moments. A hype moment is hype because someone had to work very hard to set it up, and it usually happened unexpectedly. When every moment is a hype 200 hit reset combo, it's not really hype anymore, but routine. You stop thinking of how cool everything is, and just consider the button presses you're doing to the other guy. Meanwhile, he puts down his controller and reaches for his soda.
In the olden days, this was pitched as a good game for casuals, because apparently, tutorials will teach you all you need to know for taking on stone cold killers in real matches. Now, let's think about this. You have essentially a MvC2 clone - a hyper fighting game - and you're saying that casuals should play this, because your tutorials will totally make them good at fighting games. I'll let you guess how this worked out in the long term.
As an experiment, skullgirls was a success. Thanks to it, we now know for a fact that tutorials don't make you good at fighting games. We have conclusive evidence that hard mode singleplayer boss fights don't prepare you for actual human opponents, no matter how many times you fight them. It's been proven that in order to get good at fighting games, you have to play a lot, and if you play a lot, you're gonna lose a lot. To attain the most git guds, you have to fight players who are far above you skillwise, and it'll take many sessions before you adjust to such veterans' abilities, and finally take a match off them. Because of operation: skullgirls, there's now hard evidence that casuals are casuals because they're casual, and if there's one thing casual people hate more than losing, it's going into a match knowing you're gonna lose, because the other guy practiced his 86 hit Ms. Fortune reset combo for 860 hours, while the casual in question has a total playtime of 8.6 hours, 86 minutes of which were spent fighting human opponents.
Obviously, this isn't a game for casuals. Obviously, the game did much better with the hardcore audience, right? Wrong. Other than resets, touch of death combos, and the occasional zoning war, there's just not a lot to it. It's as if they believed they could for real make a game for casuals, so they didn't bother putting any depth into the game, and it suffers a lot because of it.
Once you've got your fat combos down, that's it. I want to say that there's more, but there isn't.
Many people played this game with their online community of choice, and most of them have the same story. They bought the game, it had some pretty cool characters, they picked their waifu, played a couple hours, then one guy developed a fat combo, and it ceased to be fun, because they had to develop their own fat combo as a response, at which point matches were all about landing that fat combo. Their one waifu wasn't really viable, because assists and health regen are MUCH stronger than a moderate increase in life and damage, thus forcing them to add two more characters to support the one character they wanted to play.
I'm not gonna cover any of the dev/publisher issues, but suffice to say, many mistakes were made, and hopefully lessons were learned, as this was Lab Zero's first game.
Overall, it's a very late 90s fighting game; the kind that just scream 'we're making this game, and we've got some ideas, but we really don't know what we're doing, or how to fit it all together.' The graphics are great, the music's pretty nice, the voice acting goes from great (Ms. Fortune, Big Band, the announcer) to average, but the gameplay is just...not fun. It's not meaty enough for people who play fighting games, and not intuitive or basic enough for new players.
Despite the production values, the lack of depth and options (very common problems among late 90s fighters, even if they happen to have been made in 2012) just kill it.

I love this game.
It's a 2 v 4 player online combat game, not normally my thing but I truly LOVE this.
I think the price is pretty spot on. The community is great, almost always have a "good luck and have fin" (not a typo, in game joke) at the start of a match. In all the matchs I've played I have only ever seen criticism of a player once.
The controls are so easy, I am a true deep dyed in the wool controller user, but even I play this mouse and key, and the control of your character shark or diver feels very natural.
Okay I have two tiny gripes so lets get them out the way. i) The matchmaking can be very skewed, I've seen level 5's paired against level 100's, but they are the exception and not the rule. ii) A couple of the maps can be very biased towards one particluar team, i.e. very open so good for sharks, or very enclosed so good for divers. You can still win on them but it's much harder. That's it, thats all I personally get irked by, but, that said I still love the game.
The upgardes are very natural, and balanced, both diver and shark, that said, they don't feel O.P., they can be beat, you just need to understand them.
Yes there are microtransactions, BUT, they are not essential and don't actually skew the game, they are for skins, either for characters or tools, you still start the game on an even setting so as I said, they are not essential.
All in all, a great game, give it a go, most I know have loved it.

In this game, you play a single character, Van Helsing, who is followed by a ghostly teammate, Katarina. You don't have to choose a class before playing, and just develop your character along the way, using several skill trees.
Basically, you can eradicate a significant amount of monsters by using either a sword or a gun. Each weapon has its specific skill tree with numerous styles of slashes and shots. Each one can be leveled up, or customized with additional powers, triggered by Rage. Also, you can wander in the side of magic by learning strikes blending physical and magical damage, even pure magical damage. If not enough, you can learn passive abilities and active spells, that can take advantage of some specific situations or simply save your butt - leaving you with a fair amount of combinations to craft.
The amount of damage you do or can endure is proportional to basic weapon and armor stats, plus the different levels of your character stats and skills, combined with the multiple bonuses you can get from gear. Very similar to Diablo 3 or Torchlight 2. So don't fall in love with that particular weapon or gear if the next one is seamingly up a notch, the impact could be tremendous.
On top of that, your translucent female sidekick is not only witty, but can be used either as a melee fighter, a ranged shooter or a decent support. She also can level up and has her own gear and skill tree to become a tactical partner or a stat multiplier.
At this point, it's pretty clear that this game targets an audience that loves to analyse how hundred skills relate to each other, carefully crafting the most badass character possible, something like "hit once, obliterate many". It's a good thing to have a significant amount of depth that way (remember Titan Quest !) but for me it was just like "too much". So I decided to focus on a restricted number of skills, low enough to keep me focused on the actual map cleaning.
The game is linear, with some quests on the side. The levels are not really beautiful but varied, and the enemies compensate lack of intelligence by sheer number. Luckily, the dialog between Van Helsing and Katarina are funny so you can have a good time playing them.
Something that kinda puzzled me was the introduction of a micro-game of Tower Defense. Not that it wasn't interesting or refreshing, but it seemed that the developers decided to put everything remotely cool in the game, thus pushing it in the Land of Blended Genre where chances of survival are slim. Luckily, the Tower Defense micro-game is nicely done, but too much thin for consideration.
Overall, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is a good Hack & Slash, that can satisfy seasoned players, but could be daunting to newcomers.

Before I start I want to state that I'm usually the person who thinks game reviews give way too high scores for lots of things.
But this time I feel 65 is too low. Yeas, the game has its problems, but it makes up for it big time.
– The atmosphere and the level designs are top-notch. The future is futuristic but not far-fetched, and the memory-excange aspect is really thought out on how it may affect society. The graphical design really helps too.
– Remember Me is almost purely story-based and it shows. The voice acting is decent at worst, great at best. The story itself unfolds in a perfect rythym and the two large and several smaller twists are not too clichéd to make them tiresome.
– The Memory Remix minigames add an easy but very unique puzzle type in a somewhat "timetravel changes the future" kind of way. Depending on your taste they may be the absolute high or low point of the game. (Though in latter case you probably wouldn't pick it up in the first place.)
Granted, the combat difficulty may vary for people. It's usually pretty easy even on highest difficulty but there are two ro three arena fights that are gimmicky and really frustrating.
– The music is just plain awesome.
– The achievements beside "kill n enemies" and "do x move n+1 time" are really fun to do, a rare thing in most games.
– Unskippable cutscenes. And since the game is story-heavy it makes up almost half of NG+. It really hurts replayability.
– Linear level design. The levels are very unique and make up for it somewhat but you are always on a corridor no matter what.
– Short. Playing it casually can net an about 8 hour gameplay, I finished every achievement in little less than 20 with two playthroughs.
– Combat and camera system can be against the player soometimes.
– Though many people complained about the controls I found the PC controls very well ported, combat was easier for me than in the Arkham games. The only bad point is the Spammer (your "gun") which most of the times would simply not go into aim mode.
– Combat may seem repetitive as you use only four combos over and over but the Combo Lab customization system is pretty  innovative and makes combat a somewhat tactical challenge that can be adapted to various play styles.
Altogether I'd say that the game is worth it for the story only, it's so good that you can replay it over and over again just like your favourite movies. If I'd have to give a numerical verdict it'd be around 72/100.

The mechanics of this party game are great. I love being able to whip this game out and everyone can play as long as they have a smart phone... but it gets old rather quickly, especially if you can't find new people to play with. I'm seeing a lot of up-votes and the down-votes are not being taken seriously. I'm going to have to be that guy here and advise you not to buy this game in its current state - at least for said price of $25. The positive reviews are warranted, but would I buy this game for $25 if I knew what I know now? Absolutely not. This is for two simple reasons.
1. There really are only two games worth playing in this pack: Fibbage and Drawful. You could argue You Don't Know Jack, but if you'd played it once, it's nothing knew. Besides, if you have more than 4 people in your party, you can't play this game, so it is almost always excluded at most parties. Word Spud isn't even a game. End of story. I wouldn't pay a dollar to play it. Lie Swatter is ok, basically a guessing game between two questions and the luckiest person wins. I never played it enough to see how many questions it contains.
2. Fibbage and Drawful are the bread and butter of this pack. These together would be worth the $25, IF they actually had a reasonable amount of stock questions. From what I've heard Fibbage has around 200, and Drawful has ~600. Drawful obviously has the most replay value, but Fibbage seems to always be the favorite at parties. Unfortunately, after a few short hours, you see more repeats than you'd like to admit. Now if you like being the host of a party and don't mind the repeats, this isn't so bad, as long as your guests are different people every time.
However, I really don't understand why new questions have not been implemented. Or why there isn't a way to have the community submit their own, or at least create your own for your own game. I'm sure the framework was never built to do those things, but why they thought 200 questions would surely be enough is beyond me. Even with Drawful, you begin to see repeats fairly quickly.
What's worse is the developers state it is impossible to get repeat questions until you've gone through them all if you host on a single system. This has been contested by several gamers and I too challenge this statement. I've only hosted on one computer and seen repeats within a few hours.
I might as well also note there are a lot of bugs: throwing people out of games, randomly not being able to select answers, etc. They are a nuisance, but don't really seem to deter me or the people I play with as the games themselves are so lighthearted in terms of competitiveness. If that is something that is going to bother you, then I would add that to the list of reasons why not to pick this up at its current price tag.
The developers themselves said they won't add new content unless the demand is there. Well consider this my demand.  I want to support these guys, but I feel a little cheated. I expected more out of this game than 5 hours. They've opened up an interesting platform, but I think they or someone else could do this genre better justice and increase replayability. They state you’re gonna need more than one party for this, and that's absolutely true. Because otherwise you'll burn out your audience real quick!
UPDATE (1/5/2016): This review received more attention than I expected, so with the successor out on steam now, I feel compelled to give an update on the state of the game. It appears the developers due indeed believe there is demand for more content. Unfortunately that content is in the form of a sequal and a price tag of another $25. I can't speak for the this game's successor, but I can give an update on this games current condition. Unfortunately, there isn't much more to say... This game resurfaced for me on New Years Eve with a (reasonably) fresh audience. The game was still littered with bugs (i.e. no one being able to enter in answers, freezing, booting players, no input recognition, etc.), and the newcomers seemed to agree that only Fibbage and Drawful (though primarily Fibbage) was worth playing. Overall an enjoyable experience for the newbies, but a little lackluster for those who had played with me before. Simply put, the game still lacks polish and solid content.

But those time-critical sections are essentially the game's "boss-battles" despite being mostly a fight against the terrain itself.
I heartily recommend Ori - easily the best, trickiest, and most ingenius platformer since Braid (and with a decent bit more content).
Two tips: first, one can copy save-games, if you decide you want to fork your play-throughs with different abilities, say. Second, persevere. Often the next safe-place is just one perfectly-timed jump away from where you keep dying. ;-)

I played through the game single player and was left with this, "oh ok...and then?" hollow feeling.  Towards the end between items and levels it pretty much negates the difficulty and puzzles.  The narrative is pretty standard fantasy, aloof wizard, sneaky thief and meat head warrior go to the place and get the thing.
PROS:
+ Graphics
+ Music
+ Atmosphere
+ It's fun
+ starts off as a good puzzle platformer
+ Story starts off interesting
CONS:
- Quit Game nag to buy Trine 3...EVERY TIME
- Music can sometimes drown out diologue
- Characters become too powerful for the games own good negating the puzzle aspect of the game
- Faux wood...apparently in trine land there's things that look like they're made of wood but are made od marshmellows?
- hit box wonkiness
- anti-climatic
YET I still recommend it.  Why? It's a fun game you have to look at as a small indie game from 2009 which lacked the resourcs of huge AAA studios. Yes I know it's no excuse but it helps understand it's short comings.  See for this it wasn't like a lot of games that shall remain nameless, where the short comings where not because of studio size or budget or man power but "we need something for a season pass".  BTW this is about Trine 1 not 3...just saying.
Towards the end it feels like going through the motions.  In the beginning it was "shoot the rope and slam the wall like some rube goldberg machine" towards the end it's "Planks, platforms and boxes...everywhere! I have no time for you platforming puzzels".  Or "I could move the heavy box then grab it with my shield and break the wall OOOOOOr I can just thunder hammer and break everything breakable on the screen"
It's like the difficulty curve doesn't match how powerful the characters get.  The last level feels like the devs knew this so they just throw things at you to throw things at you.  You die, rarely, not because of a mis jump or an attempt to solve a puzzle goes bad but because that wooden beam isn't wood, it just looks like wood OR a mob spawns where you're jumping mid jump and it's hit box is more important than yours so you Super Mario bounce into lava.
It's that last level, that kinda gave me the "oh ok" feeling.   You get to the base of the tower, some lich is there for...reasons. the thief says "hurry jump on the platform".  I was expecting something like the infamous level in Ori and the Blind Forrest then a boss fight.  What I got was a "hurry as in take you time there's no rush laval moves slow after all" and nothing.
This is where the short comings of the gameplay meets the short coming of the story.  The story starts off like the typical fantasy "reluctant hero(s) in the wrong place at the wrong time thrust in to this world saving adventure" even going as far as to touch on the character's motivations, yet it just ends.
I was expecting a "we got the mcguffin but lets continue to work together to save the land from this lich" what I got was "This lich that coated the world in darkness and raised the dead, hit him in the face once it's his only weakness yay you win! NO QUESTIONS"
I know the story isn't important, the game is mostly fun but if they're going to add a narravite then it something that will either add or take away from the game.
Overall again, I do recommend it.  It's a fun game and made me want to play Trine 2. It has it's short comming and would suggest either buying 1 and 2 or getting it on sale.  It's an amazing game lumps and all for $2.25 during the 2015/6 winter sale.

I cannot sing the praises of this game highly enough. As you can see from mine and others' play time, this is not a long game, though it is large and bold and amazing. This is an experience and an incredible one at that. To start with, the game itself, the core, physical properties, are flawless. The graphics and environments and characters are positively gorgeous and it's so easy to simply immerse your whole being in this game. The sound design, the lighting, there is not a single complaint I could make about how the game looks, sounds and feels to simply be a part of.
Secondly, the psychosis. This is a story of Senua, of her journey, and her mental illness. This game was put together with so much attention and love and detail from all corners, from people who have these actual experiences and scientists who study it, it is an amazing and perfect capture of these experiences, of what this life can possibly be life and the stigma and issues that arise with it. If for no other reason, this game is a master piece for the love that went into crafting the psychosis experience and representing it properly.
And the gameplay itself is phenomenal. The puzzles are simple at their core, but made complex by the game world and the connections you have to make. There's exploration to be had in small amounts of a world that is beautiful and amazing. The combat is pure and simple and fluid and still challenging at the same time. There was not a single battle in this game that I ever felt was unfair, either too easy or too hard. Every single one was good and solid, some were harrowing and difficult, some felt overwhelming because the enemies just kept coming, but all of those were good things, all of those made the experence so much greater and more than it could have been without them, and the way the game progressively gets more complicated both in combat and in the puzzles, is simply marvelous.
And, though I won't spoil anything, each section is wholly unique. There are some things in this game that I have never seen done before, and if I had heard them explained to me, I would have said it would be a♥♥♥♥♥♥experience. But it isn't, it was amazing and perfect. This is the only game I can think of that has ever sucked me in so completely, to the point where I finished the whole thing in a couple of sittings simply because I didn't want to stop. I could speak endlessly about how amazing this game is, I could sing its praises for years to come. But really, all I can say is you need this in your life. Get yourself a good pair of headphones, put them on, and immerse yourself in Senua's story, and don't look back. There will be emotion and excitement and fear and it will be one of the greatest games you have ever played, that I promise.

In a world where so many games pad out the content with tons of meaningless fluff, Hellblade is a refreshingly tight 6-8 hour experience. The game does an excellent job of putting you in the main character's shoes and telling a story that is compelling, harrowing, and dark. This isn't a happy-go-lucky tale of redemption or revenge. The subtitle Senua's Sacrifice is there for a reason.
While the storytelling, presentation, and character portrayal in Hellbalde are all excellent, your mileage may vary when it comes to the combat gameplay. The combat is slightly more involved than it seems early in the game, but it is not the focus of the game, unlike previous Ninja Theory games. I enjoyed the combat for what it was, but some fights late in the game got a little tedious when you start fighting more than a couple enemies at once. The camera is very close to your character, giving a claustrphobic feel to 1v1 and 1v2 combat encounters. However, the system just wasn't built for fighting many enemies at once, so when the game makes you do that, it can get a bit frustrating.
There is also a lot of puzzle solving in Hellblade, most of which I found to be very enjoyable. The puzzle designs in different ares of the game vary enough to keep them interesting, even though most of them revolve around finding the proper perspective to change what you are seeing.
If you tend to enjoy story-heavy games and Hellblade looks interesting to you, go ahead and give it a shot. Ninja Theory tried something very ambitious with a small team, and for the most part succeeded. The game isn't perfect by any means, but it is definitely worth playing.

The New Colossus seems like a great continuation to the amazing Wolfenstein: The New Order. The previous game -- The Old Blood, kind of lost me. Its idea of a storyline seemed to be "let's introduce a bunch of new characters and kill them off ten minutes later, that way we don't have to develop any of them!". TNO, on the other hand, had amazing character development, both for the main cast, and, what is no less important -- for the enemy. The Nazis in TNO actually managed to induce a feeling of strong discomfort and hate in me, which TOB somewhat failed at -- they were kind of just there to scream "ICH BRAUCHE VERSTAERKUNG" and for you to shoot at (not to mention they turn into zombies halfway through the game?), and Wolf 2 is doing great in this regard so far. Frau Engels is an absolute menace, and the way she's acting, even at the very beginning of the game, is positively disturbing. I can't comment on much else story-wise just yet, unfortunately, as I still have to play the game more.
Technically, this game is a mixed bag. Performance seems fine, but it's a bit on the crashy side. For me, the game crashes under following circumstances:
I'm amazed they managed to ♥♥♥♥ up something this basic, but I'd imagine this will be fixed ASAP. That said, both of these crashing conditions are perfectly avoidable, so the game remains both playable and enjoyable.
Additionally, we have mechanical changes. The weapon switching wheel is now assigned to a key instead of being brought up with the scroll wheel, and using the scroll wheel simply cycles through the weapons you have without bringing the wheel up. I'd love to say I'm in favour of this change, since it lets you switch weapons more quickly, but I'm so used to TNO's and TOB's wheel system by now that I keep messing it up whenever I try to switch weapons. I suppose that's entirely on me, though.
The Laserkraftwerk has been seriously improved compared to TNO. You don't have to awkwardly try to make a rectangle anymore, you just shoot and it burns the whole bloody fence/vent gate/whatever you're aiming it at.
The main menu is honestly hard to navigate. It's designed to be used with the keyboard or a controller, and while it does respond to mouse input, changing options requires you to press teeny tiny little arrows instead of having a drop-down of some description or, you know, just clicking on the option to cycle through the possible settings. TNO/TOB had this done better, but again, this isn't a deal-breaker of any sort.
Aim assist is ON BY DEFAULT for some insane reason, even if you're using a mouse to play. For the love of all that is holy, switch it off right away if you want to enjoy this game at all.
Overall, I'm really enjoying Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus so far, and I'm excited to play more of it and see what comes next. From a technological point of view, the game's less perfect than the former entries in this series, however, it's not enough to stop me from enjoying the game, and I expect these issues to be addressed soon enough, anyway. But the gameplay, and, especially, the story, have me hooked, so I'm not going to wait for a patch just to continue playing.

A phenomenal game for scifi enthusiasts, especially those into cyberpunk tales. While it has its rough edges due to a mixture of heavy ambition and first experience in game design, it's a worthy addition to your library for its well realized world and soundtrack that combine to overcome its occasional frustrations. As other reviews you may have read note, the camera can prove a little stiff and the combat system can seem a little clumsy, but these are easily dealt with. The camera won't kill you and if your combos are built either to maximize damage or quickly regenerate your health, neither will the somewhat clumsy combat system.
What's so clumsy about the combat system, you might ask? It's not the customization, that's for sure, which personally I found to be a fascinating, if mild, innovation on the typical combo system. While you do only have limited combos to work with that cannot themselves be customized (e.g. you cannot configure a five punch combo, though you may cycle through the three punch combo to "make" a six punch combo, if you like), each hit of the combo can be given its own effect. There are S-Pressen (special attack) cooldown decreases, power pressens to increase damage, regen pressens to restore health with each hit, and chain pressens that double the effect of the previous pressen. These each give every combo chain its own unique blend of effects besides purely compounding damage and unlocking special moves for use, which made it far more interesting than your typical combo system to me.
However, where this falters and where the combo system becomes somewhat clumsy, is that while it will remember your progression in the combo for an individual enemy, this momentum is lost upon the next enemy. Slightly more frustrating is that any hit taken, and you will take hits, resets the combo forcing you to go through it again. On its own, this wouldn't be that big of a deal, except that each encounter is not entirely well balanced against the combo system, as each combat area becomes crowded with enemies that tend to refuse to separate. If each encounter had had fewer enemies, a better ability to draw them apart, or simply a better defensive option than flipping away from or over them, this wouldn't have been as clumsy. Unfortunately, that's not the case, but each time you do achieve a combo, whether appropriately or not, you'll feel a sense of accomplishment and generally, the game itself does a good job of rewarding this with fantastic music and sound effects following your combo progression, as well as an experience bonus for longer chains.
If you think you can stand for that, and are looking for a fascinating scifi vision of the future, with a beautifully realized world design and invigorating soundtrack, not to mention a genuinely compelling cast of characters to learn about, you'll have an experiential gem on your hands. Please don't miss this for its faults, play it for its ambitions.

Rogue State is a handsome mess. I've tried to like it, I spent on it 7 hours, and 12 more after some pause, and in the end I feel robbed.
The game lets you feel like a ruler in terms of stress and management, but not in terms of making a difference. Sometimes the game doesn't seems to answer to your choices, sometimes it's misguiding/arbitrary, and sometimes it feels too cruel or even too sugared.
About choises:
You can disallow the death penalty and give amnesty to previous ruler's allies, but anyway NPCs will say that you executed them publicly, and sometimes the game will obliviously suggest to punish your subordinates with nonexistent measure.
Random regular events – one of important gameplay features – contributes to the feeling of powerless. Event can ask you to deal with, say, ecological problem, and the only way to resolve it... is to encounter this crisis not before X turn. Not before you'll be allowed to build infrastructure, because you need will to have specific construction. That could add some drama or 'realism', but you can never solve crisis later, not even for a month, and it doesn't always makes any sense.
About misguiding:
You can lose the game while having 100% approval of every person and institute in the county just because pretty UI doesn't helps you to understand objectives. It feels like cheating, and the game cheats you repeatedly. After every walkthrough you'll earn some XP to unlock new gameplay features. Unfortunately, some of them are mediocre, and others just have no effect (literally).
About cruelty or sugary:
It's just another form of inability to play as you want. You can build liberal paradise, but your subordinates will anyway fail to interrogate prisoner without killing him, because it is mentioned in a dialogue, and dialogues doesn't react on your play-style, they all written for default "dirty heartless dictator" style. Sweetness is the opposite: if you wish to be a strict ruler, you can forbid hamburgers or western haircuts, but the most severe measure you can inflict on liberal manifestation is... turning blind eye on it.
I'm afraid that Rogue State actually has only one real way to win it, a pretty precise set of steps. Any other steps are of no significance or wrong. It's not awful – many components of the game are very decent – but I can't recommend it.

I've heard a lot of folks say this is a beautiful game, and it turns out they're right. The story is simple yet touching, and the music and visuals add a lot. This is one of the few platformers I've played in which it's relatively easy to navigate the entire map based on landmarks and striking backgrounds. (That there's a mini-map also helps, though.)
The gameplay is also excellent. You get new abilities along a gentle slope, but must master each one in turn. And I mean master - certain sequences required many run-throughs to perfect. But those time-critical sections are essentially the game's "boss-battles" despite being mostly a fight against the terrain itself.
I heartily recommend Ori - easily the best, trickiest, and most ingenius platformer since Braid (and with a decent bit more content).
Two tips: first, one can copy save-games, if you decide you want to fork your play-throughs with different abilities, say. Second, persevere. Often the next safe-place is just one perfectly-timed jump away from where you keep dying. ;-)

This game takes difficulty through requirement of perfection too far.
Many segments require perfect execution, which leads to running the same sequence tens or even hundreds of times trying to clear it. There are almost no areas that can be cleared on the first or even the fifth try, because in most cases any given 'challenge section' is many screens wide. And just for icing, for those trying to be completionist, there are many hidden areas and items in places you can't return to, but appear inaccessible unless you figure out the stunt. Each save slot is a single playthrough, so you cannot back up to an area that has been closed by game events without doing the whole game over.
Additionally, very early in the game, you acquire the ability to jump off of enemies and enemy projectiles, and about as soon as this happens the gameplay changes to basically force you to try to avoid killing enemies as you have to use this to progress. Unfortunately, enemy firing arcs are fairly random and due to the aforementioned need for pixel perfect jumping, a lot the repetition you experience won't be because you did anything wrong, but just because the enemy shot at the wrong angle that time. What could have been an interesting and unique mechanic instead becomes a frustrating exercise in randomness, as this can kill you anytime from the beginning of a sequence to just short of the first safe platform in minutes.
To top it off, the health bar is basically meaningless, as almost nothing actually deals only one point of damage and most terrain obstacles can instagib, the leveling tree is arranged such that you basically have to level everything at once so there is no real choice, and the save anywhere system is negated by level design and a need to use the same resource to clear many areas, meaning it is quite possible to put yourself in a situation where your having saved means you cannot clear the area and have to start the game over again.
What this means is that you will spend hours not experiencing the beautiful story, not experiencing the excellent graphics, and not experiencing the incredible music, but doing the same platforming challenges over and over and over until you want to scream at your computer. Hard can be fun, dieing can be part of the experience, but not to the extent that this game requires. Only a masochist should purchase this game.

I got this game from a friend, before I played it, I had seen maybe the first half hour of the game. I'd seen other people struggling to play the game. Then I decided to play through it myself.
First off, the games graphics are absolutely gorgeous. It's a 2D game that doesn't feel flat at all. There's so much to look at on every screen! Sometimes the screen does feel a bit 'busy' and it can be tricky to tell if something is actually going to hurt/kill me or not.
The music in the game is fantastic as well. I enjoyed every minute of it even if when I was getting frustrated with some of the gameplay aspects.
The game is a platformer, and the controls feel more or less solid. Sometimes wall jumping or jumping would feel just a bit off, but I'm guessing that was more my errors rather than the game messing up. The ability to save at any point was both a blessing and a curse. Sometimes I would forget to save, and I would have to redo a difficult jumping sequence over.
There were a few things I disliked about the game, the first was all the death traps. Especially the lasers. I made a comment about playing it that one of the developers must have a thing for 'death laser porn'. Be warned! This game has some brutal death traps. At least the game prevented me from creating a save point in an area where death traps were.
I think my least favorite part of the game were the dramatic 'escape sequences'. Much like Metroid games, when Ori finishes a dungeon, he has to rapidly escape the area.  This happens not once, not twice, but three times in the game. If I died at any point along the escape sequence, I would have to restart from the very beginning. Let's also factor in the fact that they featured instant death traps and they were timed in one way or another.  Honestly, I feel like it was a dramatic part of the game that could probably have used a bit of tweaking/playtesting to make it less stressful for the player.
Overall:
Pros:
A fun platformer with some unique movement abilities
Great Music
Great Visuals
Cons:
Too many death traps
Platformer (might be a con for some people).
I'd give the game a solid 8/10 myself.

This is a flawed political and financial sim where you try to balance your treasury with approval from your various social factions, the military and cabinet ministers, while keeping an eye on your neighbors and possibly developing some fancy secret project on the side. You get 5 years, i.e. 60 turns, which you have to survive and hopefully rack up a good score.
The good:
- A good breadth of approaches are possible. You can please some factions while neglecting others, you can be a corrupt kleptocrat, you can be a warmonger or a peacebroker, side with the USA or Russia, oppress or empower the ethnic minority, and more.
- It's varied. Each playthrough randomizes the events you get, the resources that become available, population faction membership, ministers and the big late-game crisis (such as a recession or terrorist threat). Makes for lots of replay value.
- There are collectibles, including game modes with alternate start conditions, and some easter-eggy unlockables.
The Bad:
- The military aspect is atrocious, or at least woefully underexplained. I never have any idea why my units are winning or losing. I don't know what forces the enemy has since they're not shown on the map, and I don't understand why my buildings are getting destroyed when I have forces at the border. It's so bad and obtuse, I almost gave the game a negative rating.
- Expensive superprojects have a chance of failure. This shouldn't be. If you put millions and millions into a project and it fails, you may as well start over. Very ill-conceived system given how tight your budget is and how much money is involved. Maybe instead there should be multiple levels of funding that get you more bonuses the more you invest in the project.
- The intelligence system seems like a lot of expense for little gain. 50 million might get you a tidbit of info that you can use one time to increase relations with one neighbor by a bit. I just didn't find it worth the expense. It's super-insulting too when you pay tens of millions just to get a morsel of info about a leader that Wikipedia would have told you. I know you can get more indepth stuff, but the expense is just unacceptable. If you could direct intelligence spending on specific areas, or the investment needed for each type of intel was more transparently explained, it would be a much more engaging mechanic. See, like the military aspect, the game seems to think uncertainty is an involving game mechanic, which it can be but not when you don't understand what is happening or why. The rules need to be clearer and better represented in the game. Uncertainty should come down to the player making informed choices knowing the risks, not to being left in the dark about vital information.
Other remarks:
- As with real life, it all comes down to money. Practically everything takes money. It's really easy to get people to love you if you just throw enough money at their problems. Which is good if you want a financial sim, but perhaps not so good if you expect a complex political sim. Once you've tried a playthrough or two, you'll get the picture that, while it's easy to keep most everyone happy and stay in the green in the early and mid-game, the late game throws you a curve ball that - you guessed it - takes lots of money to solve. So you learn to be frugal and squirrel away cash into the treasury for that stormy, stormy day.
Verdict: It's clear this team put a lot of effort into this game, and this is why I'm giving it a positive rating, but key aspects are too half-baked and underexplained for it to be consistently fun. These are things that can be patched, and that would make Rogue State a real gem.

THE BAD: Ultimately, the game is just a matter of answering politically-oriented questions with the end result being that some points go here and other points go there, while trying to maximize your total points across all piles (each pile being something that can acccumulate influence, like a faction or a country).  In that sense, it can get boring (especially in the long run), but I pardon it on account of its price.
THE SIMILAR: The policy and faction aspect of Tropico is clearly visible here, but not the SimCity-aspect of Tropico.
Overall, worth a try.
