The story of B.J continues. Fast paced action, gore and killing a vast array of enemies, not all completely human. (See bottom if you’re just interested in the pros and cons list)
First off, is it worth it? In my opinion yes. I have been eagerly awaiting this game and it delivered. I believe this game to be very worthy of anyone’s time. My current playtime is slightly wrong as I have a alt+tab habit and have probably in total left the game running whilst I quickly doid something else a total of around 4-5 hours collectively. I have seen complaints of a “short” 10 hours to finish but if you find yourself breezing through the enemies and finish quick then you did this game an injustice. To start, crank that difficulty up until you find dying a hard thing to avoid.
Next, explore! I can’t stress that enough. Walk around ‘EVAS Hammer’, watch Max destroy a pool table with savant like skill and listen to the strange, funny or heartbreaking conversations the crew has. Try your hand at stealth too. Enemies don’t raise the alarm just because they found a dead body and it seems most levels can be done almost completely in stealth if you have the patience and don’t mind the use of the old quick load button. Stop to read a few of the letters, postcards and other things to get a chilling idea of life under Nazi rule from the side of the oppressed and the oppressors.
Now the technical side. Great graphics, a noticeable improvement over ‘The New Order’ and ‘The Old Blood’ A few glitches here and there but that is to be expected in the world of PC gaming where every permutation of PC configuration is impossible to account for. The game runs nicely. Vsync caps the frame rate to 60 but without it I was getting well over 100 consistently. A few of the graphics settings need some clarification however.
Without Vsync the pre-rendered videos had noticeable tearing but honestly I have yet to find a game that didn’t do that with Vsync off. The only annoying problem I had was that the mouse decided its speed should be ‘13’ every time the game was launched. Changing it to what I want worked but only until the restart of the game. However this and a few other barely noticeable things are all will no doubt be addressed as the game’s life continues.
Bethesda and Machine Games have released something great and by the way. If you are one of the people that finds yourself online crying over Bethesda because of some of their business decisions. Stop wasting people’s time by leaving negative reviews just because Bethesda had a hand in a game like this. Vote with your wallet you morons, not with words of hate for a company that has helped release fantastic games like this and so much more.
Pros:
Fun, fast paced, gory action with available stealth options a plenty
Highly customisable graphics settings (excluding texture detail)
Quick reload upon death or load of quick save. Also quick save is instant without pausing game
Unique upgrades and ‘Contraptions’ that can greatly alter your play style
Heavy duty story mixed with funny moments (Max winning chess was my favourite)
Additional side missions taking down ‘ubercommanders’ in previously visited but changed locations
A home base filled with things to find and people to visit in on
Perks that increase B.J’s skill as you level them up
Over the top and larger than life characters and scenarios (Not a game that takes itself seriously)
Controls well and allows a player to use aim down sight or not with minimal difference
(EDIT) Forgot to mention the fantastic, heavy soundtrack. An amazingly great detractor from almost every other game that sticks to easily produced techno crap
Cons:
A few graphical glitches (skyboxes on a level or two went a little weird)
Mouse speed resetting after every launch (Could be a problem on Razer Synapses side however)
If you want to play on easy, not read anything or attempt stealth, this game will be short for you
Missing an indicator or notification to let you know a side mission is available so you don’t miss them
Some graphics settings need better explanations on what they do, some have nothing helpful at all
A few props during people’s conversations floated in air or beside their hands
A few crashes here and there. Windowed borderless does help stop some of these however
Steam overlay was perhaps pushed a little too quickly and seemed to be the cause of a crash or two

I liked it.
The visuals are pretty amazing, the fake 3d on my monitor worked well with them too.
The memory remix mechanic is cute though it's impossible to fail, just a matter of repeating a short segment until you've found all the glitches required.  You only do it about six times in the game so it's not a constant thing.
The game has an interesting plot and they've put considerable thought into the ramifications of a single technology.  In some ways, the plot or at least the background, resembles Syndicate Wars a little.  I guess all Cyberpunk dystopias look a little bit alike.
The gameplay mostly falls into parkour that is almost but not quite on rails and Over-The-Shoulder brawling which is quite a lot like Oni with punch/kick combos that you customise a little with various side abilities like regen/damage/cooldown as well as some special abilities that you build up focus for.  The fights aren't so frequent that you get bored and there's enough variety in enemies to keep it interesting.
All in all, a very well executed cyberpunk game with a dash of philosophy to it.
Time to complete: 14 hours at a casual pace.

is the obvious second in a series of time management games loosely based on the titular hero of ancient legend. While lacking any cohesive story, it is easy to forgive in light of excellent music, visuals, and gameplay. Casual gamers, this one's for you.
Once again, your mission is to direct a cast of workers to gather resources and build, repair, toggle switches, etc. in pursuit of a level goal. It keeps itself fresh by adding mythological characters, special abilities, clicker minigames, and puzzles. This title isn't anything terribly different from the first game, but it succeeds in pushing the bar a little bit higher. Add the impressive audio and visuals, and you've got a simple recipe for success.
There really isn't much to say negative about this game, but if I were to improve on it, the expert difficulty needs to be more balanced, and the game could use a more detailed tutorial. On one hand, it's nice from the perspective of letting the player learn through discovery, but on the other, it can be frustrating to figure out how to beat the developer times, when certain details you may never find. Ultimately I gave up on challenging dev scores beyond the achievement, because some of my best efforts were thousands less than the posted times. I'm still not sure what I'm missing.
Achievement hunters: This is a relatively easy 100% aside from "beat 10 developer times." Here's the trick: First, the description is wrong. You only need 5. Second, you can get this easiest in the earliest game stages (since shorter and less complex design), and the "boss" stages, the 10th of each section. These are simple to complete quickly but will require you to click birds out of the sky to get the extra score needed to beat them. With a bit of practice, it should take under an hour to do. You may need to exit the game for the achievements to register.

I've only played this for a few hours so-far, but it's because I've had to surgically remove myself so I can go to bed O_o
TLDR:
I am LOVING this game! Ninja Theory's live motion capture technology is a breakthrough that takes storytelling to a whole new level. In my opinion, the price is more than fair considering what they've delivered in the first couple of hours I'v played. Even if this game isn't really your thing, it is a perfect opportunity to send a message to the industry that the proverbial bar has been set.
The long version:
Sure, I've only played this game for a couple of hours, but like I said before, I'll be up all night if I let myself. In the developer videos/interviews during the making of this game, Ninja Theory (NT) made it clear that they wanted to make a change in the industry by providing a AAA but without the typical pricetag. Sure, the combat system may seem shallow to some, but I felt it was fluid, challenging, and still quite fun. Seriously though, this game isn't about the combat, it's obvious that they want to tell a story.
NT's motion capture has enabled the protagonist to feel real and human, and the actress did a fine job. A big part of the game is Senua's struggle with her inner doubts/feers which are portrayed through whispers that you really need to hear through decent headphones to appreciate. At first, I was worried it would get annoying, but it turned out to add a layer of depth to the game that really drew me in. I felt NT is putting a lot of effort to really make you feel like you are very much a part of the story, and even a part of Senua in a way.
The gameplay/character motion is fluid, and I haven't noticed any glitching or stuttering. The puzzles I have come across have been engaging, but not overly frustrating, and seem more a part of the story than some one-dimensional brain teaser. The world layout also feels very organic and looks nice. Yeah, there are times when I wonder why I can't just climb the thing, but I don't feel it distracting from the experience. The graphics are nice and the animations cleverly done.
Are there some imperfections, sure, but so far nothing distracting. I definitely recommend this game. The price is definitely worth it. As I mentioned before, I see this as one of the games to get behind to really send a message to the AAA industry that well-polished titles don't all have to be $60+ and rife with microtransactions. Also, give Ninja Theory your support so they make more games like this one! Will you buy the freaking game already!?

There's so many levels I want to review this game on, all could be rated very highly exclusively on their own but they culminate here to create a truly unique and immersive experince that is a marvel of wonderful stroytelling. The world is beautifully rendered and created, even the scenes of horror have an underlying elegance to them that you can't help to appreciate. The motion capture, and especially facial captures for Senua herself, are so realistic and and fluid you can read every emotion going through Senua simply by looking at her face. The sound, particularly the voices and minute auditory cues given from the environment, are so well thought out and implemented I appreciated this game on an auditory level that I've never experienced before.
The gameplay, while not ground-breaking or particularly complicated, had a simple elegance to it that allowed enjoyment of the game without distracting from the storytelling or environment. The combat specifically was kept simple but fluid: strikes, parries, dodges and guard-breaking kicks, make for a system that is un-cluttered easy to learn and with just enough depth to feel satisfying when you string it all together succesfully. The overall mood and setting of the game was well-established and allowed you to immediately get lost in Senua's world and experience it with her. It's dark, it's gritty, bloody and raw but it also has a beauty that Senua holds close and allows herself to experince when she feels at her lowest points. It binds together struggle, defiance, despair, loneliness, loss, hope, victory, and strength in just the right mix to keep you fighting without ever thinking this is a hopeless journey.
This game is scary, in some parts downright terrifying, but not in the traditional way that some games have achieved this such as Amnesia or Outlast. It grips you in an anxious hold that has you holding your breath and fighting back a rising panic as you continue to push forward. These are not jump scares or cheap thrills, it's an oppressive feeling of powerlessness that you must overcome at several points of the game.
Most importantly though is the story. Simply put: It's brilliant, thought provoking and entertaining. Senua's story is equal parts heart-breaking and inspiring. The pacing reveals key elements of her history and who she is as a person in such a way that new developments satisfy your curiosity but always leave you wanting to know more. Senua herself is an amazing character, so well thought out and believable, that it's hard not to feel for her and her situation. Quite important to note too is that while Senua is not a character defined by her psychosis but rather a character full of personality and life who is living with a psychosis that has influenced parts of her life.  It's exciting to say that I learned so much in playing this game, not just on a scientific or historical level about psychosis, celtic myth and culture but also on an empathic level. The game brought with it an understanding of how another person can perceive the world and that even if I can't see it how they do that doesn't mean there's anything wrong or broken about their reality. It shines a light on mental illness and psychosis in a truthful and often-times brutally honest way that I think very few other mediums have achieved.
This game won't be for everyone, achievement hunters, high-score heroes and those in search of a fun time-waster to fill your evenings will probably step away disapointed. For those in search of an amazing story, fascinating character and beautiful visual and auditory experience then this is a gem.

Alright, I'm just going to say this... This game is really great, and I would recommend it to any one. Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful 2D platformer taking place in the (fictional) Forest of Nibel. You play as Ori, a spry little Forest Spirit, who is too cute for some people to handle, and a childhood that some people can't emotionally handle. Some of the story is cliche
but it is still a story I fell in love with. With a set of characters seen in the game, and an antagonist with a backstory we all couldn't guess, this game is practically a Disney film with controllable characters.
Now time for the actual constructive criticism:
This game almost REQUIRES you have a controller. I played through the whole game multiple times (on another account) and also managed to get some of the more difficult achievements, such as Elite and Supersonic. The keyboard is just way to hard to master with this game, giving you some sections of the game with clunky controls, making it nearly impossible. Another thing about this game is the way it handles bad PCs. The way they built the engine (Unity) the FPS is not allowed to drop under 30 or so FPS, so to counteract this, the game will run in slow motion, making cut scenes and certain escape scenes with music that is supposed to fit run out of sync, frustrating almost anyone with this problem. This game has about 5000 megabytes of data, but still runs extremely slow on my PC, despite it being able to run Warframe at 60 FPS with Bloom and other video settings active. Other than that, this game is a work of art, and should be played by everyone, but this is also a game that is hard to enjoy, since it is so hard to begin with. 90% of bad reviews I've seen mostly complain about difficulty, which is what this game was DESIGNED to have. this game would have nearly 100% good reviews if not for some people's problems with difficulty and challenges. So go spend the money on this game, and get it... It's really great.

An argument could be made that Lego is too late. Minecraft has existed since 2011 and it single-handedly became one of the most commonly recognizable and referenced games for a whole generation of gamers. Yet, Lego always puts a spin on things. With a clickity-click-snap of enthusiasm Lego Worlds takes on sandbox gaming.
FIRST IMPRESSIONS
As soon my astronaut character crash-landed onto the first world, I noticed the lack of story-driven linear action Lego puzzles. Here, you are thrown into a sandbox world of free-to-choose missions to acquire gold Lego bricks. These bricks are the only way to power up your spacecraft for further travel. Upon investigating some bright lights emanating from the ground I received my first item, the Discovery Tool, which enables me to carbon copy items for use in the game world. It mostly felt like a Ghostbusters proton pack as it was huge, requiring two hands to hold it. However, the fun of it was being able to quickly copy - as well as projectile shoot - anything I could scan and unlock with it. I immediately filled the screen with as many chickens and pigs as possible.
Subsequently, you unlock a handful of other tools during the tutorial levels. You will use the Landscape Tool to add or delete the landscape.  There is a Copy tool
that allows you to select portions of your game world to save for later.  This was by far the most interesting tool. Want to keep that rainbow colored lollipop for a garden in the sky? Then this is your tool.  Next, you’ll find a Paint Tool, a Build Tool for carefully building brick by brick, and a Free Build Tool that merges all these into one work tool.
I really feel that until you unlock medium sized worlds, the sandbox gets repetitive.  Before, I had seen candylands, junkyards, pirate ships, and a “Fruit Ninjaed” version of all those combined. Now, I find swamps with full sized buildings and characters in a Swamp biome. Travel over the mountain and there are pyramids with a large Sphinx and some Lego mummies roaming about an Egyptian biome.  It’s finally an adventure.
Still, for hours I pretty much went about looking for gold bricks. I got past the magical fifty gold brick number and all I got was a bright level nine badge.  I was expecting more, and that was where Lego Worlds kept falling short. Expectations did not match up with the in-game achievements. This occurred over and over.
CONTROLS
The usual Lego game controls are present here with the added ability to create and edit the environment. Climbing trees and traversing terrain feels effortless. Where I had issues was with the camera angle.  I often got too close to an object while another character was nearby, tilting the camera angle out of position. This happened quite a lot with monsters near treasure chests. Some side quests had the same effect. Two or more NPC’s would be vying for attention and blurring all their word bubbles into each other. These camera issues are annoying.
There was also an issue when playing local co-op. The option to drop out is either well hidden or excluded from the game. This is really frustrating for young kids when one of them wants to go play something else and the other wants to keep playing.
Building and editing Lego structures is a bit of a mixed bag. While I could destroy to my heart’s content, using a controller or keyboard controls felt a bit like operating a claw machine at an arcade. I’d think everything was just fine, lay down my bricks and miss by just enough to make the end result look like a mess. Painting can be done in giant sections or slight dabs. However,  I mostly relied on splattering paint everywhere like painting with a ketchup bottle on a canvas. While it is certainly possible to design vast feats of architecture and visual eye-candy with Lego Worlds, more than likely you will flounder a bit using either a controller or keyboard.
GRAPHICS AND SOUND
If you are used to Lego games in the past, expect nothing too different. What you will get with Lego Worlds are a lot more blended color hues in the landscape, extra shadows, and some reflections. What is hard to describe is the way in which these all meld together. The way the sun hits the bricks while climbing a tree, or the first time you come across fireflies is something that stands out in your mind. Game transitions are seamless. You could be spelunking the caves by lantern-light until a cyclops and skeleton chase you into the ocean and immediately start swimming through the murky depths amoung sharks and stingrays. Each one of those drastic environmental changes comes off very smooth from one section to the next at 60FPS with a mid level card with just a few FPS drops in local co-op.
Sonically, the music score is adventuresome yet light hearted. I was never noticeably annoyed by repeated sections. If i turned the sound off I found myself wanting it back on. It generally informed me of when things were going on in game as well, so I’d say it’s a good soundtrack for the Lego genre
GAME CRASHES
I’ll size up the situation first.  I have two elementary age kids with controllers in hand, having fun building and exploring with one of their favorite and most familiar franchises. It a a co-op gameplay with smiles and laughs all around.
Then, the game suddenly died. I hear, “What!!? I spent forever building that!” coming from both of them at the same time. I try to calm them down and say we can do it again. They listen, and we reboot to start over. It is going well and they are playing from where they roughly left off.
Then the game died again. This time I hear, “For crying out loud!” and “ You have got to be kidding me!”. Once again, we reboot and try again. As a matter of fact, it happened five times in total. By the fifth time, I had two weeping kids who were frazzled.
After some best guesses, I discovered that the FPS was the main culprit. While the FPS looked okay on my screen, in reality it was jumping all over the place.  I needed V-Sync on. Once enabled, Lego Worlds mostly stopped crashing.
FINAL THOUGHTS
So, I sit back and ask my kids, “Is this better than Minecraft?”. “No!”, they both reply in unison. My 2nd grader answers, “It’s like a friendly Minecraft.”. It struck a chord with me.
The quests are repetitive, with only a half chance of getting anything back in return after 20+hrs.  Each biome seems filled with lots of fetch quests, a few coloring quests, and some basic building and copy quests. I would literally kill for some Lego platforming puzzles quests right now.
If you have played Minecraft and are burnt out from digging for resources, you will get even more burnt out. However, there are quite a lot of game objects that are plain fun to use. Want to kill someone with a glow-gun, go ahead. Got stuck in a hole? Well, a jet pack will take care of that. It’s the magic of these items that defines Lego Worlds. Even though I have a need to dive deep into the sea and explore, I’d rather try to make a replica of Castle Greyskull out of candy-canes. The downside is that the actual application of the tools within Lego Worlds can be frustrating. Try to make a house, and you will feel how inaccurate the placing of single bricks really is.
My last thoughts are that despite the game crashes, repetitive quests, constant digging for gold bricks, excessive menus, and fumbly brick-building the game is still quite engaging for anyone who enjoys sandbox games. Minecraft is still Minecraft, there is no huge rivalry to be made here with Lego Worlds. There are comparisons to be made, but you won’t find yourself saying, “This is such a Minecraft ripoff”.  It’s a Lego sandbox that is perhaps the truest version of that idea that has ever existed.  There is still more to unlock and I am having a great time both by myself and with my kids. Now excuse me while I ride a land shark and chase down a Yeti.

This game has a very odd charm to it and real reward that makes me keep going back to it over and over and over (it's a good game).
So what is the game's objective? To become a Master Builder!
But this is no easy feat! You must collect 100 bricks in order to get that far.
In order to avoid the bore of simpling giving everything to you and have the game be a mega-grind to 100 bricks, the game has unlockables that can be achieved only at certain points. These unlockables are actually really damn useful. The camera is helped to get the right shots and the grapple helps me get out of deep caverns (which is all the time).
There is no shortage of stuff to collect. I mean it. Also, you think you can just discover everything and be done? nope! The game has you interact with characters who have simple tasks or perform some feat to get a brick, set, money, or item to make it feel like an achievement. I feel like I actually earned most of these bricks (some of them were from chests underground) with hard work. Each character has something to get that another character can give to you so it connects everything.
What is your reward for getting 100 lego bricks? Making your OWN worlds of grand sizes. Honestly, that is a kickass reward. If the game had simply given you all the unlockables and the ability to make worlds right at the beginning, it would've been an incredibly weak game. As it is now, it is awesome and I can't wait for future updates.
However, one major gripe I have with this game is actually building. In order to build, you need to go into a menu, select another menu, select a tab, and pick a brick. This can severely hurt creativity and slows down the progress you can have.

The New Colossus is worth $20-$30. It's a good game, with a lot of loving detail and fun gameplay put into it, but it's definitely not as enjoyable in its story, tone, and characters as The New Order (TNO), which I would strongly recommend you buy instead if that's what you're looking for in your linear shooter.
As I said before, it takes a couple of steps foward in terms of gameplay. The gunplay is as fluid and punchy as ever, with really fun weapons and mechanics that mix up the encounters, like the battle stilts and shoulder tackle of doom. The melee mechanics are improved with better throw/slash detection, a new animal-grapple mechanic, and some really great kill animations with the axe. This game also does body awareness better than easily any other FPS on the market. Fast turns have intertia, you get knocked on your butt from explosions (and can shoot from prone), getting punched wobbles your view, and the lean system is still the best there is.
TNC unfortunately takes several steps back in the story and pacing department, which is the make-or-break characteristic for a linear-focused FPS like this. To make it brief, TNC commits to a much wider array of characters, topics, and unfolding events, but ultimately suffers from this wide focus and combining it with a more schlocky Tarantino-esque tone. Compared to TNO, many characters that are introduced end up underdeveloped or end up reduced to foils or comic relief. It certainly doesn't help that there are far more unique characters in this game than in TNO, which means the story's main attention is on the main characters and spread very thinly on the supporting cast.
On the tone: this mega-pulp Tarantino tone works pretty well for the purposes of gratuitous Nazi-killing and the occasional story beats (the Super Spesh character and a hilarious disguise sequence comes to mind), but it ultimately undermines the story by diluting the player's emotional investment in certain important characters. For instanced, the main villain here is like a zany cartoon character compared to the absolutely menacing one from TNO, and her villanous presence onscreen is sabotaged by poor writing and interactions that feel very forced. Many characters feel like they are seemingly shoehorned into the plot and/or act in ways that don't really make sense (like a pregnant woman going on a really dangerous assault operation, wtf). Even worse, new faces with lots of character, like the alcoholic anarcho-communist Horton and his New Orleans pals get almost no story exposure outside of their initial reveal. There's a lot of wasted potential here for likeable, flawed characters to shine like they did in The New Order.
The worst sins that this sequel commits are ones that you'll see in other games like Mankind Divided. There are parts of the game where they reuse levels for gameplay - as in combat levels, not hubs. They signpost some boss fights pretty poorly; in fact, I didn't even realize what was the final boss until after I had beaten the game. The story finale is abrupt, has plot holes like you wouldn't believe, and feels half-baked in its execution. In all, these problems made Wolf 2 feel like a middle child in a trilogy, hence my use of Mankind Divided as an example.
I had really high hopes for this game to expand on The New Order's potential. It's still a really fun shooter and when story vignettes and the pulpy tone align, it's a right riot of a time. However, it just kind of falls apart in so many ways in the story and characters, which are the aspects of its predecessor that made it such a surprisingly compelling experience.
Inexpensive, pleasing to the eye game, which has quite a thematic way of chracter progression. Recommended.

Rise of the Argonauts is a great blend of RPG elements and Action.
The story itself is an epic tale from Greek Mythology, where a great king seeks to resurrect his lost love with the power of a legendary artifact called the Golden Fleece.
The game itself is not really open world, but the levels themselves are very expansive and provide a lot of interesting and memorable characters, as well as multiple ways to go about solving certain quests.
You don't receive XP in a certain skill tree for your actions like most other games, but you instead get "Deeds" for, well, doing deeds both great and small, and you may dedicate them to one of four gods of your choosing to progress in level with the chosen god.
While a lot of people complain about the combat, I don't see what's wrong with it.
For those who like powerful swings which crush their enemies, there is the mace, along with Ares, the God of War.
Those who prefer their strikes to be quick and deadly are best suited to the spear, favored by the Godess Athena.
And those which like to cut through enemies with speed and cunning will take to the sword and the God Hermes.
I've seen people put negative reviews because their kills got stolen by their party members. Honestly you'd have to be a fool to not get at least 90% of them, so you'd do well to ignore the reviews made by kids who can't bother to learn the game and how to fight properly.
Overall the game is great, I've beaten it 5+ times and it's a gold mine of lore and interesting characters for those who are fans of Greek Mythology.

The marvel vs capcom 3 is back (again!) to take you on a ride!  Keep in mind this review is coming from the perspective of someone who has bought this game three times:  regular edition on console, ultimate edition on console, and now the ultimate edition on PC.  While I may not have many hours on the PC version, I have put in a lot of time in the console version.
If you're looking for a fun, casual fighting game to get into, this is the one.  If you're new to the MVC series, the key mechanic that makes these games unique is having three characters instead of one.  The way this works is that while the game is still technically a 1v1 battle, players can call in their other characters to either do a single move to assist in their combos, or swap them out to give one a chance to heal.  There's also a super meter that can store up to five charges, which allow you to pull off incredibly powerful moves, and "x-factor," which can only be used by each player once per match to provide them with a useful yet temporary buff.
The gameplay is fast, yet frantic.  The game encourages insanely long combos, since you can call in supports at the end of a combo to keep your opponent from recovering, and you can cancel animations by activating your hyper combo.  These are very fun to pull off, but incredibly frustrating to get caught in.  In casual games with friends this shouldn't be an issue, but if you ever play online be prepared to just not stand a chance.
Speaking of online play, I had some issues with hackers on the console version, where I would have to face off against two galactacuses at the same time.  I would imagine these issues would translate over to PC as well, but I honestly don't have enough experience to tell you if this is the case.  Luckily, however,  I did do a few matches online with friends, and the lag wasn't noticable at all.  Obviously results will vary, but I think they did a decent job with the netcode.
for offline play, you pretty much have three choices: arcade mode, missions, and heroes and heralds.  arcade mode is your standard fighting game arcade mode: fight a few enemies and then defeat a boss.  It's fairly short and on normal and easy it's a pretty simple task.  depending on which character got the final hit on the boss, you'll get a short comic book-like epilogue.  It's usually just a small reference or joke about the crossing universes, for example in she-hulk's ending we see her judging a case with phoenix wright and miles edgeworth as the defense attorney and prosecutor.  I didn't feel as if these were massively rewarding, but they're better than nothing.
Missions are basically just a tutorial for normal mode.  They require you to complete a few combos for each mission, and there's a set of missions for every character.  It's a lot of content, but not necessarily very interesting.  The combos range from "anyone can do that" to "oh my god this is actually impossible."  I found that sometimes I would "pull off" a combo but it would still not consider it complete, so either the detection is off or the timing is VERY precise.
I honestly didn't really care about heroes and heralds at all.  you pick a side and you get like these cards that give you buffs that very slightly alter the gameplay.  I felt like it was very grindy and not very interesting, but it's easy enough to just avoid the mode altogether.
There's a lot of characters in the game (less than MVC2 unfortunately), but they all feel unique.  There isn't really any character I would consider a clone of another.  There are some that definitely feel a bit cheesy (looking at you, iron man and doctor doom), and a few I would consider underpowered, but I think they did a pretty good job with the cast of characters.  It even includes two DLC characters for free.  I thought Jill was pretty fun to play, but Sheogorath or whatever the second one is called felt a bit clunky.  Maybe i'm just bad at playing as him.
The sound design is really good.  The music is lively, the sound effects are great, all the characters sound like themselves, and best of all the character select theme is still "I wanna take you on a ride."  Also, the art is pretty good as well.  The game is technically fairly old, so don't expect mortal kombat X levels of detail, but the art style they chose has aged pretty well.
Overal I think the game has aged pretty well, and has remained of my favorite fighting games for years.  Also, Phoenix Wright is the best fighter in the game and don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

There's so many levels I want to review this game on, all could be rated very highly exclusively on their own but they culminate here to create a truly unique and immersive experince that is a marvel of wonderful stroytelling. The world is beautifully rendered and created, even the scenes of horror have an underlying elegance to them that you can't help to appreciate. The motion capture, and especially facial captures for Senua herself, are so realistic and and fluid you can read every emotion going through Senua simply by looking at her face. The sound, particularly the voices and minute auditory cues given from the environment, are so well thought out and implemented I appreciated this game on an auditory level that I've never experienced before.
The gameplay, while not ground-breaking or particularly complicated, had a simple elegance to it that allowed enjoyment of the game without distracting from the storytelling or environment. The combat specifically was kept simple but fluid: strikes, parries, dodges and guard-breaking kicks, make for a system that is un-cluttered easy to learn and with just enough depth to feel satisfying when you string it all together succesfully. The overall mood and setting of the game was well-established and allowed you to immediately get lost in Senua's world and experience it with her. It's dark, it's gritty, bloody and raw but it also has a beauty that Senua holds close and allows herself to experince when she feels at her lowest points. It binds together struggle, defiance, despair, loneliness, loss, hope, victory, and strength in just the right mix to keep you fighting without ever thinking this is a hopeless journey.
This game is scary, in some parts downright terrifying, but not in the traditional way that some games have achieved this such as Amnesia or Outlast. It grips you in an anxious hold that has you holding your breath and fighting back a rising panic as you continue to push forward. These are not jump scares or cheap thrills, it's an oppressive feeling of powerlessness that you must overcome at several points of the game.
Most importantly though is the story. Simply put: It's brilliant, thought provoking and entertaining. Senua's story is equal parts heart-breaking and inspiring. The pacing reveals key elements of her history and who she is as a person in such a way that new developments satisfy your curiosity but always leave you wanting to know more. Senua herself is an amazing character, so well thought out and believable, that it's hard not to feel for her and her situation. Quite important to note too is that while Senua is not a character defined by her psychosis but rather a character full of personality and life who is living with a psychosis that has influenced parts of her life.  It's exciting to say that I learned so much in playing this game, not just on a scientific or historical level about psychosis, celtic myth and culture but also on an empathic level. The game brought with it an understanding of how another person can perceive the world and that even if I can't see it how they do that doesn't mean there's anything wrong or broken about their reality. It shines a light on mental illness and psychosis in a truthful and often-times brutally honest way that I think very few other mediums have achieved.
This game won't be for everyone, achievement hunters, high-score heroes and those in search of a fun time-waster to fill your evenings will probably step away disapointed. For those in search of an amazing story, fascinating character and beautiful visual and auditory experience then this is a gem.

A very pretty game, both from a graphical and art style standpoint, which will permit this game to be one of those games that time will not diminish based on its appearance. The music is very nice, and it has a simple but emotional and entertaining story.
The game plays like a platformer with some shooting elements, and is really a Metroidvania style game at its core. Although the world isn't massive or anything, a few teleportation/fast travel spots would've helped cut out time that was spent just for the sake of killing time. Considering the game auto-aims attacks, I could just click wildly and everything died that I came across, and I was having to run across the entire game world to get to something, so it was just a time suck with no relevant events or things to do.
The game's difficulty is a bit...peculiar. Most of the time, you move about at your own pace, and taking the time to assess an area before just "going for it" can pay off in better execution and survival, as well as giving you more time to possibly spot secrets. Speaking of secrets, there are things you can interact with which will reveal parts of the map, and there is a skill tree thingy which will let you upgrade your abilities as well as uncover hidden items to boost your health and energy...although I never found one health upgrade because it wasn't marked on the map.
Back to the difficulty, though...when you complete one of the game's major sections, a very fast-paced 1-2 mistakes-gets-you-killed section will start up. You cannot save during these and every time you die, you have to start the whole segment over. These are some heavy rage-inducing segments unless you're just crazy good at platformers and don't mind doing the same part 20-30 times over and over again trying to do it perfectly. I would have much preferred checkpoints during these, or at least the option of having checkpoints if more hardcore individuals would like to turn the option off and welcome the annoying fast sections.
All that said, this is a Metroidvania game that looks and sounds very pretty, has some good gameplay, and despite rage-inducing parts and failed to flag one of the health upgrades despite this being promised by a skill in game, this is over all an enjoyable game I am glad to have played through. If the developer would add the missing health upgrade marker to the map and add the option for checkpoints during the fast segments, this could be an excellent experience.

The New Colossus is worth $20-$30. It's a good game, with a lot of loving detail and fun gameplay put into it, but it's definitely not as enjoyable in its story, tone, and characters as The New Order (TNO), which I would strongly recommend you buy instead if that's what you're looking for in your linear shooter.
As I said before, it takes a couple of steps foward in terms of gameplay. The gunplay is as fluid and punchy as ever, with really fun weapons and mechanics that mix up the encounters, like the battle stilts and shoulder tackle of doom. The melee mechanics are improved with better throw/slash detection, a new animal-grapple mechanic, and some really great kill animations with the axe. This game also does body awareness better than easily any other FPS on the market. Fast turns have intertia, you get knocked on your butt from explosions (and can shoot from prone), getting punched wobbles your view, and the lean system is still the best there is.
TNC unfortunately takes several steps back in the story and pacing department, which is the make-or-break characteristic for a linear-focused FPS like this. To make it brief, TNC commits to a much wider array of characters, topics, and unfolding events, but ultimately suffers from this wide focus and combining it with a more schlocky Tarantino-esque tone. Compared to TNO, many characters that are introduced end up underdeveloped or end up reduced to foils or comic relief. It certainly doesn't help that there are far more unique characters in this game than in TNO, which means the story's main attention is on the main characters and spread very thinly on the supporting cast.
On the tone: this mega-pulp Tarantino tone works pretty well for the purposes of gratuitous Nazi-killing and the occasional story beats (the Super Spesh character and a hilarious disguise sequence comes to mind), but it ultimately undermines the story by diluting the player's emotional investment in certain important characters. For instanced, the main villain here is like a zany cartoon character compared to the absolutely menacing one from TNO, and her villanous presence onscreen is sabotaged by poor writing and interactions that feel very forced. Many characters feel like they are seemingly shoehorned into the plot and/or act in ways that don't really make sense (like a pregnant woman going on a really dangerous assault operation, wtf). Even worse, new faces with lots of character, like the alcoholic anarcho-communist Horton and his New Orleans pals get almost no story exposure outside of their initial reveal. There's a lot of wasted potential here for likeable, flawed characters to shine like they did in The New Order.
The worst sins that this sequel commits are ones that you'll see in other games like Mankind Divided. There are parts of the game where they reuse levels for gameplay - as in combat levels, not hubs. They signpost some boss fights pretty poorly; in fact, I didn't even realize what was the final boss until after I had beaten the game. The story finale is abrupt, has plot holes like you wouldn't believe, and feels half-baked in its execution. In all, these problems made Wolf 2 feel like a middle child in a trilogy, hence my use of Mankind Divided as an example.
I had really high hopes for this game to expand on The New Order's potential. It's still a really fun shooter and when story vignettes and the pulpy tone align, it's a right riot of a time. However, it just kind of falls apart in so many ways in the story and characters, which are the aspects of its predecessor that made it such a surprisingly compelling experience.

I really enjoyed Rise of the Argonauts. Yes, it's quite easy and not very long, the plot is kind of stupid in places, the loading times disguised as cutscenes (I'm talking to you, gates to the Acropolis of Mycenae) become tedious because there's much running back and forth, and it's not the best looking game out there. Why did I like it then?
Well, I'm a sucker for Greek mythology and I think this game gets the atmosphere right. Mostly. Don't get me wrong, the legendary characters, places and stories of old are misplaced, mixed and butchered without remorse, when not completely made up. If you want a more canonical depiction of Greek myths go play Apotheon (seriously, go play it, it's awesome!), this is more like a fanfiction or an alternate reality but still feels Greek and mythological enough.
I specially like the god alignment system. Dialog options don't influence the plot but they do influence gameplay because your dialog choices are aligned with one of four deities (Athena, Apollo, Ares and Hermes). Winning their favour by choosing their dialogs or dedicating your deeds (ingame achievements) to them lets you level up in their respective skill trees and unlock different powers and buffs. To me it feels very satisfying to devote yourself to a god (Athena rules and anyone who disagrees will eat my spear), it really gets me immersed.
The dialogs and characters are mostly well written. Each of your companions have different personalities, and they interact between them and with the enviroment in different ways (Pan is snarky and will go on about old legends and trivia, Achilles is obnoxious and will brag about being the best fighter ever, and so on). Like Mass Effect, you take your ship (the Argo, a steampunk-ish mechanical Greek galley) to different locations and decide which companions will go ashore with you. Of course it's much more limited and samll than Mass Effect, with only five or six main locations or so, and only four companions to choose from, although you collect a few other characters with whom you can speak while on board the Argo.
The combat, although not very tricky, is fluid, fun and bloody, and can get quite spectacular once you start throwing god powers all over the place.
Aesthetically, it's good enough. Some of the enviroments look pretty and colorful, like Iolcus palace (I really liked the guards openning the doors for you, I know it's probably there just to hide a loading time but it made me feel like a king and I've seen too many magical self-openning doors in games to appreciate the detail), while others are much more dull and uninspired. The bronze in your armour is shiny and many of the armours and wepons themselves are not too overly fantastical in design, which I like.
I haven't experienced crashes or major bugs that I remember, as many reviews say, and I played for several hours at a time. I guess I got lucky. I bough this game on a sale for dirt cheap (1.75 EUR) fearing that it would be awful or crash on me, but I was pleasantly surprised and, after completing it, I woudn't mind having paid more for it.

I really, really wanted to like this game.  It shows so much promise, but for every step forward, it takes 3 steps backwards.
First, the game is a beautiful reimagining of the Greek myth of the Argonauts and the Golden Fleece.  The art direction is absolutely gorgeous - the environments are great, your armor and weapons look unique and interesting, and all the characters manage to look "larger than life" while still fitting into the game world.  The main characters, that is, because there are only 3 NPC models in this game.  At one point, I was mediating a dispute between three merchants, and they were all the same person.  It really breaks immersion to walk through a city full of clones.
The writing is really well done, and the conversation system (where you can pick responses that align with certain gods - like a witty response to appeal to Hermes or an aggressive response for Ares) works very well!  But NPCs converse by stiffly holding the same pose and moving only their mouth, or repeating the same hand motion over and over, which is often distracting, sometimes unsettling.
The combat just kinda sucks, really.  I like that you can switch between the Spear, Sword, and Mace, but they all play the same: just wail on your enemy until it dies.  There's not strategy, it's just button mashing.  It's also a real tragedy that there's a finite number of enemies in this game, and it's VERY POSSIBLE for your Argonaut allies to steal enough kills and prevent you from reaching max exp.  So you get these really well crafted characters, but just end up resenting them for stealing your kills.  Plus, the lack of a lock-on systems is BS, I can't count how many times I've whittled an enemy down to kill him with a thrown spear, only to have my character do a 180 and throw it at someone offscreen.  Then one of my allies kills the weakened enemy, because of course.
The cherry on the top is that this game is an abysmal port.  Apart from screen resolution, there's no visual settings at all, not even a LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH option.  Plus, frequent crashes to desktop, which are inexcusable in my opinion.
It's a little embarrasing.  This game could have been great - like, legitimately great, but they ♥♥♥♥ed it up so bad, I'm kind of amazed actually.  I wish I could recommend this game, but I can't.  Watch a youtube playthrough, though, because the story is pretty grand.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT:  Having played the game to completion, I'm now fully qualified to say this game is absolute trash.
Despite all the good things I said about it in my original review, my feelings about the game as the end credits rolled were overwhelmingly negative.  The developer, Liquid Entertainment, should be ashamed of themselves that they took something with so much promise and potential and made it so irredemably terrible.  Whatever good qualities this game has are so thoroughly drenched in filth, it's really not worth a playthrough to experience them.
Don't buy this.

I honestly came into this one expecting to hate it. People had panned the combat as difficult or confusing, and the game to be nothing special.
Lucky for me I still went ahead and picked this up (at a steep discount, though, so take that for what it is).
From the moment the game started, I was intrigued by the setting. Though full of sci-fi tropes, the game still managed to capture my interest and imagination, and I found myself caring for the protagonist as she made her way from beginning to end. I even found myself worried that she was, at times, too trusting of those around her and I worried that she would make the wrong decision - and though I had hoped at times I could make the decisions for her, the linearity of the gameplay did not take away from the final product.
As for the combat, I personally had no trouble figuring it out. The 'build a combo' system isn't quite what I expected - what I had expected was something more difficult. Basically you get four different combinations of X and Y presses on the controller (or your keyboard equivalent). Over time you unlock different 'powers' to place in each of these slots... so if your combo is X-X-X you can have one X be a powerful hit and the other be a heal, or maybe something that lowers the cooldown of your presens (big power moves). It made sense to me, and I managed to adjust and play with the combos to suit my playstyle and for different parts of the game (easily done on the fly).
Getting the combos to work wasn't an issue either... but be warned, this isn't a button-mashing game. For the most part, combos all require calm, regular and deliberate button presses. If you are accustomed to going crazy with the controller, you will be frustrated as getting any of Nilin's (the main character) powers to work properly requires combos to succeed.
tl;dr
Graphically impressive game with a linear, yet rewarding story, interesting and appropriately challenging combat with some climbing, discovery all in a great science fiction setting. Game clocked in at about 9 1/2 hours for me, which I think was about right. Great buy, especially on sale.

Remember Me was an emotional experience, an immersive glance into a potential future, and a journey into questioning morality.
Overall, this game was unbelievably fantastic- it took place in such an interesting, immersive world to the point where you wanted to look around simply to learn more about it. The story was beautifully written, the protagonist was and will always be one of my absolute favorites, and the twists and turns in how the game played out kept you wanting to learn more, wanting to see how it would all end.
That being said, the ending was... Not perfect. Albeit it was decently epic and it introduced another interesting concept on top of the already interesting "memory industry" dynamic, it was also somewhat cliche, in all honesty.
In addition, I have to agree with some of the criticisms on the gameplay- my first playthrough was on Memory Hunter (hardest difficulty) and a lot of the time it felt like "see if you can time your dodges right while simultaneously throwing out punches between dodges to get your focus up". In other words, it sometimes felt kind of like *press space, okay, punch twice, space again, punch twice... and so on*. Then again, my standards for gameplay in narrative-oriented singleplayer RPGs is usually decently low, so I thought it was fun enough. Tedious at times, definitely.
The best way I can summarize how I felt/feel about this game is: it was basically another Dishonored with (decently) worse gameplay. Same immersive feel, both extremely interesting worlds, both well-written stories and characters, both beautiful art direction, etc.
Do I recommend it? Hell yes.

Pros:
+Deeply moving storyline with excellent character development, rare for a game to have a female protaganist that I actually care for.
+The best level design I have seen since Half Life 2. Around every corner is something that makes me say "wow".
+Beatiful visuals (after an essential tweak) and a vivid, colourful world.
+Dynamic and fluid combat mechanics with a number of strategies available.
+Parkour is smooth and simple to master.
+Memory Remixing is a stroke of genius, and can be an emotional rollercoaster.
+Fabulous music that adds well to the immersion.
Cons:
-Levels can sometimes feel a little too linear, despite the game being non open-world by design.
-Memory Remixing, probably the game's strongest point, is simply not explored enough.
-Very little replayability aside from completing all collectibles.
-Rather duff final boss, despite the superb and moving build-up.
-Combat and some other elements are poorly explained with no tutorial leaving the player to figure out what to do.
-Default game has a stupid film-grain effect which ruins the visuals, but this is easily removed (PM me).
-Camera difficult to control, FOV can be restrictive and is not editable.
-Although it functions well, parkour remains fairly simplistic and could have been expanded.
Overall I really enjoyed the game experience, despite the cons. This game recieves 9/10 bacons.

Remember Me: Initial Impressions
PC gamers - if you've picked this up cheaply as part of the Steam Summer Sale, it's definitely worth a look, but USE A CONTROLLER. You'll love the nostalgic button-mashing and find yourself mentally yelling "C-C-C-COMBO BREAKERRRRRR!" every time you get hit in the head. I know, I know -  I had to dig my dusty Xbox 360 controller out of my two-year-old's toybox, but it was worth it for the fantastic dodging of raining blows and fighting fury. From my kid. Not the game.
Ahem. So far, Remember Me is visually stunning and sounds sublime, but I'm lamenting the lack of a free(er) camera to take in the sights with. As it is, from a third-person restricted perspective, Neo-Paris is breathtakingly beautiful in all its splendid squalour. I just wish I could go off track and explore a little more, which brings me to my next point about the game's linearity.
I think people have been a little harsh in their reviews of this game, although I'm only a couple of hours in. Yes, the combat is repetitive (again, try a controller) AND the gameplay is horribly linear, with no detours or optional quests so far (this was all the more amusing after The Stanley Parable) BUT the exquisite setting and the science fiction concepts are enough to make me want to go beyond the first act.
There's a lot of cliched, derivative gameplay and characterisation here - leaping around and hanging off walls, deranged bandit\raider\splicer-style enemies (what are they even called again? Leapers, yeah, that's it. Leapers) and the resulting comparisons between Nilin and Lara Croft are inevitable, but I'm choosing to view this game as an enjoyable pastiche of days and games gone by. There's enough familiarity to make it playable, and enough novelty to make it memorable.
In short, give it a go if you've got it. We'll see how the rest goes.

So here's the thing...
-This game isn't for everyone. It's absolutely a "Chill" experience, so if you're expecting a fast action game like COD or an easy builder like Minecraft, look elsewhere. It took a certain mind set to keep me playing beyond the 10+ hour mark (namely drunk and/or high).
-This game pretty much requires mods for the best experience (low flight, fast actions, SHUT UP!, as well as several graphics mods).
-This game is MUCH better now then it was at release. Yeah there are still bug aplenty (like the stupid way-point markers getting stuck on my screen or the annoying inability to view blueprints without a free slot) but for the most part you'll just be battling the sporadic FPS which for me is either a solid 30fps, 60fps or 14fps and random graphical glitches (who doesn't love invisible mountains?)
-THE GRIND... yeah you're gonna be grinding for everything, often, so if that's not your thing look elsewhere.
-The combat is meh at best. You've got special classes for both your starships as well as your multitool which confer special bonuses based on the class. A fighter class for your multitool will give higher damage bonuses then a mining class much like a fighter class starship will do higher damage than an explorer class. There are also different tiers (ranked C to S) which further increases the bonuses. All of this is great except while you can keep multiple ships, you can (as of yet) only keep one multitool. Which is very unfortunate as there are multiple weapon types each of which is unique (oddly there are weapon racks that you can place as a decoration but can't hold a multitool).
-THE GRIND... seriously, there's a lot of it and trying to find the exact planet, in the exact system, with the correct resource you need is sheer luck.
It might sound like I'm being very critical of this game (and I am) but that's only because I've come to like it so much. I've recently started replaying the game and the new updates since release have significantly improved the game. If it had released as it is now it would have been significantly more well received and if the next update is anywhere near as good as they say then I'm even more hyped.
So, in conclusion:
If you want a game to simply chill, relax and explore then this is your game, but if you want a fast paced action game or in depth story driven RPG look elsewhere.
Also photo mode is pretty amazing, and for the love of god let me rearrange my suit / ship / multitool upgrades without destroying them!!!

You know, I only bought into the series after seeing Trine 3 and thinking of how great this seemed. Maybe I'm one of the select few who looked at this and thought it was amazing. I've started the trilogy at the third game and even with the stupid and menial bugs/glitches I have seen, I would have to say that I really enjoy this game. I have enjoyed the concept and even though I have started at the last installment, I plan to venture into the previous games of the series. If, according to the reviews, this is the worst game of the trilogy, I look forward into heading backwards into the previous games. All in all, after seeing the value just in watching the trailer video for Trine 3, I bought into this series. It didn't take but a few minutes into this game that I have enjoyed the concept of Trine and looked forward to the depth and intrigue into this game. I can understand the feeling that there may have been a rush to push this third sequence, but for what it's worth I appreciate all aspects of this game. I would not rate this game a 10/10 in any means. but for the value of buying this trilogy on sale I feel the money is well spent. Even if you invest time into one of the games in this trilogy, it is money well spent.
Long story short, do not over look this game due to the negative reviews. It's a great pick up for the sale value. Today 12/1/15 the trilogy is $15 of which I think Trine 3 is worth the value. Watch a let's play or a walkthrough before you count this game out for the mixed reviews. You wont be disappointed, unless you highly detest the type of game, not the story or value as a whole. A very pretty game, both from a graphical and art style standpoint, which will permit this game to be one of those games that time will not diminish based on its appearance. The music is very nice, and it has a simple but emotional and entertaining story.
The game plays like a platformer with some shooting elements, and is really a Metroidvania style game at its core. Although the world isn't massive or anything, a few teleportation/fast travel spots would've helped cut out time that was spent just for the sake of killing time. Considering the game auto-aims attacks, I could just click wildly and everything died that I came across, and I was having to run across the entire game world to get to something, so it was just a time suck with no relevant events or things to do.
The game's difficulty is a bit...peculiar. Most of the time, you move about at your own pace, and taking the time to assess an area before just "going for it" can pay off in better execution and survival, as well as giving you more time to possibly spot secrets. Speaking of secrets, there are things you can interact with which will reveal parts of the map, and there is a skill tree thingy which will let you upgrade your abilities as well as uncover hidden items to boost your health and energy...although I never found one health upgrade because it wasn't marked on the map.
Back to the difficulty, though...when you complete one of the game's major sections, a very fast-paced 1-2 mistakes-gets-you-killed section will start up. You cannot save during these and every time you die, you have to start the whole segment over. These are some heavy rage-inducing segments unless you're just crazy good at platformers and don't mind doing the same part 20-30 times over and over again trying to do it perfectly. I would have much preferred checkpoints during these, or at least the option of having checkpoints if more hardcore individuals would like to turn the option off and welcome the annoying fast sections.
All that said, this is a Metroidvania game that looks and sounds very pretty, has some good gameplay, and despite rage-inducing parts and failed to flag one of the health upgrades despite this being promised by a skill in game, this is over all an enjoyable game I am glad to have played through. If the developer would add the missing health upgrade marker to the map and add the option for checkpoints during the fast segments, this could be an excellent experience.

So, brief thoughts: the game is amazing.
It took everything that worked in the New Order and improved it, and the story is outstanding.
I mean, it's not that it tries anything particularly new, but the New Order and the New Colossus stand out by taking unrealistic characters and making them human. All of the relationships in both games have believable and enjoyable dynamics, with real chemistry. The New Colossus doesn't trailblaze in this regard save for the fact it's an expansion of the same in the New Order, but the progression only gets more and more enjoyable.
And the gameplay, oh my god. The gameplay alone makes me want to come back again and again. The combat is so fun; it truly offers you the room to decide your own approach, without penalizing you for not going with stealth.
I mean, there is a HUGE incentive to go in guns-blazing; you get to kill more Nazis, which is what this game is all about. Wiping out the Nazis, like a true American.
My only complaint is the pacing. The ending felt out-of-left-field, though it was well done. The action is steadily escalating, so you think a final boss fight is going to occur..... then you're at the end. And you might not even realize it until the credits start rolling.
9/10, will play again, and recommend it to any old-school FPS fans.

The ideas are there.  The story progression is very cinematic and pretty much seamless.  The in-game logs are great if you want some backstory or history of the world of Neo-Paris... Graphics are pretty top-notch and inventive for a dystopian future.
The combo lab is a great idea.  However, the execution is awful.  The horrible delay and laggy controls just absolutely KILL this game for me.  I just must be used to instant cancels or something.  But there are times you'll attack, see an impending attack being telegraphed, and you'll hit 'Dodge' but Nilin will insist on NOT dodging, or just ROLL right into the attack.  I'm gonna try and beat it, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥..
EDIT after beating it (1/10/16) :  It's definitely a different experience and worth a sale purchase.  The story, the world of Neo-Paris, is worth some of the trouble going through the game.  Granted, I was playing on Memory Hunter and not sure yet if things are different going through on the Normal Difficulty.  The game does suffer from repetitiveness, and the main idea behind the combat needs to be fleshed out a little more.  But overall, the combat can be fun at times if everything goes right.  There are certain enemies in the game that can make the combat quite troublesome -- later on in the game there are robots that have a huge explosion radius that sometimes are very hard to dodge in closed-in hallways and rooms.  There are also lady cyborgs that show up in the second half that sometimes you won't know are there and will get in a free shot at you.
The dodging is still very finnicky, and there are telegraphs like sounds or visual animations, but you have to be super careful in your button presses, for the system likes to commit to attack animations.  There aren't very many cancel options and it can become grueling at times.  But I feel it is well worth the trouble to experience some feels towards the end of the game.
With that said, this is a game I'll probably play through again.  The game is pretty linear, but there are a few minor secrets you can find throughout the game, and sometimes just looking at the sights and finding secrets is a good break from the somewhat frustrating combat.
I HAVE changed my recommendation, because after beating the game and sifting through the artwork and story of the world -- a LOT has been put into the artwork, story, and characters.  I feel that the gameplay was kinda cut short because of that reason and who knows whose fault that is (theirs or Capcom's).  But all in all, I feel Remember Me does deserve a chance, and if DONTNOD were to go back and address certain gameplay issues with a (spiritual) sequel to this, I'd be more than willing to give it a go.

Remember Me is an exciting and immersive fighting game set in the sci-fi world of NeoParis. The campaign should take anywhere from 8-10 hours and is broken into 8 episodes. Each episode generally brings new, more difficult enemies along with some fantastic top of the line scenery. Seriously, one of the best features of this game is its environment. It's absolutely beautiful.
The game's story is fullfilling as well. Despite what others may say, the story is captivating and emotional. You can feel the main character's pain, Nilin, as she attempts to cope with relearning all her past actions as a memory hunter. You'll finish each episode yearning to know what happens next.
The combat is crisp and rewarding, and plays similarly to Batman. The variety of pressens available - aka the types of combat moves (power, regen, cooldown, and chain) - add variety to the combat system. On top of that, each combat move is unique so you can customize your combo bars in which ever manner pleases you most.
There are also S-Pressens, which are special power moves on a cooldown. These allow you to activate powerful abilities that will come in very handy during boss fights or other tough situations. There are 5 unique S-Pressens that come with their own special effects and purpose throughout the game.
I would highly recommend this game to any gamer who enjoy a story centric campaign with fighting elements.

Okay, Let me first start with this: Yes, they did lie or stretch the abilities of this game and what you can do through launch, but that doesn't change the fact of what this game is now and what it is to be in the future.
(Read Bottom For Overall)
No Mans Sky is an adventure RPG-type sandbox (To a degree). Most negative reviews are of those who have spent more time trying to critic it for what it doesnt have rather then play it for what it does.
When you start off in the game, you are already given an objective with a fairly easy guide to how to achieve it. The game is easy to learn, so there is no complaining about that. It does take time to do things in this game but not in a fact where you just sit still for hours and hours grinding, but more so an action-based adventure that you partake in to achieve goals such as getting supplies, looting bases, and interacting with other life forms.
This game is beautiful, and if you don't believe me, check out some screenshots I have taken
Other then being aesthetically beautiful, the game has a real given for adventure. Once repairing and obtaining your ship, you're able to explore an endless galaxy with dozens of different planet types as well as dozens of different weather patterns, species, and wildlife on planets. There is also tons of differents types of planets, like hot planets, temperate planets, hostile planets, poisoness planets, raining acid planets, raining magma, ice planets, peaceful planets, water worlds, and many more.
Not only that, but the game is constantly updating, whether it be adding new items, vehicles, planets, species, or fixing bugs and adding small details, it is in a constant point of making itself better.
Throughout your time on No Mans Sky, you are broadcasted different objectives and side missions you can complete other then going straight for the main goal of achieving the Atlas or getting to the center of the universe. You can ingage in space combat with either hostile cargo ships, bandits, or fleets of ships trying to destroy friendly frieghters. Some of these battles can be easy, but some can be very challeging at points, and it involves a lot of skill for flying and shooting. You can also be given coordinates to different temples to where you can learn different species's languages as well as find crashed ships that you have the possibility to repair and take as your own. You also can break into different bases to loot and find coordinates to other bases or objectives around the planet or system.
Yes with every game there are negatives, but this game should not be shamed on for what it doesn't provide to the players.
First off, it was promised to players to have multiplayers, and in some degree there is, but you can not interact with those players, which is a really big negative. Though even though it doesnt have multiplayer, this game runs and plays like a singleplayer game.
Next is time. This game takes a while to complete, or more/less play. You need patience with obtaining certain goals in the game, but realistically it does make sense to where you need to go or what you need to grab.
Dying is a pain. If you die, you lose everything in your inventory worth while achieving, so storing most of your valuables in your starship is a big go to, but being that your starship has limited room, sometimes it is agrovating getting items to which you cant take or finding out which items to get rid of because you dont have enough room.
You need to play with stradegy. If you spawn on a cold planet and you need to get something far away, you need to learn how to conserve your supplies to when you REALLY need it as well as finding shelter around your area for when you need to rest or heal. Also paying attention to what is around you is HUGE, because finding resources could be difficult if you dont know where to look, because sometimes they could be right next to you.
Overall this game is honestly fun to play in the end. It's time consuming (in a good way), its challenging but fun, and overall just a gem of a good time. Though I will agree this game is not completely worth the 60 dollars, but if it were on sale for 30, I would definitely suggest giving it a try.

99% of you are expecting Elite: Dangerous. If you want Elite: Dangerous, go buy Elite: Dangerous. If you already have Elite: Dangerous, carry on playing Elite: Dangerous. If you haven't played Elite: Dangerous and want to explore a huge galaxy without or without your friends, trade all the goods, shoot all the things, buy all the upgrades, etc. then buy Elite: Dangerous. No Man's Sky is NOT Elite: Dangerous.
Still here? Okay, No Man's Sky isn't a game in the traditional sense. Think of it more of a chillout experience, the sort of thing you play during that downtime between "proper" games. The basic game loop is set up such that you can jump in for as little or as long as you like and still make some progress, but really sustained gaming sessions for hours/day/weeks on end will just drain your ability to enjoy NMS for what it is. You'll be doing a LOT of resource collecting. No, really, a TON of resource collecting. You'd better enjoy resource collecting, because that's what you do for about 90% of the game, all of which serve to push you to new star systems and new planets -- mostly windswept, desolate hellholes, but push closer to the center of the galaxy and you might (MIGHT!) finally get that lush forest with the stampeding dinosaurs you saw in the trailer.
Is it fun to play? Maybe... That all depends on your ability to ride the wave of grind and whether or not an aesthetic reward (the occasional beautiful vista) is enough of a reward. Hello Games, to their credit, have been politely ignoring the vitriol surrounding the game and have pushed out a number of updates that add some interesting features, including base building for the sandboxers and new land vehicles for the explorers. It's not quite enough to push NMS into the realms of a bona fide sandbox experience to rival Minecraft, nor is there anything vaguely resembling a triple-A gaming experience on offer (which makes that $60 price tag, still there a year after release, nothing short of ridiculous), but if you can wait for a sale and want something you can dip in and out of while occupying your brain with something else (maybe your favorite gaming podcast) then by all means give it a whirl.

Before I begin, I'd just like to say I've been playing games for over 15 years and rarely feel the need to share my opinions with the internet. The reason I felt compelled to write a review in this case is the game's quality and subject matter, combined with my own life experiences.
As for specific elements of the game, let's start with the sword combat system. It's fairly barebones and doesn't provide much of a challenge, but thanks to fluid animation and impressive enemy design can feel quite satisfying once you get used to the flow of it. With that being said, the majority of playing time is spent exploring and interacting with linear environments and protagonist's hallucinations, for example by solving puzzles. It's worth noting that many sections feel more like an intense psychological horror rather than usual action/adventure. In my eyes, Hellblade's biggest strength is the dark, oppressive atmosphere that's cleverly constructed by use of surreal graphics, binaural sound and mature writing. Overall, I think all of the above elements combine to form an experience that's unusual but at the same time well designed and thematically coherent.
Perhaps more importantly, Hellblade is also a well-researched and deeply moving study in severe mental illness, specifically psychosis. It goes above and beyond what I've seen on the subject in almost any game. It not only asks questions about the nature of reality as we experience it but also provides commentary on relationships of those suffering from mental illness with their family members and society at large. If you are affected by these issues directly or through your loved ones, the game will speak volumes to you. Even if you don't have this kind of baggage, I believe you will still be presented with a lot to ponder over. Personally, I struggle to think of even a handful of other games (and I've played a few good ones) that actually made me look differently at those close to me and reevaluate, as was the case with Hellblade. That is why I'm recommending it to you.
