This game would have been a lot better if there had been more combat. Seriously, only like 1/3 of the game was actual combat, while the rest was just walking around and talking to people, which gets tedious really quickly.
Not that the combat was anything spectacular, just your standard hack'n'slash fare, only really, really easy. The enemies spend a lot of the time standing there and letting you attack them, i literally never used the block button. And if you do get down to low health, you can just walk away for a few seconds and your health regenerates. I didn't die until the final boss fight, and that's only because it took me a while to figure out how i was supposed to kill him.
The only real positive was the interesting character progression system, where you complete deeds (save a villager, kill X enemies, etc.) and then dedicate those deeds to one of four gods to gain favour with those gods, and gaining enough favour with a specific god grants you a skill point to spend on that god's skill tree, with each god representing a different combat style.
The story was OK, but the whole plot of the myth has been completely changed (instead of collecting the Fleece to restore his fathers kingdom, Jason only wants it to resurrect his dead wife) and all the characters are there, but they are completely different from their mythic counterparts, especially Medea, who instead of being a key part of the story, is just another Argonaut.
All in all it was a pretty average game, but being a big fan of Greek myth i found it mildly enjoyable, despite being annoyed by the changes from the myth. However, I can't recommend it given how most of the game is spent in boring conversations. If there had been more action, I would recommend it, but sadly, there isn't enough to keep the game interesting.
I also encountered frequent crashes at seemingly random points, but I can't say for sure if it's the game or my computer. However given that i can play more recent and far more graphically demanding titles than this, it seems likely that it's the game that's at fault.

Rogue State... the humoristic post-revolution country management simulator.
A nice idea, layout and attempt to deliver a realistic experience but the game have not what it takes to give us sufficient interest and life span.
[Game refunded: Review won't be updated]
The revolution is over and King Salman is dead. You are the leader of the new government of Basenji: a fictive country of Middle East based on the name of a dog. It's up to you to restore the pride and power of your state and create a reign that last for thousand years...
The intro is nice, based on pictures well drawn. The game takes place in your office and situation room. Every selections of menus makes your avatar ( a man or a women) move across the rooms and open/use appropriates elements related to menus. The game looks nice, only characters are a bit "frozen" and loose in realism. Something very nice is the presence of a newspaper. You can check some important info  and every headlines feature photographs depending of recent news. The only really problematic thing about newspaper is the color of text. When some white letters are on black and white photos it lacks in transparency!
Nice oriental tunes that stick to the atmosphere of the tile. Voice acting is correct but not impressive. Nothing special to say about this aspect of the game.
Choosing the office of the character is a good and a bad idea. Especially if any menu selections forces you to wait for your avatar to move and activate the selected item related to it. Need to check relations and trade? Select the phone and wait your man or women to take it. Need to read newspapers... wait him or her to cross the room to open it. Ect... ect... ect... Very annoying especially about trading and diplomacy. But let's talk about gameplay would you.
You are the leader of a so called Rogue State. After having created your president/future dictator, you must appoint your ministers and your brother Farouk to vacant roles.
The first issue of the game is the presence of Farouk, a general famous in the revolution and loved by the people.
You can't trust him and sacrifice a part of your ministry for him. Considering he's a burden, you are forced to put him in the worst job: intelligence. Every other seat are important and quite early shows the limits of the game:
Lacks of information (funny when you think that intelligence is a dark and useless aspect of the game).
So you have 3 others politicians, randomly generated and members of 1 of the factions of the country: Patriots, Capitalists, Fundamentalists and Liberals.
The game acts around turns where you have to do actions and try to give the best of the time you have at disposal.  To manage factions you have to choose Policies and try to balance popularity between every faction. In general to please your people acts around reading the newspapers to see how much percent of factions compose your country and after you try to balance the most important ones and please them with buildings and ministry favors. Consider that policies can change from a turn to another without any drawbacks and you have a first clue of how simplistic the game is.
But this is not all because in Rogue State you can build things...
At beginning you must rebuild the country and industries. Few choices with not much impact crosses your path, like amnesty for previous members of brought down government or not. This part sum up quite badly the reconstruction of a country after war. When done you can produce 2 resources and access to 3 panels: Army, Social, and Economic.
Very simple, a building rarely give permanent bonuses and quite often asks for a lot of funds to give a one-time bonus that might be spoiled by a random event. Because events are common in the game.
Indeed every turn has events, completely random that influence factions, popularity and loyalty.
Very often you have to sacrifice a faction and even pay lot of money to get rid of these unpleasant events. 40 % of your country is full of capitalists? Only focus on money and do not care of environmental events.
Many fundamentalists? Nevers authorize western corporations in your country. Ect… ect...
Extremely boring, it is amazing to see ridiculous events such as the Meteorite when if you have a space program... you can put a device on it and change its course... But if you don't it will blow one of you buildings.
Goodbye freshly built Stadium! Goodbye Sweetshop!
Ridiculous.
But that's not all. A building requires money. You can trade with the 3 neighbor country bordering your country.
You take your phone and give a call to each leader to find the best prices and sign contracts for export or import.
Resources are random and very often you won't have the one you need to please your factions.
Of course good relations gives better prices, also the market influences the prices.
But to know what kind of resource your neighbor needs depends of intelligence... and if you remember that intelligence is a completely unexplained element.
Add to that the fact that every phone calls uses one of the 4 segments of time that composes a turn... you bet that trades are horribly basic and falls into boredom very quickly.
Rogue State tries to play at war too. That's why the situation room is right next to your office...
You can buy troops, influenced by Army buildings in terms of price and deployment time. Each unit has attack and defense. And of course, the more powerful the more expensive.
There is a situation map where you can move your "pawns" and declare war but without any infos about attackers or how to manage fights.
You can also manage intelligence and secret projects that takes time and money but bring (apparently) very powerful effects... but you won't have time to see them finished.
Because: You remember of Farouk ? Your dear brother waits a moment of weakness to turn upside down your government.
And it's where the game fall into a waste of time because you are forced to mass tons of units and rally many favors to temporary slow the revolution prepared by Farouk (don't forget to click on the button on top right because the game doesn't even takes time to explain this...).
It is so empty and baffling that i never succeeded to survive this moment.
Even if i had 3 factions pleased and a nice popularity but not much money... i've lost the game.
Because in Rogue State you build, makes your country a safer place by building tons of institutions and nobody gives a @@@ about it. Even taxes are unexplained and you can tax 50 % of your income and know absolutely nothing about its effects of the population....
Ridiculous.

Rogue State is a disappointment. Too simplistic, the game falls very quickly into boring text reading and random events that causes havoc into your miserable tries.
Even managing your ministry is a joke where ministers acts stupidly and asks for ridiculous actions.
Even if there nothing wrong with them!

This is an absolutely brilliant game for a casual multiplayer session with a couple of friends.
First of all, I'm not sure I'd play it singleplayer, as the storyline is lacklustre (something about magic and an ancient artefact, I think) and the gameplay laborious. but add another player and that's where it really shines. It plays like a platformer/puzzler hybrid and two or three players combining the different abilities of the characters makes for endless fun.
Secondly, play with an Xbox controller (or similar). The keyboard/mouse controls are not so great, but it's really fluid with a controller - and this is coming from a PC gamer who has almost never used a gamepad.
Essentially this game has you (and/or your friends) as a wizard (with abilities to conjour boxes etc), a knight (with a sword and magical shield) and a thief (with a grappling hook and bow). All of these abilities are well bnalanced, and you will find yourself having to use all three characters as you work around the puzzles in your way. There might be any number of solutions to a given puzzle, so it's worth trying all the characters.
Finally, this game has recieved a graphical overhaul and looks absolutely beautiful. The 'theme' is a very colourful fairytale look, with locations from enchanted forests with colourful flowers, giant leaves and massive snails to underground caverns with glowing crystals and bottomless pits. It's essentially a 2.5D game (3D animation in a 2D plane), but don't let that put you off - the backgrounds and lighting are very impressive.
Definitely a 9/10 - loses the one point for the weak storyline and crazy boss level, but it's still a really fun game. Definitely worth picking up.

Rogue State fills a specific niche very well - very challenging, procedurally generated( never the same twice), self aware, and valuing content over presentation/story. At it's core it is a strategic political simulation game putting you in charge of a middle eastern country.  There are also strong emphasis on survival over crafting the your country as you see fit.  Surviving is difficult, and unlike other mangement survival games like Long Live the Queen there is some randomness, which can ruin the experience for some, but it also increases replayability. Many things threaten your survival, revolts from factions within your populace (patriots, liberals, captialists, and fundamentalists), your power hungry brother, your military, your own government's cabinet, your neigbors, democratic rebellions, disease, envnironment and financial crises, and even the meddling United States.  It may take several playthroughs to see all of these threats, and the most problematic threat to your power is almost never the same on back to back new games.
Though random, you do have hints to what you should focus on that are simple to miss, such as paying attention to random events, analyzing the breakdown of people who are in each faction or using information gained through your intelligence agency. However, that being said there are some good things that are always good -  keeping a large surplus of money around of diasters and investing into your economy and social programs with somewhat high taxes.   I also like how this game can be subtle.  You are actually a dictator and one of the scenarios confirms this when a group threatens your regime with a democratic revolution.  This is easy to overlook because the game rewards you for being a benevolent dictator, and the absence of elections during the whole game is easier to miss than you think when the game doesn't paint you as the stereotypical evil dictator.
This game may turn off some with its unpolished retro graphics and empasis on strategy over a story, but I believe it targets a specific target demographic well.  If you are ready for challenege, can overlook a somewhat dated presentation, and are aware this is more of a survival/management game that rewards for you playing to the situation faced rather than roleplaying as you see fit, this is the game for you.

I am a "latecomer" to FO3; that is to say, I didn't even think about playing it until I confided to a friend or two that I would like to play a game that's "like Skyrim, except with guns."
To be sure, this game is much, *much* more than just Skyrim with guns.  From the intro screen, to the environment, to the NPC conversations, to the ever-important Pip-Boy menus, this game is relentlessly and beautifully immersive.  I can count on one hand the number of times in which I felt so much as if I was part of the world generated by the game, and FO3 is definitely one of the proud few.
FO3 also has an impressive and compelling storyline that has a lot of "heart and mind" invested into it.  Even the DLCs- some of which are definitely "out there" as far as plot and setting are concerned- bring a worthwhile component to the overall gaming experience.  I never once felt that I was doing a quest or handling a conflict just so I could "get it over with," in fact I appreciate the design and flow of the several different quests such that they are able to be intermingled with each other- and not necessarily the ones that follow the main storyline either!
To wrap things up, FO3 is an excellent RPG as imagined through an innovative FPS, open-world format.  The graphics, variety of NPCs and enemies, weapon selection, environment design, clever application and/or tweaking of scientific and historical fact, brain-teaser puzzles, and dramatic encounters are all well-done and worthy of applause.  I think this game has something for everyone, and would gladly recommend this game- even today- to someone who asks for one or more of the experiences that FO3 offers to the player.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is one of a number of games released in the last few years that succesfully tackles a popular but well-worn genre, and manages to be both faithful to the genre style, whilst streamlining the experience, leaving it feeling both new and deeply nostalgic at the same time.
This game is one of the more fun isometric RPGs I've played, and I'd call myself a harsh critic of the genre. This and Torchlight 2 are probably my favourites, and share a lot in common in terms of updating and streamlining the experience. TIAVH is generally a well-made game, and despite some issues with player-character pathfinding, I can't really fault the production quality. It has wonderfully schlocky voice acting, humourous dialogue, lovely visuals, a deep, deep skill tree that you'll never completely discover in one playthorough, a streamlined inventory, tonnes of enemy types, plenty of wonderful locations, and LOTS of loot. The game also rewards you regularly with achievements, which keeps you pushing forward.
With that being said, it doesn't reinvent the wheel, meaning that some of the clunkier core mechanics of the isometric RPG classics remain intact. Expect repetition, a relentless onslaught of enemies, lots of useless loot, and sharp, frustrating spikes in difficulty, particularly towards the last 25% of the game.
While this does stick to a classic (and some might say tired) formula, the depth of the skill trees, the frequent validation by achievements, and the sheer personality of the characters and the world keep me playing onwards.
Even with any gripes I have towards genre, I'd recommend this for full price, as the sheer depth of content will surely leave you feeling satisfied with your purchase. I hear that the sequel is even better, and I can't wait to play it!

I'll be the first to admit that this is an odd action adventure game. The combat relies on the execution of well-timed combos. Combos which you can and must define yourself. An interesting idea that breaks with usual genre conventions, but ends up feeling not really satisfying. Maybe because this mechanic forces you to perform accurately timed button presses all the time, which keeps the player from truly enjoying some sort of flow of combat.
Another quite interesting aspect is the ability to remix memories. Basically you have to manipulate an ingame cutscene, which you can forward and rewind, to ultimately change the outcome to the one you desire. From a purely gameplay perspective this is indeed questionable, but it's an interesting variation of storytelling and does build atmosphere. You don't get to do this often during the game though.
The rest of the gameplay mainly consists of horribly stilted platforming, trivial puzzles and walking around a scrictly linear path. Doesn't sound too exciting overall. The reason why I still immensly enjoyed Remember Me lies in the unusual science fiction scenario that manages to build an immersive atmosphere. Certainly not for everyone!

This review would be positive, except for one thing dragging it down: Glitches. There is a bug that prevents the host from using a controller in co-op, and with absolutely horrid KBM controls, this is practically gamebreaking. Using a controller in single player makes the game think you are trying to drop in a second local player. Secondly, alt-tabbing will change the game resolution back to the lowest setting every time, as well as lock your mouse into a small square of movement both in game and on your desktop. Oh, and each time I quit the game, my refresh rate is lowered back to 60. Add on to that things like your character randomly being stuck in one direction when using a certain tool, button prompts and lables randomly not working until you leave the world, and everything being locked behind boring repetitive quests, Lego Worlds is a bit of a mess.
Currently the developers say they are aware of the controller bug, but it's been a problem since release and there is still no patch. This isn't something you let sit for days. Lego games have always been sort of buggy, but this just proves TT has an issue when it comes to anything beyond a single player movie clone.
Also, a lot of the positive reviews of this game are from the alpha, before they locked being able to create your own world behind 100 gold bricks.

This game is Early Access done right.
I bought this game the day it released, I've always been a fan of Lego games, ever since the first Lego Star Wars for PS2. The idea of an open world PC exclusive seemed too good to be true, and upon playing the game for the first time, it almost was. You could generate a randomized level, run around to get some studs and unlock some objects and weapons, but there was nothing to do, it felt really empty. I disliked the game for the reason people are currently slamming No Man's Sky, it's big but it's empty and there's nothing to do.
Fast forward to yesterday, I was scrolling through my Steam library and I stumbled upon this game again, but this time, I noticed a news article that said that this game was now out of Early Access. My first thought was "A game actually left Early Access? That's new.". I launched the game and immediately felt like I was in a 100% completed, full game, all because of one big element; the cutscene.
This game now starts with a cutscene that gives you a rundown of what you are, what you're doing, and what to expect. Then, upon starting a new game, you get another cutscene! This one is sort of a secondary, more specific intro. You then get a few tutorial worlds to unlock the tools you'll be using and get the hang of the controls (which, as a first for a Lego game on PC, actually work just fine with a keyboard and mouse!). You get a warm and inviting voice guiding you through the first few worlds, but it doesn't feel like the typical modern hand-holding tutorial, if you want to run the other way and launch chickens into the ocean, you can do that too.
The only thing I would change is the ship. I had mentioned No Man's Sky earlier, and honestly, this game would be the perfect replacement for that if, instead of the ship flying being a loading screen, you could actually fly between worlds openly. However, considering how far this game has come since it started, I wouldn't rule out open space travel in the future.
Overall a solid 8/10 for a game in general, 9/10 for a Lego game, definitely worth the money and time.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a game that I didn't want to like, largely because I was familiar with the developers and their previous exploits, and initially, I was confronted with a powerful intro that, for a few moments, made me wonder whether or not I was capable of liking the game if it could pull itself along.
The fact of the matter is, it could not.
When I first heard about the game, I heard that Ninja Theory was producing another action game. I didn't give a crap, because it was Ninja Theory. These're the guys who called game stories trite, and in the same breath, decided to make a game about a half demon, half angel demon hunter and his brother who kills unborn fetuses.
That kind of says something, doesn't it?
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice lacks the redeeming qualities of a 'good game,' it instead wants to sell you on its story, but unfortunately, there's a problem with that. It starts you off with a fair introduction to Senua's psychosis, of the different voices in her head. Immediately, these voices are played a production manager's idea of playing around with surround-sound, and while the effect is somewhat distasteful, the implementation is actually quite impressive.
Approximately two and a half minutes later, you're off the boat, the voices are immediately dialed back, and Senua's psychosis becomes less psychosis and more a hamhanded tool for narration. Instead of managing to put you off, or giving you any real reason to doubt Senua's abilities to proceed, these voices are instead, time and time again, used for exposition.
Oh, but right, there's a story there? It's supposed to be interesting, right? Well, before you can get through that, you have to go through the gameplay rotation. In Senua's Sacrifice, there are three main gameplay elements you will be continually faced with. You have the "find the shape game," which will ONLY begin AFTER you proceed to "look" or "focus" upon the gate you need to use to exit the area.
And that find the shape game? You're finding nordic runes, hidden in the environment. Of course, like any typical find the shape game, once you've done it, the game's over and the object or shape hidden immediately sticks out like a sore thumb, but once again, you have to begin this game at the gate. Walk past something you recognize as a Nordic rune? "Focus" on it and see the rune in particle effects in the air? Go walk to that gate and come back bub, because this is a Scripted Linear Narrative Experience™.
But hey, we've gotten past that, so what're we onto next? Well, there's the combat that's intersparsed between the find shape game and the other major gameplay... Mechanic? Anyway, that combat basically amounts to a Light combo, Heavy finisher system,  in which the animations are fairly fluid, there is a certain degree of flow and responsiveness, but there is both no real challenge presented by the enemies except when they outnumber you and neither is there any reward for doing well.
Except wait, jeeze, I'm sorry. You came here for the STORY right? God, I'm so sorry, but you see, you have to just go through this one little, teensy, tiny thing to keep going on through the story, and can you guess what that is? If you said "A time-limited sprint from point A to point B that kills you if you go the wrong way/don't stay in the lines/don't do what the developers wanted you to do" weeeeeell, Johnny boy, you might just be right. And oddly accurate at guessing which part of the bottom of the barrel Ninja Theory scraped off of to come up with that idea.
So, I mean, hey. This game might, MIGHT have a cool story to it, or some interesting characters or ideas, but Ninja Theory tried too hard to make the normal concessions of a game blend with their narrative experience and failed, presenting instead a hurdle for you to cross the more you want to be engaged by the story. Also, the people who support this game are pretty tumblr-esque, so expect this review to go up in flames for my explanation of what awaits you should you try to boot up Senua's Sacrifice.
And if my hours on record with this particular game causes you to doubt, the accuracy of my statements regarding the gameplay loop after 30 minutes or more should prove my point. This game offers little bits of itself in the form of lore and story, dangled between the mangled carcass of a bad, bad game.
Oh, yeah, and it's completely ♥♥♥♥ing broken for a whole bunch of people. Not myself, but big folks like Jim Sterling and such, also, don't backtrack. No. Really. Don't backtrack in a Ninja Theory game.
...I ♥♥♥♥in' warned you.

I cannot recommend this game highly enough. Everything about it is incredible. The visuals, the graphics (I'm making a difference here because they're both awesome), the sound design, the music, the story. And I'm not even finished with the game yet. Maybe I shouldn't jump to conclusions like that, but Hellblade is just something else...
First, the visuals (as opposed to the graphics). The environment is just stunning. The weather effects are incredible. The background - if you can call it a background since the level transitions are so fluid I for one never even noticed them (the level transitions) - is breathtaking.
The graphics. I couldn't believe them when I first saw the game. Hellblade's graphical capabilities are next-generation, and yet the game ran great on my computer, which needs a bit of upgrading. Senua doesn't have any regular interaction with the environment, but so what, who's looking at the ground when the polygon count is so damn high?
Everyone was talking about the sound design in the game, the binaural audio. Let me tell you, it really is incredible. You need headphones, a good pair if you can. Then, sit back (don't sit back, you're playing a game!) and be engrossed in the world and mind of Senua. It's such a unique experience. I would suggest turning off notifications as well, to get that full experience, with no distractions.
The music is so great. It picks up during combat and cutscenes (not always, though). Since the game is set in an ancient Celtic and Norse time, you get this epic music themed after the time period. I won't spoil it.
Speaking of spoiling, the story is beautiful. I don't think it's something that a person playing this game can really relate to, (trying to save your lover from the depths of the Norse version of Hell, and at the same time suffering from psychosis) but you play a woman warrior who suffers an unimaginable amount of pain, but does not give up. It is a story that makes you want to keep playing, thinking, she can do it, she can do it, oh my god she can't do it, oh my god she CAN do it! I love it, and Senua is now one of my heroes.
In conclusion (wow, did I just make a high school-worthy essay? That's kinda sad, honestly) this game's got just about everything. Even the combat is simple and fun. I read from a user named Morti
I couldn't agree more. This is a game where you absorb yourself into it, and you have no distractions. You experience the story. 11/10. The extra 1 is for surprising me with how amazing it is.

This journey will keep your interest from beginning to end, and then you'll want to play it again.

I've had about 15 people download this to play no problem.  I've heard Skype screenshare might also work but I haven't tried it.  I've had nothing but poor experiences with Skpye so I can't be bothered to try it anyways.
My process: First off I gather up the people I'm playing with in Teamspeak (Mumble/Skype/Steam Voice Chat/etc also work), it's usually just whoever is there and then we'll try to get a few more in, prefarably 8.  Next I open up Teamviewer and start a presentation, making sure I have my performance meter set as high as it will go.  I am then given a code to give to everyone that they put into the Teamviewer app and they instantly join my presentation no problem.  I give them all some time to look at my cute wallpapers while I wait for everyone to join of course.  When everyone is in I open up the game in windowed mode and display it on my second monitor.  You CAN do this with one monitor but then either your display will be really small for everyone or you will have to write down your answers via phone/tablet.  I click on the preview settings on my Teamviewer and have it display ONLY the game on the second monitor, then my primary monitor is open for answer input/whatever else you want.  Start the lobby, have everyone join Jackbox.tv, make sure they can see both your screen on Teamviewer and their input device (we all use the web browser) and you're ready to go.
The problems with my method:  I have been disconnected from team viewer one time in the 8 hours I've played this game with everyone and had to have everyone join a new presentation.  Also there is VERY NOTICABLE FPS lag and it can look very bad, but everyone agrees it is completely playable since there is no delay.  I would not reccomend this method for anything other than playing party games.  By the way, only one person needs to buy this game, everyone else just watches the Teamviewer/web input device.

This is a great pack of games marred by its terrible multiplayer support.
There are 5 games included in the Jackbox, and of these You Don't Know Jack, Drawful, and Fibbage are the ones you're buying, with Word Spud and Lie Swatter filling in the gaps.  I've supplied a mini-review of each game below as well as a remark on the bad multiplayer, because this is the kind of game that thrives on a party.
YDKJ 2015 is more of what you love: a trivia game full of satire and rib-rubbing, with in-jokes and pop culture sprinkled healthily over top and a healthy dollop of the just plain bizzare.  It is somewhat of a Jeopardy for the MTV crowd, and is even split into individual 'episodes'.  Once you've played through all of the episodes, you'll start to repeat questions and the game loses some lustre, but that should not dissuade you, because You Don't Know Jack is famed for its writing and the snide side-remarks of its host.  You're definitely getting your money's worth with YDKJ alone. (9/10)
Fibbage is a game of lying to your friends.  A Jeopardy-like question is phrased, but with a missing word and its up to you and your friends to supply a word to fill the blank.  Once done, all the submissions are displayed with the TRUE answer, and its up to you to puzzle out which of the words is the truth, and which are your friends' submissions.  It's great fun, but can be ruined by the game not having sufficient duplication-detection.  This is a problem when someone typos a word, or adds "the" or "a" in front of a similar submission by someone else, which causes the game to display both (now obviously wrong) submissions, which makes it very easy to discern the truth.  Only a minor problem, because the game is still a blast despite this.  I've yet to play through all the questions, but my understanding is that there's not nearly enough.  That said, what's there should keep you reasonably occupied.  8/10
Drawful is identical in nature to Fibbage, with the exception that instead of being shown a phrase and filling in a blank, you are instead asked to draw something.  It's easily the best game of the set, and art skill is not required.  In fact, the worse you are, the better it is.  Once you're done drawing, friends add a title to your artwork, and then try to guess the "true" title from the list of submissions.  The game is incredibly sneaky, and will even misspell some of the "true" titles in an attempt to make them appear to be user-submitted.  It's great fun, but loses points for not having any kind of erase function (a big problem when your are tapping your phone to keep it awake during the game).  It's easily the most fun I've had with this whole pack so far though, and still earns top marks despite (or because of) people instantly resorting to drawing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.  9/10
WordSpud is a stream-of-conciousness typing game.  A word is displayed, and its up to you to complete a phrase using that word.  The end word of your phrase then becomes the beginning word for the next player, and so on.  Players yea/nay each submission, and the number of yeas/nays are given as points.  This is where the game falls apart, because it relys on charity.  It's easy to simply "nay" each submission and subtract points from your friends.  There's no objective scoring, and each game devolves accordingly. 5/10
Lie Swatter is a game to bust out if you've got a real bone-fide party going on.  Anyone can join a game in progress, and the game supports up to 100 players.  The game displays a statement, and its up to everyone playing to buzz in whether its Truth or False.  Some good trivia to be found here, but the game lacks personality.  The game is really You Don't Know Jack "Lite", with all the weird questions but with none of the charm or satire of YDKJ's over-the-top host.  6/10
__________
This is all well and good, but there is a crucial flaw in every single one of these games:  The Jackbox does *NOT* support local multiplayer, *NOR* does it support online multiplayer.  Instead, it horribly butchers both.
Let me explain: The Jackbox has controller support, but only for single player.  If you have 2 or more players (and you should, because its a f---ing "party pack") then you *must* connect through "Jackbox.TV", a website set up specifically for this purpose.  Players use their phones, tablets, or laptops and navigate to the site, enter a 4-character code and join the game.  Each player is controls the game by typing, drawing, or tapping the virtual buttons on their device.  In theory, this is great.  In practice Jackbox.TV requires a relatively new smartphone.  If you're using Windows Phone, Blackberry, or an Android device older than 4.X, or an older i-Device, you're♥♥♥♥♥♥outta-luck.  This is a total bummer for a game that purports to be able to be played "on your phone or tablet".  Even on a laptop, IE is not supported and you must use Chrome or FF.
This ruins the fun by a significant margin.  You'd think that if someone's phone is incompatible that you could use one of those controllers sitting around, but the Jackbox bizarrely removes support for controllers in multiplayer.  It's a crippling blow to a great game.  If you have multiple controllers, a keyboard, and multiple mobile devices, each should be able to connect and play, but instead only mobile is supported for multiplayer, and even then only mobile devices meeting the very specific criteria of being able to support WebSockets (there's a website to check if your browser supports websockets).
You Don't Know Jack is very time-sensitive, and it's frustrating if your mobile data ends up being fractionally slower than someone elses'.  Again, something that controllers have solved years ago, but someone at Jackbox Games thinks that you only own one controller.
Do your research.  The Jackbox still gets a "yes" from me but honestly it's a close one.  The "phones-only" multiplayer really cripples this otherwise great pack of games.  It could easily benefit from having a free app that provided better support for phones that don't have WebSocket-capable browsers, or by supporting controllers and the keyboard in local multiplayer.

In a cliched world of action RPGs involving medieval/fantasy type settings, it’s refreshing to discover Neocore’s 19th century steampunk gothic-noir type game,
The game’s ambience of nighttime villages and murky swamps accompanied by a greatly appropriate soundtrack will keep you playing until your index finger gets numb.
Character class and selection is so varied the game will probably warrant more than a single playthrough to flesh out all of its possibilities. Upon seeing the blank skill tree when first starting out it’s almost mind blowing to wonder where you’re going to put all of the skills, perks and auras the game allows you to. It’s not quite the endless skill tree as
but it’s deep enough you’ll feel your character grow as you play. Enemies come in waves, overwhelmingly so. I played a range character and being able to kite the enemies helped somewhat. If you decide to play as a melee class I think you’ll have your work cut out for you.
Neocore is a small publisher out of Hungary, and big publishers could take some lessons from these guys. I’ve never had the desire to play an RPG through more than once until I played this. Despite the trappings, however, all is not perfect. There was no game manual included in the download, and for the developers to instruct players to read online forums and watch online videos to learn simple instructions about the game bears little in the way of professionalism. Once I learned how “rage” (the energy required to do super attacks, acquired through killing NPCs) worked I was able to accomplish much more. Some creatures in the game had an attribute called Abomination. I never did find out exactly what that was. And the final boss fight involved a lot of lag for me. I died many times because I simply lagged out. Definitely not a deal breaker, but it made that final fight more difficult than it had any right to be. This may or may not be an issue affecting anybody else. I have a state of the art rig, and I was surprised the lag even occured.
Still, I’m glad I found this game. I look forward to playing through it again, experimenting with another class. And then I’ll look forward to tackling Neocore’s sophomore effort,

Once in a while, a game surprises you.  It might have a surprisingly epic scope, innovative gameplay, or familiar gameplay done exceptionally well.  It might put an innovative spin on an old franchise, or deconstruct long running video game conventions.  Then there's little gems like this.
To the Moon took me only about three and a half hours to complete.  That's a long time for a movie, a short time for a video game.  It's also "one of those story games" that's mostly if not completely linear.  You don't "do" much, except see how the video game medium can be used to help make a simple story touching.
There's this old guy.  He's dying.  You and your collegue are there at his request to alter his memory.  He always wanted to go to the moon, but never got around to even trying.  Then there's the issue of his late wife, who seemed nice but sad and unable to effectively communicate why.  Why does someone who spent most of his life married to someone with emotional and communication issues but who chose to reach out to him, now at the time of his death want to change his memories to something radically different?
Maybe you've seen "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" or know enough about it to feel like passing on this game.  Some guy used to be happy with his significant other.  Now he's not and wants to forget her.  The thing is, it's not that simple.  It wan't for the younger couple in Eternal Sunshine, and it isn't for this elderly couple, one who died and the other about to.  The game's simplicy and relatively slow pacing compared to film enable the characters and the player to see how a lifetime of experiences can both culimate in and complicate a simple wish.
It also enables them to see how a person someone just laid eyes upon isn't just another extra in one's own life.  Early in the game, the elderly man's memory is frozen in place with dismissive ease.  It's just a memory, one they've even seen already.  It's not like he's real.  Later, by the time the situation gains urgency -- he's dying, remember -- the two people working on his memory have learned enough to become invested in his life.  He's no longer just a job, even when he still is.
There are some twists in the game, but only because the two people employed to work on the old man's memory are just learning about a life already lived.  The real twists happened long ago.  Now it's the aftermath.  Except, their invovlement creates one twist more, and this one will affect them as much as their subject.
It's gotten to the point I can't really say more without being pretentious.  Play the game.  Feel the feels.  You might like it more than Mikey likes Life cereal.

Remember Me is a strange game -- a game with so much potential that is never fully realised. BUT this is by no means a bad game. The combat is enjoyable, and the story to a degree is good -- and at least it is a personal one (you're not out saving the universe). That said, the gameplay mechanic that is truly novel is the memory-hack, where you repiece someone's memory for a different outcome. It comes into play only at very important story milestones, so they're few and far in between, but that makes them special. Perhaps if the game had been longer and more open ... I am not sure. As it is I would still recommend it, but you can't help the feeling that you would have wanted to spend more time in its world.

Ok, I'm gonna review this after only a few hours play, but short of any game breaking crashes or up coming mind-blowing gameplay, i think i can speak to this game.
I had skipped it at launch, because of all the bad reviews at release. Its now been several months, so I assume that any problems have been patched. So far I have not encountered any technical issues. Will update if I do.
What do I think? I think its an awesome game and a worthy successor to Deus Ex. Judging by the start only, its almost better than that lackluster sequel we had few years back. The story has a very strong French distopian feel to it, that only the first Deus Ex pulled off.  The maps are gorgeous to look at, but limited and linear..."game-like" not open world, but still very  effective.  More than good enough. If Splinter Cell can do it, why not this game?
So why was everyone hating on it?  Probably has something to do with the fighting system. to be perfectly clear, I hate all button mashing fighting games.  Memorizing X Y X X, block, jump x is not my idea of fun. you may disagree.  The recent batman games looked amazing, but I hated that fight system. didn't stop everyone from praising those games! So why the hate here?  I don't know, feels the same to me. I'm probably missing some mind-blowing nuance that a fan boy reading this may point out to me.  I just set the game on easiest difficulty and enjoyed the story.
And that is my final point, its a slick and beautiful to look at story experience. all the negative reviews have tanked the price, so especially on sale you can probably get it for song.   I would recommend it to any fan of futuristic sci-fi.

Remember Me is a strange mixture of Batman Arkham (the fighting), Tomb Rider (the jumping), Portal (the puzzles and sometimes environments) and Bioshock (the distinct world and atmosphere) with a touch of Chris Nolan's Inception.
You play as Nilin, a memory hunter - able to enter the head of any person and remix their memories, changing this very person forever. The setting is NeoParis, year 2084. The design and detalis are amazing - from claustrophobic, futuristic corridors to beautiful vistas that blend classical architecture with neo skyscrapers, you will discover every flavor of NeoParis, even though the path is always straightforward and linear. The story is gripping and mature. The feel of the game and the concept alone are the reasons to play this title. Remember Me has its flaws - the pontential of the game is not really realized and the borrowed elements from the abovementioned games are sometimes poorly executed, but not to the point where it ruins the experience.
Unfortunately, the price tag feels a bit inadequate - the game was a pleasure to play, interrupted by several nuisances here and there, nevertheless, worth half the current price. I recommend Remember Me, but grab it while it's on sale.
PS.
Oh, I just noticed the game is 28€, not 50€ as it used to be. Well, I guess it's worth it.

Great graphics and a good story are unfortunately the only good things I can say about this.
This game is as repetitive as it gets. Litterally every damn boss fight is exactly the same. The combat system itself is based off button-combinations you need to push to do combos. This gets repetitive fast, and really isn't fun anymore after half of the game. Especially since you encounter horde after horde of enemies, that only change very slightly throughout the game.
On top of that I have not had that many game breaking bugs and glitches in a game for a long time. I had my audio randomly not work, my character getting stuck ing fighting-mode, instead of going back to parcouring my way through neo-paris, I had my character not attack an enemy, and I had a cutscene not play when it was supposed to, making me replay half a chapter.
All in all, not worth the trouble.

Kinda like a mix between Deus Ex Human Rev and Batman Arkham Asylum, solid but not as good as either of those in gameplay terms. Interesting story, strong visuals and imaginativeness but a real lack of interaction with both the environments and many of it's hinted inhabitants. As for the core dynamics, the core idea is great (remix memories) but happens few and far and when it does is far too linear to hold you (imagine if you were able to remix / change memories of any inhabitants you found the street to help you progress, now that would have been awesome).
Even in terms of the many climbing sections in the game your very much restricted and spoon feed the way (this is the free-flowing climbing you may be use to or expect due to the likes of Assassins Creed series.
Giving it a 6.5 / 10 overall due to bugs (had to replay a boss due to not being able to progress without all the minions out the way first, nearly got uninstalled there and then), the heavy linear nature and lack of interaction / exploration when such great art is on display. The strenghs come in the solid Batman-like free-flow combat (although not as good), wonderous visuals and strong story, worth it on a discount for sure.

Still hunting that Rex though, haven't seen it on my game yet. The amount of content this game has is a lot and you do get blueprints (it builds the whole set for you in seconds) for things like Shogunate Castles (Large), coffee shops, laundries, etc... If you like LEGOs, this game won't disappoint, it just lacks narrative.

I really enjoyed previous YDKJ games, but this version is so bad as to be unplayable, because it does not have controller support. Controllers are fast, precise, and offer tactile feedback. And for god's sake, let players use the keyboard. If the keyboard has n-key rollover and all four players are willing to crowd around it, let them do it. It wouldn't be fun, but it might work better for them than using smartphones. Or maybe I have controllers incompatible with the game and I want to use JoyToKey to kludge them into working. Even that would be sloppy and lazy on your part, and you failed to meet even those low standards. But, not only does this game not allow you to have more than one player to play using the keyboard, it actually allows NO players on the keyboard. That's right, this game lets NO ONE play on the computer hosting the game. A minimum of five devices is needed to play this game with four players. Good job!
The point is this: give your players options.
Trying to play this game using smartphones, the ONLY WAY the game works, was an awful experience. It was a decent idea, but it does not work well in practice. The lag is a serious issue, which should not happen when everyone's in the same room. Minimal lag is acceptable for most of the game, but completely ruins the Jack Attack. We tried more than one phone that didn't work, which led to one player being forced to use a laptop. She was at a disadvantage because clicking a button with a mouse is slower than on a touch screen. Even that's no picnic, though. It still takes a significant amount of time to look at the phone and press the button, something you DON'T have to do with controllers, as they offer tactile feedback. It's a little thing, but these little things add up. Even worse, oftentimes when we would press the button, the input would simply not register. Some players were at a serious disadvantage because they had more lag than other players. Our phones, like most people's, are set to go dark after a few seconds of disuse, which is the desired behavior at all times except when playing this game. This is distracting and frustrating, because enough time passes between each question for the phone to turn off, and it's not uncommon for you to get caught with your phone off when it's answering time. And god forbid it's locked by then. You have to remember to turn your phone on ahead of time, or continuously rub your finger on the empty area of the screen to keep it awake. You think it doesn't sound like a big deal, but it really does significantly detract from the experience, knowing you have an unreliable piece of garbage in your hand that will screw you over unless you pay constant attention to it. Changing the setting is a hassle, needs to be done again once the game is over, and results in your battery dying even faster (which this game does a pretty quickly already.)
The idea to use smartphones was clever, but flawed in execution. Failing to support ANY OTHER INPUT MODE, even the DEAD SIMPLE keyboard, was a catastrophically bad decision, and it ruined this game entirely.

After (re)playing New Vegas for a bit I decided to revisit this review and go with a negative instead. Fallout 3 really isn't a worthy successor to the franchise. Of course I went full completionist with it now as I did in 2008, but most of it wasn't time well spent, I admit. Also, reviews are for people looking to purchase now, not 9 years ago when the context was much more favourable for F3. If you're a more casual gamer and not a life-long follower of all things Fallout, skipping this episode and going straight to NV may not be a bad idea.
Yes, the main quest, more significant side-quests, Liam Neeson and some of the DLCs do have their moments, but there is space between 'good enough' and 'spectacular'.
The dreadfully boring D.C. area world map (you probably won't even remember where the main settlements are) with all it's generic metros does not do justice to Fallout and it's obvious the developers had tight constraints in both manhours and max CPU cycles used. Most NPCs have no significance and numbly follow their dumb AI routines. Your actions have very few consequences upon the in-game world. If Megaton provides a disappointment you're in for a lot more of those down the road.
I'm grateful Bethesda picked up probably my favourite game of all time and made it a sequel after almost 10 years without turning it into a family-friendly cash cow, but they did dumb it down a lot even so.

It's very slow paced, and there are some systems that could use a little more work.  But to me, No Man's Sky is just blissful.  It's by turns exhilarating in its vastness, yet gorgeously relaxing to just bum around in.  The worlds I've seen have been incredibly beautiful; from lush forests and tundra, to the bleakest, barren, poisonous rocks, they've all been an absolute pleasure to explore.  The spaces between things don't make the game boring to me, they make it immersive, and render each new discovery something special.  As a fan of games like Dear Esther and Abzu, this is a simple delight, yet one so grand in scale, and with far more gameplay possibilities than those games, now with base building as well as resource gathering, crafting, trading etc. that I could lose myself in it for a long, long time to come.
This is the first time I've written a Steam review, and I felt compelled to do it because of how much scorn has been poured on this game, and how much I love it.  Sony may have marketted No Man's Sky poorly, but Hello Games have created something wonderful here, that both needs and deserves the support of its players.  I'd be sad to see their future plans not come to fruition because of a rough launch and a reactionary public.
Realistically, I guess I couldn't recommend this game to just anyone, but to people like me, I can't recommend it strongly enough.
Instead of running with the money, the devs are listening to it community and taking in and implementing suggestions.

First thing first....I enjoy these tables (and am growing to LOVE them!)
EDIT: 11/5/17 Everything said below about these two DLC tables being easy....just not true. While play is simple enough, for both of these tables it is quite challenging to achieve high scores or lengthy game time. Challenging enough, I believe, to satisfied even advanced players. (Reviewer has over 1,000 hours in Steam pinball.) New, in-games rules for each table explain the complexity of each table, which had been somewhat concealed until now. Key-binding is nice!
Malzbie’s Pinball Collection (MPC) is Steam’s newest pinball choice, and it’s very easy to do much worse. Admittedly, Day One is a difficult stage at which to judge a game, especially one from a new developer (at least new on Steam.) But there are things that can be said from the start, both positive and negative.
Not having my Razer Orbweaver handy, I tried using my Xbox Afterglow, but it showed no sign of life with MPC. (EDIT: I've since been told that an Xbox wiill work if plugged in after game launch.) Unfortunately, this review is based on using a keyboard in landscape mode, so it’s less than optimal, but there was still a general feel for all three tables. Malzbie's Pinball fails to offer a RESTART feature of any kind (though has promised it eventually) and is the only pinball this reviewer has ever seen where both flippers rotate lane light in the same direction. (Presumably, future tables will behave more normally.)
The free table provided with the game is called “Time To Fight Back”. It’s a military air force themed table (and in my opinion the weakest of the three.) The ball felt just slightly laggy, but wasn’t noticeably so on the other two tables. This is the first table I can ever recall playing where both flippers cause lane lights to change in the same direction (which the DEV indicates is deliberate, and not to be corrected.) While not really a particularly original table, still a solid beginner / average player table.
“Carnival” takes one of the most common themes in all of pinball, and instead of simply reusing the same things seen from the beginning of time, adds some features less used, and even things this player has not seen before (with this theme.) This table takes a more advanced player to keep a ball in play for long, or to get a high score. Looks good, sounds good, plays good. (Grammar bad…I know. Mine, I mean.)
“The Garden” is a very nicely designed 3-D garden themed table. It’s a simple table to play, the primary goals being to grow flowers while pumping water from a well in order to help them grow. For me, the simplest of the three tables, and one that might become tedious to advanced players, but I really liked the concept and the look very much. (When I say “simplest”, I don’t mean that the average player will necessarily consider it to be so, but it’s not a terrible complicated table. But it is an exceptionally beautiful one.)
[EDIT: 10/29/17 Portrait mode is now working, and it's a thing of beauty! ]
MPC comes with fifteen achievements, but I’m not sure that artificially loaded high scores to be beat is really fair or appropriate (especially at what seems to be higher levels than average players are likely to make.) And having an achievement for highest score (against both real and artificial scores) will leave out 99% of all players, and may not be well thought out. Perhaps I misjudge the player interest, but the achievements seem to be designed for more advanced players than do the tables themselves. (EDIT: In the past hour scored 57M on Fight Back, which had an artificial HS of either 25 or 30M, so I may be mistaken....)
On the “Unfortunately” side, there is no automatic detection of resolution or hardware, and almost no settings for anything (graphics or otherwise) that pinball players have begun to take for granted (but which most indie pinball DEVs have needed to add after the fact.) The physics is intermittant, with the ball often changing "weight" suddenly. No binding of keys either, and these deficiencies can be enough to kill a game, regardless of positives. These tables may not be difficult enough to fully satisfy an advanced player, at least not in a month that has seen two far more advanced pinball games released on Steam. And at $1.99USD each, MPC tables aren’t the cheapest available on Steam either. (But they are FAR from the most expensive, one of which has left me personally underwhelmed like very little other Steam pinball in the past 2+ years.)
There are seven more MPC tables lined up for release (and it's my current intention to acquire every one), but much may be based on how willing players will be to request changes and improvements based entirely on the free table. (A free table being the standard for Steam pinball, so we’ve all seen this transpire multiple times.) If the single DEV continues to respond quickly, Malzbie’s Pinball Collection may become a popular and successful Steam pinball game. Time will tell, and I personally hope for the best for MPC (but I’d be happy if EVERYONE released a Steam pinball game.)

This is my first time playing visual novel game in form of 2D animation point-of-view, and it totally worth it. The game is fantastic and beautiful in many aspects.
Let me elaborate:
1. Graphics 10/10
Visual novel games I usually play are never based on 2D animation style, they are always in point and click style with art backgrounds and characters. This game use a totally different style. There are no character artworks, no background artworks (like other usual visual novel games). But don't get me wrong, the developer is very capable and smart to execute the 2D animation style into visual novel game. I don't get bothered at all by the pixel 2d arts they are using, it's rather excellent to drive the atmospheric element any good visual games should transfer (in form of visual experiences) to the player. I feel very satisfied with their 2D assets of choosing, from characters, animations, 2D backgrounds, and environments.
2. Story 11/10
It's beautifully written, well-planned, and really match with their soundtracks, and the characters. Everything they put into the story from the beginning till the end is a masterpiece. I couldn't describe it any longer because it will spoil the story and it won't be pretty, so I highly suggest you just play and enjoy the ride. It's totally worth your time. I sit, play, and always curious as to what would happen next in the storyline.
Bottom line is: It's like playing a really good visual novel game and watching a beautiful story-rich movie at the same time.
3. Dialogue 10/10
A good visual novel games should have a vast array of interesting conversations, and this game totally knocked it out. It feels like each character has a well-planned development for their personalities.
P.s. I laughed a lot when Dr. Eva and Dr. Neil argues. One of the in-game best scenes.
4. Sound effect and Music 10/10
Ah yes, the music also hits me every time they put different themes into the scenes. Whether it's a sad scenes, a curious one, or even a funny remarks, the devs are always capable of pairing excellent choices of sound/music with the present theme. Oh, and despite there are lots of in-game characters that say the piano plays of "To the River" is repetitive, I kinda like it.
Conclusion:
If you are into visual novel games, this one is a must buy.

My review may be slightly biased as I had the opportunity to BETA test this game early on through to release. I've seen it grow into the immersive, challenging, and beautifully addictive simulation that it is now. I think that's a key point to make here - this may look like a game but it's more akin to a 'strategy simulation'. There is no 'easy win' path that, once discovered, works each time.
Some of the other reviews here cover the main mechanics so I'll keep this short. The game is loaded with random events inspired by real life meaning that each play through is always different. You play with the hand you're dealt and see how the cards fall.  Certainly, the good decisions you make and the tools you implement along the way will help to swing things in your favour - be it a change in policies or a perfectly pitched national broadcast - but you can never please all of the people all of the time and the randomness of real life can quickly change your fortunes if you react wrongly. Then, of course there's your scheming brother Farouk to contend with.
This is almost a survival simulator as much as it is a strategy title - the goal being to stay in power for as many turns as possible. Some times you'll win, most times you probably won't - but you'll have a darn good time trying... because once you get comfortable in the dictators chair you'll be itching for the next turn... and the next... and the next... which seems to me an accurate reflection of the life of a dictator, and the hallmark of a good game.
Just make sure to siphon off enough funds to enjoy your retirement... if you make it.

I received an early copy of Rogue State and have been playing it (primarily off Steam) for a while now.
The game is a turn-based strategy simulator of a middle-eastern dictatorship with deep, interconnecting mechanics.  Each session of the game is very different: your neighbours, the distribution of goods, your ministers, and most importantly the events that will occur are randomized, and this has made each playthrough very different and interesting.
The graphics in the game are, admittedly, retro, but the artwork is very well done and the animations are clean.  For a turn-based strategy game, it does the trick.
The writing of the game is often funny, and the voice acting is very good (and everything is voiced).
Rogue State is admittedly very challenging, but I like a challenge.  Managing the support of the four factions in your country, managing your budget, and managing the production of infrastructure and special projects is a tricky balancing act, and early on, I lost often.  However, when I won, I felt like I really earned it!  I found that I could get further and further on each playthrough as I figured out how to better keep everyone (or everyone that mattered) happy without going totally broke.
This game has that "one more turn" compulsion that I get with Civ.  I recommend it!

First off, do not even think about playing this game if you have not played the original trilogy, and not just because the original trilogy is better. It will spoil the trilogy's ending and I don't think you'd want to have that spoiled. Which leads to my next point...
The very existence of this game cheapens that ending. If you've seen it, you'll know what I mean. The original trilogy was wrapped up nicely with a pretty bow on it, and while it did leave some questions open, I felt there was simply no room for a sequel to it.
So it's no good if you liked the trilogy's ending. What if you hated it? Well, I won't spoil it, but I can tell you that if you hated the trilogy's ending, you will not like this one any better.
The game's story involves time loops, and some pretty complicated ones. It can be difficult just to make sense of the plot. I couldn't even figure out if a certain character was alive or dead in the final timeline. Unfortunately, the use of time loops also makes for repetitive gameplay, especially if you're not good at solving the puzzles. I got tired of hearing "GOOOAAALLL!! DON'T GOOOOO!!" well before I heard it for the last time.
But it's not a horrible game. If you simply cannot get enough Deponia, or if you have to play every half-decent adventure game that exists, then by all means get it. But I think most people have better options to choose from.

Minor pacing issues and graphical errors aside, this is a brilliant horror game with some heart pounding moments of terror. I recommend it to horror fans everywhere!

All the games are wildly different in their enjoyment, but they are all positive in my book!
You Don't Know Jack, the classic of the bunch. A cheesy gameshow with traditional trivia interspersed with a few more unusual rounds, like a quickfire true or false and a round which singles out the current loser to get themselves back into the leaderboard. It's decent, but the time based answering means that it's unsuitable for streaming and the 4 player max player count makes it less appealing when there are many friends or family over. Still, it's solid fun.
Fibbage and Drawful are the gems in the pack. Both support 8 players and both have a greater focus on player driven interaaction. Meaning your terrible drawings, guesses and lies become part of the whole game leading to some of the best fun you will ever have with party games.
Fibbage however lacks content, after playing for half an hour or so, questions started repeating. Drawful, on the other hand, took a very very long time until something even resembled a possible repetition. (Drawful is much harder to get a feeling of repetition since the answers and phrases are all so esoteric and outright nuts (which only adds to the fun).
I explored the gamefiles, and saw an explaination. Fibbage only has 200 or so questions, while Drawful is closer to around 600. A rediculous disparity when both games are really great.
Flyswatter and Word Spud are special situation games. They are neat, but cannot really stand among their peers. Flyswatter is basically a game you play if you have A LOT of people who want to play a simple trivia game in the form of true or false questions.
Word Spud is the subjective game of the bunch, where how you win is directly related to what kind of people you play with it. Words are stringed together, one player at a time; whether you want to be smart, funny or write poop and pee jokes is entirely up to you and judged accordingly; as each input is judged by everyone else.
Being able to pretty much play all games (aside from You Don't know Jack) through streaming and also being able to play through mobile, tablet and web browsers makes this one of the most unexpectily well realised, accessible party games released in the last decade.
It is one of those technologies that wouldn't have worked 5 years ago, but now it is in the most fertile of environments, and it thrives.
Boy, I just hope they add some more Fibbage questions though, or workshop support.

Ori and the blind forest is a must-have game. It's not perfect, but what it does well more than makes up for its flaws. The game manages to create a beautiful world with characters full of personality without the need for words. Its tight controls and challenging gameplay help to create an engaging metroidvania experience. To sum it up in three words:
Pros:
Simply put, Ori and the Blind Forest is hands-down the most beautiful game I have ever played. The whole forest is wonderfully hand-painted, and the quality you see in those trailers isn't just picking the good parts. Seriously. The whole game looks that pretty. The animations are also spot-on, if not as flawless as the environments. It also has some pretty killer parallax scrolling effects. This game is the culmination of 30+ years of 2D art design, as if every 2D game since the beginning has been working to create this level of quality in it's visuals. Absolutely beautiful from start to finish.
The music is also amazing. In most cases, it fits perfectly with the gameplay and visuals, helping to sew together a colorful, immersive aesthetic design that makes Ori and the Blind Forest incredibly atmospheric.
The characters are brought to life beautifully, and this game is a textbook example of characterization without dialogue. Here's one example from the game that perfecly demonstrates this concept:
Naru, the big, motherly creature that adopts Ori, has slow, ponderous walk in which she throws her arms back and forth in a very stylized manner. If you take a look at Ori's walking animation, you will notice that it is almost exactly the same. No matter how different Ori is from Naru, you are reminded that he loves her as a parent figure and keeps a part of her with him wherever he goes. Just from this tiny detail, you can see how close the bond between Ori and Naru is.
I'm a fan of metroidvania games, so Ori's gameplay was very good in my opinion. As with any good metroidvania, there are plenty of interesting areas to explore and satisfying powerups to collect, and for the most part the game leaves you free to advance the plot at your own pace. It's also suprisingly hard. In this game, you will die. A lot. It even keeps count for you (I died 404 times in my first playthrough).
Cons:
Let me start out by saying that Ori and the Blind Forest is an EXCELLENT game. Moon Studios definitely deserve your money, so please don't let me persuade you not to buy this game.
In certain parts of this game, collectibles necessary for 100% completion are located in one-time areas. By one-time areas, I mean sections where you cannot backtrack and are locked when you complete them. This is unacceptable. This is the one flaw with this game that cannot be overlooked. A good metroidvania should never do this to their players. Either: 1) don't put collectibles in one-time areas 2) Don't create one-time areas 3)Let the players know when they are entering a one-time area so that they know to be sure to get the collectibles. Ori and the Blind Forest does none of these things, so I highly suggest that you look up the missable collectibles if you're aiming for 100%.
Now that that's out of the way, here are a few miscellaneous nitpicks:

The fourth installment of the Deponia franchise, honestly, leave me a little mixed.
On the one hand, it's Deponia. I greatly enjoyed the original trilogy, as it had a great story and solid gameplay, so Doomsday had a strong foundation of characters and mechanics to draw from. It also added some new mechanics of its own, which were hit-or-miss. I liked traversing through time portals, but the timed segments were fairly annoying, especially near the end where there were multiple tasks you needed to complete in order to progress, and if you didn't finish them all once time ran out, you were forced back to the beginning of the sequence to do everything over again.
On the other hand, and this will be a bit spoilery, but the game did feel a lot like a middle-finger to the fanbase, story-wise. Before playing this I had already heard that this was the case. A sort of response to the negative reaction the not-quite-happy ending of the previous game had. Personally, while I thought the end of the third game was sad, I didn't hate it by any means. Still, while I was not part of that crowd who disliked the ending of Goodbye Deponia and, in fact, knew the kind of ending that was coming, I couldn't help but feel that, where Goodbye Deponia comes off as bitter-sweet, Deponia Doomsday just comes across as bitter. It's a lot like watching a friend get drawn into a childish argument with someone over something stupid. It's embarrassing to watch.
I won't claim that Doomsday is a bad game. As I said, it has a very solid base both in characters and gameplay. This is one of those instances where I get really annoyed by Steam's binary "Recommended or No" system, as it leaves no room for the grey areas in-between. However, as a fan of Deponia in general, I'd have to say that you're probably better off either giving this one a pass, or at least waiting until it's on sale.

All in all, I considered this to be a brilliant capstone to the series.

It strung very well on nostalgic feeling toward old characters and locations, while not overusing them all - just to keep things familiar and beliavable, and there was a lot of new things so it feels like a new game. It is also commendable how well executed was whole time travel theme, both in terms of gameplay and keeping logic of story, and of course of jokes. Охотник за нечистью очень приятно и литературно выражается, идеально сохраняя образ; его подруга каждые 15 минут выдает остроты; окружающие персонажи продуманы и прописаны настолько, чтобы каждая из отведенных им фраз звучала свежо и интересно. The game follows a quest of Van Helsing and his companion, the ghost Katharina, who try to get to Borgovia to stop a mad scientist. Along the way you encounter dozens of different enemies throughout numerous different environments. Some of these locales look stunningly beautiful: you traverse through a muddy forest fighting hideous monsters and evil spirits and also join the resistance in a town to fight the soldier-machines. These machines add the steampunk part of the game - with all the traps and contraptions you find they make the game even more diverse.
One of the things I liked about Van Helsing was its atmosphere. Sound effects and the score are excellent and I liked the sarcastic conversations between Helsing and Katharina. One-liners are common from them as well as from enemies and there are numerous references to other video games and films throughout the game. In order to find all of them it's worth hovering the cursor over all objects in every environment - Van Helsing might collect a quest item or just make a funny comment.
There are many sidemissions, of course, as it is common in this genre and there's even one that takes you throughout the game. You just need to carefully look everywhere and open all chests, containers, destroy all barrels and boxes as you might find the next piece of the puzzle. It's worth mentioning, though, that not all items are related to a quest, still, they will be part of the corresponding tab in your inventory.
Normally, Van Helsing wields two swords and two pistols. You can decide which way to go from there in terms of customisation. Beside these two tabs there is also one called Tricks (active spells) and Auras (passive skills). Every level-up grants you ability points (the good-old attributes we are talking about here), skill points and occasionally reputation points, but the latter is not related to quest but more to the annihilation of strong beasts. Your reputation can then yields you perks - the list is gradually increasing and you can pick more and more of them along the way.
Katharina, the ghost companion is a bit similar to the pet we have in Torchlight. She can do the shopping on behalf of us and can also pick up loot by category. Her behaviour is completely modifiable. Of course, she has many skills and also attributes - her skills either make her stronger or support Van Helsing in combat.
While there are no other companions in the game the abovementioned customisation I described for Van Helsing is the Hunter class only. With the added DLCs you can play as a Thaumaturge or Arcane Mechanic. I hear they are pretty fun and diverse, too, so this is all the more in favour of the longevity of this game.
Van Helsing is pretty cool game considering it is a relatively low-budget hack 'n' slash. It is filled with content and there's high replayability due to the 3 different classes, more difficulty levels, hardcore mode, online cooperative mode in the game. I look forward to playing with its sequel. In the meantime, if you are the fan of the genre Van Helsing should be in your library. Word of advice: buckle up as the game can be pretty challenging even on normal difficulty setting!
