FULL DISCLOSURE: I received a free copy of this game prior to release for review. It is your right to disregard my criticism as invalid because of this fact. That said, I assure you that this has never affected, and will never affect, any of the content of my reviews.
Rogue State is a management game, where you play as the leader of a middle eastern country. The whole idea is that you led the rebellion, man or woman, that overthowed a previous tyrannical power, and the people look to you to rebuild, and propel the country into prosperity. It is procedurally generated, with new countries, ministers, and events each game -- but there is one major constant that is present in every single game; your brother Farouk. He will be trying to undermine everything you do, and if you let your popularity dwindle Farouk will make his move and take over leadership by force. In addition to this you might have to deal with war, environmental and social issues, terrorism, financial crises, debt and more, so there’s a lot to pay attention to.
I’m gonna begin this review at rock bottom. This game is presented abhorrently. It looks and plays like it was made 20 years ago. I mean, I don’t think there is any aspect of this game that couldn’t have been done in the 90s. Maybe aside from the resolution. In addition to the aesthetic issues, it played in a 4:3 aspect ratio and 30 fps and I don’t think it’s possible to go any higher than that. To me this reeks of trying to be overly-ambitious with the visuals; personally I think a top down pixel approach definitely wouldn’t be anything special, but it would be a lot cleaner and palatable than this; just as an example. If I try and twist it into a positive, then maybe you’d like the presentation if you have nostalgia for 90s point and click games? That’s the kind of visual vibe I get from it.
Presentation is important, but it can be completely overruled by solid mechanics. I thought about this for a while, but I think the best description of what this game is like, is Long Live the Queen but randomly generated. I feel like, at first, that seems appealing to Long Live the Queen fans (which I’m one of by the way, I loved that game) but actually that makes the game extremely challenging. I feel like if you knew everything in advance that was going to happen, you could maybe beat this game and reach the final turn 50. However, since you don’t know anything that’s going to happen, other than a few key events,  it becomes a game of luck rather than one of strategy. Everything can be going perfectly for you, but if suddenly you have a terrorist problem and you have to begin putting money into the intelligence agency, you can quickly find yourself in debt and you reach a point where, even if you stop the terrorists, your country hates you and Farouk takes over. This is compounded by the fact you are constantly pressured into spending money in the events that occur every turn. It’s very hard to deal with these situations when you are given such a tiny timeframe to combat them in. One of the more cool mechanics, though,  is that you have to make a speech every year and you pick what the leader says in the speech. Again, it’s cool, you have to make sure you don’t contradict yourself and stay relevant,  but even then it does get repetitive and eventually I just found it unreliable and clicked through it out of boredom. There are some fun ideas here, but ultimately everything is tainted by that unfair difficulty.
The story is really just furniture, but the theme is pretty interesting to me. I like that you have the opportunity to run the country in whatever way you please. It’s a pretty good role-play game I think. There’s some social commentary mixed in with the turn-by-turn events which is interesting, and there's some pretty funny writing here and there. There’s a potential neighbouring country you can have called Chickenstan, and you can unlock a perk which allows you to understand the ancient chickenstan language. I will say that there are a couple of groaners in there in terms of the writing, but I have a suspicion that was what they were going for in those situations.
Now it’s time for me to say whether I think it’s worth it or not. The game is $13 at launch. I’m just going to be blunt; for most people I wouldn't recommend this game. I was kind of joking about this earlier, but if there really are people who are nostalgic for this kind of look, and are really into the idea of role-playing as a middle-eastern leader then yeah sure I’d recommend it -- but I feel like that is an incredibly tiny subset of people. Frankly, you’re only really going to like this if you're big into management games, and even then there are better management games out there. Prison Architect is a great game that allows you to actually build the prison as well as set things like policies, prison schedules etc that offers everything that Rogue State does only better. Even smaller games like Game Dev Tycoon and Long Live the Queen get a bit of an edge over Rogue State. It’s a shame, but that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I'm excited to see more from this developer, but Rogue State is one you’ll probably want to give a miss.

Let me start by saying that I am one of the lucky ones that experienced very little performance issues; I am running the game in 1440p resolution maxed out and I am able to maintain 140+ FPS most of the time. However, no matter how good a game runs; if it's bad it's bad
TL;DR: wait for %50 off at least before picking this up
Pros:
-Stunning graphics, one of better looking games out for sure
-Fun gameplay, very fast paced and satisfying with good variety
-SFX are robust; be it the satisfying gun-shot sound, the explosions or the huge mech enemies
-Some, though rare, funny moments in cutscenes
Cons:
-Terrible storyline: it's basically your typical corny action-romance movie fake deep ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, the writers are trying to force a romance sub-plot that has no place in a game like Wolfenstein, and they’re doing a bad job at it too.
-Terrible cast of characters: the writers tried to give every character a unique personality, but they tried too hard and most of the main cast turned out to be annoying. Anya is bland, Grace is a snarly pr*ck and BJ is trying too hard to be poetic. The characters with interesting personality (like Fergus and Sigun) didn’t get enough air time.
-Not enough content: The campaign took me 12 hours to beat and I was going out of my way to find collectibles; 3 hours of those 12 are cutscenes. The side quests are boring, repetitive and don’t incline you to play them at all. There is also a lack of variety in weapons; you only have 6 weapons, 2 of which are impractical due to the unavailability of their ammo type. So you’re stuck with only 4 weapons that you can actually use all the time. There are only 3 upgrades to every weapon and most of them don’t make the gameplay any fun.
-Lackluster soundtrack: After the outstanding work Mick Gordon delivered in Wolfenstein: The New Order, The Old Blood and Doom, I expected the soundtrack to be just as good in this one. What I got was a main theme that’s a remix of the first game’s main theme and generic rock music playing in the background that did nothing to hype the gameplay. I also found that the music was too low even when maxed out, you are unable to lower the SFX in the setting too so if you want the music to be loud you will need to tolerate the deafening sound of gun-shots.
-Slow storyline progression in the beginning, but extremely fast towards the end; making the final credits rolling in an unpleasant surprise.
Conclusion: One of the most disappointing sequels ever. The developer put so much emphasis on a terrible storyline with a terrible cast and kicked the gameplay down to a 2nd priority.

I'm not going to sugarcoat it-- The ending is bittersweet.
You go through time repeatedly, and redo puzzles over and over until you finally figure things out. It's a bit tedious with the gameplay, but I can't bring myself to dislike the story... Or even the ending.
In America, we're used to happy endings. Almost all movies and books end with a happy ending, and Goodbye Deponia didn't have one. It caused outrage from the fans. We grew to love these characters, and yet the ending wasn't what we wanted. So Daedlic Entertainment created this game... In a way, from the very beginning, it was a giant middle finger to the naysayers.
It's still very funny, and in my opinion worth playing (though, admittedly, with a walkthrough, cause things are just not that obvious this time around), however there will be a lot of people who dislike it. It does not have an all-around happy ending for the original pair. However, previously, it was disappointing. This time, it was somehow... poetic. From an artists point of view, it's majestic. From the fans' point of view, it probably won't be. That's why there's so many mixed reviews... That, and, probably people are tired of the timeloops.
****SPOILER BELOW****
The difference here, is, Goal gets to say goodbye to Rufus... That simple change in the ending made me enjoy it so much more than I had before.

So, remember how people hated the ending of Neon Genesis Evangelion, so the creator went ahead and made End of Evangelion?
This is kind of like that.
The game is reasonably fun (though some of the puzzles are a bit much I would say). But the writing of the game has such contempt for the people playing it; as if to say "you should not play this game."
Well, I'm going to have to act in defiance of the writing by recommending it.

Let me get this straight, I'm a huge Daedalic fan and so far loved all their point-and-click adventures. (I even bought them up to four times due to an unfortunate real-life adventure. :D )
Deponia 1-3 was great and I am one of those unthankful idiots that was disappointed in the ending. I guess life has the most unhappy endings, so I wish for happy ones in made-up stories, okay? ;)
I waited long until I finally purchased Deponia Doomsday and I thought it was nice that they gave Rufus another chance. Yes, he's a pain in the a**, but still quite a fun character I grew fond of.
So yeay, another Rufus maneuver, another chance to make things right....right?
Far from that. I agree with other players here that it doesn't really fit into the whole Deponia story, that it feels a little bit like a desperate attempt to fix something and then in the end only wanting to directly punch everyone in the face. I could hear the devs laughing, while I watched the credits puzzled and thought: "That's it? Seriously?"
Don't get me wrong, there are nice riddles, the familiar scenery of Deponia, you finally get to Elysium (*cough, cough* only to destroy it *cough* Darn it, Ronny!), there's Goal and close to the end the story takes a turn that makes your head ache. No, there's nothing missing that makes it a nice point-and-click adventure. But I felt like the title "Doomsday" couldn't have fit any better. At some point I think the devs just stopped caring. For example Rufus walks over a dead pigeon several times...maybe funny, but rather lines up with all the jokes that really went to far in this one. It just keeps going, Rufus is sometimes so awfully rude and annoying that I wished I had an option to change his attitude after all. Plus you don't really want Goal and Rufus to be together, because you want to spare her from this unbelievable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
And then basically all other characters you knew don't exist in this one. No Bozo, only a little bit of Lotti at the beginning and (thank god) only a small part for Cletus as well.
And after going through this really effed up portal madness you get to the ending, only to find out that this must be the most disappointing revival of a protagonist in a game ever. I hated it. And of course now they made sure that there is no chance for Rufus to return ever again. (You read that right. Finito!)
Sorry Daedalic, I love you but this was no big fun to go through.
I still recommend it, if you're into point-and-clicks and twisted stories. Also I guess this would work without playing the trilogy first...maybe that would even be more fun.

For the most part I enjoyed the original Deponia trilogy. There were some flaws though, especially with gamebreaking bugs, jokes that went too far, and an unsatisfying ending.
This new game has some enjoyable moments, especially with being able to visit Elysium (finally), but it brings all the flaws of the earlier games and then some.
*** Warning, Spoilers Ahead *** (not that it matters too much since the game has been out a little while now)
Gamebreaking bugs are back, and in this case it's right in the middle of one of the jokes taken too far scenes with Rufus squished between fat old guys in a sauna. The only fix is to load an earlier save and not click on things in the order that triggers the bug. Conveniently, Daedalic support has a downloadable savegame right at the beginning of this scene, but still haven't actually fixed the bug.
The story involves time travel and time loops, and while the first part of the game is okay, by the end there are so many loops that it's just plain confusing and doesn't really make any sense.
On top of that, the ending is more unsatisfying that Deponia 3, with Elysium crashed and nearly everyone dead, at least in the present.
And then there's the marketing for this game:
"Can you change Deponia's fate? Do you have what it takes to change Rufus' past, present and future without accidently destroying the whole planet?"
That sounds like it's targeted right at players who were unsatisfied with the ending in Deponia 3. However, as I've already mentioned, this game has a worse ending. This made me feel like this game is one giant cruel joke from the devs to spite the players who complained about the ending of the original trilogy. It lures you in with the promise of a better ending, only to sucker punch you at the end.
So do I recommend this game? No, not really. It might be worth playing (if you can get it for cheap) for someone who really enjoyed the first three games and wants more puzzles and jokes, but it doesn't add anything worthwhile to the story.

The game has a good storyline, but the Greek mythology is very scrambled. Don't expect this to be like a Percy Jackson book in terms of accuracy.
There are 3 weapons - sword, mace and spear. The game lets you work out which ones work best where, and there are several (at least 4) different weapons for each slot, as well as armour as well.
The god powers are fun, but suffer from being really awkward to actually fire up in combat, since you have to push the button then hold it for a few seconds, and you can only have 4 on "quick"slots, so if you use more than 4, you have to constantly be swapping out.
The combat is good, better than Skyrim's 'click, block, repeat", but not Kingdom of Amalur standard. The combos are pretty basic when you learn the patterns, and the executions in the game are little more than slowed down hitting people, which is fine by me.
The upgrade system is quite different from other games, since you can dedicate deeds ♥♥♥♥♥♥you've done, like "I mow this lawn in the name of Hermes!") to gain points to put into upgrades, with each upgrade tree upgrading one of the weapons, or your defense, and giving god powers.
The story is short but good, with a nice variety of combats and environments, and a (very small) bit of branching its all very fun. The ending, however, is very abrupt and rather dull, and has a rather rushed feel to it, like the devs were working into the night because the game needed to be put on disks the next day.
Overall, there is some potential for replayability, and the game itself is solid but short. 8/10.
EDIT: I noticed a few people saying you'll need to navigate without a map, which isn't true, as there is a map in the pause menu for all places. However, its not likely you need it except to remind yourself of your current quests, seeing as most areas are very linear.

If you have read the general negative buzz, let me respond to three of the points that seemed to be harked on the most. Linear level design, clunky controls and uninspiring combat.
1. The game is to linear- Fair. The game is built with linear levels with hiddens areas for collectables. I didn't think linear gameplay is nesessarily a bad thing merely a design choice. The game is supposed to play like a cinematic action/ Sci-fi movie. Cutscenes aren't tremendously long the game and quick time events are at a minimal. You aren't going to feel like you are playing Xenosaga or Heavy rain though, this is still very much an action game. But in reality the game's audio and voices are fully realized and it really is a treat to sit back and enjoy the experience.
The story is the driving force and sticking to it plays to its importance. Ever hear people complain about doing remedial tasks when you should be saving the world? Like  running off the beaten path to catch someone's chickens (zelda). This game alleviates alleviates those issues by keeping things important and relevant.
Now if you simply don't like that idea, then this game isn't for you, But in my opinion linear games in a 3d environment is a matter of taste not a design flaw.
2. Controls- I have read many reviews about clunky and glitched controls. I have played through the game 4 times and have only had two minor glitches that did not effect gameplay. As far as clunky I completely disagree. hitting buttons feels precise and having a dodge that can be activated on hit or on block makes Nilin (our protaganist) feel fast and light on her feet. But i think I might understand why people may not like the platorming...
Since the game is a very visual experience, climbing, jumping and navigating when in platforming mode, Nilin has tons of unskippable animation. If you are in a rush to complete jumping from one ledge to another, then you are just going to feel a bit slow in this game. But moving speed on objects can be rushed so if you choose to play with a sense of urgency, you may, otherwise you will be moving at ponderous speed (most likely) enjoying the background. It may be slow, but you will rarely ever get missed or delayed inputs once you are acustomed to the pacing.
3. combat- People complain that it is rather simplisitic. I disagree. Maybe the animations you choose for nilin's attacks seem unconsequential, but the added benefits are highly important. dealing more outright damage (causing override), keeping healthy, or cooling you special down faster. there is a ton of strategy in your attack choices. Even deciding how long combos will be plays into the games meta game. Longer strings will be hard to pull off but will give added benefits in later hits. small strings will be very reliable but will award medicore benefits. Its the opposite of a fighting game mechanic, instead of hits meaning less near the end of string and scaling down. The benefits scale up incentivizing players to try longer strings. But admittedly I wish there were major diffrences in attack animation similiar to Clover Studio's "God Hand".
But all in all I think this game generated unfair reviews in general. With Tons of interesting content, pretty visuals, and an amazing soundtrack. Remember Me might be the sleeper hit you missed.

After beating Remember Me, I can understand, why this game has so mixed reviews. I cannot even fully make up my mind.
Let's start with some of the really good stuff:
The basic idea, the world they created is great.
The story is very ambitious and - let's say - powerful and is partly very well told
Here and there the game develops a cineastic quality, which is rarely if ever seen in videogames
The visual design of the levels, of the characters etc is good.
Later in the game, it just serves you big chunks of story, with almost generic dialogue patched between - they cannot keep up with their own ambition.
In regard to gameplay, the game oscillates around mediocre.
You have the rather uninspired brawl-sequences, where you have combos, dodges and some special attacks. There is a little running around, but the game always shows you the way, you are basically on rails. And then there are very boring climbing sequences, they rarely pose any challenge and obviously serve only the purpose, that the game does not consist of (mediocre) brawl after brawl.
Especially later in the game, when the storytelling becomes stale and the levels get longer, it gets boring and almost a chore to finish.
Although in doubt, I do recommend this game.

Trying out a new style of review here. Totally NOT influenced by a critic. Here goes.
Note: This is my first Bethesda RPG game AFAIK. So I'm heavily biased towards this game.
Pros:
- Decent storytelling
- Interesting locations
- A story that, while cliche, has enough to interest you
- Interesting NPC's with character
- Varied enemies
- Cool♥♥♥♥♥combat system, "V.A.T.S." that lets you target body parts or even disarm opponents, with luck's blessing
- Character progression. Wanna make a charismatic lady-killer with the aim of a sniper? Sure. Go ahead.
- Pipboy! With radio stations and a map! Kill enemies while jamming to Cold War era tunes!
- Desolate atmosphere. Lack of colours make you feel hopeless as you scavenge around cautiously whilst searching for supplies and ammo.
Cons:
- Somewhat clunky combat. The firing animations for automatic weapons and the choice of a semi zoom-in instead of iron sights when you aim feels weird.
- The downtown area is a maze. You have to use the metro system to get around roadblocks and rubble. This could also be a storytelling and progression tool to prevent progressing too far, but I'm not sure.
Verdict: It's a decent start point to the 3D Fallout universe (post-isometric games). While I recommend New Vegas as a better starting point, this is where it all changed. For better or for worse, I'm not sure. So, if you like shooting mutants and running around in your very own suit of power armor then by all means get this game. Keep in mind that the game is nearly 9 years old and it hasn't aged graphically well. And the shooting mechanics will feel dated.

UPDATE: So, I finally came around to finishing the main story. It took me nearly 18 hours to complete on the hardest mode available when you first launch the game. Like many others stated, the ending is an extremely unsatisfying cliffhanger. It makes it seem as if everything you just did had no contribution to the story in anyway. I'm sure this is so people purchase the seasons pass or wait for "Wolfenstein 3". Another thing to mention is towards the end of the game, levels were reused which really had me rolling my eyes and had me reconsider whether the purchase was worth it. I don't think the price tag for this game is justified with what is offered. Should you purchase at full retail price? No. Should you purchase the game at a reasonable sale? Hell yes. Although the game does have a lot of side missions/content to offer (a lot of which I haven't even begun & not sure if I will), I think most people will purchase this game for its story. With all that being said, i do have to commend Machine Games (or rather Bethesda) for not shoving in anti-consumer RNG loot boxes into this game. It's sad that this has to be something that is appreciated nowadays but that just how it is (until people stop supporting these scummy business practices atleast). In conclusion, the game is just currently not worth its price in my opinion. Wait for a sale.

Let me start by saying that I am one of the lucky ones that experienced very little performance issues; I am running the game in 1440p resolution maxed out and I am able to maintain 140+ FPS most of the time. However, no matter how good a game runs; if it's bad it's bad
TL;DR: wait for %50 off at least before picking this up
Pros:
-Stunning graphics, one of better looking games out for sure
-Fun gameplay, very fast paced and satisfying with good variety
-SFX are robust; be it the satisfying gun-shot sound, the explosions or the huge mech enemies
-Some, though rare, funny moments in cutscenes
Cons:
-Terrible storyline: it's basically your typical corny action-romance movie fake deep ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, the writers are trying to force a romance sub-plot that has no place in a game like Wolfenstein, and they’re doing a bad job at it too.
-Terrible cast of characters: the writers tried to give every character a unique personality, but they tried too hard and most of the main cast turned out to be annoying. Anya is bland, Grace is a snarly pr*ck and BJ is trying too hard to be poetic. The characters with interesting personality (like Fergus and Sigun) didn’t get enough air time.
-Not enough content: The campaign took me 12 hours to beat and I was going out of my way to find collectibles; 3 hours of those 12 are cutscenes. The side quests are boring, repetitive and don’t incline you to play them at all. There is also a lack of variety in weapons; you only have 6 weapons, 2 of which are impractical due to the unavailability of their ammo type. So you’re stuck with only 4 weapons that you can actually use all the time. There are only 3 upgrades to every weapon and most of them don’t make the gameplay any fun.
-Lackluster soundtrack: After the outstanding work Mick Gordon delivered in Wolfenstein: The New Order, The Old Blood and Doom, I expected the soundtrack to be just as good in this one. What I got was a main theme that’s a remix of the first game’s main theme and generic rock music playing in the background that did nothing to hype the gameplay. I also found that the music was too low even when maxed out, you are unable to lower the SFX in the setting too so if you want the music to be loud you will need to tolerate the deafening sound of gun-shots.
-Slow storyline progression in the beginning, but extremely fast towards the end; making the final credits rolling in an unpleasant surprise.
Conclusion: One of the most disappointing sequels ever. The developer put so much emphasis on a terrible storyline with a terrible cast and kicked the gameplay down to a 2nd priority.

So let me start by saying, you should give this game a whirl. I had a bad experience, but you might not. But listed below are the reasons why I tried it, and just asked for a refund within the hour.
1. Holy damn its hard: So as a diver, its really damn hard to survive. When sharks approach, you get a heartbeat sound that increases as they get closer. But just that. In a really, really, really dark game where they can come out at you from literally any direction, its not particularly helpful. You have like a split second to try and decide which direction they are coming from. And then they suddenly lunge out from the dark (Cause that's their primary ability is lunge which is fast as hell). You really have no reaction time. And yes, you CAN buy little scanners to help you. But they work out to like.... 20 feet. It still jsut does not give you nearly enough reaction time to these sharks.
2. You can't pick a side: The game automatically picks if you are a diver or a shark. You can't decide "Hey next match I wanna be a shark!" You just have to roll the dice and sort of hope. Of the 4 games I played, I got diver all four times (And lost 3/4 matches). Some days you just wanna eat a dude and this game doesn't give you the option to do so.
3. Micro Transactions: Ok so the transactions are just for like, skins and stuff. So its not game breaking. But I'm always going to ding a game for micro transactions because I think the whole concept is a plight on the gaming industry anyway. On a plus side, you get daily quests that give you skin rewards if you complete them. Though I would just dump the microtransactions and just use that.
4. Lack of Development: You have a set amount of things you can buy and no real character development. I've always been a fan of some sort of level system that rewards you for playing well and letting you develop your character more to your playstyle. Like in my case, I REALLY would like to be able to detect these sharks just a little sooner. So if I had a character development, maybe I could have something to improve that. Right now its just the same character and the same 6 weapons you can choose from and deployables that don't seem to help.
5. Destroyable deployables: This is my final grief. I bought a little auto turret to help try and keep the sharks off us. Cause hey, robots are a lot faster than me. I've come to accept that. The sharks can literally just charge in, and destroy it in one hit. That's it. No refunds, and you can't replenish it. The only way you can get another one is if you die. I've dropped like 10 of these damn things and each shark just giggle and ate it. While I'm under deployables, the water mines can blow you and your team mates up. Of the land mines I did drop, I killed more team mates than sharks (And got killed by my team mates mines).
So all in all, I just did not have fun with this. It was annoying to try and look around and guess which direction these sharks were going to zip out from. Above? Below? Around? Who knows. All I know is I'm tired of getting rammed by a hammerhead and getting insta-killed in a place that is filled with narrow walls, super dark corridors, and little reward for my time.

Trying out a new style of review here. Totally NOT influenced by a critic. Here goes.
Note: This is my first Bethesda RPG game AFAIK. So I'm heavily biased towards this game.
Pros:
- Decent storytelling
- Interesting locations
- A story that, while cliche, has enough to interest you
- Interesting NPC's with character
- Varied enemies
- Cool♥♥♥♥♥combat system, "V.A.T.S." that lets you target body parts or even disarm opponents, with luck's blessing
- Character progression. Wanna make a charismatic lady-killer with the aim of a sniper? Sure. Go ahead.
- Pipboy! With radio stations and a map! Kill enemies while jamming to Cold War era tunes!
- Desolate atmosphere. Lack of colours make you feel hopeless as you scavenge around cautiously whilst searching for supplies and ammo.
Cons:
- Somewhat clunky combat. The firing animations for automatic weapons and the choice of a semi zoom-in instead of iron sights when you aim feels weird.
- The downtown area is a maze. You have to use the metro system to get around roadblocks and rubble. This could also be a storytelling and progression tool to prevent progressing too far, but I'm not sure.
Verdict: It's a decent start point to the 3D Fallout universe (post-isometric games). While I recommend New Vegas as a better starting point, this is where it all changed. For better or for worse, I'm not sure. So, if you like shooting mutants and running around in your very own suit of power armor then by all means get this game. Keep in mind that the game is nearly 9 years old and it hasn't aged graphically well. And the shooting mechanics will feel dated.

Technical issues aside, I'm dumbfounded at the number of negative reviews this is getting from Steam users. (70% are positive, so I don't know why it's not 'mostly positive' but whatever)
The game is absolutely phenomenal - gameplay, audio and visual fidelity, technical performance - improved over TNO and TOB in literally every way. I will concede that the story has some pacing issues, you may or may not like certain characters, and the ending shows up out of nowhere. What this game manages to pull off though is insane. The gunplay, my goodness - it's fantastic. And the level design compliments the gameplay perfectly. The asynchronous gameplay and all of the found story telling, ughhh, so good.
You know the lobby shootout in the Matrix and how nuts that was the first time you watched it? The hospital shootout at the end of Hard Boiled? This game feels like the first time I watched those films. Dual wielding SMGs, bobbing and weaving enemy fire, moving from pillar to pillar as you wipe scores of enemies efficiently with a mix of lead and melee attacks. Charging head-first down a corridor full of nazis with your shotgun, blasting nazis as you go; my goodness - THIS is wolfenstein. It's challenging, it's heavy, it's visceral, it's funny, it's emotional. All of these complaints about the game being too political are absolute nonsense. Wolfenstein's been doing this longer than literally everyone. LITERALLY, everyone. This is the natural next chapter of the story they set up with the first game. BJ's not here to change your daiper - he's here to topple a regime!
Modern audiences are fickle, and there's a whole generation of gamers that didn't grow up on fledgeling PC games and don't understand the contribution id made to games as a whole. While this is made by machine games, is so wonderfully carries the torch of the franchise.
I do understand there are a number of players, and a fair number of them at that, who had technical issues getting the game running. Those are fair points to consider, but I hope they come back and change their reviews once the hotfix gets their clients fixed because it's a shame that a title like this should be seen so negatively for something a minority of the player base is experiencing. I personally didn't experience any issues, my game ran like a dream - but I've been on the other side of that coin before and I know what it's like. With the amount of polish this game has compared to most modern games at launch, I'm positive these issues will be fixes very quickly, if not already.

So let me start by saying, you should give this game a whirl. I had a bad experience, but you might not. But listed below are the reasons why I tried it, and just asked for a refund within the hour.
1. Holy damn its hard: So as a diver, its really damn hard to survive. When sharks approach, you get a heartbeat sound that increases as they get closer. But just that. In a really, really, really dark game where they can come out at you from literally any direction, its not particularly helpful. You have like a split second to try and decide which direction they are coming from. And then they suddenly lunge out from the dark (Cause that's their primary ability is lunge which is fast as hell). You really have no reaction time. And yes, you CAN buy little scanners to help you. But they work out to like.... 20 feet. It still jsut does not give you nearly enough reaction time to these sharks.
2. You can't pick a side: The game automatically picks if you are a diver or a shark. You can't decide "Hey next match I wanna be a shark!" You just have to roll the dice and sort of hope. Of the 4 games I played, I got diver all four times (And lost 3/4 matches). Some days you just wanna eat a dude and this game doesn't give you the option to do so.
3. Micro Transactions: Ok so the transactions are just for like, skins and stuff. So its not game breaking. But I'm always going to ding a game for micro transactions because I think the whole concept is a plight on the gaming industry anyway. On a plus side, you get daily quests that give you skin rewards if you complete them. Though I would just dump the microtransactions and just use that.
4. Lack of Development: You have a set amount of things you can buy and no real character development. I've always been a fan of some sort of level system that rewards you for playing well and letting you develop your character more to your playstyle. Like in my case, I REALLY would like to be able to detect these sharks just a little sooner. So if I had a character development, maybe I could have something to improve that. Right now its just the same character and the same 6 weapons you can choose from and deployables that don't seem to help.
5. Destroyable deployables: This is my final grief. I bought a little auto turret to help try and keep the sharks off us. Cause hey, robots are a lot faster than me. I've come to accept that. The sharks can literally just charge in, and destroy it in one hit. That's it. No refunds, and you can't replenish it. The only way you can get another one is if you die. I've dropped like 10 of these damn things and each shark just giggle and ate it. While I'm under deployables, the water mines can blow you and your team mates up. Of the land mines I did drop, I killed more team mates than sharks (And got killed by my team mates mines).
So all in all, I just did not have fun with this. It was annoying to try and look around and guess which direction these sharks were going to zip out from. Above? Below? Around? Who knows. All I know is I'm tired of getting rammed by a hammerhead and getting insta-killed in a place that is filled with narrow walls, super dark corridors, and little reward for my time.

I am leaving a note here because it's the only place my past self would look. He's an egotistical prick who reads his own reviews constantly. In all honesty I don't want to communicate with him directly, so the rest of this post will be written in a detached, story-like format. It serves the same purpose, I figure. All I need to do is warn myself, but in the past though.
Anticipating the release of Wolfenstein 2, in September I am going to boot up No Man's Sky and play it until the game's release. The basic idea is that it would lower my standards so far down that I couldn't possibly be dissapointed. After The New Order and The Old Blood, my expectations were unreasonably high. The trailers for The New Colossus weren't doing anything that bothered me and I needed to drop the hype fast. It has a tendency to destroy the games it's supposed to support, and I'd hate to be oversold on something I might have otherwise enjoyed.
The plan worked up to a point, but I fear space and time won't sustain itself long enough for me to experience the game I destroyed reality to properly enjoy.
Allow me to explain.
No Man's Sky is an illusion. The game mechanics feed you progression, but it dawns on you eventually that your progression is meaningless in the absense of a goal. Almost the entire game is centric around the concept of discovery, but there is no planet you visit that does not already have aliens living upon it. You travel to the centre of the galaxy only so that you can get further away from it and travel to the centre of the galaxy again. Were this an ordinary game, these examples would be hard to forgive, especially given the marketing push for this one in particular. To emphasise this hypothetical excercise, i've selected not to recomend No Man's Sky, but that's not canon to the time travel plot arc i'm currently working on.
After prolonged hours in this game, I came to realise that these illusions were intentionally visible. Like a shower curtain concealing the shadow of an armed stranger entering the room. It was done to incite fearful anticipation, and to encourage the foolish to pull the curtain aside. I decided to confront these illusions and travel away from the centre of the galaxy instead.
It was at this point that I began to hear screaming that I didn't know speakers were capable of. The sounds were crystal clear, like pure water dripping from the circular speaker holes. The screen was awash with hyper realistic gore, and what looked like severed body parts arranged to spell out anti religious statements and unpopular opinions on videogames with cult fanbases. I turned off the Gameboy Colour. That's the last time I purchase a haunted Pokemon cartridge from a convicted serial killer of serial rapists of serial killers. That man was part of an ugly feud that spanned generations.
Looking up at my PC, I see that my ship had continued on it's course while I was playing Pokemon: Nuclear Holocaust Green. I set my Gameboy aside. From what I could see, a sort of space storm had surrounded my ship. Through flashes of space thunder and nonsensical space rain I could see the clouds in front of me darkening. Something was approaching. I heard screaming to my left. The Gameboy had turned back on. I pushed it off my desk and into a small bin. Looking back at my monitor, it would appear that my ship had crash landed on a new planet. This was strange for a number of reasons, one of which being that while there are mechanics for repairing a crashed ship, there are none for actually crashing one.
I find it difficult to talk about the rest of my journey because i'm not entirely sure how much of it I can legally disclose. Put simply, it was the most joyful experience i've had with a game and it just kept getting better the more time I invested into it. As I proceeded away from the centre of the galaxy, I encountered features like destructible, physics based terrain. There was in-atmosphere dogfighting and true control over my ship. I was playing the most robust and free form game i'd ever seen. It functioned as a space flight simulator, but worked perfectly as an on foot action game. On less hostile planets it was a zen like experience with a convincing ecosystem full of surprises and new behaviours. I could play the game without ever setting foot on a planet if I wanted. I can not overstate the sheer versatility of the game I saw develop before my eyes.
But as is law when writing about a videogaming oddity on the internet, all good things must become scary at some point. I had played shot for shot what was shown in the trailers. The sand worms, the huge monster knocking down trees... all of it. As I ventured further away from the center of the universe, I wasn't discovering new features. Features were being restored. The only explanation I can give is that they cut down the game as it grew closer to release. Sean Murray seemed nervous in his later interviews for No Man's Sky, and after what I've seen, I think it may be outright fear. The game was simply too deep. It was too open ended. It was a game that was totally dynamic and randomised, yet every feature seemed hand crafted, expertly developed. Many would ask if it's even possible to have a truly randomised sandbox game of such infinite scale that has the depth and quality of an infinitely smaller, more linear experience where every feature has been given the attention it deserves. That's a good question.
As I proceeded back through the game's development, it was becoming apparent to me that this game was bigger than any of us were ever intended to know. This would set a precedent for gaming so far ahead of it's time that the industry would be unable to sustain it. The creators of No Man's Sky had to choose between their game, or gaming itself. I see now that they chose wisely. I began to explore game worlds before beta, before alpha and then before the development of the game itself. The further back I went, the more huge the game became, the more I was drawn into it's world and the more helpless I was to stop the events i'd set into motion. I was now playing the No Man's Sky that never existed, that never was and should never have been. Time itself began to tear, as a man in the present was now playing a game so far back in the past that it never existed.
The best way I can describe it is that two timelines were made to intersect at one point. The fact that one timeline does not exist added friction to this event. It's a bit like two timelines doing that gesture where you make a ring with one hand and point with the other, then move the finger through the ring you've made a few times.  Time has rended itself apart, ribbons of it's fabric hanging between the past that never existed and all that has occurred in my timeline. While that's very unfortunate for me, as I was excited to play Wolfenstein 2 and it seems like I may have messed that up a bit, it does mean that because of hard to explain time stuff, this review should be posted at some point in your present.
To put it simply, don't play this game. It is a disgusting, putrid illusion. All of it.
PS- Sorry your future self still sucks at writing. Read a book or something.
PSS- If we want to talk theories, I think Sean Murray probably found this game in an underwater tomb of some kind.

Shortly put, this is a game that really shows that videogames are art. (in case you didn't know that already)

As the fourth installment of a trilogy (that's not a joke. It's in the trailer), Deponia Doomsday does fit in with the story really well. The key conceit of this adventure game is time travel, trying to chance the previous events of the previous three games. However, there are tons of new characters, and and only brief repeats or cameos of things you have already seen. However, with time travel being the overarching theme, there are some good and bad consequences. The good: shenanigans. So many. it's like Back to the Future 2, where you get to interfere with things in the past that you've already interfered with. There are time travel duplicates out to wazoo. However, the bad: There are several puzzles that are only solvable by rewinding time, meaning you end up having to do the same tasks over and over, only to find out you don't have everything you need to complete it until you solve one thing first and do another time loop. So the game is much more linear than it otherwise would be. There are also timed puzzles with a countdown clock in which you have to perform certain actions in a time crunch before a time reset, which is super stressful and doesn't allow you a lot of time to puzzle it out on your own or plan anything. There are also lots of lowbrow jokes (farting, pooping, boobs, and old man sweat), so be prepared. If that's your thing, enjoy. Personally didn't care for them much.
So, overall: It's good. If you liked the previous games, you'll like this one. Same great art, voices, humor, music (literally the same music. I didn't really notice anything new), but with some new twists. I found myself cheating with walkthroughs a few too many times during the countdown sequences just because I was getting so sick of repeating. There are also some nonsensical puzzles that are inherent to any adventure game, where the devs clearly had a plan in mind and it's only obvious once you have all the pieces, but you can't GET the pieces if you don't realize what the devs want you to do.
So, yeah. Buy it if you like the series or enjoy puzzle games. The story is worth it, I think. Just don't expect perfection.

Recommended, with big caveats. (Note that I've played all of the Deponia games.)
The humor and voice acting is great, much of the puzzles are fun. A part of me wants to give this an enthusiastic thumbs up, but I'm on the edge of thumbs down.
The fact that there is a simple game breaking bug that *most* people hit that they haven't seen fit to fix (SAVE BEFORE GOING INTO THE SAUNA) should be enough to stay away in most games.  There are also infuriating timed events, particularly near the end of the game (at the *least* they could pause the timer while the character is speaking and you can't do anything). Said timed events at the end of the game will leave you that much less satisfied with the ending (which many are unhappy with, story-wise).
The polish is lacking, and seems to stand out more near the end of the game. Mouth animations sometimes don't play when the characters speak, and the volume levels aren't consistent with the voices- which is a particular shame given the quality of the writing and acting.
I personally found very few of the mini-games enjoyable, but thanfully they're skippable. I wondered to myself how much better the game would have been if the resources from developing "action" mini-games would have gone towards fit-and-finish for the game.
There were a couple of unfortunate puzzles that might drive you to walkthroughs. Notably one where you can pick up an item if you *look* at it three times in a row. Ugh.
Pick this one up if you see it on a major sale. They don't deserve more than $5 if they can't fix the sauna bug a year in. Stay away if you get frustrated easily or you want to finish without consulting online resources.

Fallout 3 is a great game, in fact it's one of my facourite games of all time. So far I have done 10 or so full playtroughs in both Xbox 360 and PC and I enjoyed every single one of those. The world is well built, having plenty to explore which generally gives somewhat good rewards but fluxuation happens in both better and worse.
The weaker aspect of the game is the main storyline which goes all over the place has somewhat lackluster ending, which is somewhat fixed in 'Broken Steel' DLC. The lack of strong main storyline is supplemented with heavy use of sidequests and these are the meat of the game as many of these sidequests are memoriable and interesting, altough slightly dimnished by the karma system which promotes player for being either super good or super evil thus making some choices easier for the player to make.

The combat it functioning and while there is clearly superior playstyle the game does offer and sometimes even promotes the use of other methodes as well.
Modding is very prevelant and allows for quite large changes to be made to the base game, greatly enhances the game. Altough it might be a bit fiddely got them working.

Now for quick rewieve of the DLC that come with the "game of the year edition"
Operation: Anchorage is radically different from rest of the game as it takes place in a simulation. Your playstyle is heavily restricted and the DLC is extremily linear. The story is quite bland as well. Gives good gear as a reward tough.
One of my favourite DLC's. The Pitt gives wide range of playstyles and choices for the player while also allowing for great freedom to explore the area, with few story explained expections. The setting and the story are also fantastic and the DLC also includes one of the few real moral dilemmas that blurs the line between good and bad.
Broken steel fixes the ending of the base game and alters the world greatly while giving you ok story and new area. Generally does everything alright.
Point Lookout gives the largest new area with new characters and plotpoints. The story is done well and the settings is good. The only negative are the enemies which in many cases have been made to be either cheatingly strong hitters as they ignore your armour or are simply bulletsponges. Generally well made DLC
Mothership Zeta is probably the weakest of the DLC as it's concept is wuite ridicilus and the characters are somewhat dull or unrealisticly calm. The enemies are also far too bulletspongy. The story is quite dull and the map is generally uninteresting as it's always either small corridors or open rooms.

Remember Me is a game full of beauty and intrigue. It’s clear a lot of thought and hard work was built not only to craft an interesting world to inhabit, but also explore. It’s really too bad the mechanics and story weren’t up to par for the task.
Remember Me is a action-adventure-brawler that takes place in the year 2084 in a heavily cyberpunk inspired city of Neo Paris. In this world a new technology exists that allows memories to be exchanged, modified and removed, allowing citizens to remove unpleasant memories and replacing them with good ones. Nearly everyone in society has taken up that opportunity.
The player plays as Nilin, a member of the “Errorist” movement fighting to get rid of said technology that they believe has enslaved much of society. The game starts up with the player tuning in just as Nilin seems to be having her memory removed rather painfully. As far as amnesia as a narrative framing goes, this one is at least somewhat interesting. From here the player is guided mostly linearly throughout the rest of the game, which consists of alternating between competent melee combat and samey exploration.
Basic combat is handled by using different combinations of the X and Y button on the XBox controller. While fighting Nilin automatically locks on to a nearby opponent, though the game never really explicitly tells the player which opponent you’re locked on to. Switching between enemies is simple, as moving the left analogue stick in the general direction of an opponent causes the player wants to start attacking them. In my experience though switching to a new opponent ended any combo I was in the middle of, which can be a pretty big problem. More on that a bit later.
Besides combos the player also has special attacks that are used once they have enough energy that is gained through attacks on the enemy or when Nilin is attacked. The first special attack unlocked is pretty standard and makes Nilin faster and more powerful allowing the player to jam on whatever buttons they want for a few seconds and generally do a lot of damage. This is useful for clearing out enemies, but little else. Another stuns enemies for a while allowing the player to get in a few good combos. My favorite ability allows the player to turn invisible for a brief period and take out any one enemy before becoming visible again, a power I used as frequently as allowed later in the game.
The special attacks are critically important to the game later on as enemies become stronger and more plentiful, or have some sort of effect that makes attacking them less effective. This would be neat, if they allowed the player to use special attacks more frequently. After the activation of a special attack the player cannot use it again until a cooldown has ended. This in itself isn’t a bad idea, except in a lot of cases the cooldown was so high that it made combat pretty frustrating, especially when the special attacks is the most fun part of the combat.
As the player progresses through the game they unlock combos and “Presence” through gaining “Presence Points.” The combo systems is unlike anything I’ve seen before. Each presence corresponds to a specific button press that is used in combat, which is then equipped to a button press in any of the combos. For example, if I unlocked a presence labeled as “X” I could equip it to any part of a combo where the button “X” would be pressed. What this does is vastly change the effect of any of the combos.
In total there are only four combos throughout the entire game ranging from three button presses to eight. When the player earns enough PP they can unlock one of four kinds of Presence. The first Presence unlocked gives each hit a bit extra damage, allowing the player to disorient enemies and finish them off for some extra PP. The second gives the player a small health boost with every hit. The third reduces the cooldown time for any special attack currently in a cooldown phase. The final is a sort of enhancement presence that enhances the presence for the previous button press in the combo.
The different kinds of presence can be stacked in a row for greater effect allowing the player to define exactly what each combo is really good for, or allow them to make a specific combo a sort of catch all for everything they could hope to want. Though, because of the ability to gain health during combat, I only ever died once through the entire experience while I played on the medium (recommended) difficulty setting.
The problem with this system arises when the player actually gets into combat. Typically while in combat the player has several opponents, and they tend to gather near the player. This causes the scenario to occur where the player is attacking an opponent when another opponent starts to attack them. Thankfully when an enemy is about to attack there is a clear indication over their head, and a simple press of the A button causes the player to dodge out of the way and keep the lock on their current enemy. However, I’ve found dodging out of the way inconsistently ends the combo I was in the middle of. Most of the time I only ever completed one of the larger combos when I was fighting a single enemy on their own. Every other time I had to deal with using a smaller combo I knew I could finish off before being attacked.
Overall, the combat felt entirely too stiff and mechanical. It gave me very few chances to feel like I was pulling off cool moves since I was being interrupted so frequently. It often seemed that enemies were designed to only start attacking while I was in the middle of an active combo. The special moves helped with getting some enemies off my back, but the most useful ones took so long to recharge and the combos that I had set to reduce the cooldown were so constantly interrupted combat felt drawn out and frustrating.
There are a handful of boss battles, but a good majority of them involve the player fighting hordes of enemies while the boss takes pot shots at them from afar. The boss battles are painfully extended, mostly because there are only key moments where damage can be dealt or require a special attack to end it’s cooldown time. At the end of each boss battle there is a quick time sequence with timed button presses and occasionally some button mashing. The best thing I have to say about the QTE in this game is that it isn’t offensive and I only ever failed one once.
Between combat the player spends a lot of time navigating the environment. This includes a lot of climbing over ledges, jumping over pits and shuffling along building edges. This wasn’t bad per se, but I never felt like this was particularly interesting. These sequences are almost entirely linear in nature and rarely have any sense of urgency. There are a small amount of collectibles scattered around like health and special power boosts, as well as small amounts of information on the world. The former is often given away with hints that show the location of the boost from a different angle. Though frequently the location of the boosts are so obvious that the need for a hint can feel almost insulting.

Ultimate Marvel vs Capcom 3, the infamous "fighting game on crack" with all of its crazy broken gameplay finally hits Steam, containing the previously-delisted Jill and Shuma-Gorath, all costume DLC, and utilizing Steamworks for multiplayer. Now I finally have a reason to get rid of my Xbox 360. God bless, Capcom.
+Runs on the MT Framework 2.x engine, so performance will be very well optimized, even on low spec setups. Other games that run on MT Framework 2.x that you can use for performance references: Dragon's Dogma, Resident Evil 6, Devil May Cry 4 SE, Resident Evil Revelations.
+Faithful port of the PS4 version, gameplay is completely intact and identical to the original last-gen versions.
+Supports resolutions up to 4k. Uses FXAA, and can use antisotropic filtering if forced through your graphics drivers.
+Natively supports both Xinput and DirectInput controllers.
+Uses Steamworks for multiplayer (take notes Capcom...).
+- VSync is forced on by default and cannot be disabled through config files or in game options. Must be force disabled from graphics drivers.
+- Does not support ultrawide resolutions (Letterboxing/pillarboxing will occur for anything other than 16:9).
+- Can crash with certain on screen overlays (minor issue but worth mentioning, I experienced consistent crashes with MSI Afterburner running).
+- The netcode is apparently UNCHANGED from the console version. UMVC3 on last gen consoles had spotty netcode at best, so don't come in expecting flawless online play most of the time. It's nowhere as bad as Street Fighter 5, but it's certainly not on the level of Fightcade/USF4/Skullgirls/Killer Instinct.
-There seems to be a minor audio issue where after a certain amount of time in game, the audio will become severely muted/deafened. Also, Frank West has some certain sounds mixed up (Tools of Survival sometimes plays a zombie sound effect) that as of writing this review, have not been patched. Hopefully Capcom gets on a bugfix quickly.

I was gifted this as a joke, and can't believe I'm doing this, but I'm recommending it on the basis of it being, well...kinda fun.
It's a casual, on-rails real time strategy (RTS) game. You assign workers to tasks by clicking their destination, but they can only move along set paths and have to clear obstacles to get to additional resources, building sites, and end-goals in each level's self-contained one-screen map.
The Greek-mythology-lite story is pretty dumb, and clearing the levels is hilariously and mock-ably easy. But like many casual games, trying to earn 3 stars on each level raises the stakes to a fun level. Getting the 3rd star requires beating the level before the timer reaches the "Gold Time" mark, which turns each level into a trail-and-error efficiency puzzle.
For example, on one level I attempted 4-5 times to get the 3rd star, there were 5 branching paths from a central path to the end goal with 2 farms (which produce food) and 2 worksites (which produce wood) near the starting point. First attempts focused on resource gathering and left obstacle-removal until later, and failed. Focusing on clearing obstacles ran up against resource shortages. Finally I figured out a perfect balance of selective resource gathering with one worker while clearing just the right paths with the other to clear all the end goals just before the timer dinged. Pretty satisfying!
If you go into this with appropriate expectations - a pretty goofy casual game with some light but entertaining strategic challenges - you could have a good time. If you enjoy playing RTS games solo but can't handle the constant pressure of scrolling all over the place, this might also be a good fit.
For a harder efficiency-focused strategy game, definitely try the harder but less clicky and goofy "Spacechem," or the turn-based "Desktop Dungeons."

A year after the release, this game is still full of disappointment and frustration.
1) Everything is slow AF. Menu transitions are slow. UI animations are slow. You have to hold button for a full goddamn second to trigger any action (there's a mod though which removes this delay in most places). Doing anything feels like it's taking eternity and a half.
2) Crafting and inventory system is really awkward to use. Amount of inventory slots you have is tiny compared to the number of items you'll need, so you constantly get "INVENTORY FULL" message. You can't talk to NPCs when your suit's inventory is full. You can't move things from exocraft to suit inventory directly, you have to transfer them to the ship first. Crafting a few of the same thing is awkward, because you need to craft one item in an empty cell and then manually stack it with existing item. It like the crafting system was slapped on later, but somehow it is a vital component of the game.

Honestly, I do not think No Man's Sky is a bad game, but it is nowhere near the best. The gameplay is fun for a while, getting resources, doing the storyline, making a base, getting vehicles for your use on world, getting new ships, etc. Then comes repetition. It gets dull. This game is a perfect example of how you shouldn't trust blindly in the masses' opinion. For me, at least.
I'll preface this short review by saying that I got bored after 1 hour and complained about it to my friends. The game was bland and crashed a lot at first, nothing special really happened.
But then I gave it a second chance and I started looking into it a little more. Learning the languages seemed to affect very little but it's actually really fun; crafting the next best thing is the classic progression system that everybody loves and roaming around the planets on your exocrafts, shooting stuff and making profits is everything a gamer dreams of in a sandbox. I speak for myself.
There's a lot to do for at least the 25 hours I've played. I've been doing quests, exploring planets and identifying animals and plants (the true sandbox experience), and I haven't even scratched the surface on spaceships or more importantly, base-building. I honestly don't see what's not to like about all of this in a sandbox game. And maybe that's the key: people seem to forget this is a sandbox game and that sandbox games don't have endless hours of objectives to do. You make your own fun. Just like in Minecraft, Terraria, Garry's Mod or any game of the sort.
The only negative aspects I have to say about this game is that there are a few bugs, a few crashes and the exocraft vehicles, although fun, are kind of irrelevant. Their purpose turns obsolete with inventory expansions, advanced mining tools and for fast travelling... Why not just take the ship? They're great for finding ruins and that's about it.
For a sandbox experience? 8/10. It's not incredibly groundbreaking but it is incredibily fun. Give it a shot and remember that the masses also think Justin Bieber is a good singer.

Fallout 3 is a great game, in fact it's one of my facourite games of all time. So far I have done 10 or so full playtroughs in both Xbox 360 and PC and I enjoyed every single one of those. The world is well built, having plenty to explore which generally gives somewhat good rewards but fluxuation happens in both better and worse.
The weaker aspect of the game is the main storyline which goes all over the place has somewhat lackluster ending, which is somewhat fixed in 'Broken Steel' DLC. The lack of strong main storyline is supplemented with heavy use of sidequests and these are the meat of the game as many of these sidequests are memoriable and interesting, altough slightly dimnished by the karma system which promotes player for being either super good or super evil thus making some choices easier for the player to make.

The combat it functioning and while there is clearly superior playstyle the game does offer and sometimes even promotes the use of other methodes as well.
Modding is very prevelant and allows for quite large changes to be made to the base game, greatly enhances the game. Altough it might be a bit fiddely got them working.

Now for quick rewieve of the DLC that come with the "game of the year edition"
Operation: Anchorage is radically different from rest of the game as it takes place in a simulation. Your playstyle is heavily restricted and the DLC is extremily linear. The story is quite bland as well. Gives good gear as a reward tough.
One of my favourite DLC's. The Pitt gives wide range of playstyles and choices for the player while also allowing for great freedom to explore the area, with few story explained expections. The setting and the story are also fantastic and the DLC also includes one of the few real moral dilemmas that blurs the line between good and bad.
Broken steel fixes the ending of the base game and alters the world greatly while giving you ok story and new area. Generally does everything alright.
Point Lookout gives the largest new area with new characters and plotpoints. The story is done well and the settings is good. The only negative are the enemies which in many cases have been made to be either cheatingly strong hitters as they ignore your armour or are simply bulletsponges. Generally well made DLC
Mothership Zeta is probably the weakest of the DLC as it's concept is wuite ridicilus and the characters are somewhat dull or unrealisticly calm. The enemies are also far too bulletspongy. The story is quite dull and the map is generally uninteresting as it's always either small corridors or open rooms.

I can't believe I'm doing this, but I'm giving a Deponia game a negative review. It's not just because I'm still salty about the ending, and don't expect the ending to change that much; I'm just going to warn you right now. I'm glad that I didn't buy this game at full price because it's sadly not worth it.
Of course it still has the same fun cast and great new characters, and of course the same great, sarcastic, slightly narcissistic Rufus that we all know and love, but there was a lot about the game that I found unsatisfying, and it wasn't just the garbage ending.
Let's start off with the pros-
-Great characters
-The new time function definitely turned the game around, made it more interesting
-Great music (as always, but we didn't see much of our banjo playing friend which kind of sucked)
Now for the cons-
-The new time function, while a fun game changer, was also quite annoying and confusing at times because it made the game much too difficult, I found myself pausing way too much and having to end up looking at a walk through just to figure out what I had to do before the timer ran out.
-The false hope that the ending just might be better. Lets face it, most of us bought this game in hopes that the ending would be better, or at least different and SPOILER WARNING:
-Some of the plot seems a bit rushed and pointless
So I just want anyone who reads this to know that I LOVE the Depoina series as a whole, but this game just disappointed me on SO MANY levels. And it was not just the ending that angered me.

This is hands-down the best party game I've ever played. For the price of You Don't Know Jack alone, you get multiple great games, including an amazing Pictionary-style game that manages to not only have its own identity, but exceeds Pictionary in some ways, mostly in terms of quality of the prompts. I can't say Pictionary has ever asked me to draw "words" or "#throwbackthurs."
Meanwhile, Fibbage manages to take the YDKJ-level of trivia questions and combines it with trying to fool your friends into choosing your convincing yet wrong answer. Would you guess that there's a group of people who celebrate by bashing each other with bags of fire ants? Neither would I, which is why I got 1000 points by tricking my friends into thinking it was feces.
YDKJ is, of course, the best at what it is, and 2015 keeps with the trend of "ARE YOU ♥♥♥♥ING SERIOUS" trivia, so while there's nothing really new about the gameplay, that's not necessarily a bad thing. Don't fix what isn't broken, after all.
Word Spud is the only game that really falls flat for me. The description really doesn't explain what it is, so I'll attempt to do so. Have you ever played the driving game where you say a word, and then your friend has to say a word to go after that one that still makes sense? It's that. That's the whole game. They made a video game out of that. There's scoring, but the points are based on your friends voting on whether or not they liked what you said. There's literally no incentive to say "yes" to anything, so the game falls apart. I see the potential for a Cards Against Humanity-style "everyone puts something in and then you pick the funniest answer" game, but they instead made... this. It's fun for one round, but I don't plan on coming back to it.
Lie Swatter is essentially something you can put on to fill time at an actual party. Since it's the only game that supports more than 8 players, it works well for larger groups who don't want to leave anyone out. Unfortunately, since it's been designed to accomodate such large groups, the gameplay suffers, and it's essentially a game of True or False. It's certainly more fun than Word Spud, but nothing to write home about. Definitely reserved for things like family get-togethers, weddings, and the like.
For those concerned about how multiplayer works, don't be. While a couple of reviews have groaned about the smart device requirement, it really shows how creative the people at Jackbox can be, given the right tools. A game like Drawful has always required you to either play a Flash game on your computer or use some kind of accessory on your console, but in this case, if your device can run a modern web browser, you can probably use it to play these games (while I haven't tried using the WiiU gamepad, I would not be surprised if it worked). Fibbage would be outright impossible with any other input method, simply by design. While I can understand the frustration with YDKJ not using controller input, and I don't know why they didn't increase the amount of players thanks to bypassing the controller limitation, it's a small price to pay, when smartphones and tablets are as ubiquitous as they are.
Oh, and if you're looking to play online, I've found a solution (requiring multiple monitors) that involves using Google Hangouts to broadcast your screen that's hosting the game and having all of your friends play by watching the Hangout. Skype, unfortunately, has such terrible video quality that it's unwatchable, but I'm sure many other video conferencing applications will do a similarly good job. The game runs in Windowed Borderless, so you don't have to worry about constantly alt-tabbing, or anything, and the latency from Hangouts is short enough that you can all laugh at the same things at the same time. If you really want to have fun, you can even broadcast the game on Hitbox.tv, because the latency is short enough to where your viewers can competently play, albeit with a 4-second delay. Twitch is functional for playing Drawful, since you have so much time, but Fibbage and YDKJ are far too time-focused. I'd personally recommend streaming on your preferred site and then advertising the Hangout somewhere in the chat or on the page, for anyone wanting to join.
While I'm concerned about the amount of content, considering multiple-hour play sessions are a regular thing, I've been playing a combination of only Fibbage and Drawful for nearly 8 hours with not a single repeated prompt, yet. I would definitely purchase add-on content, if any became available, as well.

Hardest no I've ever written.  I love the games in the party pack.  They're a lot of fun.  My family and I have managed to get a few hours of entertainment out of them and I have immensely enjoyed the content.  You Don't Know Jack 2015 and Fibbage both feature Cookie Masterson, which is really the most important thing to know, with Drawful being the surprise hit of the pack.
You Don't Know Jack is a classic trivia game show environment where each question is posed, then each player is able to give their answers. Cookie is condescending and evil towards the folks who get it wrong, something that often provides a great spot of humor.
Fibbage XL is a fill-in-the-blank trivia game where each player gets to enter an answer, right or wrong, and then those answers are shuffled in with the real answer, at which point each player gets a chance to guess.  Points are awarded to players who get the question right, and to the players who are able to "trick" the others into guessing.  There are a few problems with Fibbage, mostly relating to the use of the language.
Fibbage's "true" answer can easily get lost in the mix.  For example, say the answer to a question is "Grand Canyon" and you type in "the Grand Canyon" and your friend misses a letter and types in "Gran Canyon."  You now have three VERY similar answers, with two of them being functionally correct, and the game won't detect it as being the same as the "correct" answer. This is both the source of fun in Fibbage, and a source of frustration.
Lie Swatter is a pseudo-trivia game where players must either answer True or False to the statements given.  Some of the "lies" are remarkably difficult to spot, and players will enjoy trying to guess them.
Drawful requires players to attempt to draw things from the given category, and then other players will try to guess what has been... done.  After guesses are made, players must determine the true name of the category.  Like Fibbage, Drawful suffers from answer ambiguity in that adding articles or making typing errors can render the true answer indistinguishable from the fakes, but c'est la vie.
Word Spud, the low point of the pack, is a word association game played by taking random turns adding to the words given previously.  So a 5 turn word order may look like this: Banana Split Decision Election Politics. Points are awarded by players voting on whether the given words were acceptable, so basically the points don't matter.
The games scored as individual games:
YDKJ - 9/10
Lie Swatter - 9/10
Drawful - 10/10
Fibbage - 9/10
Word Spud - 6/10
So why No?
Pseudo-technical issues.  This game doesn't have actual local multiplayer support.  Internet connection is a MUST, so no taking this game to a party center unless they've got wi-fi.  The game requires that you sign each player into Jackbox.TV - admittedly not that difficult since you can do it from desktops, laptops, cell phones, tablets, toasters, etc. and use your "room code" to start the game.  However! This connection to the online service
give you actual online multiplayer, either.
and streaming services have a significant enough delay to where YDKJ players would have a significant host advantage... sometimes by more than 10 seconds.
It gets hairy in practice, though - the people playing the game have to be comfortable with their individual devices, or one of you has to be technically inclined enough to be able to make sure everyone's devices are operating as expected for the entirety of the game. So if you've got a friend or relative or partygoer who doesn't have a cell, they're not playing, making this the least casual-friendly party game to date.
This leads me to my next problem - while I understand the need for the screen for Drawful, Fibbage, and Word Spud, I can't figure out why YDKJ and Lie Swatter aren't controller compatible.  I should be able to hand each player an Xbox 360 controller (or use my Big Button controllers) which require LITERALLY no technical experience to use and put each player on an even playing field.
That's ultimately my biggest problem with the system as it stands at release - in practice, the game is literally unfair.  My parents are in their fifties and my mother's an amputee.  We can't really play on an even playing field because my ability with the phone doesn't match theirs.
So, if you're going to get a group of friends together and they're all on equal footing in the smartphone world, then fine - this is a great game.  If you're going to include anyone else... nope.  Nope nope nope.

(I'll just put the most important point here before all the context and complaining: I bought this game because the steam page lists "Full Controller Support", but this doesn't have that, as only one of the games in single-player mode supports a controller. It should be "Partial Controller Support" at best. So my purchase was based on a false claim.)
The one, and only thing I bought this game to do was to play You Don't Know Jack with my family around thanksgiving. I have a set of controllers and was extremely disappointed that the previous release didn't support them. This does support controllers, however! Well, sort of. It supports Controller, singular.
It only supports a game controller in single-player YDKJ mode. To play multiplayer, you have to use smartphones (or other computers) to load a browser-based controller app. This sounds neat but was plagued with problems - trouble connecting, getting disconnected a few times per game, phones falling asleep between questions because of no input for 15 seconds, laptop turning off the screen mid-game because of no input for 15 minutes, etc.
Several of these issues (and locking up the first time I tried to screw someone, which was when we gave up) are likely because of being rushed out before thanksgiving - and I appreciate the effort, and all of us agreed that the bugs are reasonable for it being brand new. But several of them are fundamental design issues. And none (except the screwing lock-up) would have been a problem if I could have used the controllers I already bought, have used for years, and have already used in the Xbox 360 version of YDJK released 3 years ago.
Of course, that's not the only reason to buy the game for many other people, since there are several other game modes, but that was the only reason I got it, and mostly for the short window of family gatherings. But the other games would have had the same issues with the smartphone controllers. I also feel deceived, as I bought it because the store page clearly says "Full Controller Support" and it absolutely doesn't have that.
