I had a ton of fun playing this game. First playthrough was on the hardest difficulty which felt realistic, as in, you take about as much damage as the standard enemies do. This forces you to slow down a bit and really plan out attacks. I would typically use stealth until it hit the fan then would need to move quickly and use cover. The lean mechanic works very well to get a few good shots off. Once the action starts, it's all about mobility. The AI is a good balance of smart enough to flank you, but dumb enough to have fun with. You always feel like you have the upper hand, but it takes real work to survive a firefight.
The second half of the game has some awesome gameplay twists that keep things fresh and while always linear, introduce some interesting level design changes to accomodate some new toys.
The story is good. I enjoyed it, and while slower in pace for the first half, it picks up in such an over the top fashion later, you can't help but laugh at the absurdity. Very comic book like in nature. It could be argued that the cutscenes are frequent and on the longer side, but they are well acted, directed and fun to watch at least on a first playthrough. The loading is hidden by the cutscenes, but you can skip them once the load is done.
I did have a few technical issues. Some freezes here and there but after I locked my fps to 90 in EVGAs Precision X, it seemed to fix all of it. Not sure why, but the game seems sensitive to high frame rates on my overclocked system.
End game content is very fun and keeps the action rolling after the credits. I'm excited to see where the series goes next!
Also wanted to comment on length. 17 hours on hard for first playthrough is pretty good for a linear FPS. I'm sure it's much faster on a lower difficulty, but if you have competent shooter skills, the game should be played on the hardest to start.

Been playing piano since I was young, and graduated in Music Ed recently. I've used online free music theory stuff similar in kind, so I am comparing it a bit. Since it was on sale for $1>, I thought I'd give it a shot.
Pros: Good as a game for newbies. Starts out very simple. Probably does get more challenging with the learning curve. Allows background music to be turned off, and muting strings.
Cons: I felt that it needs an accurate visual aspect. For example, clicking on a digital keyboard that shows you and plays back low keys and high keys. I felt that if the strings were a violin or guitar string, it would be more real-life accurate, high pitches and string note location in relation to each other. I thought that having background music was distracting, which you could argue that it helps listening against distraction but I think it hinders accurate listening. I thought the layout and menus could've been better, as well as different color schemes. Wasn't really feeling the lavendar/purple gradient.
I obviously didn't play very long, but it didn't pique my interest as something I would use as a tool in the future, except for younger kids who could possibly take something away from this. Maybe it's just too simplistic for me. It could turn out to be much more challenging for a seasoned musician as you move forward in the game, but I didn't really want to put the time into it seeing as I don't really need this for myself. Maybe the whole strings theme didn't relate with me since I've learned (as well as all my college classmates and musician friends) music theory based around the piano. This game is just a different aspect.
Bottom line: I wouldn't personally recommend... but that goes without saying I don't think that it can't find it's place with someone out there.
If you're still curious or feeling unsatisfied with my answer, give it a go. :]

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice isn't just a videogame; it's a work of art. You cannot possibly imagine a game with this quality sold for 30$, it's insane. It might only take 6-7 hours to complete, but every single minute of this game is unforgettable and, ultimately as a whole package, becomes one of the best games of 2017. More than that, Hellblade is most certainly that breakthrough the gaming industry needed, but not in a way it wanted it. At the end of the day, probably few will appreciate the scale of what hellblade brings to the table.
There isn’t anything like this in the market. The binaural audio really comes as a fundamental tool to try to bring the audience as close as possible to one of the most recognized symptoms of psychosis and probably the most difficult one to portray: auditory hallucinations. This is what makes the game unique. Few games depend hardly on their sound design like Hellblade does. Fortunately, this is the best aspect of this game and probably one of the best sound designs of all time in a game. Voice acting is also excellent and music very good. This game should be the best in this category, at least this year.
The power of the Unreal Engine 4 is already known within the gaming community, but Hellblade still manages to surprise. The portrayal of visual hallucinations is very solid and the overall graphics in the game are pretty impressive to look at. Probably, the best feature about the graphics quality can be admired on the main Character's (Senua) expressions and motion design; it's really breathtaking how many emotions are transmitted through her and how it helps to really bring her and her story to life. As with most Unreal Engine videogames, Hellblade runs very well even on mid-range PCs. It feels fluid either on 30 fps or on 60fps.
The entire story revolves around Senua and her quest to save her lover's soul while facing all kinds of fantastical trials that just might or not might be all fabrications of her own imagination; all of this revolves around the mysterious and interesting Norse mythos. Almost at the end, the quest abruptly transforms into one of self-acceptance. While the story wouldn’t be anything to write home about under normal circumstances, in here it all cames back again to the way it is delivered and displayed; that's definitely what makes this game so unique. There are few psychological games that manage to bring out such an appropriate atmosphere of fear and helplessness, Hellblade nails it. It also encourages the player to keep going and see how Senua's tale will unfold pretty much till the credits roll.
If Ninja Theory wasn’t such a famous game developer people would be calling this game an indie game. Thing is, it really is almost an indie game, at least when you take the publishing measures of it into account. It would be best, though, to call Hellblade: Senua's Scrifice an independent AAA game. Ninja Theory developed and published this game on their own and released it at the base price of 29.99$. It’s rare for developers do this kind of stunt and, personally, I feel the game is worth every penny. It's very rare when I sit and focus on one game and even finish it. Hellblade made me sit through 3 nights and finish it while I enjoyed every minute of it, then I watched about 25 minutes of the development/educational video they included which brought me almost to 10 hours in total for in-game time. For a videogame of this quality, quite honestly, at the base price it is a steal for the awesome experience it delivers.
This is probably where the game doesn't manage to be spectacular. Action is very fluid and beautiful to watch at, but very simple. Don’t expect combo based systems like on DmC, expect something more on the lines of Heavenly Sword. Then again, Hellblade is a story-oriented game, so combat comes off as a bonus. Then, we have the puzzles that, again, are very simple and tight. Honestly, the puzzles are not really interesting and while most are really easy to solve, some require very specific positioning, so much so that the whole thing feels extremely restrictive at many points in the game. This doesn’t really tamper with the game's overall experience, but this aspect of the game could have been a lot better, even for a story-driven game.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is not a game for everyone and it won't be appreciated by everyone who plays it either. It is a very disturbing game to its core with the usual dose of violence audiences seem to love. The thing is violence here is represented in such unique way throughout the game that it doesn't feel cliché at all. The psychological aspect of the game has been researched and compared up with real-in life experiences to bring out the gamer closer to a psychosis scenario. The characters are fleshed out and make the story captivating and interesting. The graphics are very good and the sound design is just brilliant. Hellblade is definitely one of my favorite games this year and I will probably remember it for a long time and compare to other games that attempt to go the same way this game went. Because Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice has become a shining reference for the psychological genre and I doubt that, out of the few games that will try out to go this same path, there will be any that actually surpasses it in the near future.

Let me start by saying I haven't beaten this game yet, but at level 26, I'm far enough in to give a review. I'm going to list pros and cons and then expand upon them down below. I'm not really going to touch upon the story all that much.
Pros:
Story is alright (nothing special, but it's better than most of what you'll find these days)
Nice level design
Game provides a challenge (both a pro and a con, see below)
Katarina is a pretty cool character
Varied enemies
Cons:
Framerate tanks to below 30 in some areas if you can believe that
AI partner is useless
Game provides a challenge (both a pro and a con, see below)
Very lame skilltree as a mage
Voice acting is pretty lame (Van Helsing isn't too bad, Katarina is hit or miss and the rest of the NPC's are pretty bad)
Combat is boring
To start off, you play as Van Helsing's son (yea, THE Van Helsing). Something is wrong in this city that your father cleared out years ago and you must save the day. You are accompanied by Katarina, a ghost who is bound to serve your family. She is your partner in combat and can either be a melee or ranged specialist. She also levels up and has her own skill tree.
This game does a few things right. Level design is something you will notice upon loading up a new area. The areas you prod around in are generally large and look pretty good. So far I've been through a small village, forested areas, a mine, a sewer, secret laboratories, The Ink (kind of a take on The Fade from Dragon Age) and a big city. Each location has impressed me thus far. Also a plus is Katarina herself. Trudging around the game by yourself would get pretty boring. Her presence, combined with the banter she has with Van Helsing is decent enough to where the game doesn't feel so grindy. Also a plus are the various types of enemies with different abilities. The game groups up different enemies constantly, and some of the battles can be very tough.
Unfortunately, for every thing this game does right, there's two things it does wrong. Firstly, the game tanks to below 30 FPS in certain areas. This is on a 4770k with 2x 7870 Myst Editions. It's happened in two areas so far. It's not in one little spot on the map, either. The framerate keeps tanking throughout the whole area. If I leave the area, I start getting great frames again. As soon as I go back in, it tanks again. I guess those areas were just very poorly optimized. Next, combat is weak at best. I am playing as a mage, and combat doesn't feel good at all. None of the spells you can unlock feel good/forceful, and some of them require you to keep clicking your mouse button to charge up a spell, draw a line on the screen for a wall of fire, etc. This wouldn't be such a problem if you weren't fighting 20+ enemies at a time, and if your AI partner was competent. Katarina is utterly useless. I thought setting her up as a melee specialist would let her tank damage and draw enemy aggro as I hit them from range with my spells. Not quite. Enemies run right by her as if she's not even there and book it straight at me. This leads to every battle turning into a StraCraft-esque kite-fest, which gets old, fast. To make matters worse, you cannot command Katarina to attack a target. You can setup behaviors for her where she'll attack your target, the weakest target, the most vulnerable target, or the target that is attacking you (which is all of them), but you can't click on a target for her to attack. This means you have to aggro the enemies yourself. Not a problem if you're playing a sword-wielding badass, but as a mage it's terrible.
As I mentioned the game provides a challenge. Some of that is due to good enemy design, but most of it is artificial. Katarina being terrible and enemies running straight for you are the two biggest culprits of that artificial difficulty. Also contributing to this are some of the enemy groups you will run into. For instance, there is a part in a laboratory where you run into 6-7 Champion versions (the enemies have different tiers, Champion being the toughest) of this one enemy that has the ability to raise undead, trap you temporarily, form a temporary barrier, lay down an AOE poison spell, and an AOE spell that just drains your health as soon as you step into it. The fight went something like this. Step into area, trigger aggro on the 6-7 enemies, they cast raise undead to the 50+ rat-like corpses on the ground, use barrier so I can't go anywhere, use trap to hold me in place, cast poison or the other AOE spell on me while the rat things beat on me and I'm dead in seconds. I died 10+ times in that one place, due solely to how cheap the enemies were. This type of nonsense happens every now and again.
When it comes down to it, I can't recommend this game. If only the combat matched the pretty visuals...

I can see that if you were a Fallout 3 fan you could have been super underwhelmed with Fallout 4 as you might have been expecting a whole lot more, but as a huge Fallout 4 fan I was just so happy to be getting more Fallout, period!

It's not the greatest new IP to come out recently, but it isnt as bad as the scores may lead you to think. I've only just hit the final hours of the game, and it's definitely not worth the full price. Get it on a sale, it's too short to merit anything beyond $15, but definitely worth your time.
-The graphics of the world are amazing in some areas, even with them on low I found the world to look rather stunning, it's a shame there's so little going on where you're supposed to be. I would have to interact with the enviorment more. It is indeed extremely linear, so if that turns you off just stop right here.
-I personally loved the music and sound effects, though I do wish they had used some scores in more location or at least not where they did. I sometimes found myself listen to what seemed to be battle music in an average climbing section, though the majority of the time it fit the mood. I don't know if it was just me, but I experienced quite a few audio bugs. Multiple times I had duplicate sounds playing over each other, and the audio cut out entirely in some sections.
-The story is definitely alright, but having just finished DX:HR my expectations may have been a bit high :P There are a few plot twists and I really enjoyed it, though I did wonder why I had to revist so many areas.
- The combat, everyones favorite gripe. I recommend playing with a gamepad if you have it, I found some difficulty in managing everything, as unlike Arkham City or the majority of other games you dont have large amounts of time to react, or a counter. Unfortunately the dodge mechanic is rather lacking. I often found myself trying to dodge an AOE attack only to rebound over the back of the guy next to me and still be in the blast radius. Which is sad considering it's your only escape tool. The 3 hit combo is rather useless in my opinion, but being able to see the moves you'll use in the combo lab makes it fun to create the flashiest combos etc. I loved the design of the S-pressens, but losing all of your focus if you die was incredibly frustrating.
-The controls are a bit finicky, as you can tell from my difficulty with the dodge in combat. Often in climbing I found myself headed back the direction I came when I wanted to back eject instead. Overall it definitely felt like it was designed for consoles in mind, but it's nothing too difficult.
-DLC I found the majority of the dlc moves to be rather useless, but the Spinning Bird Kick is incredibly handy as the last hit of a combo, as it's rather an aoe meelee move, and as the last hit does alot of damage. The rest I never really used, but I loved that one.
It's definitely not the greatest game ever, but its a fun few hours of distraction, and I hope we'll see a more expanded universe from this IP in the future.

Yet another crazy installment of the Deponia series from Daedalic Entertainment and this one is just as good as those that came before it.
Story: 9/10
------
I must admit the story was surprisingly good in this game, the fact that the story runs "parellel" to the 3rd game made me a bit skeptical at first, but the game was full of suprises and originality so I loved every minute of it. Like other Deponia games its chock-full of humor, drama and crazy situations, you'll never be able to guess what's coming next. The story will get very confusing at times I must warn you but since I'm already a fan of games like Bioshock Infinite and anime like Steins;Gate, I was not overwhelmed. I think some may find the ending a little dissapointing but I think it does give us a little more hope for Rufus and Goal compared to the ending of the third game... Which I suppose is a central theme of the game so I won't bash Daedalic for that.
Gameplay: 9/10
-----------
It's a point and click adventure so theres obviously not much to say here, but what I will say is the timetravel mechanic was very cleverly done and makes this relatively small game feel a lot longer. It also mixes things up compared to the previous games so you won't feel like the series has just gone on too long. Some of the puzzles are incredibly difficult to figure out though and I did have to look at a walkthrough maybe once or twice but overall the puzzles were great in this game.
Art: 10/10
-----------
The art is one of the things I love about all Daedalic games and this one does not dissapoint, gettting to finally see Ellisium was wonderful and Deponia looks as awesome as ever.
Conclusion: 9/10
-----------
If you're a fan of point and click adventures, puzzle games or good narrative I would deffinately reccomend this game, however you are going to have to play the first three before you play this one. If that seems like a daunting task to you I reccomend playing Anna's Quest, still my favourite Daedalic game. That game will give you a good idea of whether you're ready to attack the Deponia beast.

6.5/10 Honestly, it was enjoyable to play another Deponia game, but it was the weakest of the four games. I was so excited when I saw that there was another game, so I finally bought it. While I'm glad that I played through it, it didn't have as much of the charm that the other games had, nor did it have as much of the familiar humor that made them so thoroughly playable. I'll admit, it became very tedious at times. I am not always the biggest fan when it comes to time travel games, and this one became overly tedious because I had to keep replaying certain scenes so many times through. It became very monotonous (Much like this review..?) If you've played the other three games, I would definitely recommend buying it, especially if it's on sale. However, DO NOT start with this one. There is also a lot of humor that will be lost on you if you haven't already played through the other games. Something that I did enjoy was how the creators of the game explained everything so thoroughly, and wrapped up the ending so nicely. Everything came together in that confusing- yet very descriptive, backwards cliche of a used kleenex type of ending you only get when Rufus is involved.
And yes, if you aren't annoyed yet, or haven't noticed, I tend to rate games that don't have their own ESRB rating, and do my best to remain as close to their rating system as possible.
MATURE: Some Sexual Content/Brief Nudity, Suggestive/Sexual Dialogue, Language, Mild Violence. (In all honesty, the violence isn't anything more than a TEEN rating, it's more for the suggestive content and language that this earned a MATURE).

Skullgirls is a 2.5D beat-em-up  in the vein of the likes of Virtua Fighter, Mortal Combat or Street fighter. It offers however a really rather unique single player story mode and graphically has a lot more of a "Cartoony" quality to it that I personally found very endeering.
a unique story and really quite wonderfully drawn graphics offer a unique gaming experience which; when coupled with a wonderfully jazzy music score, really makes this game pop out as a quite wonderful little time killer, all of this week I have regularly found myself pulling away from other tasks to play a few rounds on here and play through quick matches.
If all this was was a simple single player game I would be content but left feeling empty. Luckily skullgirls comes with enough additional extra content in the form of mini challenges, online modes and unlockables to keep the replay value ticking over on this one for a good long time...

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice isn't just a videogame; it's a work of art. You cannot possibly imagine a game with this quality sold for 30$, it's insane. It might only take 6-7 hours to complete, but every single minute of this game is unforgettable and, ultimately as a whole package, becomes one of the best games of 2017. More than that, Hellblade is most certainly that breakthrough the gaming industry needed, but not in a way it wanted it. At the end of the day, probably few will appreciate the scale of what hellblade brings to the table.
There isn’t anything like this in the market. The binaural audio really comes as a fundamental tool to try to bring the audience as close as possible to one of the most recognized symptoms of psychosis and probably the most difficult one to portray: auditory hallucinations. This is what makes the game unique. Few games depend hardly on their sound design like Hellblade does. Fortunately, this is the best aspect of this game and probably one of the best sound designs of all time in a game. Voice acting is also excellent and music very good. This game should be the best in this category, at least this year.
The power of the Unreal Engine 4 is already known within the gaming community, but Hellblade still manages to surprise. The portrayal of visual hallucinations is very solid and the overall graphics in the game are pretty impressive to look at. Probably, the best feature about the graphics quality can be admired on the main Character's (Senua) expressions and motion design; it's really breathtaking how many emotions are transmitted through her and how it helps to really bring her and her story to life. As with most Unreal Engine videogames, Hellblade runs very well even on mid-range PCs. It feels fluid either on 30 fps or on 60fps.
The entire story revolves around Senua and her quest to save her lover's soul while facing all kinds of fantastical trials that just might or not might be all fabrications of her own imagination; all of this revolves around the mysterious and interesting Norse mythos. Almost at the end, the quest abruptly transforms into one of self-acceptance. While the story wouldn’t be anything to write home about under normal circumstances, in here it all cames back again to the way it is delivered and displayed; that's definitely what makes this game so unique. There are few psychological games that manage to bring out such an appropriate atmosphere of fear and helplessness, Hellblade nails it. It also encourages the player to keep going and see how Senua's tale will unfold pretty much till the credits roll.
If Ninja Theory wasn’t such a famous game developer people would be calling this game an indie game. Thing is, it really is almost an indie game, at least when you take the publishing measures of it into account. It would be best, though, to call Hellblade: Senua's Scrifice an independent AAA game. Ninja Theory developed and published this game on their own and released it at the base price of 29.99$. It’s rare for developers do this kind of stunt and, personally, I feel the game is worth every penny. It's very rare when I sit and focus on one game and even finish it. Hellblade made me sit through 3 nights and finish it while I enjoyed every minute of it, then I watched about 25 minutes of the development/educational video they included which brought me almost to 10 hours in total for in-game time. For a videogame of this quality, quite honestly, at the base price it is a steal for the awesome experience it delivers.
This is probably where the game doesn't manage to be spectacular. Action is very fluid and beautiful to watch at, but very simple. Don’t expect combo based systems like on DmC, expect something more on the lines of Heavenly Sword. Then again, Hellblade is a story-oriented game, so combat comes off as a bonus. Then, we have the puzzles that, again, are very simple and tight. Honestly, the puzzles are not really interesting and while most are really easy to solve, some require very specific positioning, so much so that the whole thing feels extremely restrictive at many points in the game. This doesn’t really tamper with the game's overall experience, but this aspect of the game could have been a lot better, even for a story-driven game.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is not a game for everyone and it won't be appreciated by everyone who plays it either. It is a very disturbing game to its core with the usual dose of violence audiences seem to love. The thing is violence here is represented in such unique way throughout the game that it doesn't feel cliché at all. The psychological aspect of the game has been researched and compared up with real-in life experiences to bring out the gamer closer to a psychosis scenario. The characters are fleshed out and make the story captivating and interesting. The graphics are very good and the sound design is just brilliant. Hellblade is definitely one of my favorite games this year and I will probably remember it for a long time and compare to other games that attempt to go the same way this game went. Because Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice has become a shining reference for the psychological genre and I doubt that, out of the few games that will try out to go this same path, there will be any that actually surpasses it in the near future.

Whenever there's a take on an old classic, there's a big problem of living up to the feeling of nostalgia in the player's mind. There's no disappointment here.
Bad Caterpillar offers a great throwback for people who grew up playing centipede or millipede. Very enjoyable game, and I would highly recommend it to younger people who never experienced Atari arcade machines in their heyday. Simple concept, with great playability.
The only problem with it, is goals for replayability. In the arcade you always had the high scores table tempting you to play again to climb the charts and get your name on there. On Steam, most high score based games eventually get their high score tables polluted by hackers showing impossible scores, Steam achievements could have been used to create more incentive to play more.
I detest it when games have ludicrous amounts of achievements, and make it VERY tedious to 'perfect' the game. I was happy to see that this game didn't do that, but felt it should have had some more, to keep people coming back a little longer.

Bad Caterpillar is a straightforward clone of the arcade classic Centipede with some new power-ups. I wish it did a little bit more differently, and particle effects are overused, but it does capture all the correct gameplay beats quite nicely. If all you want is a Centipede-like game on Steam, this will definitely do the job. Smooth gameplay + online leaderboards make Bad Caterpillar my favorite version of this game at the moment. For $2 it's a great effort. I recommend playing with mouse controls, they're extremely responsive and generally the best way to enjoy this style of game if you don't have a trackball.

I really like the idea behind this game, but I feel like it's a far cry from what it claims to be and I can't recommend it in its current state. I think the developers have their heart in the right place and maybe they're a little too familiar with the content to see some of the things I feel are shortcomings. With that in mind I have several criticism which I sincerely hope are taken constructively because I want to see this become the game I thought it would be.
I don't feel like I'm learning anything. It might be fun if I already knew something about music, but even when I pass a tier I don't feel like I understand what I did. I wish there was more of an educational element.
The help/cheats aren't very helpful. They just give you answers. I'd consider slowing down the music, or playing the chord clearly without the music, or playing the notes in the chord one at a time to be more helpful. Using the cheats doesn't actually feel like it's helping, just postponing my next failure.
After failing the only option I have is to start the tier over. There is no guidance for your mistake, nothing is clarified. At the very least I'd like to try it again without credit to see if I can recognize my error. I would hope for a lot more feedback. Show me where each string falls on a scale and which ones I cut/left and which ones were correct.
I'm on tier 15 and I still get presented with stages that I think are easy and I cut strings after hearing them after a single pluck. Within the same tier sometimes I get completely stumped. This has been happening to me since tier 5. I feel like if this game had a suitable educational element, I'd have an explanation for this seemingly random difficulty.
Some things I'd like to see in future versions:
-I'd like to play with my eyes closed, but the interface requires a mouse. It'd be nice to have ASDF...or 1234... assigned to the strings.
- More music. The music is lackluster. Some songs have too much delay before the chords. If you're troubled with a tier, the music can be tiresome.
- It'd be nice to have the option to mark what I think is the root/3rd/5th as I make my progress.
- There's a constant audio static which I believe is intentional (maybe like a record?) that would be very nice to shut off.
Other bugs:
the disabled state for he 5th cheat button is the 3rd button
The drop shadow on the string cut button is cut off on the bottom
all 3 circles for the play chord, mute and settings buttons have flat bottom and right sides

Not played a whole lot yet but I played enough to get the general idea, very interesting concept, executed almost like a cheap mobile game but this is actually ridiculously useful for gaiging in note recognition by ear, kind of like the "gateway drug" to more advanced theory. I thought I was terrible at doing note recognition by ear (spoiler alert: I am) but after the first few levels of this game I felt myself getting better at it. It eases you in with some really blatantly obvious dissonant notes that give you a basic idea of what a wrong note sounds like, just more extreme than the more subtle ones later in.
There are a few cop out options ( show root note and third, on the start levels using them both pretty much wins you the level, removing any kind of auditory 'training' for lack of a better term.) this minor flaw becomes redundant when more strings come into play. I think it dilutes the experience a tad but it's good they have those in there, I try to avoid them as much as I can because I'm trying to train my ear here, not complete levels.
It also highlights the chord in the puzzle once you complete it, have a notepad handy and this is a fantastic way of writing down some new chords to learn, a nice sorta 'reward' and if you were stuck on the puzzle for a while you can already recognise individual notes when you try to play said chord on your instrument of choice, they get broken down for you during the puzzle, not the manner of an arpeggio but you have to play the individual notes and recognise out of place notes. This will be very handy for tuning by ear and i seriously cannot wait to dig into this more.

String Theory on PC / Steam
Score 10 / 10
2016 STEAM AWARDS "Just 5 More Minutes" Nominee
[This review has been updated following a complete second ‘Standard’ game playthrough following last week's patch 2016.02.26. Score before the patch 9 / 10]
Recognizing chords and matching notes to music is a fun experience in this musical game. All levels of musicianship from newbs to card carrying long hairs will benefit from this software including those with formal training in solfège. I purchased this software on day 1 because I thought the concept was cool… and I was right. I have made extensive notes for musicians in this review. On with the show….
The background music plays (BGM) and you pluck virtual strings that may or may not be in harmony. Pick the right strings and cut the bad ones. This game introduces simple 2 and 3 note chords; forget the musical theory you do not need it; just enjoy the experience. Game levels 1-20 are straightforward and can be completed by everybody. Go ahead and dive in….
Each level represents 5 chord challenges which must all be correctly resolved to progress to the next level. The complexity progresses gently through increasing the number of strings in a chord, increasing the number of alternative strings, mixing the order of Majors and minors, and finally inversions. Every time I finished a level I kept saying to myself  “just one more level before going to bed”. I went to bed late, a few times. There are a total of 40 levels.
The game really takes off at level 21 with the introduction of 4 note chords, 7th chords to be precise, driving up the difficulty. I did find myself occasionally misidentifying the tonic or the third; patience and concentration is required especially when surviving chord inversions. Following the patch I can confirm that all sonic puzzles resolved to either Major 7ths or minor 7ths as per game instructions; the game will challenge you with alternatives such as Major 6ths, dominant 7ths, and minor Major 7ths but they were not solutions in these puzzles.
Achievement notes: Achievements are linked to completing levels with specific BGM. Playing alternative modes changed my BGM when I resumed ‘Standard’ playthrough. Check the achievement requirements and reset the BGM manually through ‘options’ while in-game if necessary.
Honorable mentions
1. Many different styles of music are represented here and are sufficiently varied to keep us interested. Chapeau :hat1: to the music director.
2. Lots of extra game modes including Chaos and Endless.
3. Steam accoutrements including huge numbers of achievements, cards, and leaderboards. Woo!
4. Special thanks to the devs for opening a line of communication to allow for questions that I had about the game; they have been responsive to their players with the patches.
5. This game is the first in its genre; genre defining. Honour this.
Last words
I often pick up my guitar while jazz or rock is playing and determine the chord progressions and spend some time improvising on the spot. This game fulfills the same role of learning the key of the sound space but just using a computer instead. I really took this game to heart and wanted to prove to myself that I have internalized all my intervals, an exam so to speak that I passed with just a slight bruising of my ego! Musicianship is great for the mind; it teaches the qualities of perseverance, gives improved memory and concentration including better academic performance, and has proven protective against the afflictions of aging (alzheimer’s and dementia).
Buy this software if you are a musician at any level or the least bit curious (or shy).This fun musical game is genre defining and is the logical evolution of using computers to help us train our minds in the realm of music.
My scoring system 10 / 10
9 / exemplary execution of the genre don’t miss out, for fans of the genre and the curious alike
8 / for well done not a must play, fans of the genre and newbs will be happy it is well done
7 / for calibrated expectations only, fans of the genre would not miss out if they skipped this
6 / only for serious fans of the genre for whom game play with bugs is acceptable
5 / enough bugs to make me unhappy

Basically the only thing I would change would be to give the strings a more satisfying animation or sound when you cut them, like a really good guitar string snap or something.

I would probably characterize it as a musical rouge-lite: you must choose the outlier note correctly for each level on a tier without making a mistake and having to start over at the beginning of the level set.
String Theory scratches the itch for both listening to music and engaging in challenging gameplay without having to compromise on one or the other. It has smooth gameplay and a light interface that makes everything accessible without losing utility.

In the french tradition of studios like Ubisoft, this game holds your hand from the beginning and doesn't let go EVER. You are like a child being led through places that you just want to explore and interact with, but the game strictly forces you to follow its linear, obvious path, pointing out every little move that you have to make with little indicators. You are not trusted to draw even the most trivial of conclusions on your own, and the fluid and exciting (although also obvious, throwaway easy and repetitive) combat is interrupted most inconveniently by the game forcing you to pause, and go to a menu to equip and try this new move or another that it just gave you, even though the strategy for every attack and every enemy is pretty much the same. To sum up, the game has breathtaking visuals and an engrossing story, and has absolutely nothing to offer in the gameplay department. It just guides you through like a tourist excursion, never letting you or asking you to think or try anything, but only executing its commands in a timely fasihon. Deponia Doomsday.
The 4th game of the series of the Deponia games is (so far) the last game.
Let me tell you as a big fan of time traveling this game really caught my interest. Not to mention it finishs up the game series quite..in an unique way.
If you like time travel, Point 'n Click adventures, black humor, silly puzzles and the Deponia series itself you should give it a try

Full disclosure: I recieved review code for the game from the developer/publisher.
This most recent entry into the Deponia series is a well-written capstone for the series, as well as an exploration of the dangers of time travel, at Rufus' expense.
He's still a cynical, selfish, scheming oaf. Maybe not quite as bitter in the beginning as he once was. Not to worry... He'll get there-- and he's still just as much a failure as he was before. This entry has some interesting puzzles, some justg as good as trying to catch one's recalcitrant toothbrush, but ultimately it still falls afoul of Dev Logic. The biggest problem I had with this entry were the occasional QTE that required fairly good reflexes to survive. Fortunately, they tended to be repeatable, so not a total loss.
In the end, a solid puzzle/adventure game, good for a score of 70. If you like adventure games, then get the game. If not, then give it a pass.
Man... And I thought Homestuck had a lot of time shinanigans. If you like temporal nonsense, and like to theorize about non-deterministic time travel. This game is for you.

Whilst I don't mind running around with all my items at the ready clicking on everyone to progress the story, I mean that's what a point and click is, Doomsday took the p#@s with this game by adding a new feature,
, whilsts its fun in the first act it gets old fast as you have to spend hours running about not only to get the items but to then get them in order and in time to procced. This game almost forces you to get a guide and it almost feels like i payed £24 for a tabbing out simulator. If you want a game with wacky yet logical puzzles, get the first three but pass on this one.

I would rather suggest playing through the first three (Deponia, Chaos on Deponia, Goodbye Deponia) than suggest this one.

Skullgirls  was a game I had been curious to play for a while and while I cant say I have yet 100%-ed the game (I have yet to play the bulk of the DLC) I can say that after playing most of the main game campains I have a pretty good grasp of how this game works and functions.
Skullgirls is a 2.5D beat-em-up  in the vein of the likes of Virtua Fighter, Mortal Combat or Street fighter. It offers however a really rather unique single player story mode and graphically has a lot more of a "Cartoony" quality to it that I personally found very endeering.
a unique story and really quite wonderfully drawn graphics offer a unique gaming experience which; when coupled with a wonderfully jazzy music score, really makes this game pop out as a quite wonderful little time killer, all of this week I have regularly found myself pulling away from other tasks to play a few rounds on here and play through quick matches.
If all this was was a simple single player game I would be content but left feeling empty. Luckily skullgirls comes with enough additional extra content in the form of mini challenges, online modes and unlockables to keep the replay value ticking over on this one for a good long time...
The only issue I honestly had with this title was its controls. I have been using a gamepad to play this title preferring it over a keyboard configuration but no matter how hard I try there are some moves in this game that I simply cannot perform with the gamepad. the special moves and cobos are fiddly to the point of utter frustration...though knowing how to use these moves can often help tip the scales in battle I have rarely had to rely on them at any point and random mashing sometimes seems to get the job done well enough so I cant really complain too much about that.
I can reccommend skullgirls as an essential Sale game, if it's ever going cheap in one of the sales pick this up you will most definately not be dissapointed.

This is a really great game, and I have the confidence to say that before even completing it. The controls are fluid and satisfying, the game design reminds me of this brilliant mash up of Donkey Kong Country, Metroid, most Mario games, and Rayman Origins/Legends. On top of all of that, the game is drop dead gorgeous, the story is engaging and heart wrenching, and the soundtrack is a great accompaniment to boot.
However, as someone who plays platformers in such a systematic, calculated, completionist fashion, this game rubs me the wrong way in certain areas. For those who play games aiming to get 100% completion - especially in games that reward you greatly for doing so - be wary of Ori and the Blind Forest. There are giant sections of the overworld that you will be completely locked out of after completing certain parts of the story, and you are NOT warned when you are crossing these paths. I discovered this after quite a long time of rummaging through the map trying to 100% each section of the overworld, rendering all of that time useless.
I understand that this game isn't just, "Collect all the shiny things, get to the finish line, and gawk at your 100% completion," that's fantastic. In fact, I'm glad this game doesn't make that a priority. Any good platformer can be completed by picking up absolutely none of the secrets. BUT what this game DOES do is highly reward players who DO seek out every nook and cranny of the overworld for secrets. Why they decided to highly reward players only to reprimand them against their own will later on when missing ONE item in a later unreachable part of the overworld is beyond me.
I can only assume they trap players like this in order to force them into replaying the game for achievements and for 100% completion. I hope that's not the case, but that's what it feels like. It makes an otherwise flawless game feel a bit more plastic.
Long story short, if you are a fan of platformers, you absolutely must play Ori and the Blind Forest. Just try not to think about all of the pickups/secrets and just enjoy it for what it is, at least the first time through. Even though the secrets will be tantalizingly displayed on your map, resist wasting your time to get them if they're out of your way.

The story is a little above average. Senua is a mentally ill girl who is descending into hell in an attempt to have the gods bring back her dead lover. Through her journey we learn about Senua's past of being an outcast because of her illness and the story of her and her lover. From the prologue, we are in Senua's mind, and can constantly hear the schizophrenia-like voices talking, at some times berating her, sometimes egging her on, and even just narrating the story. It's certainly a unique aspect of the game, and very unsettling, but the voices really do grind on you quickly, especially when some of them will just repeat similar things for whole sections of the game. The story, however, doesn't really fit the length of the game, and by the end it feels like you've heard some of the same things over and over again.
The puzzles are intriguing at first, mostly using perception of the environment to create rune symbols to progress. However again, the game goes far too long for the same kind of puzzle to stay interesting. There's hardly anything added to the puzzles between the first and the last in the game and you will feel like you're just doing the same puzzle in a different room. Many games that choose to focus on puzzles will at least add aspects to them, increasing the complexity or just changing it up a little, this does not.
Lastly, the combat. It's a touchy topic around this game, anyone who seems to criticise the combat just gets mets with "it's more about the story, it's not meant to be Dark Souls." That's all very well, but it isn't a small part of the game. There is a LOT of combat, and it really isn't good. There are very few attacks, very few different enemies, and often the encounters are very long with a lot of the same enemies spawning ad infinatum. The worst part of the combat is that one enemy will attack you at a time, but as soon as an enemy is off the screen, whether due to the awful camera control in battle, or literally just spawning behind you, it will rush to attack you completely out of sequence and will often blindside you and hit you. (Also, usually this is accompanied by one of the voices saying "behind you" right as a mace slams into your face.) I could understand sacrificing a complex combat system for a better story experience, but if that's the case, there shouldn't be SO MUCH of this frankly tedious fighting in the game.
The appearance of the game is amazing, and the environments are a combination of beautiful and disgusting, often with corpses littering the area. One thing that really frustrated me from the beginning is that there is no "Motion Blur" or "Film Grain" options in the menu, and to remove these effects you need to directly edit the game files. Both of these really annoy me in AAA games, when so much effort has gone into producing a beautiful HD experience, then some person went "great, now put a fuzzy filter over everything" and motion blur honestly gives me a headache. These sorts of things should never be a locked-on option.
If it were less pricey, I'd feel better about the game, but a walking simulator with a frankly slow and uninspired story should not be this expensive.
Such a unique experience.

A rather short, but great and unique story driven experience of suffering and psychosis.
You know you can expect some ♥♥♥♥ed up♥♥♥♥♥♥if the very first credit you see in the intro is for a psychosis consultant.
The basic premise of this game is that you are a person suffering from psychosis, making you hear voices, halucinations, constantly twisting your mind.
This game is absolutely gorgeous, with exception of texture quality. The lighting and the effects are superb, the character looks absolutely incredible but the world textures are not quite on par in terms of resolution. I don't know if the game auto limited their size/quality but the settings were cranked to the highest it would go (very high) and you can clearly see the the lack of crispness when you look at them a bit closer. From the distance they look great but it's when the character is close to a wall or a floor is when it's most obvious.
The game also has a photo mode which let's you position and frame the camera however you like and apply some preset grading and some stylish effects. Despite the dodgy textures, I spent a lot of time in photo mode taking screenshots because the game just looks amazing.
Here is where some might be turned away by this game. It is a very story driven game and the gameplay revolves around finding symbols in the world to unlock gates, activating "narration beacons" and some combat.
The game doesn't tell you how to do anything and it's mostly figuring it for yourself but you quickly get the hang of what to do since it's the same task just different locations/symbols.
The doors are sort of like puzzles. You have some symbols (runes) on the door that keep them locked and you have to find patterns in the world that resemble those runes to unlock the doors. It's not that hard to find these locations, the game even starts showing bunch of symbols in the air around the areas where those symbols are.
The combat only happens in predefined "arenas" and it's quite simple but satisfying. You have your basic light/heavy attack, block and dodge. There's not that many enemy types but each enemy has it's own set of moves and does require a slightly different strategy.
There's also this thing called "focus" that is like some special ability that fills up when you attack/dodge/block and it slows down time letting you go berserk on the enemies.
There are also boss fights and I wouldn't say that they were neither hard or easy. They have a few stages and won't make you frustrated in any way if you know what you're doing.
The game has this "if you die too many times the game restarts" thing and I think that is the reason why the combat and boss fights are rather simple and not too hard to beat. I died only once in the game and it was in one section where your vision is distorted and for some reason the game turned me in a wrong direction. But if you want to make combat harder there is an option to do that.
I cannot say how realistically this portrays psychosis but seeing the dev blog they consulted with experts on psychosis and even portrayed things that actual people with psychosis experience. Heck, the part with symbols and runes is from people actually mentioning how they notice patterns in real world that make sense to them.
The game points out that it's best played with headphones and you really should. You constantly hear voices talking in the back of your head, questioning your decisions (or you questioning them), always making you uneasy. They would often mock you for showing weaknesses but would then scream to go back as you go further towards the danger, into the darkness.
I don't want to say too much about the story as it's pretty much all spoilers but I think it's pretty good and it did make me feel uneasy at times and making me panic in situations where there probably wasn't any reason to panic.
In the end, if you don't mind games that revolve heavily around the story and have fairly simplistic gameplay you will most definitely enjoy this game. And if you like to take game screenshots, this is heaven for you.

It's a grand continuation of the tradition of single-player first person shooters, a dying breed these days amongst the stultifying preponderance of multiplayer garbage and open world icon-collectathons. The art direction is gorgeous, and, importantly, the writing is high quality and the voice acting is that rara avis, both well acted and well directed. It's quintessential over-the-top, absurd yet heartfelt and thoroughly pulpy Wolfenstein. For almost the first time in a singleplayer FPS, I found myself actually wanting to look at every collectible: the amount and quality of concept art is impressive, and the faux Nazi pop songs that you find in the form of records are absolutely hilarious gems.
I actually found stealth to be a more viable option than others have reported. As long as you're not fixated on stealth killing every enemy perfectly, you'll be fine. The dynamic of trying to pick off the Nazi commanders before you're spotted, then transitioning to the ridiculous bloody slaughter once you're inevitably spotted, is just as strong in this game as in TNO and Old Blood.
Gripes: The combat and movement are a little floaty. Getting damaged doesn't really feel like anything, and neither does firing most of the weapons. The campaign is super short and ends anticlimactically, clearly setting up the paid preorder DLC, which feels exploitative and predatory--not a shocker coming from Bethesda these days. (I never, ever preorder, and I have no plans to buy this game's DLC campaigns until they're on sale. Doesn't detract from my pleasure with my purchase of the main game though.) The sidequests feel perfunctory and not well signposted--it seems like you're supposed to go out and get the two other "special" upgrades in addition to the one you originally chose in the course of the campaign, but the plot never (until the free-form epilogue) offers you a clear moment that says, "OK, here is the point at which you go out and do those sidequests." And then the game's over with you having unlocked only 1 of the 3 cool special toys. That was my experience, anyway.

I bought my copy of The New Colossus day before its release for a good price. I had very little info about the sequel to 2014 reboot of Wolfenstein franchise.  I played the original and enjoyed it for what it was, a single-player story driven FPS, but it did not leave any lasting impressions.
The New Colossus did not start well, error message right at the start left me with no choice other than to search internet for solution--and I was found relatively quickly, I had to instal latest Nvidia drivers.
Once I installed latest drivers from Nvidia, the game started and played flawlessly on high settings in 1080p on my i7-4790k with GTX1070--rock solid 60fps, no noticeable slowdowns, no broken geometry or texture popping. Only other problem I have encountered from start to finish of the game were 2 game freezes during loading. I have not fiddled with video settings at all, the game run smoothly and looked amazing at default high settings.
The game offers continuation of alternative history of WW2. The story was decent with several great characters that were flashed out as much as possible in a FPS game. The story absolutely parodies current political situation and does not shy away from controversial topics such as racism, sexism and spreading of neo-nazi propaganda. It is all in good fun and cartooney approach but there are some graphical moments not for feint of heart.
I liked the gameplay because it is simplistic in its focus--provide well crafted experience focused on killing enemies, pure and unadulterated mayhem, with optional stealth that worked good enough. Weapon selection is limited to standard set of armaments including pistol, sub-machine gun, assault rifle, electricity-based gun and grenade/rocket launcher. There is also few heavy weapons that can be picked up from static gun posts or from fallen enemies. They have limited ammunition and must be carried in both hands slowing you down and forcing you to drop them on the ground if you want to use some of your standard guns. Gunplay is fine, each weapon feels differently.
Length of the game is decent, I have finished the story at around 25 hours on Do or Die difficulty setting. Some parts of the game were rather difficult but nothing impossible. Enemy AI is very mobile and once alerted to your presence they can often surprise you  by flanking you or coming from behind you. I always found it better to soften enemy forces by applying stealth early in the game levels--this is certainly recommended approach on higher difficulty settings when captains are present on the battlefield.
I still have several ubercommanders to kill via helm navigation map, which is some kind of meta game on top of story missions. These kill missions are happening in locales you visit during story missions with slight modifications to what enemies are present, their placement and new collectibles.
Character perk and weapon upgrade systems are good and fit the tune of the game. Character perks are gained naturally by performing specific actions, e.g. killing enemies while dual-wielding or performing stealth takedowns. These perks improve certain aspects of your character--mostly quality of life improvements but some of these perks are very powerful.
Weapon upgrade system is simple enough but efficient. Upgrades provide improvements to a gun or even add new functionality to it. Upgrades can be toggled on and off so you do not have to worry whether you will like it or not. Weapon upgrade kits are relatively rare but you get enough of them to upgrade your favourite weapon or two. Side mission provide access to additional weapon upgrade kits.
All in all, Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus was very positive surprise for me. High quality production value with slightly goofy story that does not take itself too seriously. Once I overcome initial problem with incompatible GPU drivers, the game run smoothly without any major issues. Visuals and sound are great, music fits the theme and some tunes were outstanding. Gameplay is fast-pace with clear focus on combat with light elements of stealth that never felt cumbersome. Enemy AI is serviceable but it will not amaze you.
All I have to say is...AWESOME! Fisrt time to purchase and play on Steam. Not a big fan of gaming, but when I have the time, this was a great experience.

Depth is a fun little game with a novel premise- but it's very flawed, and I think how much enjoyment you get out of it is going to boil down to how much you enjoy scares.
I've always had a pretty big fear of deep ocean waters, shipwrecks, etc. Could never explain why exactly, it just gives me the creeps. I also really enjoy a good scare, so I'd been interested in Depth for quite awhile and hopped on board during the free weekend.
In short, the game doesn't dissapoint: it is indeed a game about divers vs some homicidal sharks and it does it very well. It didn't quite scare me nearly as much as I thought it might, but playing as a diver is a blast and is perpetually tense. Playing as the sharks is a bit different as it's a lot less about scares and more about trying to win, which is very skill-curve dependent.
PROS:
------------------------
+ The asymmetric gameplay is pretty well handled. It doesn't provide anything new or groundbreaking, but does a great job of packaging it with the underwater premise. As the divers, you collect bling, escort a rover, and try not to get horribly eaten. As a shark, you want to kill everything that moves. There's a charming simplicity to it.
+ The level designs are great. The thematics are really strong and provide each side with a different take: as a diver each level is like a freaky uncharted haunted house where you never know when a monster will pop out. As a shark, the environments give you lots of possible obstacles and oppurtunities to get the drop on your victims.
+ A lot of love went into the shark designs; even though the DLC money grubbing is there, it's clear they have a lot of fun making these beasties and it never stops being unnerving fighting them. The different species of sharks also have enough differentation in their stats that you have options to tinker and experiment with, finding one best suiting your needs.
CONS:
-------------------------------------------------
- The playerbase. It should be apparent with the sale and F2P weekend there's a bid to revitalize the playerbase...Mostly because it's almost all but gone, save for a lot of grizzled, ill mannered veterans. If they're not souring the game with trash talk (trust me, having a shark suddenly start ♥♥♥♥♥alking you takes a lot out of the horror part) , they're just ragequitting the moment something goes awry. And when these guys travel in packs, you're suddenly left with an empty lobby. I got in a game, and less than 3 minutes in one guy got killed twice, got fed up, quit, and all of his buddies too. And suddenly I was stuck alone with a bunch of bots. This has happened on both sides numerous times.
- Loot stuff. It's the same♥♥♥♥♥♥as TF2, it sucks but whatever, all the stuff in the base game is perfectly viable and you can largely ignore it.
- The gore is pretty piddly for a scary game. Hardly a deal breaker, but I think some more in-depth (HURR) wounds and gore could ratchet up the scares even more. Like really, it would be cool if killed divers and sharks just clouded up the water with so much blood you could barely see anything but red.
TL;DR
-----------------------------------
Depth's strongest selling point is it's unique spin on assymetric FPS gameplay. It's a fun little way to get some good jump scares that feel immersive and emergent rather than the trite, scripted sorts you would find in a conventional horror game. If you're just looking for some good aquatic scares, Depth is a great title to pick up on sale and kill a couple hours time trying not to get horribly murdered.
Having said that, it's not a very good competitive game and it's more competitive players will do a lot to sap the fun out of Depth's creepy premise so I'd say if you're going to pick it up, you should be doing it because you want the fright of a watery grave, rather than some ill misplaced need to find a new challenge.

What Van Helsing may lack in overall polish and length, especially for a hack and slash game of this type when some of its contemporaries seem to march on forever, it certainly makes up for with particular East European flavor and largely successful attempts at humor. If Van Helsing has one thing going for itself it's the fact it happens to have a very well defined atmosphere as well as some tangential gameplay additions you would not necessarily expect, mainly in the form of tower defense game and some separate scenarios unlocked towards the end.
That's not to say the negatives don't rear their ugly head; from a single playable class, unless you buy the remaining two in the form of DLC/complete version, wonky and unclear itemization which will make you return to old RPG territory and simply look for basic attribute bonuses, and sometimes outright weirdly paced difficulty. Latter could be the failing of my own poor character building skills, but somewhere around The Old Town area difficulty seems to ramp up for no real reason other than perhaps the introduction of particularly annoying new enemy types. Ending is also an obvious cliffhanger, which may or may not annoy you depending on your take on the final boss.
You will be in familiar waters if you have any experience with the genre in general, although your patience may be tested at certain parts as you struggle with camera spazzing out and somewhat obtuse quest directions leading you astray. Still worth checking out, though.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is hack n slay RPG in the style of Diablo or Torchlight.

What I also like about it is the overall world and the atmosphere, plus it has some humor in it which will probably make you smirk from time to time.
Plus the game is quite player friendly, you're able to reset your skills easily for Van Hellsing and Katharina and identifying items doesn't require a spell (which lead to the question why they actually implemented that feature because now you're only required to right-click and wait 2 seconds)
Things I don't like are for example the huge hordes of enemies you can encounter. Although the battles are fun (which is important because this the main thing you're doing) I was sometimes feeling like the developers just smashed as much enemies as possible in an area which sometimes leads to exhausting long battles against 30 or more enemies at a time. Also, the story isn't really exciting but that doesn't matter that much in that kind of genre. Graphics are also quite good and support the atmosphere of the game.
All in all: 78/100, worth buying!

Remember Me brings to the table an absolutely sublime world known as Neo Paris. The designers have gone all out to craft a world that feels believable but is nevertheless, bursting, with novelty and creativity. Life has been brought to this world by a first rate graphics engine and texture art that produce stunning lighting and sharp detail. The score also merits special mention. Holding everything together is a fairly engaging story with a few surprises up its sleeve. Gameplay includes some novel elements (memory `remixing' and the combo lab, for example) that keep things feeling fresh and made the experience enjoyable--even for someone not usually fond of the `brawler' genre.
The main shortcoming of the game is that it holds your hand too much. Everywhere you go, the next move you need to make is pointed out by an obnoxious orange arrow. Hesitate for just a moment during a boss fight, and a window pops up telling you exactly how to exploit the enemy's weakness. This excessive mollycoddling ultimately detracts from the player's sense of agency, making those gorgeous environments feel even more linear than they actually are.
My advice: buy the game and enjoy the scenery. Just don't expect Skyrim.
My playtime for a leisurely playthrough of this game: 13 hours.

It's finally gone live, and there's a bit of controversy.
The game was famously open world, and a lot of people really enjoyed the freedom that this provided. However the last patch before they hit 1.0 removed much of the open world component, and threw in a lot of quest type stuff, very much like the earlier Lego games.
To be honest, the game needed a *bit* of structure, but it is now definitely unlike the game that was advertised in early access, and has moved away from the style of game that a lot of people shelled out their hard-earned money for.
I liked it when it was open world, but I don't hate it now.  The quests can be a bit repetitive, but they're OK. There's still a bit of open world freedom, but nothing like the scale of the original game.  Not even close, at this stage.
I genuinely believe that they should re-introduce the open world aspects as an option. A lot of people played that way, and loved it. A lot of people PAID for the game for that precise purpose.  It seems a bit weaselly to then go ahead and change the game completely.
Having said that... I'm enjoying the new mode. I'm still going to recommend the game, even though I think they've done their player-base something of an injustice.

An objective review for the most subjective of games.
To the Moon isn't so much a game as it is a visual novel. The gameplay is extremely limited and consists mostly of walking from one story segment to the next. I'd go even so far to say that there are some unnecessary play sections that mess with the story pacing. There are some play sections that enhance the story but these also are limited and rare. The graphics are sharp, nicely colored and have a good amount of detail. The soundtrack is absolutely stellar and elevates the game to a higher level. I just wish these compositions had full orchastration because it's that good.
So as you might come to expect the story is brilliant. It walks a fine line between sentimental and dramatic and knows when to be subtle. With a lot of media that have this "feels" tag surrounding them I feel like the story is trying to force me to get emotional. However that is not the case here at all and that is a huge testament to the structure and writing in this game. Especially the use of recurring motives makes this game memorable and leaves you satisfied after the perfect ending.
Going into details about characterization, writing and so forth is trivial. If you want to talk about this game you should sit down next to someone and discuss it. This game is a gem that deserves all the praise that it gets and everyone should try it. Because I for one, would sure as hell like to play it for the first time again.

Hey, it looks really good, and the soundtrack matches how it looks. Too bad then, that the gameplay does not match up. A paint-by-numbers metroidvania with incredibly sloppy platforming. Since so much effort was clearly put into the artwork, very little effort seemed to go into designing fun platforming environments.
With multiple abilities that interact with walls, the organic and "painted" look of the walls and platforms means that the game's definition of a wall may not line up with your own. The need to have everything react to your movement means that a good number of floating platforms are tied to a physics engine, making their movement very erratic. Coupled with the massive difference in ground and air control you have means you will fling yourself off of platforms because they moved out from under you after you landed. Left me feeling more frustrated than challenged during many of the platforming areas.
Overall, I can't recommend it, with better games in the same genre on Steam, for the same price (or cheaper).

At first i brushed it off and continued playing, but then a 3rd voice came through: "what if this is what he wants us to think" at that moment i began to question my own thoughts and ideas and was beginning to think that i did indeed do something wrong.
Even the voice over at times felt like it was speaking directly to me as it mentioned asura's mental state and the theory that it was just an illusion and in her head. i say this because, i have had similar thoughts and ideas to this, what if i was already dead and im dreaming right now, or im in my own personal hell. in this modern age, games and story lines that go with them become better over time, however this story in particular, or should i say experience spoke volumes to me and gave me a better understanding of my own mental issues and problems - tho it has not completely fixed my problems- it has shown me to accept that it is there and move on with life. On a side note, i found the combat system awesome. highly recommend this game to anyone

As a fellow game dev, I am really impressed with the work that Ninjatheory has put into Hellblade: Senuas's Sacrifice.
Senua's rig and her animations are absolutely on point, very natural and well made. I've been keeping up with Ninjatheory's developement-diary, since my startup was discussing using similar mocap methods for our future project. Senuas face scan and her emotions are amazing and really make her look almost as in real life. I have not seen this amount of detail in any game before!
The transitions between the player being in control and cutscenes are on point as well, for the most part it feels like the whole game is just one big event, no loading screens, nothing to degrade the experience of playing. There are some loading screens, but they are really well hidden, good job Ninjatheory!
The camera rig feels a little weird at first, but I got used to it quickly. The camera is kind of close to Senua, but all it does is amplify the fact that everything is 'crazy' in this game, so I respect it as a wise choice to use the camera this way.
The only issue I have got with the camera rig is that there is no wall-clipping protection, I think you should implement that, it's only a short script after all.
Shaders and image effects are amazing, some may find them overused, but I think the shaders (for effects, not the normal shaders I mean) and image effects are some of the best I've seen thus far. It looks beautiful and also pushes the atmosphere further into feeling like a crazy dream. I've not seen this amount of post effects used this well before.
I have no clue how you managed to achieve some of the effects, especially the one where the whole world goes from normal to fiery hell after Senua touches the shrine (I forgot the god's name).
Now in the beginning I said we were developing our own games and we made a weather/skybox system for it. At the time I developed it, I strongly believe it was one of the best weather systems in gaming. It can easily simulate every weather condition - you name it. Skybox looks good, volumetric clouds and everything. Sunlight and galaxy/moon rendering. However, I think, I've been dethroned. The weather in Hellblade is just out of this world good! I don't know wether it has all the functionality as my system, but the things it does in game, it does perfectly. The clouds look amazing (I don't know wether you use normal hdr skyboxes and blend between them or something else), but they are so good! The raindrops look completely real, it's insane! Lightning is also on point! Also, I love the light rays from the sun and the whole volumetric lighting feel!
The ocean's look great when they are calm, but I think the way storms are simulated could use some love from the devs. The ocean just looks too opaque imo. I believe those were just some choices regarding time budged, but if not - please make the oceans look a little nicer during storms!
Sound. This is insane and some of the best use of sound I've ever heard in games. The way Senua's voices help when in combat or during normal game play is genius. The way her voices interact with each other is amazing. The deep voice talking to senua after she defeats the first two gods is so well placed (I know it's just a deep voice, but it's simply perfect for this setting). The only thing that seems off some times is Senuas voice herself, I know the actress wore the mic on her head while doing the performance capture, so sound is not going to be perfect. Maybe next time get some one else to hold a boom mic overhead or something, and maybe try to make the whole room a bit less reflective to sound. I'm not an audio engineer, so I can't really say what's wrong with Senua's voice, those are just some things that come to mind. Unlike the other voices it just feels like she's not really there. I'll try to find out what's going on next time I play the game.
Environment. Now I did not even notice some things regarding the environment for the first hours, since I spent my time drooling at how well Senua's character was made, but after some time I took a closer look at the environment.
It's really well made, and looks good. Some things that could be done better, but aren't really needed, would be:
Interaction with foilage: Bushes could bend a bit when Senua touches them, instead of just having a fixed collider and Senua not being able to walk into them.
Some props could be of a higher lod, some of them just felt a little low poly compared to the rest of the word.
I suppose you are using some kind of lod system but I noticed some stuff flickering when I walked away from it, not really a smooth transition between lod's. But that really only happened two times.
Other than that I just love the environment, it does exactly what is needed for the atmosphere of the game and everything is well made, design wise and regarding technology.
Ninjatheory's goal was Indy AAA, did they achieve that? Nope. They somehow surpassed many AAA games. I know you can't make a new the Witcher or a new GTA with your budged. But those games you were aiming at, you easily surpass.
This game is just one of the best games I've ever seen. It may not fit everyone, but it is doing everything it want's to with absolute perfection. I think this is sending a strong message toward every studio, indy or AAA, it shows you that you can make awesome pieces of art with every budged as long as you choose the right style for your budged.
Now I hope you opened the gates for more companies to make the technologies you developed even more affordable, since I don't have $10M for my own games, but man, I would love to have the tech for characters like Senua available to me! I think this game really puts the final nails in the coffin for the traditional publisher-developer style and raises Indy games to a whole new level.
