The hardest battles are fought within the mind. Let me tell you that's true, I've fought many myself. This game reached me in ways no other game has.
I have some really complicated feelings toward this game but I do feel it's a game that deserves to be played and appreciated. I won't say it's supposed to be liked, or certainly not enjoyed -- akin to the movie "The Road," a comparison I keep coming back to, I'm not sure it's *supposed* to be enjoyed. Of the words I would use to describe this game -- bold, audacious, vulnerable, insanely risky, meaningful, impactful, significant -- "fun" wouldn't crack the top fifty. Playing this game is not a good time. And if you're of the belief that games are supposed to be fun first and foremost, I can't entirely blame you for passing on this one. But I feel you're missing out on a remarkable achievement in design and artistry.
This game is an experience the likes of which has never really been seen before. Sure, the hack 'n slash combat gameplay is itself anything but groundbreaking. Neither are the admittedly repetitive puzzles. But it's just so much more than the sum of its parts. It's hard to even describe in words. Senua's journey is an incredibly arduous one to take, but it's one that if you're sufficiently hooked in, you can't walk away from.
Hellblade's sound design is nothing short of exquisite. While the game is very visually stunning as well, it really is the sound design (along with the hauntingly sublime performance of Melina Jeurgens) that immerses you and puts you right in the midst of the harrowing ordeal this game throws at you. We all do it with movies, if they're especially good ones -- we come out wondering what major awards it might win. Hellblade absolutely must win the audio design award at Geoff Keighley's gaming Oscars thing in December. I don't even care what the other nominated games are. In a game I consider a monument to "video games as art" in its own right, the music and sound design in this game is its own work of art.
A section that I keep thinking about over and over again is "trials of Odin" section. While I will try to be as spoiler-free as possible, I will just say that this section embodies something I've tried to explore in my own writings and have had to experience in my own life as well. One of the most remarkable contradictions I've experienced -- comfort in a crisis. A shimmering harbour in the bleakest of storms. It's a beautiful thing that I hope you never have to experience, because to know this beauty you have to be taken to the absolute depths of hell. It's a place I wouldn't wish my worst enemy to go to, yet having someone there to give you "a little help, a little hope" is the most incredible feeling of peace and safety a person can have. And Melina Jeurgens and Hellblade take us there. It is not an easy place to go to -- no part of this game is easy to go through -- but it's something to experience.
The whole experience of this game is one that I don't think a game has ever offered. I keep going back to "The Road" -- meaningful and impactful art that is not easy to take in. And this game to me stands alone as a work of art. People talk about Shadow of the Colossus when they talk about games as art, and deservedly so. This game needs to lead in that conversation as well. Art isn't (necessarily) about feeling good, and certainly not about having fun. As I said before, this game somewhat sacrifices the fun factor for its artistic value. That artistic value is in taking you to places you've never had to go before, or at least I hope you haven't. They are complicated and not easily described places, but you will have a better understanding of yourself and your fellow man and woman should you go to them.
I am glad the "vote" at the bottom of this review box is whether you would *recommend* the game, not whether you liked it. The former is an exceedingly easy question to answer. YES, I recommend this game (I may not ever be able to answer whether I "liked" it), it is something every gamer should play whether they come away liking it or not. Do be aware that you may have been misled about it. It is not a Dark Souls clone. Combat is sparse and sparing. Much of the game is spent walking "alone" -- or as alone as you can get. But this journey is one you need to at least try, I promise you that.

Resumo: Deponia Doomsday é um belo jogo da franquia Deponia baseado no estilo de aventura , point-and-click (ou seja, basicamente tudo que você faz no  jogo é na base do clique) e comedia. Criado pela Daedalic entertaiment Deponia conta a historia de Rufus um cara que esta cansado do mundo pos-apocaliptico e devastado pela poluição no qual ele habita (Deponia), e tenta de tudo pra deixar a sua cidade (Kuvaq) e chegar a Elysium , uma cidade planando no céu livre de toda a triste realidade que ele vive. Sua jornada nesse jogo é guiar rufus até elysium (novamente^^) mas dessa vez você tem a habilidade de viajar através do tempo e espaço O 0 O.
Graficos: O que dizer dos graficos... Deponia Doomsday como sempre esta lindo, os desenhos são bem definidos , cada linha e detalhe feito com  bastante equilibrio entre efeitos animados e realisticos, a daedalic como sempre deslumbra e brilha nesse aspecto.
Trilha Sonora: Esse é outro aspecto em que o jogo realmente brilha , deponia possui uma trilha sonora original , envolvente , empolgante e emocionante (tudo ao mesmo tempo). Sem contar que cada capitulo da historia é introduzida com uma canção, original, cativante e MUITO engraçado, chamada as canções do Huzzah (link de uma das canções):
Gameplay: Como todo o jogo point-and-click nao havia muito o que mudar nesse quesito, porém , a daedalic se superou e tornou o gameplay em varias partes do jogo bastante interativo , o que adicionou bastante ação em varias situações.
Jogos point-and-click são muitas vezes descartados , e nao recebem muita atenção por que o publico acredita que o estilo vai ser tedioso e nao muito interessante.Deponia veio provar que todos que pensavam assim (Inclusive eu)estavam errados,o jogo é muito bonito, a historia é bastante interessante, e MUITO MAIS MUITO engraçada. Eu desafio você a jogar deponia e nao rir pelo menos algumas vezes.Sinceramente é um dos melhores jogos Indie/point-and-click que ja joguei.

It's a grand continuation of the tradition of single-player first person shooters, a dying breed these days amongst the stultifying preponderance of multiplayer garbage and open world icon-collectathons. The art direction is gorgeous, and, importantly, the writing is high quality and the voice acting is that rara avis, both well acted and well directed. It's quintessential over-the-top, absurd yet heartfelt and thoroughly pulpy Wolfenstein. For almost the first time in a singleplayer FPS, I found myself actually wanting to look at every collectible: the amount and quality of concept art is impressive, and the faux Nazi pop songs that you find in the form of records are absolutely hilarious gems.
I actually found stealth to be a more viable option than others have reported. As long as you're not fixated on stealth killing every enemy perfectly, you'll be fine. The dynamic of trying to pick off the Nazi commanders before you're spotted, then transitioning to the ridiculous bloody slaughter once you're inevitably spotted, is just as strong in this game as in TNO and Old Blood.
Gripes: The combat and movement are a little floaty. Getting damaged doesn't really feel like anything, and neither does firing most of the weapons. The campaign is super short and ends anticlimactically, clearly setting up the paid preorder DLC, which feels exploitative and predatory--not a shocker coming from Bethesda these days. (I never, ever preorder, and I have no plans to buy this game's DLC campaigns until they're on sale. Doesn't detract from my pleasure with my purchase of the main game though.) The sidequests feel perfunctory and not well signposted--it seems like you're supposed to go out and get the two other "special" upgrades in addition to the one you originally chose in the course of the campaign, but the plot never (until the free-form epilogue) offers you a clear moment that says, "OK, here is the point at which you go out and do those sidequests." And then the game's over with you having unlocked only 1 of the 3 cool special toys. That was my experience, anyway.

I bought my copy of The New Colossus day before its release for a good price. I had very little info about the sequel to 2014 reboot of Wolfenstein franchise.  I played the original and enjoyed it for what it was, a single-player story driven FPS, but it did not leave any lasting impressions.
The New Colossus did not start well, error message right at the start left me with no choice other than to search internet for solution--and I was found relatively quickly, I had to instal latest Nvidia drivers.
Once I installed latest drivers from Nvidia, the game started and played flawlessly on high settings in 1080p on my i7-4790k with GTX1070--rock solid 60fps, no noticeable slowdowns, no broken geometry or texture popping. Only other problem I have encountered from start to finish of the game were 2 game freezes during loading. I have not fiddled with video settings at all, the game run smoothly and looked amazing at default high settings.
The game offers continuation of alternative history of WW2. The story was decent with several great characters that were flashed out as much as possible in a FPS game. The story absolutely parodies current political situation and does not shy away from controversial topics such as racism, sexism and spreading of neo-nazi propaganda. It is all in good fun and cartooney approach but there are some graphical moments not for feint of heart.
I liked the gameplay because it is simplistic in its focus--provide well crafted experience focused on killing enemies, pure and unadulterated mayhem, with optional stealth that worked good enough. Weapon selection is limited to standard set of armaments including pistol, sub-machine gun, assault rifle, electricity-based gun and grenade/rocket launcher. There is also few heavy weapons that can be picked up from static gun posts or from fallen enemies. They have limited ammunition and must be carried in both hands slowing you down and forcing you to drop them on the ground if you want to use some of your standard guns. Gunplay is fine, each weapon feels differently.
Length of the game is decent, I have finished the story at around 25 hours on Do or Die difficulty setting. Some parts of the game were rather difficult but nothing impossible. Enemy AI is very mobile and once alerted to your presence they can often surprise you  by flanking you or coming from behind you. I always found it better to soften enemy forces by applying stealth early in the game levels--this is certainly recommended approach on higher difficulty settings when captains are present on the battlefield.
I still have several ubercommanders to kill via helm navigation map, which is some kind of meta game on top of story missions. These kill missions are happening in locales you visit during story missions with slight modifications to what enemies are present, their placement and new collectibles.
Character perk and weapon upgrade systems are good and fit the tune of the game. Character perks are gained naturally by performing specific actions, e.g. killing enemies while dual-wielding or performing stealth takedowns. These perks improve certain aspects of your character--mostly quality of life improvements but some of these perks are very powerful.
Weapon upgrade system is simple enough but efficient. Upgrades provide improvements to a gun or even add new functionality to it. Upgrades can be toggled on and off so you do not have to worry whether you will like it or not. Weapon upgrade kits are relatively rare but you get enough of them to upgrade your favourite weapon or two. Side mission provide access to additional weapon upgrade kits.
All in all, Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus was very positive surprise for me. High quality production value with slightly goofy story that does not take itself too seriously. Once I overcome initial problem with incompatible GPU drivers, the game run smoothly without any major issues. Visuals and sound are great, music fits the theme and some tunes were outstanding. Gameplay is fast-pace with clear focus on combat with light elements of stealth that never felt cumbersome. Enemy AI is serviceable but it will not amaze you.

This game looks like a simple Centipede clone, but don't be fooled -- this is functionally Centipede III, or maybe more accurately Centipede IV, because it adds enough to account for two sequels--which, admittedly, could have come out decades ago, but they didn't. Also I guess it's more accurately described as a Millipede variant, since it includes many if not all of the Millipede enemies and more.
First off, this game adapts the Centipede controls very fluidly to desktop mouse or trackball movement, which has always been a bit of a back-port to Centipede which expected the large arcade trackball. BUT. That's not the important part.
What the devs have done here is add some features to Centipede that were developed for later arcade games but never before adapted to this particular vibe. To wit:
It borrows the falling capsules bit from Arkanoid, which was also ripped off by lots of Space Invaders variants over the years but it never landed on Centipede before to my knowledge. Other elements are added from latter-day shoot-em-up games, like selectable characters with different attributes, and bombs--although, in this game, you actually have to HIT something with the bomb in order for it to explode.
All in all, among the straight arcaders on Steam that genuinely behave EXACTLY like oldschool cabinet arcade games, this is one of the best I've played. A refreshing surprise that I picked up just because of its low price, but I feel like I'd have pumped more than four quarters into this machine so I got my money's worth pretty well.

It's good old Centipede with autofire and powerups to make things more interesting. To balance things out, bugs take more hits to destroy (you still die in one hit, of course), and you can't get any extra lives besides the 3 you start out with. Additionally, each level has a time limit, after which everything goes haywire, the caterpillar speeds up and spiders spawn all over the place, making it very difficult to survive. Overall, easier than the original, though later levels are pretty intense, and there's always the challenge of getting a high place on the leaderboard.

This is one of those games that is way more worthwhile than it's metascore would lead you to believe. It's not perfect, but it's engaging, it's gorgeous (especially if you've got a rig that can crank the settings up), and the story is solid with punctuated moments of impressive depth.
The combat and traversal isn't wholly unique or innovative, really, but it's done well enough that it doesn't feel prohibitive to progressing through the story. The combat in particular, while it can take some getting used to, does allow for some creativity on the player's part, and can be customized through the swapping of individual strikes to form combos to suit your playstyle, or different situations.
The memory sweeping mechanic is an interesting one, and probably had the most promise of anything in the game, however it winds up being under-utilized, with only a few points during the game giving you the opportunity to use Nilin's signature skill. The process itself is neat at first, but sort of unravels into a time-consuming trial-and-error experiment, with no real indication of which triggers that the player can control will actually have any desirable effects. Honestly, my one hope is that DONTNOD get's another crack at a game set in this world so that they can really hone this particular aspect of the game maybe create something really cool the next time around.
Anyway, this game wound up flying under many radars, between the fledgling developer, the new IP, the middling reviews... But it's definitely worth your time, especially if you're looking for an action/adventure game featuring a strong and interesting female protagonist, and a beautifully realized world, wrapped in a quality storyline that will pull you along to a satisfying end.

Highly recommended for those who like cinematic games. The graphics are pretty unique and the combat is relatively similar to your typical beat 'em ups.
The game's main feature is the story though, and because of this, everything is practically linear. It's practically impossible to get lost, since many branching paths just lead to a dead end, and the only things you can interact with are the things that progress you through the story. This might make some people lose interest, but because the story is quite immersive, it makes up for the linearity.
Combat is pretty straightforward since you only have 3 options: punch, kick, or dodge. You'll then be able to equip special powers into combo strings, which can help you hit harder, heal yourself, or even grant special ability cooldowns. You gain all of these as you progress through the game, and each chapter practically (and conveniently) introduces a new element up until the finale. Animation is rather fluid and satisfying to watch, making for a rather entertaining experience whether you're playing or watching the game.
Controls are a bit wonky at times though, but the game is quite forgiving and leaves you at a place close to where you left off in the event that you die. Camera angles can get a bit weird too, but only in certain spots without any events going on at the time. Overall a great experience.

Skullgirls is a beatiful looking 2D fighter and shows the world the difference between "Advanced graphics" and good art direction. It accomplishes with an indie studio what countless triple-A developers manage to ♥♥♥♥ up with office blocks full of programmers and artists, it has art design that is memorable, literally iconic, and undeniably charming. The music, the art style, the characters, everything sits together in this wonderfully charming game.
Having said that, it's not the perfect game. God only knows what's going on with the plot because I can't fathom what it's supposed to be and the story mode is crying out for voiced cutscenes.
The other complaint (Which I suspect is the reason some bought the game) I have is that the skill ceiling is very high, and the floor is very low. If you didn't quite internalize the tutorial, you can spend hours getting beaten down by the final boss and the best PvP players can stomp you easilly. Some kind of ranking system might be in order. Maybe one's been added since I last checked not sure.
But these are just nitpicks. Don't let them fool you into thinking that this is anything less than an exempliary indie game.

I bought this game today thinking that I'd play for a little bit then hit the hay. Welp here I am 9 hours later at 5 in the morning with the story beaten. To sum up my experience I've made a pro and con chart to help you understand if you should buy this game.
Pros:
-The sound track was amazing. It changed everywhere you went and flowed with everything you did.
-The art was astonishing to say the least. From mushrooms to rams, all of it was detailed perfectly. Every new part of land you encountered changed colors vibrantly. All the things that you see in the game can, and will move in some way. Your actions, the AI actions and many objects all interact with the environment.
-The game play was very smooth and very manageable. There were only a few times where I actually had to practice a new move they give to you. The controls were simple enough that my 5 year old sister could master them.
-The map that they throw you into is giant. If i could compare this map to something I'd compare it to darksouls. Everyother path has a shortcut or a secret and the only way to get around is to walk there yourself.
-The story was touching. I'm not going to give anything away, but i did shed a few tears here and there. Punched a shark after this game's credits to regan my manliness.
-The fact that everything was so well done and everything had an animation got me thinking, "uh oh, this is gonna lag so hard the whole game," but on the contrary, everything ran so well my frames didnt drop below 50 the entire time. My Laptop is not one to brag about and my graphics card can just about handle the medium settings on 8-bit games.
- And finally, the amount of stuff you can do afterwards. I havn't done much yet because I was so preoccupied with the story, but I know for a fact I still have to max out my skill tree and get the rest of the power-ups.
now for the cons:
...I think I've made my point.
This game is a must have for anyone any age, any size, any gender and I give it a straight up 10/10.

As a fellow game dev, I am really impressed with the work that Ninjatheory has put into Hellblade: Senuas's Sacrifice.
Senua's rig and her animations are absolutely on point, very natural and well made. I've been keeping up with Ninjatheory's developement-diary, since my startup was discussing using similar mocap methods for our future project. Senuas face scan and her emotions are amazing and really make her look almost as in real life. I have not seen this amount of detail in any game before!
The transitions between the player being in control and cutscenes are on point as well, for the most part it feels like the whole game is just one big event, no loading screens, nothing to degrade the experience of playing. There are some loading screens, but they are really well hidden, good job Ninjatheory!
The camera rig feels a little weird at first, but I got used to it quickly. The camera is kind of close to Senua, but all it does is amplify the fact that everything is 'crazy' in this game, so I respect it as a wise choice to use the camera this way.
The only issue I have got with the camera rig is that there is no wall-clipping protection, I think you should implement that, it's only a short script after all.
Shaders and image effects are amazing, some may find them overused, but I think the shaders (for effects, not the normal shaders I mean) and image effects are some of the best I've seen thus far. It looks beautiful and also pushes the atmosphere further into feeling like a crazy dream. I've not seen this amount of post effects used this well before.
I have no clue how you managed to achieve some of the effects, especially the one where the whole world goes from normal to fiery hell after Senua touches the shrine (I forgot the god's name).
Now in the beginning I said we were developing our own games and we made a weather/skybox system for it. At the time I developed it, I strongly believe it was one of the best weather systems in gaming. It can easily simulate every weather condition - you name it. Skybox looks good, volumetric clouds and everything. Sunlight and galaxy/moon rendering. However, I think, I've been dethroned. The weather in Hellblade is just out of this world good! I don't know wether it has all the functionality as my system, but the things it does in game, it does perfectly. The clouds look amazing (I don't know wether you use normal hdr skyboxes and blend between them or something else), but they are so good! The raindrops look completely real, it's insane! Lightning is also on point! Also, I love the light rays from the sun and the whole volumetric lighting feel!
The ocean's look great when they are calm, but I think the way storms are simulated could use some love from the devs. The ocean just looks too opaque imo. I believe those were just some choices regarding time budged, but if not - please make the oceans look a little nicer during storms!
Sound. This is insane and some of the best use of sound I've ever heard in games. The way Senua's voices help when in combat or during normal game play is genius. The way her voices interact with each other is amazing. The deep voice talking to senua after she defeats the first two gods is so well placed (I know it's just a deep voice, but it's simply perfect for this setting). The only thing that seems off some times is Senuas voice herself, I know the actress wore the mic on her head while doing the performance capture, so sound is not going to be perfect. Maybe next time get some one else to hold a boom mic overhead or something, and maybe try to make the whole room a bit less reflective to sound. I'm not an audio engineer, so I can't really say what's wrong with Senua's voice, those are just some things that come to mind. Unlike the other voices it just feels like she's not really there. I'll try to find out what's going on next time I play the game.
Environment. Now I did not even notice some things regarding the environment for the first hours, since I spent my time drooling at how well Senua's character was made, but after some time I took a closer look at the environment.
It's really well made, and looks good. Some things that could be done better, but aren't really needed, would be:
Interaction with foilage: Bushes could bend a bit when Senua touches them, instead of just having a fixed collider and Senua not being able to walk into them.
Some props could be of a higher lod, some of them just felt a little low poly compared to the rest of the word.
I suppose you are using some kind of lod system but I noticed some stuff flickering when I walked away from it, not really a smooth transition between lod's. But that really only happened two times.
Other than that I just love the environment, it does exactly what is needed for the atmosphere of the game and everything is well made, design wise and regarding technology.
Ninjatheory's goal was Indy AAA, did they achieve that? Nope. They somehow surpassed many AAA games. I know you can't make a new the Witcher or a new GTA with your budged. But those games you were aiming at, you easily surpass.
This game is just one of the best games I've ever seen. It may not fit everyone, but it is doing everything it want's to with absolute perfection. I think this is sending a strong message toward every studio, indy or AAA, it shows you that you can make awesome pieces of art with every budged as long as you choose the right style for your budged.
Now I hope you opened the gates for more companies to make the technologies you developed even more affordable, since I don't have $10M for my own games, but man, I would love to have the tech for characters like Senua available to me! I think this game really puts the final nails in the coffin for the traditional publisher-developer style and raises Indy games to a whole new level.

The hardest battles are fought within the mind. Let me tell you that's true, I've fought many myself. This game reached me in ways no other game has.
I have some really complicated feelings toward this game but I do feel it's a game that deserves to be played and appreciated. I won't say it's supposed to be liked, or certainly not enjoyed -- akin to the movie "The Road," a comparison I keep coming back to, I'm not sure it's *supposed* to be enjoyed. Of the words I would use to describe this game -- bold, audacious, vulnerable, insanely risky, meaningful, impactful, significant -- "fun" wouldn't crack the top fifty. Playing this game is not a good time. And if you're of the belief that games are supposed to be fun first and foremost, I can't entirely blame you for passing on this one. But I feel you're missing out on a remarkable achievement in design and artistry.
This game is an experience the likes of which has never really been seen before. Sure, the hack 'n slash combat gameplay is itself anything but groundbreaking. Neither are the admittedly repetitive puzzles. But it's just so much more than the sum of its parts. It's hard to even describe in words. Senua's journey is an incredibly arduous one to take, but it's one that if you're sufficiently hooked in, you can't walk away from.
Hellblade's sound design is nothing short of exquisite. While the game is very visually stunning as well, it really is the sound design (along with the hauntingly sublime performance of Melina Jeurgens) that immerses you and puts you right in the midst of the harrowing ordeal this game throws at you. We all do it with movies, if they're especially good ones -- we come out wondering what major awards it might win. Hellblade absolutely must win the audio design award at Geoff Keighley's gaming Oscars thing in December. I don't even care what the other nominated games are. In a game I consider a monument to "video games as art" in its own right, the music and sound design in this game is its own work of art.
A section that I keep thinking about over and over again is "trials of Odin" section. While I will try to be as spoiler-free as possible, I will just say that this section embodies something I've tried to explore in my own writings and have had to experience in my own life as well. One of the most remarkable contradictions I've experienced -- comfort in a crisis. A shimmering harbour in the bleakest of storms. It's a beautiful thing that I hope you never have to experience, because to know this beauty you have to be taken to the absolute depths of hell. It's a place I wouldn't wish my worst enemy to go to, yet having someone there to give you "a little help, a little hope" is the most incredible feeling of peace and safety a person can have. And Melina Jeurgens and Hellblade take us there. It is not an easy place to go to -- no part of this game is easy to go through -- but it's something to experience.
The whole experience of this game is one that I don't think a game has ever offered. I keep going back to "The Road" -- meaningful and impactful art that is not easy to take in. And this game to me stands alone as a work of art. People talk about Shadow of the Colossus when they talk about games as art, and deservedly so. This game needs to lead in that conversation as well. Art isn't (necessarily) about feeling good, and certainly not about having fun. As I said before, this game somewhat sacrifices the fun factor for its artistic value. That artistic value is in taking you to places you've never had to go before, or at least I hope you haven't. They are complicated and not easily described places, but you will have a better understanding of yourself and your fellow man and woman should you go to them.
I am glad the "vote" at the bottom of this review box is whether you would *recommend* the game, not whether you liked it. The former is an exceedingly easy question to answer. YES, I recommend this game (I may not ever be able to answer whether I "liked" it), it is something every gamer should play whether they come away liking it or not. Do be aware that you may have been misled about it. It is not a Dark Souls clone. Combat is sparse and sparing. Much of the game is spent walking "alone" -- or as alone as you can get. But this journey is one you need to at least try, I promise you that.

But, the Story is the main point of this game.
And i won't spoil anything. I don't want to.
All i will say that this game is pretty disturbing... At least, it was for me. Maybe because i can relate a little bit.
Play it. You won't really regret it, and it's 6 hours long, so you won't lose much time.

Deponia Doomsday is possibly the final (final) game in the Deponia game series, and with the newest game, we get the best experience as well. Because, Doomsday is probably the best part of the entire series.
You probably played Goodbye Deponia, and thought to yourself "Man, that ending sucked" And you're probably craving for more, and then see this game, and ask yourself "Is this worth it? Will it give a better ending than the one in 3?" Well, I can answer that easily. The ending in this game is a lot more satisfying than in Goodbye Deponia, but I won't go more into that because it's not possible to do it without spoiling it.
In Deponia Doomsday, time gets rewinded to the very beginning, even before Deponia 1 happens, by the cause of a time machine. You as well as McChronicle will have to use it to revert the timeline to be back like it was originally, so you will have to solve puzzles in various times and try to not cause paradoxes and destroy the ending which happened originally. I don't wanna say  too much about the story since it's the best experience when you destroy it for yourself, but all I will say that the whole time I played through it, I enjoyed myself, and the ending gave a lot of satisfaction.
Deponia Doomsday in general, seems to have a lot bigger budget than before. There's tons of new animations, cutscenes, basically things which you rarely saw in the previous games, happen here pretty often, which makes the game a lot better, and gives it more life.
Alright, let's talk about the soundtrack. The soundtrack like in the previous games, is really good. But this time there's a lot more memorable tunes, and the music in general feels a lot more lively with a bigger variety of instruments in the tracks, as well as them fitting into the current location better. They also used some tracks from the previous games, which gave a bit of nostalgia to the ones who played the previous games.
Deponia Doomsday, like the previous games in the series, is a Point and Click game, in this part we will be doing various things in various timelines, sometimes even having to decide what to do in a certain amount of time, before a time loop happens (and the decisions here matter more than in The Walking Dead) The Time Loops are kind of a gimmick, like controlling the 3 Rufuses in Deponia 3, and it's frankly pretty fun. You do various things, and then are able to rewind time and hopefully see a different outcome this time. There's a pretty hard Time Loop Puzzle near the end of the game, but completing it is pretty satisfacting, and seeing that the things you did before change the outcome what is now happening, is really great.

Very good game and great for ear training, but I'd be hesitant to recommend this to anyone without any prior music experience or education. A complete novice could probably get the hang of things eventually, but unless you already know a little bit of music theory you probably won't really understand what you're learning. It's one thing to gloss over this in the tutorial, but even in the in-game glossary, it's not explained why the first, second, and third notes in a chord are called the root, third, and fifth except that "music theory is weird". While music theory is indeed super weird, the explanation for that is very simple - the root is the first note of the scale the chord is named for, the third is the third note in the scale, and the fifth is the fifth note in the scale(you can probably guess about the seventh). As another reviewer noted, some of the note names appear to be slightly off, but that's not really a big deal here - the point isn't to memorize the the names of the notes, but train your ear to identify the relationships between the different notes. You don't get to see any note names until you've figured things out (same goes for the scale they're in) and they flash by fast enough that you probably won't even read them. This is for ear training, not memorizing chords. Another minor gripe is that a couple songs (two out of the roughly fifteen I've played so far) have relatively long drum lead-ins, four or eight bars, before the melody kicks in. That would make sense in a rhythm game, but here you end up just sitting around for a while until you can start listening for a root note. Those minor complaints aside, I'd recommend this in an instant to any musician. The first ten levels or so are a breeze if you have any prior music experience, and you'll be worried you wasted your time and money, but things get really interesting and fun after they start with inversions and 7ths. I've played several instruments for over fifteen years, and professionally over the last seven years as both an instructor and performer, and I can't recall better, more dense training in a single session than the two hours I've spent with this so far.

First off, this game is a fantastic addition to any music lover's game library. The concept is really cool and is a fun and interactive way to train your ear to hear different chord qualities. However, I do have a little beef with this game as of now. The simpler levels where you learn to identify major and minor triads are perfectly fine, but things start to get mislabled once the seventh gets involved. For example: whenever the song is in the key of A Major in these levels, your goal is to identify an A Major Seventh chord, but the chord identified as the A Major Seventh is spelled "A-C#-E-F#" (an A Major with an added sixth). This also applies to the E Major Seventh. Also, no distinction is made between a dominant seventh and a major seventh, or between a minor seventh and a minor chord with a major seventh. Sorry for my lil rant here. I just don't want people to wonder why one seventh chord sounds different than another seventh chord with the same label. Also, I've only played for about an hour, so maybe this is cleared up in later levels. :p Otherwise, this is a great game.

Books could be written about Call of Duty’s multiplayer. It could be argued that CoD, along with its other well-known competitor, revitalised the first person shooter multiplayer experience. Maybe that is true and maybe it isn’t – these discussions are best left to posterity.
It isn’t the stellar multiplayer experience however that makes this particular title the most memorable and sets it apart from other first person shooters, both then and now. It’s the first person campaign and the story that drives it that shine the brightest and even now stand the test of time.
In a day and age where the first person experience is nothing more than an afterthought in contemporary military shooters, CoD had a riveting story. An unforgettable journey. A clichéd journey, without a doubt, but a cliché we all found ourselves, inexplicably perhaps, drawn to and captivated by. Modern Warfare taught us what camaraderie is about and what a band of brothers in arms can achieve. It’s about the trust and bond between the men fighting on the same side, against all odds and overwhelming forces. It did everything right and created enough suspension of disbelief to move us. Don’t tell me you didn’t at least have a solitary tear in your eye at the end.
I still have a place for MW on my drive and even though I haven’t played it in a while, I think of it fondly. Do yourself a favour, if you haven’t played this game – get it and play it. It’s one of those games that have to be played at least once in a lifetime.

A fun game, with minor RPG elements, wonderful art style and visuals , albeit slightly repetitive gameplay and lack of character depth.
The first thing about this game is the amazing visuals. It is a pleasure to play simply to look at the environment. The detail to the characters, spells, enemies and background art is great. The voiceover of the characters is also very well done. All in all, the production and art, design elements are top notch.
The gameplay mechanics are well done - but the areas that could have been improved are the RPG elements. The gear and skills for each character are fairly irrelevant. It doesn't seem to be much of a stretch to say you could ignore all the gear and all the skills and finish the game without notice that you didn't use anything. They are merely small accents to your character - which is cool - but feels like it could have been developed more to make each character even more specialized and the party dynamic more rich.  As it stood, I used the fighter all the time and only switched to the mage when I needed a box and the thief when I needed to swing (and maybe at least half the time I could just make boxes to achieve the same ends).  This wasn't enough to detract from the fun of the game - it just had me thinking there was a lot of character overlap or lack of puzzle diversity to properly utilize each character more.
Leading to the "puzzles" - each level, each map was essentially always the same type. Eventually you get slightly different obstacles such as spinning boards, button pushing, but most of the time it was "jump, make a box, jump, make a box, (maybe swing)".  More diversity in this area would have enhanced things. Same with the story. I don't put much weight into the story, but it could have also been a lot more interesting than it ultimately turns out to me. It was only 10 hours in length for me, and I don't play very fast, so expect others could go through even faster.
With that said, it was still a very fun game. Recommended if on sale for sure.  I have bought the 2nd game (as a testament to the enjoyment of the first) and hope some of the things above are more fleshed out making it really what it could be. Then if things go well, onto the 3rd installment.

I had never heard of this game prior to it being bundled in part of the last Humble Bundle.  From what I have played so far, I can make the following observations:
1. It has similar controls to Diablo 3 (some skills have power ups that you buy using skill points you receive when you level up, some of these power ups need to be manually activated rather than an add on)
2. They borrowed heavily from Diablo 3 in that gold, potions, quest items, and essences (gems/item enhancments used in socketed items) are automatically picked up
3. Huge emphasis placed on gear
4. Leveling up is closer to Diablo 2 than Diablo 3. Every level you gain 5 attribute points to distribute among body (combination of str and vit), Willpower (intellect), Luck (magic find, gold find), and finally dexterity (important for ranged attacks), plus you gain 3 skills points to use in a skill tree. This can be used to level up your current skills, unlock new skills, or purchase the add on abilities mentioned previously
5. There is a reputation leveling system (seperate from your character's leveling up) that is similar to the system from Torchlight.  When your reputation gains a level you can unlock a new perk (an example is one of them gives you a +50 to poison resistance and increases the effectiveness of potions by 10%)
The game's setting is easily described as steampunk, you play the titular character Van Helsing (well his son, who carries the Van Helsing name) in an eastern European country.  All of the enemies have names that are Slavic in origin, and overall the game has a very late 19th century to early 20th century vibe.  In fact playing through the game reminds me of the Leviathan book series and almost like a Diablo version of Arcanum (ie less emphasis on RPG and more emphasis on hack and slash) in an odd way.
I have been playing as the mage class, and my only gripe is that you are incredibly underpowered at the start of the game. As the game progresses you will obviously gain abilities to clear enemies faster, but for the early and mid game you may feel over whelmed in no small part due to the lack of an effective AOE.

Picked this game up for $10 on sale - I absolutely urge anyone who is an avid gamer to buy it.
I have seen a lot of griping about a number of things, and I hope to put some of them to rest.  One example is that someone mentioned a seeming lack of imagination when it comes to enemies.  To that, all I have to point out is that great games like Bioshock, for example, literally had like two types of enemies - Splicers and Big Daddies.  That game is still widely regarded as a great title and this one is no different.  Enemy archetypes are low in number, but the variance in enemies is by no means small.  I found myself constantly enthralled by the evolution of enemies over time.  It definitely felt like they were ramping up the the difficulty as time went on (when playing on the hardest difficulty) and therefore I think they did fine in this department.
Another thing people have mentioned is that they felt as though the combat system was strange or too simple - what have you.  The combat system is exactly like what you would see in Batman: Arkham Asylum.  It has that sort-of fluid momentum to it that I, personally, praise in video games.  So, if you liked Arkham Asylum's combat system, you will like Remember Me's.
Things like the plot (I am about 50% of the way done) and the world seem to be wonderfully crafted.  The world especially is breathtaking.  In every chapter so far, there seems to be a subtle moment handed to the player to let them know that the environment is expansive and enveloping.  It really does well, with the majorly-accredited musical score that accompanies it, in making the player feel immersed.  The plot is interesting and holds up well to what I originally anticipated from the game.
Another major gripe seemed to be the interaction with memories and the player's ability to alter them.  This was a minor pitfall in the sense that I felt like there needed to be more examples of this throughout the game.  Still, in the examples that have occurred up to where I am currently at in the game, I have had plenty of fun trying to solve the puzzles.  Sometimes you screw yourself, sometimes you accidentally alter it the wrong way - it /has/ to be limited to some extent but it is still really fun.
I gave the game a 10/10 simply because I think it is a fantastic game overall, an wonderfully immersive experience for players, and a great addition to any gamer's collection.  If you can pick it up at $10, I would say it is entirely worth the cash if you have it on hand.
As an afterthought, here are some games that it contains elements of as a means of comparison to your tastes: The Bioshock Series, Batman: Arkham Asylum, elements of horror similar to those in parts of Dead Space and Dead Space 2, Mirror's Edge, Assassin's Creed, and even some relation to Dishonored.  Super fun game, check it out in the very least and, if you get it, I definitely recommend tackling it with a controller.

**Word of Caution to Windows 8.1 users** - Game play and graphics may not work correctly. As an 8.1 user, I've had to turn the graphics settings to low, AA off, and Super-Sampling off and I still get full pixelation and near graphics crashes in fight scenes. My GPU is the MSI Lightning HD 7950, which has had no problem running the most demanding games on maxed out settings. CPU is AMD FX 8350 OC'ed to 4.4 ghz.
Aside from the above stated problem the majority of the game runs ok on my machine and enough to be able to review it. The controls are a little weird at times and camera angles can throw off combat just a bit. But those are my only complaints with the game.
The ability to enter people's memories and fast-forward and rewind them at will to alter the outcome of your story is a wonderful concept that Capcom obviously took their time to get correct. It is one of the most original features in any game in recent history. Most of the time when a developer or publisher tries something this far out it usually doesnt end well.
The settings for this game are beautifully done and even thought it is set in the future the background world you live in is not so far out taht it is unbelievable. Too many times games set in the future leave a player unable to relate with their environment; almost as if their character is a unique specimen that does not fit into the scenery. Here, the designers have done well to understate your presence and make you just another feature of the environment.
Voice-Acting is well done as well with only a few cheesy lines from the characters so far. Lines like [sic] "The whole world is counting on you" always creep into the dialogue, but as of writing this review I only experienced one line from a main character that was close to what I just stated.
So, the story is tight, well crafted, and compliments the the way the character fits into the main environment. Some of the ideas are wildly original and actually work well in-game. Game play is good enough to get you through the game but could be better. And the graphics have some pretty serious issues for me on 8.1. Who knows, maybe its just a terrible port over to PC. Overall I'd like to recommend the game but without knowing the extent of the graphics issues its hard to do that. If this is just an issue with drivers and is fixed in a later update then that would be a major bonus.

It's a grand continuation of the tradition of single-player first person shooters, a dying breed these days amongst the stultifying preponderance of multiplayer garbage and open world icon-collectathons. The art direction is gorgeous, and, importantly, the writing is high quality and the voice acting is that rara avis, both well acted and well directed. It's quintessential over-the-top, absurd yet heartfelt and thoroughly pulpy Wolfenstein. For almost the first time in a singleplayer FPS, I found myself actually wanting to look at every collectible: the amount and quality of concept art is impressive, and the faux Nazi pop songs that you find in the form of records are absolutely hilarious gems.
I actually found stealth to be a more viable option than others have reported. As long as you're not fixated on stealth killing every enemy perfectly, you'll be fine. The dynamic of trying to pick off the Nazi commanders before you're spotted, then transitioning to the ridiculous bloody slaughter once you're inevitably spotted, is just as strong in this game as in TNO and Old Blood.
Gripes: The combat and movement are a little floaty. Getting damaged doesn't really feel like anything, and neither does firing most of the weapons. The campaign is super short and ends anticlimactically, clearly setting up the paid preorder DLC, which feels exploitative and predatory--not a shocker coming from Bethesda these days. (I never, ever preorder, and I have no plans to buy this game's DLC campaigns until they're on sale. Doesn't detract from my pleasure with my purchase of the main game though.) The sidequests feel perfunctory and not well signposted--it seems like you're supposed to go out and get the two other "special" upgrades in addition to the one you originally chose in the course of the campaign, but the plot never (until the free-form epilogue) offers you a clear moment that says, "OK, here is the point at which you go out and do those sidequests." And then the game's over with you having unlocked only 1 of the 3 cool special toys. That was my experience, anyway.

I bought my copy of The New Colossus day before its release for a good price. I had very little info about the sequel to 2014 reboot of Wolfenstein franchise.  I played the original and enjoyed it for what it was, a single-player story driven FPS, but it did not leave any lasting impressions.
The New Colossus did not start well, error message right at the start left me with no choice other than to search internet for solution--and I was found relatively quickly, I had to instal latest Nvidia drivers.
Once I installed latest drivers from Nvidia, the game started and played flawlessly on high settings in 1080p on my i7-4790k with GTX1070--rock solid 60fps, no noticeable slowdowns, no broken geometry or texture popping. Only other problem I have encountered from start to finish of the game were 2 game freezes during loading. I have not fiddled with video settings at all, the game run smoothly and looked amazing at default high settings.
The game offers continuation of alternative history of WW2. The story was decent with several great characters that were flashed out as much as possible in a FPS game. The story absolutely parodies current political situation and does not shy away from controversial topics such as racism, sexism and spreading of neo-nazi propaganda. It is all in good fun and cartooney approach but there are some graphical moments not for feint of heart.
I liked the gameplay because it is simplistic in its focus--provide well crafted experience focused on killing enemies, pure and unadulterated mayhem, with optional stealth that worked good enough. Weapon selection is limited to standard set of armaments including pistol, sub-machine gun, assault rifle, electricity-based gun and grenade/rocket launcher. There is also few heavy weapons that can be picked up from static gun posts or from fallen enemies. They have limited ammunition and must be carried in both hands slowing you down and forcing you to drop them on the ground if you want to use some of your standard guns. Gunplay is fine, each weapon feels differently.
Length of the game is decent, I have finished the story at around 25 hours on Do or Die difficulty setting. Some parts of the game were rather difficult but nothing impossible. Enemy AI is very mobile and once alerted to your presence they can often surprise you  by flanking you or coming from behind you. I always found it better to soften enemy forces by applying stealth early in the game levels--this is certainly recommended approach on higher difficulty settings when captains are present on the battlefield.
I still have several ubercommanders to kill via helm navigation map, which is some kind of meta game on top of story missions. These kill missions are happening in locales you visit during story missions with slight modifications to what enemies are present, their placement and new collectibles.
Character perk and weapon upgrade systems are good and fit the tune of the game. Character perks are gained naturally by performing specific actions, e.g. killing enemies while dual-wielding or performing stealth takedowns. These perks improve certain aspects of your character--mostly quality of life improvements but some of these perks are very powerful.
Weapon upgrade system is simple enough but efficient. Upgrades provide improvements to a gun or even add new functionality to it. Upgrades can be toggled on and off so you do not have to worry whether you will like it or not. Weapon upgrade kits are relatively rare but you get enough of them to upgrade your favourite weapon or two. Side mission provide access to additional weapon upgrade kits.
All in all, Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus was very positive surprise for me. High quality production value with slightly goofy story that does not take itself too seriously. Once I overcome initial problem with incompatible GPU drivers, the game run smoothly without any major issues. Visuals and sound are great, music fits the theme and some tunes were outstanding. Gameplay is fast-pace with clear focus on combat with light elements of stealth that never felt cumbersome. Enemy AI is serviceable but it will not amaze you.

Orphaned as a child, the young Ori is found and raised by the loving creature Naru. They live a happy and content life together, searching for fruit to scoff in the forest. A catastrophic event changes all that, causing the trees to wither and die. Being forced into submission by the deteriorating environment, the Spirit tree uses the last of its strength to give Ori a second lease on life, sending him on a journey into the unknown to save the world from being devoured by the elements.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a story driven platformer set in a beautifully designed world, with absolutely stunning artwork and visuals. With a delightful array of characters, and a beautiful, touching storyline, this is without a doubt, the most emotionally powerful platformer I have ever played. Solid and fine-tuned gameplay provides a fun and challenging experience for casual gamers and achievement hunters alike. With an incredible orchestral soundtrack (which I definitely recommend purchasing with the game), it will put you on the edge of your seat and keep the emotional juices flowing throughout.
+ Beautiful and touching storyline
+ Stunning artwork and visuals
+ Well designed environments and level design
+ Fun and challenging gameplay
+ Incredible orchestral soundstrack
+ A large amount of collectibles to keep you exploring
+ Fine-tuned controller support

The most important preface to Hellblade is that its not a game for everyone. In fact, I don't mind admitting that its not a game for me.
The most striking thing about this game is the sheer haunting beauty of the look, feel and sound. The first opening sequence gives you a pretty good idea of the dark journey you are about to embark on. The scenery is striking and haunting, the voice acting is superb and the dream-like (or nightmare-like) feel teeters on the brink between surreal and morbid. This game elevated the video game genre to an artform like nothing I've seen before.
Having said that, if you play games for the sheer adrenaline thrill of victory or to excersise the competitive muscles (like I do), this will be utterly disappointing. The combat is simplistic (just a waste of time until the next super cool cutscene) and the puzzles are easy. Much of the early part of the game is figuring out the controls and how to properly interact with the environment. The initial story is revealed in tiny pieces in a way that many games have done before. The mysterious feel is ruined by the completely unsatisfying progression. There are no levels, no itemization, no skills. It feels like insulting a Picasso, but to me a game is a form of entertainment and enjoyment. I was in awe and marvel and the accomplishment that Hellblade is, but it would be a stretch to say I enjoyed it.

10/10 -- Read below to find out why.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is definitely one of the best games I've ever played. The story is rich, Senua is a well-developed dynamic character, and the entire experience itself is something that should not be missed out on. Being able to experience and see psychosis through someone else's eyes provides an educational standpoint into the psychology of a sufferer. Several reviews posted online may suggest that this game was created solely to take advantage of a medical condition and capitalize on it for the purpose of making a buck. Truth is, various mental health sufferers have worked collaboratively on this game with Ninja Theory to provide the most authentic experience possible to educate others about the effects of strain on the human psyche (as documented within the game's clip after you beat it).
IF YOU DO NOT OWN A SURROUND SOUND HEADSET, DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME UNTIL YOU GET ONE. The experience is crucial to having a surround sound headset. You are able to hear statements, whispers, voices, and screams in certain ears that cannot be heard appropriately and as intended with traditional speakers or headsets. I'm not trying to say that the sound effects make the game, but it kind of does. Having this will truly immerse you into the experience, making you feel as if you are actually there. Some reviews might suggest that the game is boring, and you are simply running into rooms and fighting, running into rooms and fighting; it may seem this way to someone who has no sound playing, or not the right equipment to immerse themselves in the game. Having a headset TRULY makes you feel as if you are experiencing the game first hand. There have been multiple counts and occasions where this game has scared me out of my seat, where I then had to pause it to breathe, recover, and then continue my journey as Senua.
Other reviews may suggest that the combat is bland and repetitive; I, on the other hand, was completely surprised, impressed, and blown away by the way the combat looked and operated. It requires a bit of skill to appropriately dodge, parry, and block incoming attacks to prevent damage taken. It is somewhat difficult to beat some of the enemies on the default difficulty setting, but with enough experience and practice, it does ease up some, but enemies will become more difficult by the end of the game.
Last but not least, the visuals are breathtaking. The graphics make this game LOOK real. The design of Senua is jaw-dropping. Environments are detailed, with fleshed-out foliage and intricate puzzles that make each "stage" of the game different.
For a price point of $29.99, you cannot beat a one-of-a-kind experience unlike anything you have seen before (in a video game).
Please purchase this game. It will definitely take you on a trip you probably have never been on before.

In all the time I was waiting for the price to drop on this game I had read both good and bad reviews, but have personally found it to be quite enjoyable so far.
The female protagonist is certianly refreshing, though despite being a complete badass Nilin has about as much depth and complexity as the recently re-imagined Lara Croft (if not less); the reason for this being that she primarily interacts with herself and the brief moments she
have conversing with others are done via commlink and thus end up being rather impersonal.
The gameplay is mostly balanced between vertical platforming and combo-based 'beat-em-up' style combat. While the platforming doesn't really offer anything unique (missed opportunity if you ask me) it is handled quite well all the same. The combat, however, is part of what makes this game shine. Sure, on the surface it may not seem so different but the Combo Lab is quite a nifty innovation that allows you build your combos - and thus your play style - as you see fit. For each combo you unlock, you can mix and match moves (the actual button combinations are static) from various categories to build new and powerful attack strings; from power attacks to regen attacks and more.
The Memory Remix mechanic is also unique and quite interesting, though sadly doesn't see much use. What it does is let you view a person's memory and alter it by scrubbing it for memory leaks which can then be manipulated in various ways. For example: your first encounter with this power has you erasing the memory of an ill loved-one from the mind of a bounty hunter and therefor eliminating her motivation for wanting you dead.
The graphics are pretty solid and Neo-Paris is simply stunning - from it's towering heights to the murky bowels of the undercity below. Voice acting was really well done, even if the actual writing behind it often left something to be desired; Kezia Burrows (voice of Nilin) does a particularly awesome job. Music is halfway decent, too.

An enjoyable 'Diablo-eque' game starring a growly, macho-goth Van Helsing, clearly inspired more by the Hugh Jackman interpretation than that of Bram Stoker. The visuals are attractive, a sort of steampunk / magic vibe that actually reminded me a lot of the classic Arcanum (think automatons, gargoyles and electricity-suit wearing werewolves).
Van Helsing can be played as a ranged shooter (flintlocks, yes please) or a close-range sword-wielding dervish. Additional content unlocks the 'Thaumaturge' - a sort of turn-of-the-century illusionist - and the 'Arcane Mechanist' - your summoner class (fight using an army of clockwork spiders). Both add nice variety, but the game dialogue has clearly been written for the moody standard character and sometimes it sounds out of place playing as one of the DLC characters.
There are minor problems throughout, but these are often easy to work around. Some are control based (unresponsive clicks) others are gameplay based (allies not doing what they are supposed to) but compared to other ARPGS like Titan Quest or Torchlight these issues are inobtrusive. As Neocore continue to update and fix the game it continues to improve. Neocore are a responsive company and frequently comment on forum posts and respond to technical issues quickly.
Ultimately I'd recommend this to ARPG fans, or fans of steampunk / neo-gothic artwork. The plot is gibberish, but the vibe is there and all credit to Neocore for that. Having completed a Heroic Hardcore playthrough, I'd rate this as 8/10 - genuinely enjoyable, deep character development and a good post-game adventure mode.

Story: Schon die ersten Minuten des Spiels machen Lust auf mehr: Im Jahr 2084 ist es dem Konzern Memorize gelungen, eine Technologie zu entwickeln, mit der Erinnerungen wie eine Datei abgespeichert und mit anderen geteilt werden können. Jeder, der sich gegen das Regime stellt, wird in die Pariser Bastille gesperrt. Von da an führt  Remember Me durch eine packende Geschichte, die in der Mitte zwar ein wenig langweilig wird ,  dank der glaubwürdigen Heldin und der interessanten Nebenfiguren aber durchgehend bei der Stange hält.(txt.  von gamestar.de)
Technik: Schnelles Gameplay und tolle Grafik sind gut zusammengeführt und ergeben so ein robustes Spiel.
Das gute Kampfsystem ist schnell und trotzdem leicht. Das Spiel an sich ist tunnelartig und man ist ein wenig eingeschrenkt das stört aber nicht weiter.
Nilin Cartier-Wells, der weibliche Protagonist sieht gut aus und wird nicht langweilig.
Die Welt:In den belebten Gassen der französischen Hauptstadt findet man Geschäfte, und Restaurants , während Roboter ihre Bestellungen aufnehmen.Umgeben von Historischen Gebäuden  wie Notre Dame oder Sacré-Coeur, die zwischen vielen Häusern schön rausstechen.
Natürlich hat das Spiel auch seine Macken: Die Kamera spielt nicht immer mit und an manchen Stellen sieht die Grafik
dann doch nicht so gut aus ausserdem sind die im Spiel vorkommenden Kletterpassagen ziemlich langweilig und einfach. Die Kämpfe  werden immer in einem abgesperten Bereich ausgeführt dieser ist zwar relativ groß, schrenkt aber trotzdem ein wenig ein.
Dennoch ist das Spiel eine klare Kaufempfehlung und für 20 euro vergleichsweise günstig.

As others have said, a real love-hate relationship with this game. I'll just give one pro and one con, and will try to touch on things that haven't been heavily discussed in other reivews.
Pro - The themes of the game are excellent. This game takes modern-day issues about the commoditization of urban life in media and views them through a cyberpunk lens. There's a great Ghost in the Shell / Matrix vibe that runs throughout the game that makes this game a worthwhile addition to anyone who enjoys that genre, even considering all of the issues.
Con - Beyond the shoddy controls, the uninspired combat mechanics (though there are a few fun parts to fighting), the quicktime events, the boring platforming... beyond all that, the thing that bugs more more than it ought... no saving? Really? Cant' save, have to rely on checkpoints? Why?

If you've played Metroid and Castlevania, then you'd think that you would know what to expect with this game.
Indeed, it has traits and qualities that are very similar to some of The Greats in gaming. Throughout the game, you pass through areas that have powerups which can only be acquired after getting an ability from later on. There are secret paths and tunnels that lead to new places. All in all, it seems like a typical platformer Metroidvania style game, and it reasonably is in some of its traits...
But the interesting part is what isn't similar to Metroidvania games.
The central theme of this game is fragility, and it sticks true to that theme throughout the entire game. The theme is even reflected in its gameplay. Its core story maintains a smooth story-telling technique, sending you through a prologue which sets the story up, then touching upon the plot here and there. There's no burden on the player to follow really long strings of text or to keep track of tons of characters. The game stuck true to maintaining simplicity.
So I'd give the story a 9/10, for being simple, clean-cut, easy to follow, and simply put: A good story.
Anybody whose seen the trailer knows of the beauty of this game as well. The animation is seemingly flawless, and the soundtrack fits the setting. It's very rare that I feel like a game, such as this one, has truly immersed me into their world with their atmosphere. The cutscenes were also heart tugging; they were so well done, I almost felt like crying at some parts!
So I'd give the atmosphere (Which combines both music and graphics) a 9/10 as well, for its immersive abilities and fantastic cutscenes.
The gameplay is fun, engaging, refreshing, and keeps the player on their toes. I felt challenged throughout the entire game, but not so-much-so that the game felt impossible to play. It was simply fun to play. The only thing I felt might have been a little too much for the game was the ability system. For such a simple game, the ability system seemed like too hard of an attempt to appeal to all crowds rather than focusing on its core audience. Though, I admit, this isn't much of a problem I have with the game because you technically don't have to spend any ability points at all throughout the game (It's an achievement to do that anyways!). Instead of ability points, I felt like it would have been better to lean towards metroid and have abilities that, not necessarily enhances damage, but allows for weapons that have different effects.
For these reasons, I'd give gameplay a 8/10. It was very fun, engaging, and extremely exciting during some parts. The only issue is its attempt at appealing to too large of an audience by placing an RPG element to the game with the ability system, rather than keeping it down-right simple.
Overall, I'd say the game gets an 88%. I HIGHLY recommend this game to anybody, even casual gamers, because it's truly an immersive experience you don't want to miss.

I'm a huge fan of the original trilogy and I'm sad that I cannot say this game lives up to them. The art is beautiful and I enjoy the humor, but the game simply fails at very basic levels of story telling and adventure game design unlike the previous games.
In the previous three games, I felt part of the world and was interested to see what's on the other side of the junkpile. In Deponia Doomsday, time traveling completely ruins any sense of progression. You're randomly thrown into places to see what unfolds in that timeline, but none of this feels important at all. Right when you get to the climax of that scene, you just go through another portal to another random place. I no longer see interesting locations and characters, I'm just trying to identify the puzzle so I can move on in the game. I don't feel like I'm moving forward in the world or the story, I'm just getting random puzzles thrown at me.
This game tops the Deponia series with the most ridiculous puzzles. With point&click adventure games, I understand some puzzles will not click for all people, and there were some bad apples in the original trilogy. But this game has already outdone all those three, at least for me. At one point, the solution is to literally go against the control scheme of all four games. You can't just, without any kind of hinting, make a puzzle that wants you to do something that each Deponia game tutorializes you not to do. They've also added weird QTE-styled puzzles, which I find completely unnecessary.
Deponia Doomsday is still a fine looking game, but it fails to continue the Deponia series. I find it worse than any of the previous three in pretty much every way. As many other fans, I was upset with the ending of the trilogy, but I don't know if this game helped in any way. In fact, it might have made things even worse.
This is a game which must be played just by the sick people, but I'm sick, and I like it. I recommend this game to all Steam users.

A tower defence game made by Dnzy Games who are still working on their website at the moment.
They have made two games thus far and this seems to be their first to pc.
I’m not much a tower defence gamer as this is the second one I’ve ever played, the first being '300 dwarves', but there was much more on offer here than that one.
The objective is simple, your job is to stop a number of cartoon zombie waves from making their way to the exit point by strategically placing various defence towers around the grid and upgrade them as necessary. Certain towers are powerful against certain zombies and on the flip side some zombies are quite invincible against certain towers. While some are easy to work out, some levels are quite hard and will take some trial and error to work out a strategy.
For instance Cannon towers are powerful against flying zombies, but useless against everything else. Electric towers are great against poisonous spiders. Freezing towers slows everything coming through and doubling that tower with a flame tower can really chew through the health points of your enemies. Sniper towers are great against mummy waves etc.
There are 20 levels all up, with two difficulty levels normal/hard, both requiring you to get through them. The first 5 levels can be blitzed with a simple 2 tower combo, but from level 6 onwards things start to get much harder requiring a whole assortment of defence. The hard difficulty while it contains exactly the same amount of waves as the normal, it changes by giving you less money to work with and on some levels it tries to ban you from using some towers at all, usually the towers you need the most.
The assortment of enemies start from your normal zombies, flying zombies, poisonous spiders that kill soldiers quickly, mummies with a tank of health, some zombies that regenerate health, some zombies that explode into smaller versions of itself, zombies that can heal other zombies, zombies that seem to have super speed and just rush past everything and one or two more types as well.
A lot of the time your tower defences will not be enough against the onslaught, so the developers have given a few more things at your disposal to help you. You have a transportable soldier with limited health, a small collection of landmines which can placed as a booby trap and a small bomb which can be dropped from the air and helps take out a small amount of enemies. All these tools replenish on a timer. You also have three more weapons, but these cost money and do not replenish once used. Dynamite, a freeze bomb, and a satellite laser. The most helpful is the dynamite and I would often spam the last level for money so that I could buy heaps of dynamite, this way I could go for a three star rating on each level.
There are a few complaints by other gamers regarding its difficulty especially in regards to levels that have a large amount of mummies in them as they are very difficult to attend to due to their outrageous amount of hp. However there seems to be a few bugs with this game which I was able to use to my advantage and I’ll share them with you now.
1) Before actually starting a level, since the landmines replenish on a timer, you can actually lay a whole map full of landmines before you even begin.
2) As stated before some levels dictate certain towers can’t be used. There is a way around this. Spend your money that you’re allocated at the start so that your bank is lower than the price of the tower you really want. For instance a Fire tower is 120 gold coins, so you want to make sure your bank is under that. Then click on any vacant spot and click on the fire tower option. As your other towers begin to make money by killing zombies eventually you will have 120 gold coins and because you already have that option ticked with your mouse icon it will now allow you to put that tower on the spot chosen even in a level that dictates you can’t have that tower. If you want two of those towers just repeat the above trick.
3) Spam the last level on the normal difficulty, you will get 480 gold coins. Buy dynamite!
There is little to no story with this game other than you simply have to stop the waves from getting through and there is no proper ending to this game either. There are quite a few achievements but they all seem pretty lack lustre and I would much preferred if the achievements got a gamer to try various things. For example...
'Win a level with only 1 tower'
'Win the first 5 levels with only 2 towers'
'Use sniper towers only on a level'
'Have 1,000 gold coins at the end of a level'
But alas the only achievements are get level 5 on this tower, get three stars on all levels, complete all levels etc. which let’s face it most people are going to do all those things anyway. Still if you’re after something different and you like tower defence games, I can actually highly recommend this one, it should at least keep you entertained for quite a few hours.

Bought in the 2017 Steam sale like so many others.  Been playing Elite:Dangerous since Beta and dipping in and out of Star Citizen testing with some friends for a few years as reference. Pros:
- Immersive gameplay
- Addictive gameplay (just one more planet discovery...)
- Relatively seamless transitions between planets and space
- Base building click-to-block is easy and intuitive
- Nice looking vistas.
- Nice simple storyline to follow.
Cons:
- UI is a very poor port from console to PC. Click and hold action on primary button is incredibly annoying.  Poor ability to remap keys in options menu. No native ability to remap gamepad right joystick (head look) with kb/m or some Exocraft functions.

- No head tracking support at all.  Can make some USB options sort of work but it's not worth it.
