I didn't preorder NMS, because preordering a game has no benefits. You can see what happens when people preorder games in the countless amount of useless and toxic reviews here on steam.
Having played NMS for around 40h, I can say that there is a game in there, but it feels shallow and too much of a grind to me.
In a nutshell, you fly around the procedural generated universe, cataloging flora and fauna for a credit reward on completion of a planet. This seems pointless after a while to me, because once you've seen all the different types of planets, you've seen them all.
Pick a planet and make it it your home base is quite fun, but that goes out the window, once you realize that all you do is gathering resources, which at the beginning, is quite tedious in itself.
After 40h I'm now at a point where credits aren't an issue anymore and my progress is only blocked by time (waiting for resources to be ready to be collected from my farm and mining units). I don't see the point of continuing playing the game. I beat it, so to speak.
The fun here is to overcome the challenges. Built a base, create a source of income, find the largest ship. Problem is, there's nothing to do with it really. And that's my main issue with the game. There is a promise here that all the exploring and grinding for resources will pay off, but it never does, because at the point of the game where you're "rich" the game has peaked already. I realized this roughly after my 40h with the game and felt mislead.
Atmosphere is great and controls feel solid to me. Performance and stability are a mess.
Can't recommend this for $60. Game stays quite behind its potential.

First of all, like most others I was quite disappointed by the initial launch and decided not to buy the game at all back then. After the 1.2 update came out, the game seemed more likely to match my expectations but the asking price still seemed too high. During the summer sale I picked it up for around $20, and having played it around 160 hours I must say I'm quite happy with it and that price seems fair.
Sometimes NMS feels a bit like a blend of Elite, Spore and Subnautica, if you can imagine such a thing.
Mind, this is not Star Citizen or Elite Dangerous. It is nowhere near as deep, and the gameplay has been brutally dumbed down to suit console players. The flight mechanics in particular can be painful as the terrain avoidance and "assisted" speed and attitude control makes precision flying and landing all but impossible. The HUD pitch ladder doesn't even come close to a proper readout. There are also some inexplicable UI limitations like the fact that items cannot be tranferred directly between your exosuit (=backback) and your exocraft (=rover) but must go via the starship cargo hold. Items can be transferred TO your starship from anywhere, but to transfer FROM your starship it must be in close proximity. These are just the most obvious ones.
This comes on top of a fair number of bugs, like randomly getting ejected several hundred meters out of your exocraft when simply trying to get out, the "pulse drive" autopilot occasionally going haywire, or the base construction tool randomly getting stuck in color/material mode forcing a restart of the game. I guess desperately adding new features that should have been in the game at launch must have given the QA dept a bit of a backlog.
The resources in the game are worth an entire article, suffice to say that some strange design decisions have been made.  As an example, the production of glass would in most games require some form of sand. In NMS you need to find a world with oceans and free dive for an ultra rare plant that can only be spotted during the night to pluck its "fruit". Uranium, on the other hand, can be found in the form of red crystals standing 1 meter tall just about anywhere you go. This means you will be flying thousands of light years and spend several hours in order to produce a single pane of glass, while fueling your starship can literally be done with your bare hands.
Some may find the actual exploration to be a bit tedious and repetitive, in which case a game firmly about exploration clearly isn't for you and you should go look for something else. So, after all this, how can I still recommend this game? Personally, I find the gameplay to be forgiving, relaxing and fun, even addictive. If you care for lore, there's a nicely written story line waiting for you to follow, but there's absolutely no pressure and you can do so at your own leisure.

Trine is the simple fairy tale of a knight, a thief, and a wizard that are bound together by a shared, but selfish, purpose that spirals in a classic battle against evil to save the world. Just like most fairy tales, it's light on character motivation and heavy on heroic deeds. And that focus serves it. Whether it's crouching behind a shield to advance through a jet of fire, flinging a grappling hook into a support beam above to swing across a pit, or levitating a huge stone fist to drop on an offending skeleton, it's all so satisfying and it flows so well. Every puzzle is integrated seamlessly as an obstacle blocking the way to the next part of the three's quest, an obstacle that can be dealt with in any variety of ways. The thief might be able to easily swing to the next platform, but the wizard might just as easily be able to pull that platform into his jumping range and the knight might be able to break through the debris that made the jump difficult in the first place. It's this interchangeability of usefulness but specialization of means that makes the consequences of failure so enjoyable. If a character dies that character can be brought back at the next checkpoint, but until then a set of tools has dropped off your belt and you're forced to overcome any obstacles on the way without them. It's never impossible to proceed, but in the absence of a preferred strategy, you're forced change your approach, forcing you to look at those puzzles and characters left in a different light. Sure, with flawless execution you can blaze through the entire game on a single set of tactics. It's only when you don't stick that landing or dodge that attack that this short, simple game really gets to show how well it's designed. And that's when you want a game to shine. Things can be beautiful and interesting when you're frolicking along, but when you're repeatedly falling on your face, that's when you appreciate clever, polished design.

When the game is on sale, say below $25.00, it's worth a buy.
Think of this game as a 'casual exploration, shipping building game'. Some other games that I own that fall into this category are Salt and Worlds Adrift (closed beta).
If you're looking for action as in space battles or on-planet battles, NMS has that, but it is not its strong suit.
My suggestion is that you take your time, there's no need to head toward the center of the galaxy. You can have fun patiently exploring one system at a time.
I have played about 50 hours, and I see myself playing for about another 50 hours before I might get bored. I still have yet to build a base. So for about $25, the game delivers at least 100 hours of entertainment.
Positive things about the game:
1) Ever wanted to explore a galaxy full of stars and planets? Well here's a good attempt at doing that.
2) Many landscapes are beautiful and relaxing to explore.
3) You get bragging rights to be the first player to visit a star system by naming that system and its planets most any you want, I think. I name star systems after real people.
4) No PVP. The fact that no one can grief you is an absolute positive about this game. You can relax while exploring.
Negative things about the game:
1) You are not the first to discover anything in this game. There are three races of beings plus some mysterious entity that knows all about these worlds.
2) The choice of colors can be too much. I think it has to do with color saturation. It can make the worlds feel comic-book/cartoonish and sometimes be hard on the eyes.
3) All of the worlds that I have visited in NMS have life.  As a result, you're not going to have the " I discovered life ! " experience that you might have had if this game reflected the rarity of life in our actual universe. Life is too common in the NMS universe.

i avoided NMS for a year due to the colossal amount of negative user reviews, as a passive follower of the game, I didnt have a set amount of expectations going in about what features were omitted, and what the game was lacking.
this game to me is a textbook example to ignore user reviews when they go viral in one direction or another.
i am 10 hours+ in, and this game is everything I want out of a game at present, primarily escapism.
the soundtrack is fantastic, the graphics vivid and ambitious, this game is veering into work of art.
if you do not go into this game with any notion of what you want out of it, you might find that what it offers is something entirely unique.
i picked it up on sale, but i wouldnt have felt ripped off had i paid full price,
It might have fallen short of expectations set in promotional things, but as spectacle, as how it makes me feel when playing it, its right there with the best "games" ive ever played.

I was uncertain as whether to buy this game or buy into the common consensus that No Man's Sky was basically a flaming pile of liquid horse♥♥♥♥♥♥  In the end, I dropped $24 on this during the Summer sale and after almost 36 hours of play accumulated over about 6 days, I can whole-heartedly say that this game was worth every cent.  While this game offers the same challenges over and over again, you are forced to find resources in different places and keep exploring systems and planets for your hidden solutions and extra help from the 3 types of aliens.  While planets can feel similar to others, I never found 2 planets that felt like too much of the same.  Every landing feels like a new beginning and every warp feels like a massive amount of progress is being made, even if the distance covered compared to the size of the galaxy is basically 0.  Secrets are everywhere and there are multiple ways to approach your multiple problems, making No Man's Sky feel like an actual adventure and a satisfying escape from a reality lived on one single planet.  The flaws that come with this game are minor, excluding the ungodly stain of space combat, so this game is worth your while in all areas except for the void.  If you're into science fiction and exploration and can get it at a discount, then purchase this game immediately, you're likely to enjoy it.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the series at its Finest Hour.
Back in 2007, it was a big year for video games, on PC we got Orange Box, Crysis, Bioshock,etc, console players had Halo 3, AC and Mass Effect, even among those big titles, Call of Duty 4 stood out. Its predecessors, namely Call of Duty and CoD2, were already highly successful, but CoD4 was simply beyond most gamers' expectation. I still remember playing this on my roommate's PC and got totally blown away by the "One shot, one kill" mission.
Singleplayer Story: 9/10
The story is straight forward, it is not a role-playing game where you made choices, or a Hollywood movie with lots of twists, you simply move with your squad, and shoot bad guys. However, the developer still manages to put the action pieces together with a nice story, it is not perfect, but can still give you the good old "Saving Private Ryan" feeling (like it was in MOHAA). In comparsion, MW2's story tries to give you "WOW" moments, like a Michael Bay movie with lots of cool actions, but fails to deliver the glorious feel.
Presentation: 9.5/10
The presentation is top notch in 2007, some moments are still amazing to this day, like the mission "All Ghillied Up" is an instant classic, where you crawled through emeny fields in a ghillied suit, with heavy tanks and patrols moving by, it is one of the most thrilling experiences in FPS history. The graphics are surely out-dated, but they aged elegantly. The gun models, animations and battlefield atomsphere are impeccable even in today's standards, which create great immersion. The pacing of shooting scene/intermission is perfect. There are also lots of explosions, but none feels out of place.
Music: 9/10
The in-game music composed by Harry Gregson-Williams suits the pace and atomsphere perfectly, whether it is the middle-eastern showdown, or the desolate pripyat city, or the ICBM lauch field, the music always bring the scene to life. It may not surpass the later MW2's music by Hans Zimmer Team, but still excellent game soundtrack.
Multiplayer: 9.5/10
The MP mechanics was a revolution back in 2007, very fun and addictive even to this day. Most MP maps (aside from a few tiny maps) are well crafted to hold as much as 40-50 players, while still very fun to play with low player counts(8-16), also keep in mind that In later CoD (MW2 above) the player count is capped at 18, which, in my opinion, completely lost the epic battlefield feeling. This game also came before the crappy IWNet ever existed thus supports dedicated server, you can easily find a populated server with playable ping, without the worries about host-migration or host abuse, etc.
The weapons are balanced and diversified, not only feel great but actually have recoil(unlike those "laser guns" in later CoDs). The good old 3-5-7 killstreaks are simple and effective, as well as satisfying, you won't get ridiculous powerful killstreak (like nuke or AC-130 in later CoDs) but the result is still very rewarding.
End of the line
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the prime CoD experience on PC. With so many blockbuster shooters flooding the market today, you may want to pay this old game a revisit, and see what we gamers have missed all those past years.
Edit: My steam profile suggests less than 1 hour CoD4 gameplay, which is not true. My in-game stats shows I played online for more than 500 hrs, coupled with another 300-400 hrs spent playing on mods, my total play time is nearly 1000 hrs. The reason is that I used Steam key on a retail copy to avoid Steam overlay/Punkbuster incompabilites. If you don't mind losing steam overlay, I suggest you do the same, the online gameplay will be much smoother.

Doomsday is a much needed sequel to the original Deponia Trilogy. The original ending was ok, not great. This adds a lot to it, and on many levels.
This game is animated, voiced and scored extremely well, I find. There are a wide range of locations in this game, each with an organic feel and things to do that makes the environment fun to explore. This, in addition to puzzles that make sense [unlike some in the roiginal series], makes the game great to play. This game also adds a lot of new characters, as well as fleshing out old ones, which does a good job of making the universe in this game more real, and more involving.
The game itself seems pretty huge considering the large number of areas there are to explore, but without the "acts" separating things up, it may seem a bit overwhelming, so you may need to pace yourself in order to fully understand whats going on.
Definitely worth playing if you're a fan of the series, and want a proper conclusion. If you haven't played the previous ones, then there's no point in playing this one. It's not a very good jumping-on point.

Had high expectations when I originally heard about this game, but it really does not live up to them at all. After a little over an hour of gameplay, the game hasn't shown any fun or intelligent design. It tends to be a pattern of:
1) Wander around an area where there's not a lot to do other than progress forward. Sometimes you can find hidden stuff.
2) Traverse obstacles (such as walls and things) by climbing in a very slow and boring manner by picking a direction and hitting "A"
3) Fight a small skirmish of bland enemies in a very obvious arena environment by using a couple buttons and pre-configured combo moves, eventually taking them down. The core combat loop feels awful to execute, and really "dumb." It's not really worth going into much detail about the "pressen" combo system. Managing the combos is very clunky and limiting.
4) Repeat. Expect cut-scenes to be peppered in anywhere between these sections. There seems to be quite a lot of useless little snippets from time to time.
I got to a spot where I could see the main feature of the game, memory remixing. It was essentially like a video I could rewind/forward through, and look for hot-spots. I could activate these spots, then allow the sequence to play out in a different way, based on what I altered. Altering the wrong things, or not enough things will cause an undesired outcome, causing you to fail and have to rewind and make changes again until you get it right. Seems like a good idea, but a bit tedious as you have to watch the same sequence over and over again. It's supposed to make you feel like a detective or something like that, but in reality it just ends up being trial and error.
The game is visually not that great... the screenshots seem to make it look better than it does in motion. Texture quality leaves a bit to be desired, but is probably due to it being a console port. Animations are jerky and awkward. There doesn't seem to be much atmosphere in the environments that livens things up, but the environments seem moderately detailed--although nothing memorable or impressive (at least in the early stages of the game.) It seems to not run as smoothly as I'd expect, either... it runs fine, just seemed hitchy or laggy.
Interesting premise, but poorly executed. It's pretty much "on-rails", and should have probably been a movie instead rather than a sloppy in-and-out of gameplay experience. If you were interested in the combat, you'd be better off with a game like DmC: Devil May Cry. The other elements of this game are done better in pretty much any other game. I don't really have the desire to play any more of this. Tons of great reviews on meta-critic, but they must have been paid-off or something... unless the story is simply that great or the gameplay changes half-way through the game.

Looks like there's a sale going on for Remember Me right now. I just played it, and while I wouldn't recommend it for full price, I think it's definitely worth the $10 it's on sale for right now (and maybe even a bit more than that). The game is damn pretty, and the story and gameplay are pretty good considering it's a CAPCOM game. The atmosphere reminded me a bit of Omega from the Mass Effect series, and it's the same graphics engine (Unreal) which probably lended to that reminiscince. There's a unique mechanic in the game regarding altering other people's memories that's worth checking out, if nothing else. I wish it got used more, because it was fun to mess around with. Oh, and I really enjoyed the way the game used cutscenes -- they were frequent but short, and they were blended so well with the gameplay that a few of the first times a cutscene ended, I didn't even realize until I got murdered or punched in the face or something. (I guess you could look at that as a bad thing, too. :P)
Major drawback: the game is pretty short. It took me ~15 hours to play through on Normal, and I always take my time with games with any kind of collection/exploration element to them, so it would probably take a normal person closer to ~11. I guess this means the story is tighter than it might have otherwise been, though? No time for fluff or meaningless sidequests.

Great art both in fidelity and style help set this games grim dystopian cyberpunk mood for this good platform jumper, puzzle solving brawler. Platform jumping is more akin to the Prince of Persia and Tomb Raider games than it is to Assassin's Creed, meaning things are more fickle, less forgiving and not at all open-world. Comber is pretty much completely melee and flows much like the recent Batman games, but with a rather nice combo customization system to give it some spice. The games memory hacking elements end up being used only in a rather small number of cases, with the game focusing more on the stealing of memories to aid in security by-passing intrusion. Most of the character's special powers end up being much more like uber-hacking of things like doors and other machinery to add puzzles for the platform jumping aspects and as special combat powers that become nearly necessary to be victorious in various battles along the way.
Mouse support is not very good, so access to a gamepad controller is advised, and since there is no gunplay to worry about, no loss of aiming will be noticed.
As I had read that the English voice actors were not as good as the French, I played through with French audio and English subtitles and felt the experience to have been rather good.

This is probably one of the games I've been the most emotionally invested in since Ori and the blind forest. This game seemed shallow at first and I didn't understand the hype. I loved the concept of the voices in her head and the disturbing nature of the game itself but other than that I didn't really enjoy it. Oh boy was I wrong. I will not spoil any story elements in the game other than naming a few of the gods featured in the game to help with certain points I make.
You are a celtic woman who suffers from psychosis, you travel throughout a hellish world solving puzzles consisting of finding hidden runes in the area with a mix of combat during these areas too. The combat is a typical hack and slash style with evade, light attacks, heavy attacks and so on, standard for games of that genre. The combat however is not overdone in the game I feel as if the game was all combat it would get boring, the game has a very very good  balance between communicating story through voices and the world around you, exploration, puzzles and the combat.
The game has pretty well designed bosses too sprinkled throughout the game, they are not easy but not too hard you get stuck on them for hours. Speaking of hours the game is roughly around 6-8 hours long at least for most players.
I feel the story here is the main attribute people buy this game, due to this not many people are going to purchase this for the puzzles or combat, through your playthrough you'll find the story is excellent and it communicates it very nicely without just flooding you with so much information that its too much to take in at once. You get drip fed all the informaton you need throughout the games duration and it all flows very nicely.
When playing the game I urge you not to look at any gameplay of the game or read any spoilers including puzzle solutions.The game is best played blind, this applies to most games but this game relies so heavily on story that it applies to this game far more than most. That being said I made the mistake of starting with Valravn instead of Surt which is the main reason I didn't enjoy the beginning as much as the rest of the game. I found the puzzles for Valravn the hardest puzzles in the game due to the fact that I was still learning how to solve and find the clues and such for the "find the hidden rune" puzzles that persist through out the game. Therefore I recommend starting with the Surt path when given the option to. After I learned more about the surprisingly deep combat system and clues to help find the runes easier I found myself enjoying the game far far more.
When looking for the runes there are certain indicators that help you locate them without just directly showing you the rune itself. When you are in the general area of the rune you will see symbols all around you telling you said specific rune is nearby. This may be obvious for most people, I don't know ofcourse, but it took me a while to find this out so I got stuck on some of the early puzzles for some time.
The combat system has many hidden features you may not realise from looking at the controls. Senua has a tablet of sorts on her hip which will have a glowing ring around the border which slowly fills up, when this fills all the way you get one of three stacks which you can see on the tablet. You consume these by focusing during a fight and this will slow down time and let you get significantly more hits in. This is shown to you later however if you go down the Valravn path first you wont find this out until an hour or two into the game. Other than that all of the attacks you can do have combos if you use them in certain orders which is generally standard for a fighting game. You can combine all these attacks with the run button to also get different outcomes too.
I find it very hard to critique this game, its done so excellently however that does not mean its perfect. I found that the game giving the choice between two paths at the beginning is good to make it feel like your decisions actually matter however the difficulty of this beginning section is all over the place, due to both of these being available so early on most players don't understand fully how to play the game so naturally the beginning of these sections teach you new things and then ramp up the difficulty as you get closer to the end of the section, however after completing one of the two sections you move onto the other section and are then greeted by the tutorial-ish area again which is easy and gets more hard as it goes. I feel if the path was more linear say you had to do one path and then had to do the other one it would all flow a little better. This doesn't mean the game shouldn't have decisions like this I just don't feel they should be placed so early on, more decisions after the player gets through the basics would work. This is just a minor thing though I don't feel this took away from the experience heavily and I still thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrafice is a fantastically in depth game which gets even better as it goes on. Senua herself is a very lovable character you will most likely get emmotionally attatched to as you learn more and more about her. The combat has more to it than you would imagine from its simplistic nature and the puzzles whilst sometimes too hard and sometimes too easy are very fun and rewarding to complete. Hellblade is a must buy especially at the price they are marketing it at.
What an experience, what a piece of art.

This game falls in to a very small category of games that'll stick with me long after they're over. Games like Spec Ops: The Line and SOMA and now Hellblade. The story of Senua is one of mental anguish and tells the journey of a young Celtic woman who is plague by psychosis and who is on a vision quest to save the one she loves. It is a haunting, personal tragedy that is expertly told and realized in one of the most beautiful games I've played in quite some time.
A lot of people are complaining about the combat being too simplistic and while I agree that it is a simplistic system compared to Ninja Theory's past games it serves this one just fine. This is not a game that puts combat first and I'm glad it doesn't: the story deserves center stage. For people who enjoy narratives that deal with complex issues and are told in a very mature, non-sterotypical fashion then I very much reccommend Hellblade.

What I would like to see from the developers are independent graphic options for various effects. Such as motion blur, AA, film grain, and an FOV slider. The only way I got through playing it at 4K was to edit ini files to reduce those effects and increase the FOV. Even so it would get as low as 30 fps and as high as 45 fps in most areas usually at the low side of that. There was, however, a specific "Shards" area that dropped me down to 25 fps and as low as 15 fps in some instances.
I'm aware some are of the opinion that we should play an atmospheric game with the settings the developers intended to get the desired message and feel. I would mostly agree but maybe stick with my opinion of AA removal for performance and motion blur reduction for visual comfort.

The current latest of the Marvel VS. Capcom fighting game series has finally landed on the PC with all the trimmings. If you're not familiar with the game series, get out from under that rock already (unless you're the type not into fighting games).
If you are and actually like the insanity of the Capcom-made game franchise, then this game will deliver rightly, just like the version released previously on the PS3 and Xbox 360 (unless you abhor how this variant plays compared to the way older games in the franchise).
From technical standpoint on my rig... (CPU FX 8350, GPU Nvidia GTX 980Ti, 16GB RAM), things ran like butter with no hiccups, and load times feel even quicker compared to console (which is already quick enough). Graphics are the same, though this time for the problematic stages that may have induced some slowdown, there isn't to be had here.
Control-wise, I used my Hori Fighting Commander pad with the PC function turned on, and it recognized it as a 360 controller just fine. Some people in the reviews may have some issues with this. If you're one of such, either try a workaround or bug Capcom enough for them to fix it. Otherwise everything responded about the same as the console version.
Everything's unlocked, just like the store description said (though as of now, I have yet to see if they even bothered with giving Magneto his alt costume back yet) and everything feels about the same overall, with added bonus of having all sorts of resolution settings for whatever screen you're gaming on (my current one is 2560x1440). Framerate is locked, but since it's a frame-dependent fighting game, there's no need to exceed the default 60FPS.
I recommend, but only if you know what're you're getting into beforehand. This also seems like prep-work in a way for the upcoming Marvel vs Capcom Infinite...

Despite the bad start, this game has taken shape, just watch the videos the devs have put up. I have only spent 6 hours playing this game and found I could not put it down. You start off in the main game trying to repair your damaged crashed space ship. You have to find all the elements to get it off into space. What was fun for me was trying to find all the elements, accidently using some zinc to upgrade some of my equipment and that forcing me to find more. I also used this other element I needed to fix my engines. The upgrades are a must and help a great deal. The other fun part was I was on a hot planet and my suit would only keep a shield so long, so I had to either run back to get into my ship to refresh it, or find elements on the planet that I could use to recharge it. This can be a challenging game, but super fun, and when you take off from the planet you feel satisfied at repairing your ship. There will be space combat, but I have not run into it as I just got space worthy. I would get this game in a sale, just because I am cheap.

Review for Trine Enchanted Edition and Trine 2: The Complete Story. read the full review @
:D
— Characters are fleshed out in a very light way. You get a quick background on their reasons to do whatever they are/want to do and that’s it. While this could be a negative point, you don’t really need to know more than what is told to you, and from then on the plot develops over the course of the game and through their dialogue, which is pretty nice. You get just the right amount of information to be able to enjoy the characters and their misadventures.
— Characters are rather overpowered in the first game, thanks to the inventory system, allowing you to equip up to 9 artefacts to each character, improving stats or giving them health boosts (or outright giving them a second life). There is also the fact that each character has 3 ranks on their spells, and Amadeus in particular can summon more than twice the number of objects in the first game when compared to the second, including floating platforms which make it easy to bypass obstacles or reach difficult places. In the second game you have to use several skills from the three characters in combination to achieve the same results, making it more enjoyable.
— Oh my god, the visuals. Every plant, leaf, statue, EVERYTHING looks absolutely wonderful. And don’t even get me started on some of the bosses or goblins in the second game. I don’t think I ever took as many screenshots per minute as I did in the Trine games. Back when these games came out in 2009 and 2011 respectively, playing on Extreme settings with a good framerate required a pretty solid rig. But seeing as my four year old GTX670 can keep it capped pretty much all of the time, it’s not a stretch anymore.
— Occasional oddity in character physics, game has its quirks.
— Amadeus is kind of useless in boss fights. He's a wizard that can summon boxes and move objects, meaning his offensive skills are non-existent.
— Having to make movements with the cursor to summon different objects can be a headache and make the game unnecessarily hard on higher difficulties. It would have been easier to just press a specific button for each object (there are only 3 different objects anyways, 2 in the second game). Making said movements with a controller using the analog stick takes even longer than with a mouse and might get annoying after a while. In addition, the speed at which you can levitate certain objects (due to their weight) is painfully slow.
— Everything is intuitive and makes sense, puzzles are relatively easy to solve by using simple logic or by just paying attention to your surroundings. Obviously, you'll have to solve them faster on harder difficulties if you don’t want to get killed. It certainly wouldn't have hurt to have harder puzzles, though that would probably have made certain achievements close to impossible, such as completing levels using only one single character.
— Voice acting is wonderful, for some reason I can’t put my finger on. Characters seem genuinely friendly and trustful towards each other, except for the first couple of levels in the first game. Characters (especially Amadeus) have a lot of emotion behind them so it’s easy for the player to empathize with them, and all dialogue sounds natural and flows well. The narrator is nice too.
— Music is very fitting and relaxing. Goes with the beautiful art and keeps you calm and focused.
Conclusion: relaxing and fun gameplay, nice music, friendly characters and astounding visuals. If you want a nice co-op experience, go for it. If you want a good single-player experience, go for it too. Especially if you like platformers, puzzles, fantasy games and beautiful scenery.

Trine: 11 Hours played, 33 / 33 Achievements (100%)
Trine 2: 55 Hours played, 97 / 97 Achievements (100%)

This game falls in to a very small category of games that'll stick with me long after they're over. Games like Spec Ops: The Line and SOMA and now Hellblade. The story of Senua is one of mental anguish and tells the journey of a young Celtic woman who is plague by psychosis and who is on a vision quest to save the one she loves. It is a haunting, personal tragedy that is expertly told and realized in one of the most beautiful games I've played in quite some time.
A lot of people are complaining about the combat being too simplistic and while I agree that it is a simplistic system compared to Ninja Theory's past games it serves this one just fine. This is not a game that puts combat first and I'm glad it doesn't: the story deserves center stage. For people who enjoy narratives that deal with complex issues and are told in a very mature, non-sterotypical fashion then I very much reccommend Hellblade.

What I would like to see from the developers are independent graphic options for various effects. Such as motion blur, AA, film grain, and an FOV slider. The only way I got through playing it at 4K was to edit ini files to reduce those effects and increase the FOV. Even so it would get as low as 30 fps and as high as 45 fps in most areas usually at the low side of that. There was, however, a specific "Shards" area that dropped me down to 25 fps and as low as 15 fps in some instances.
I'm aware some are of the opinion that we should play an atmospheric game with the settings the developers intended to get the desired message and feel. I would mostly agree but maybe stick with my opinion of AA removal for performance and motion blur reduction for visual comfort.

Trine is a side scroll platform game with heavy puzzle elements that takes place in a medieval fairytale fantasy world. You control three characters, each with different abilitities, skills and weapons and your goal is basically to reach the end of each level by solving the enviromental puzzles with at least of your characters alive . In order to solve the puzzles and overcome the various obstacles that you will be facing, you have to combine your characters' different abilitites effectively.
The story follows a wizard, a knight and a thief that have been trapped by a magic artifact and have lost their descrete physical appearance. From now on, they can only coexist in one body each time but you can switch between them at any given moment. So they set on a journey to find information on how to break the spell and at the same time to free their kingdom from the evil dark powers that attacked it when the King died.
The presentation is nothing less than top notch, The visuals are stunning, the last time I was this impressed with graphics was back in 2004 with Far Cry and a few years later with Crysis. From the art direction, the fluid motion of the characters and the backround theme of each level to the narration and the excellent soundtrack, everything is combined in harmony to produce this visual masterpiece.
However, there are a few aspects that are on the dowside. I wouldn't say that the story is on the thin side, but I would prefer it if it was narrated a bit more seriously. By that I mean that the characters are given almost a comical tone which doesn't fit well with the overall theme of the story. As for the difficulty of the game, I found it extremely easy even on the hard level which was a surprise since this is a platformer. The puzzles were quite easy as well. The length of the game is also disputed by many, however I think it is fine, this way each level is memorable and distinguishable. If the game was bigger there would be a lot of unnecessary repetition for no reason, especially considering the short range of the gameplay diversity.
All in all, Trine is a beautiful game with unforgettable art style and smooth mechanics that despite its' short lenght, it will travel you to a world of magic and beauty for a few hours. I can't wait to get my hands on Trine 2.

Despite the bad start, this game has taken shape, just watch the videos the devs have put up. I have only spent 6 hours playing this game and found I could not put it down. You start off in the main game trying to repair your damaged crashed space ship. You have to find all the elements to get it off into space. What was fun for me was trying to find all the elements, accidently using some zinc to upgrade some of my equipment and that forcing me to find more. I also used this other element I needed to fix my engines. The upgrades are a must and help a great deal. The other fun part was I was on a hot planet and my suit would only keep a shield so long, so I had to either run back to get into my ship to refresh it, or find elements on the planet that I could use to recharge it. This can be a challenging game, but super fun, and when you take off from the planet you feel satisfied at repairing your ship. What is really cool is taking off from the planet and seeing space come into view and watching the planet get smaller as you fly away. I docked with an alien freighter who wanted to sell me his ship for more units that I had, which was 0. For those that say this is a relaxing game, I can see the point, but there is some excitement the devs have added, there are attack drones, and also some of the plants will attack you as well. There will be space combat, but I have not run into it as I just got space worthy. I would get this game in a sale, just because I am cheap.

*** English Review - Versão em português no fim
Despite the exaggerated and out of control hype at launch time, I always believed in the technical potential of No Man's Sky. There is a lot of controversy involved when we talk about incorrect or even misleading information from Hello Games before launching the game, and there was a tremendous whirlwind of criticism when high expectations were not met.
Although I liked the product proposal, even at the troubled launch, I still did not see any reason to buy it. It was, as its creators said, a beautiful canvas full of possibilities. But it was not "there" yet.
Today, after two massive updates, the commitment of HG in improving his product is pretty visible. The community also matured a lot in the period, and began to rediscover the positive aspects of NMS. So, after a long wait, I decided to invest and test the game.
In its current state, with the addition of new game modes and several new mechanics, No Man Sky is a lot of fun if you're looking for EXPLORATION, COLLECTION OF RESOURCES and a RELAXING EXPERIENCE. Do not come looking for an infinite procedural MMORPG. You will be disappointed. This is not the purpose of the game, and perhaps that is what many critics expected at the time of launch. Hence the widespread disappointment.
New updates are expected regularly. By the time I write this review, a massive "ARG" creates a new, healthy hype around an upcoming update, probably in August. Following this alternative reality game is a lot of fun by itself :)
Anyway, manage your expectations, and have fun with an unique game with vast potential. But don’t worry about the future. If you like the three pillars I´ve quoted up there, NMS is already on a very good point. And, as it seems, it only tends to improve.
********************************************************************************************************************************
A despeito do hype exagerado e fora de controle na época do lançamento, eu sempre acreditei no potencial técnico de No Man Sky. Apesar de ter gostado da proposta do produto, mesmo no lançamento conturbado, eu ainda não via razões para comprá-lo. Era, como disseram seus criadores, uma belíssima tela cheia de possibilidades. Mas não estava "lá" ainda.

Em seu estado atual, com a adição de novos modos de jogo e várias mecânicas novas, No Man Sky é bastante divertido, se você procura EXPLORAÇÃO, COLETA DE RECURSOS e uma EXPERIÊNCIA RELAXANTE. There are many games that I love and some that I hate but never before I have played a game that made me love it and hate it at the same time. Remember Me is that game.
Before we get to that some background is required. I finished it on easy and on hard difficulty, found every collectible, and did every achievement. I have spent 22 hours with it - yes, it's that short a game.
Why do I hate it, you ask?
I hate it for the promise of being something greater than what it is. I hate it for the linear design and poor controls. I hate it for being told what to do and not being allowed to find it for myself. This game holds your hand from beginning to end. There is a lot of collectibles to be found but they are easy to find. They grant you more health or power or unlock artwork but do not give you any additional information about the world. There is a lot of climbing and a lot of fighting, and some more climbing and some more fighting. Fighting is competent but pales in comparison to Batman Arkham Asylum. The climbing is boring. Don’t get me wrong, I love climbing in games, but it has to give you the illusion of choice and discovery like in Prince of Persia or Assassin’s Creed. Here you have only one route that is always obvious. The camera is lazy and stiff and does not help you at all. There is no puzzle, there is no discovery. Every ledge that you can grab is highlighted for you. You just climb and run and open doors to get to another fight.
That's not a good recommendation is it? Well, I do recommend this game for the things that I love about it, which outweigh anything that I hate about it. And what is that, you ask?
I love it for the story: this is one of the best sci-fi stories I have read, watched or played in my life. It's up there with Blade Runner, Ubik, Neuromancer, and Ghost in the Shell. It's philosophical, emotional, mature and a little too pompous for its own good. The dialogues can be a little too poetic and dramatic at times, but they still fit the story. I won’t give any spoilers, because the story is the true worth of this game.
I love it for the music: this is a journey in itself, the music defies description. You just have to listen to it, especially how it changes during the fight.
I love it for the graphics because the actual graphics deliver what is promised to us by the concept artists so many times and rarely delivered. We often see the beautiful concept art for games that we love and we hope they could look like the artist imagined, but we know that the technology is not there yet. In this case the programmers delivered. Using the Unreal 3 engine and DirectX 9.0 the programmers from DONTNOD show a vision of New Paris that will stay in your memory forever.
And finally I love it for the ability to remix memories of other characters. It is such a powerful game mechanic it is a pity it was implemented so poorly. The game allows you to remix a crucial memory of four characters in the game but there is only one right solution. It is such a wasted opportunity for branching story. It would be fun to replay the game just to see how the story would unfold if the memory of a character was remixed differently. Well, maybe another time, eh?
So should you play this game, you ask?
YES, play it for the story and the sensual feast that it is! It's a unique experience that you will Remember for a long time.

Overall a really good and enjoyable game, if you look at the discussions you see a lolt of talk about some SJW/propaganda and whatever triggers people but just ignore it. This game is just what you could expect after Wolfenstein TNO, just kill some nazis as a polish jew.
Pros:
-If you get it to run it runs better as TNO.
-Good story continuation on TNO. Really liked some of the brutal scenes and the cinematics were on point. Side characters were good enough and not obnoxious or annoying as hell. Some nice plot twists too and there is a small easter egg in Wyatt's room if you interact with the music player.
-Improved combat
-Voice acting si what you'd expect, no wonky french people with an italian accent trying to speak german. Voice acting sounds good and on point.
-No RPG crafting elements were you have to grind an hour to upgrade your weapon or get materials from everywhere. Just get an upgrade kit and upgrade your weapon.

Cons:
-Some enemies feel weak on the " Medium" difficulty(Bring 'Em On), just an example if I get the armor piercing upgrade on the Sturmgewehr pretty much all enemies become a cakewalk and if you got a god trigger finger the scope will make it even easier. You can kill the armored enemies with the heavy weapons really easy(don't know about other difficulties yet)Enemies felt stronger in TNO. The armored enemies felt scary where as now I jsut stand in their face and shoot a few times. -Some weapons are redundant at Bring 'Em On, the only 2 weapons I really used are the Sturmgewehr and the Pistole. The other weapons felt weak or useless. The pistole was much better as the machinepistole(in my opinion then), the sturmgewehr had the same damage output as the shotgun but longer range, you got the Kampfpistole(Grenade/rocket pistol) way too late in the game to really make any use of it in the main story.

Deponia Doomsday doesn't *exactly* carry on where the original Deponia trilogy left off, but it does use some relatively creatively ways to give us the opportunity to revisit the world and characters that people loved. It's a solid point and click adventure with a somewhat convoluted story, decent puzzles and interesting (if ridiculous) characters.
- Great length for a point and click
- Puzzles zany enough for this type of game but not insanely hard
- Beautifully drawn world
- Mildly amusing (not laugh out loud funny)
- Decent voice acting
- Some of the minigames were a bit tricky (however, you can skip them)
- Story gets a little convoluted at times
- Very little to interact with (usually only a couple of things per screen)
It's worth commenting on the ending as some fans of the original series clearly did not like it - however, I thought in light of the first games that it was a fitting end. It gave me the feels, anyway. The ending is certainly not rushed and is dealt with with care and attention.
If you have played through the original trilogy I would highly recommend picking this up. And if you haven't played the original games - buy them immediately (enjoy!).

I played all the Deponia games and I really like them but this one is by far the weakest of them.
Many puzzles are totally constructed. Items are placed not because it would be natural for this item to be in that location but only to allow to have a presumably funny puzzle. The problem is that this leads to many puzzles where you have simply no idea why you are doing things until you find the starting point and things make sense. Also there are many situations where you cannot continue with a puzzle because something is missing although it is already clear what needs to be done. This also leads to situations where other items would totally work to solve a puzzle but instead you are expected to do something weird instead.
My biggest concern is also the whole time travelling plot. There are some neat situations with this so I do not want to be completely negative about this. But most of the time the whole time aspect is used in a very confusing way, for example when two solutions are obvious but you do not know which one belongs to the current time line and which you are expected to do. Also time travelling is not used for clever gameplay as it was in Day of the Tentacle but instead to construct a very confusing story which gets more confusing as you progress.
Towards the end I actually got really annoyed by it because the game fails to establish a clear story path that you are following and when you get used to one location you are sent to the next one. It is hard to really get into the game and you feel like being rushed through as much content as possible. A more laid back and focus progression would have been much better.
Many thanks to Daedalic for this game, it has many great moments but overall it is trying to hard.

The funny thing about the full version is that:
1. It changed drastically with no warning. Heck, it seems as if 99% of content they could've tested or atleast shown off in the early access was kept locked at TT Games HQ. If your going to change a game this drastically, and the game's in early access, then slowly add things as they're finished into the early access. If the game started changing gradually into its finished format through updates in early access, then I would probably be fine with it, but they decided to flip the game on it's head and shake the things that made it unique and more interesting to play than other LEGO games out of it's pockets, like how a bully shakes out the dinner money of a child's pockets.
2. It runs worse than in early access. I'm no stranger to having games run like a one legged dog on my computer, but if the game runs better incomplete, then you have either added so much stuff to the point where it weighs the game's performance down or you done goofed. The full version should be a less buggier and better running game, not the opposite.
I know licensed games aren't always fantastic, but unlike other LEGO games, this one was unique and different from those ones and it seemed as though it could be the most diverse LEGO game (gameplaywise) yet. Unfortunately, they thought that the one thing that made this seem like a true video game embodiment of LEGO wasn't needed. Freedom to create. Of all the games I've played that others thing had "lost potential", this is the only one that I agree with on that.

I originally got this game for PS4 during the midnight release August 2016 and I've thoroughly enjoyed every minute! Ever since I was a kid I was fascinated with science fiction and the concept of exploring other worlds. As I grew up I struggled to find open-world sandbox games that let me just explore outer space without being burdened/restricted by a rigid storyline. This game is exactly what I've been waiting for since I was a kid!
I started following the development of NMS years before it was released and I admit that not all the hype leading up to the release was completely justified. I'll also admit that this game isn't for everyone. If you're the kind of gamer that requires rigid missions and clearly defined goals in order to "win" a game, this game is not for you. On the other hand, if you want to use your imagination, create your own narrative and explore basically an inifite universe at your own leisure, this game is right up your alley.
After almost a year playing on PS4 I started following the Waking Titan ARG that Hello Games is currently running. I'm excited to see what kind of new features may be coming in future updates. Speaking of updates, that is something Hello Games has been doing an exceptional job with. The big updates (Foundation & Pathfinder) have been well thought-out and have improved the gameplay experience dramatically. While I'm very pleased with the game on PS4 I decided to give it a shot on PC as well, seeing how it's on sale in July. I'm very much looking forward to seeing what the future of No Man's Sky has in store!

I was one of the few people who never cared for the hype, nor expected this game to have multiplayer in any shape or form. So, to me No Man's Sky is out of this world, both literally and figuratively. However, it is not for everyone so I don't expect most gamers to really enjoy it as much as me. One of the key points that keep me captivated, as many have mentioned, is the soothing effect. And then there is the exploration part; discovering new worlds knowing you will never  run out of planets or galaxies to visit is a truly unique feature. While most games are scripted and put you into a restrictred space, here you are encouraged to come out of the 'box' and explore nearly unlimited space. It'd even go as far as call it a Universe Simulator.... Of course, the universe is not without faults, but I'm sure over time the game will be improved in the areas that it's lacking.
P.S. I played a lot of Battlezone 2 as a child and I can see a lot of similarities between these two.  Especially after PathFinder update. If you remember that one, you most likely will get some enjoyment out of No Man's sky.

This was quite possibly the best singleplayer experience i've had in a long time- absolutely loved Remember Me. Another big downside for me was the large amount of quicktime events, as in having to dodge/quickly run from something under the time limit, or when a boss is at it's critcal stage, you have to perform a quick time event using combos, but there is not much time allowed and no room for errors, leading you to having to try mulitple times if you make a mistake.
Other than that it was a very nice game to play, the combat is very cool and satisfying if you hit lots of combos (also the music interaction with combos is very nice). The story is very interesting and the soundtrack is simply brilliant.

Remember Me is the kind of game you'd expect a first-time developer that's not located in any kind of development hub to make. It's a science fiction auto-platformer (Uncharted, Enslaved, etc) brawler game. It's set in Neo-Paris; in the future, climate change refugees and income inequality lead to a European Civil War which ends with people using earthquake-bombs to destroy Paris.
Combat... so, uh, I don't like brawlers. Don't like God of War, don't like Ninja Gaiden, don't like Bayonetta, etc. This is where you yell at me because my taste is♥♥♥♥♥♥or something, rather than understanding that different people have different tastes. You can go into a screen and set each button in a given combo to have one of the following effects: heal me; cause bonus damage; speed up the cooldown of my special abilities; amplify the effect of the previous button. Typically I'd set up one combo to heal me, and another longer combo to do damage and run the cooldown. Overall the combat felt fairly fluid... I'd compare it to sort of high-level play of the Batman games. I think people who like brawlers would probably find it shallow because the execution is so easy and varies so little throughout the game, but that's fine by me.
What doesn't work is the late-game combat. The back 25% of the game, you pretty much entirely fight electrified super-buff enemies. Any method of attacking them hurts you. As a result, you either need to attack them with an endless number of heal-me combo attacks (because the healing cancels out the hurting) or power up your special moves and use those to take them out. This wouldn't be so bad, but at the end of the game when you clear out a combat arena, they send a second wave after you, and so you've depleted your special moves from the first wave. It gets pretty frustrating. The early game bosses are really cool, the late game bosses boil down to defeating tons of trash mobs and then periodically being able to injure the main bosses. The boss of Chapter 7 was a genuinely miserable experience, I died about 10 times or so.
Remixing is really cool. Basically, you hack into someone's memory. You watch the memory play out. At the end of the memory, you use the analogue stick to rewind (by circling the analogue stick, so it feels like you're editing video on tape, very cool control choice). At key points in the memory there are objects you can interact with. By altering the objects, you change the way the memory plays out. It's possible the result will be a memory bug--for example, changing someone's memory so that they die is not possible because how can you remember your own death?--or it's possible you'll lead to a desired alternate outcome. Then when you pop out of their memory, they might have a moment of clarity or conscience as their updated memory makes them reconsider their beliefs. Unfortunately you only get 3.5 of these sequences in the game and the plot never deals with how deeply disgusting it is to alter a character's memory to trick them into helping you; like, to give you an example, the first remix involves changing a woman's memory of accompanying her sick husband to hospital to a memory of the hospital killing her husband in front of her, this to get her to take your side in a civil war. And the character you do it to continues to pop up later. So is this woman not going to visit her husband anymore, because she thinks he's dead? What the hell?
The game has a really distinct visual style and some amazing views. Neo-Paris combines the messy dirt of Blade Runner with the bright sterile colours of Fifth Element. So expect to be overwhelmed by colours and distracted by grafitti and trash everywhere. The character designs are basically leather and latex future badasses. The weirdest thing I found was that large quantities of food is left on the ground, and at one point I found an entire lasagna just sitting on the ground, untouched. Who the hell cooks a lasagna and then throws it out the window? But some of the views are really really inspired. I wish the game gave you more of the outsides of Neo-Paris and fewer levels inside sewers or prisons. There's somewhat significant environment reuse. You visit some version of the prison 3 times, and another level is mostly a sewer--the game only has 8 real levels. I am sure this reflects budget limitations.
The score is basically a big soaring orchestral score combined with some 70s sci-fi synth--I don't know how to describe this really, but not the kind of dark synth you think of from 80s sci-fi, a more optimistic synth--and then randomly injected with really digital, glitchy kind of techno. The combat music is really cool. If you get hit or flub a combo, the music stops. The better you're doing, the more glitched out the music gets. I felt some level of comparison to Parasite Eve in that at its best the combat music had a kind of acid lounge jazz feel, but more techno. Really cool, original score, and I'd listen to it outside the game.
Having said all this, I do have some problems with the game. The story is absolutely nonsense and the levels don't really fit together well, as if they made the levels separately and then had to thread them into a story. The dialogue is really really poetic but sometimes unclear, which makes me think that the game received fewer editing passes than most or maybe it's just the ESL coming through a little bit. The jargon-heavy nature of the script subtracts from the world rather than enhancing it--really, I need to follow the Remembrane to find the entrance to Memorize to save the Errorists. I unlocked a new S-Pressen ("Expression") or an upgrade for my SenSen and just found a Mnesist. Groan. The conclusion to the story is incredibly, incredibly stupid... I can't stress how dumb it ends up being. I won't spoil it here, but if you sit down and think about the motivations that went into starting Memorize corporation, as well as how those motivations translated into the way Memorize is ran and what it is shown doing in the game, it makes no sense.
On the whole, I'd recommend the game because of the interesting things that it does, including a biracial female protagonist and some really beautiful views. The platforming is so effortless that it feels pretty good and liberating to go through it. I'd probably recommend you play on easy to minimize frustration since I don't think you'd get a whole lot of satisfaction off of "mastering" the combat system by playing on hard. The game will never get a sequel and the developer will probably make another game, to say nothing of the way game budgets basically render stuff like this unlikely to exist more generally, so it sort of stands on its own as an interesting and unique artifact.

Well...recommending this game really depends on how much you like the story.  The combat is not very good and gets in the way of enjoying the game.
The memory bits, on the other hand, are quite good.  The remixes are what caught people's attention to begin with, and they serve as a great way to dissect the story.  Of course, there are only four of these sequences in the game, but other ideas like reliving someone else's memories to solve a puzzle, figure out a passcode, or avoid detection are excellent, and I hope Capcom focuses more on this in the future.  It is also very cool to run around in an augmented reality world.
The main problem is that the balance of the game leans heavily towards combat, so again, the recommendation depends on how much you value story.  If you really want to uncover the mystery of Nilin's lost memories and are willing to hammer through the weak combat, you will enjoy this game.  If not, pick up something with much better combat, like Arkham Asylum or City.

I honestly don't understand the reviews here.
Firstly, I had my share of technical issues with the game and it's performance. That being said I also understand how computers work and understand that it's impossible to create a game that is guarenteed to run flawlessly on all hardware configurations all the time. Most people seem to have trouble grasping this concept. I ran the game originally with async compute on before the latest patch disabled it for Nvidia cards. The game ran very well I got maybe a strange crash or 2 through my first play through but for the most part the game performed incredibly well. I finished the game on Do or Die! as my first play through. After async was disabled the game still runs fine abiet a bit slower as a result of no async computer. The game itself is beautiful, the environments are so detailed and well layered it's actually absurd there is so much environmental detail. I'm especially talking about the buildings in New York, just so much pretty stuff to look at along the way. The game's effects are stunning, but I wish they tuned down some of the bright lights in certain buildings that just shine directly in your face. Either way, couple this incredible detail with amazing music and sound design. I had heard the previous wolfensteins had rather "unauthentic" German being spoken by characters who very obviously should be speaking native German, but I don't speak German so I can't comment on that. The english banter and dialog was, as expected, over the top, vulgar and very good.
I found the game surprisingly unchallenging. Some people have noted here that they found the game more difficult than normal, which I do not agree with. Sure, there were some tighter parts but for the most part I was able to pretty easily beat the game on "hard" without having to think much. I expected the heavier soldiers and the larger machines to put up a bit more of a fight, but once I figured out their kit they were pretty much completely trivial to overcome. It's pretty hard to remain stealthed for a very long period of time, which might be the difficulty I was on, but for the most part I got like 2-3 stealth kills before something stupid blew my cover.
People who commented on the story being short, confusing, blah blah I'd ask what honestly they expected it to be like? Which Wolfenstein game had a deep well layered story in it? None of them have because that's not what the series is about. If you were expecting more from the story than you came to the wrong place. Wolfenstein has always been about (or at least the machine games ones) brutal, relentless nazi slaying mixed with dark humor and completely over the top characters and situations. The game was basically meant to have a ridiculous story. I personally enjoyed the story, I think everything about the game is fun, fast, brutal and excessive.
All in all, I thought the game was awesome and I think some of the negative reviews seem like they are from people who never played a Wolfenstein game from machine and if they did they missed the point of where the franchise has come to. I think Machine makes an incredible game and I really hope whether it's another wolf, or something in the same vein they keep at it.

I had to refund this game. I was hoping to play a relatively well working port after seeing how good the port was for the first Dead Rising that had come out earlier this year, and for the most part, Capcom has succeeded in that. The game runs well and looks just as good as it did on console. Sadly, though, the game is plagued with issues concerning controller support. Getting my Qanba Dragon fightstick to work with this game was a nightmare, as all of the buttons are scrambled to be mapped to incorrect inputs (IE: A button is B button, Home button is UP, L2 button is R1, Settings button is LEFT). I wouldn't have much of a problem with this if the game saved my input configurations for in-game, I could just navigate the menus using my keyboard, but sadly my button configurations are reset every time I quit the game. Controller support problems aside, if you were also planning on playing this game online, please reconsider. This iteration of Ultimate Marvel vs. Capcom 3 has, by far, the worst netcode of all of the ports. It is completely unplayable. How Capcom can release a game with this sort of online function is beyond me. I would be content playing offline and sitting in the lab practicing combos, but even that is an unbearable hassle with the broken controller support. I was hoping more from Capcom here, but there is where my first fault begins: hope for Capcom. Unless you're using a very streamlined fightstick/controller designed for/with an Xbox 360 setting, and are content with only spending your time in the lab practicing combos, steer clear of this extremely evidential cashgrab by Capcom.

The funny thing about the full version is that:
1. It changed drastically with no warning. Heck, it seems as if 99% of content they could've tested or atleast shown off in the early access was kept locked at TT Games HQ. If your going to change a game this drastically, and the game's in early access, then slowly add things as they're finished into the early access. If the game started changing gradually into its finished format through updates in early access, then I would probably be fine with it, but they decided to flip the game on it's head and shake the things that made it unique and more interesting to play than other LEGO games out of it's pockets, like how a bully shakes out the dinner money of a child's pockets.
2. It runs worse than in early access. I'm no stranger to having games run like a one legged dog on my computer, but if the game runs better incomplete, then you have either added so much stuff to the point where it weighs the game's performance down or you done goofed. The full version should be a less buggier and better running game, not the opposite.

Hellblade:Senua's Sacrifice is a special kind of beast.
For one, gameplay is lacking. There are long stretches were you just walk around, there's basically one kind of puzzle and combat is, except for one encounter, very repetitive and limited. Also, it is way to short.
These two factors will probably keep the game from becoming the widely recognized classic it deserves to be, which is a shame.
If you manage to immerse yourself in Hellblade, you're in for one of the most intense and unsettling experiences gaming has to offer. The mind of Senua is awash with demons, and Ninja Theory presents them masterfully. The one kind of puzzle in the game? It all revolves around perspective and perception, about finding the right angle to see the world. Combat? Mostly revolves around gaining focus, so Senua can clearly see her enemy instead of stumbling around, trying not to be overwhelmed. And walking around? That's when you get a tour of Senuas mind, guided by the many voices constantly prattling in her head, helpful, comforting, deriding, condescending, accusing.
And here is what I think to be the greatest trick of the game: the voices. They adress not only Senua, but the player as well, creating another persona and thus preventing a strong identification of the player with the character. The player is someone who seems to follow her around, guides her and can also hear her hallucinations. Basically I, who sit in front of the screen, am part of Senuas psychosis, one of the voices. And that, in the words of the Doctor, is absolutely brilliant. I started the game weirded out and a bit annoyed by the voices. About an hour in the game I was feeling tense and uneasy whenever they stopped.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is required playing for everyone who can immerse him/herself in atmosphere and story and who has even a passing interest is psychological horror and/or norse mythology. Stay away if you think story is just something keeping you from your next kill.
Hellblade it's an mind blowing wonderful experience.

Overall, it reminded me of Diablo 2 with updated Graphics... Definitely mimics many aspects of the iconic game.
Graphics were nice, and there were many extra events that just popped up that kept the player on his toes (for example... teleporting through the warp gate... only finding yourself stuck in some random location to fight out of).
Maps were pre-planned and not randomly generated, which was nice for the casual player, however the replay-ability of the game is quite hampered by this.
The drop system and the stats randomization/drop was perfect. It really felt that you and your follower got stronger as the game progressed.
The stat system was intuitive and was taken from Diablo2. For the 'mage' class, skills leveled up in an obvious path, and the progression to get stronger was intuitive when picking skills.
Downsides:
The game loads extremely slow, between maps as well as starting the game (every single time!!!).
There were times of stuttering and it seemed like the auto-detect for my video system somehow told the game to leave all the dead bodies lying about.. which made my game stutter.
Some quests were not very intuitive such as finding X of some item, sometimes the quest required you to flip over corpses... which weren't highlighted and even worse sometimes blended into the background. Hated running through an area twice to look for a specific corpse to turn over.
I would give this a game 8.9/10... but due to those graphical and quest bug/decisions... this game is a 7.5/10, a steep drop.
Looking forward to the sequel though.

this game, if you couldn't tell. I play this game on a daily basis for 2 up to 5 hours a day and I will not get sick of it. I enjoy every second of it. From the music and stages, characters and their stories, up to the developers and voiceactors themselves; I just say, that I fell in love with this game. Of course, there are some flaws in this game, that I want to say in this review, so please, if you are not sure if this game is for you, then I hope, that I'll be able to help you.
The game itself is basically what you get, when you throw Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat and your favorite anime waifu in a pot and mix it all together. It's a 2D Fighting Game with it's own certain mechanics and finally; Smooth 60 FPS. It is usually played with a Fighting/Arcade Stick, (Depends of how you call it) but on steam, you can play it with the Keyboard, XBox or Playstation controller... The choices are yours and yours only. If you prefer the Keyboard over the controller, go ahead.
The Game has a selection of 14 characters, everyone of them with their own unique playstyle. As the title says, there are mostly only female characters. I repeat;
With the exception of two characters, who are male, (Three, if you count Robo-Fortune as genderless) the rest of them are all female, but that does not matter. They all also have their own individual stories, which I like to tell you now.
The Story goes like this;
A mystic artifact known as the Skullheart has been created since multiple decades. It's power was to grant any girl's wish, if they were pure in the heart, but most of them weren't. If they were not, they turned into a creature, called the "Skullgirl", who brought chaos, death and armageddon to a teaparty to wreck her surroundings. If the Skullheart got destroyed however, it will come back 7 years later to find a new victim and the cycle goes on and on and on... Until year HellIfIKnow, where the new Skullgirls "Bloody Marie" has risen and brings havoc to New Meridian.
The character's stories are fixed and cannot be changed, whether you like it or not. Why am I telling you this? The stories of many characters end dramatically, sometimes death is included, which can be hard hitting for you, if you have a strong bound to your favorite character.
I will not tell how their story goes onward from that point, you will either have to watch a walkthrough on youtube or play the game by yourself.
Now, the gameplay is depending of what you play with. For me; I currently play with the keyboard and I improved with time. It however is definitely best played with the Fighting/Arcade Stick, so if you have one, you probably have it easy.
This is where you have to admit; Multiplayer in this game sucks
if you play with people, that you don't know. Joining a random lobby in Skullgirls will be the bane of your life, eventually making you stop playing the game even. Believe me, when I say this; You will not like the random lobbies in Skullgirls. You will get literally ♥♥♥♥ed over and over, if you started playing the game. It is recommended to get a few friends to play this game and you probably get better in it.
This game is considered in my eyes a great game, that I refuse to actually let go from. I am a Skullgirls-Addict with 150 Hours, but the hours will rise higher and higher the more often I boot it up. It is funny, you get in the mood to play it more and more, you want to learn to become better in it until you want to become the best in Skullgirls.
TL;DR: Good Game, stay away from multiplayer, if you have no friends.
Thanks to To LabZeroGames for Skullgirls and MikeZ for keeping the community uplightened

Despite the bad start, this game has taken shape, just watch the videos the devs have put up.   I have only spent 6 hours playing this game and found I could not put it down.  You start off in the main game trying to repair your damaged crashed space ship.   You have to find all the elements to get it off into space.  What was fun for me was trying to find all the elements, accidently using some zinc to upgrade some of my equipment and that forcing me to find more.  I also used this other element I needed to fix my engines.  The upgrades are a must and help a great deal.  The other fun part was I was on a hot planet and my suit would only keep a shield so long, so I had to either run back to get into my ship to refresh it, or find elements on the planet that I could use to recharge it.  This can be a challenging game, but super fun, and when you take off from the planet you feel satisfied at repairing your ship.  What is really cool is taking off from the planet and seeing space come into view and watching the planet get smaller as you fly away.  I docked with an alien freighter who wanted to sell me his ship for more units that I had, which was 0.  For those that say this is a relaxing game, I can see the point, but there is some excitement the devs have added, there are attack drones, and also some of the plants will attack you as well.  There will be space combat, but I have not run into it as I just got space worthy.  I would get this game in a sale, just because I am cheap.
Pros:

2.	Fun puzzle solving in getting the ship repaired early on.
3.	Beautiful planets full of life.

Cons:
1.	The graphics need optimization, my gpu  and cpu are pretty good and yet I run at 30 fps or lower.  It’s playable though for me.  As a side note, the game is set at a default 30 fps, so if you have the best ever you might get more out of it.

3.	Lack of a story mode in the game.  You are crashed on a planet with no idea why. It’s like you wake up with amnesia.
