I don't often write reviews but I feel like it is necessary to write one for this game.
Ori and the Blind Forest is such a great game. The art style is so beautiful, the soundtrack absolutely amazing, and the story the game is telling very sweet and lovely.
It can be quite frustrating at some points (I ragequit the game very early on and didn't wanna play it for a week; only to then complete the rest of the game in one sitting), but it definitely gets easier the more you play - even though the game itself gets harder the further you progress. Usually I'm not a huge fan of platformers, but this game had me hooked instantly - for the above mentioned reasons.
You get to spend your skill points just as you like, and you can explore and revisit areas - despite mission goals - completely freely most of the time (with the exceptions of three areas that you can't revisit) once you learn the required moves to access them.
The controls are very easy and not complicated at all, though you can't remap them if you wanted to.
Also, some of the achievements are kinda bugged; it's not that you cannot get them though, it's that it's possible that they unlock at completely random times. For example, I randomly got six achievements at once at some point when I only should have gotten one.
Even though I got quite mad at it at one point, I absolutely recommend the game because of its gorgeous art and story.

Normally I wouldn't bother writing a review for a game that already has 14,000 expressing the same view, but my last few have been pretty scatching and this one really does deserve 14,001 positives. Ori is brilliant in every sense of the word, and unlike many of my favorite games, it isn't niche in the slightest. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone and everyone.
I'd heard others describe the game as basically playing a Pixar movie before I started it. It's not the first time I've heard that said about a game, but this is the first time when the similarities went beyond the character design and basic story tone. Ori is a fundamentally lighthearted game that isn't afraid to venture into darker themes, and everything about the game reflects that. The music, level design, art, writing, and even enemies have a plethora of different tones, but they all come together perfectly to express whatever the game is saying at that moment. The story, for its part, never has more than 4 lines of spoken or written text in a row. It's overwhelmingly conveyed through the motions and expressions of unspeaking characters, and it works because of the remarkable quality of the animation.
The animation's arguably more important contribution is to the gameplay, however. Ori's movement, combining flips, spins, and even airplane arms, is wonderfully expressive, and it combines with near-perfect controls and great level design to produce a game that's simply fun. Like all metroidvanias, Ori requires tons of backtracking, especially to get the secrets, but unlike all other metroidvanias, I never got tired of it. I don't even
most platformers, but enjoyed just moving around in this game as much as Ori clearly does. Many similar little touches build up to an experience that dwarves the sum of its parts.
Ori is, at times, brutally difficult, but it's almost always fair, and I never really felt frustrated with it despite dying over 200 times.
I think that about balances out to a positive.

There are certain games that leaves a horrific scar, be it for bad or for worse; and there are games which leaves an emotional scar, making the experience sweeter and satisfying. Do not let the RPG Maker tag deceive you -- To The Moon isn't an RPG: if anything, it's on the far-end of the spectrum, simply because the game has no combat mechanics of that sort. Instead, it relies on something triple-A games sorely lack and aspire to achieve: a player-invested story built upon multiple layers. And the game wears it like a proud dogtag.
What should be the focal point is always the story. About two "doctors" that help a man relieve his dreams again, eventually finding out the entire cause of it, and granting his wish of making it To The Moon. The game straddles the line between hope and despairity; loss and gain; tragedy and happiness -- all in under five hours (counting the 2 minisodes which are absolutely must-plays).
To The Moon is an all-round experience that leaves you wanting more, and hopes that after you've gone through all the sobbing tissues right by your side, that you still have a bottle of scotch waiting for you once the game ends. Because trust me: you'll need it. Brilliant story, brilliant soundtrack -- To The Moon is one of the best gaming experiences of all-time.

I personally like new twists on old classics, so I look for influences of good oldies in newer games. So when I was first introduced to “Trine”, I was all like: here are new “The Lost Vikings” (by Blizzard, 1992): three characters, each one with his strength and weaknesses complementing each other and solving little puzzles to complete levels.
“Trine” is not, of course a copy of “Vikings”: it is more of an action, the puzzles are a bit easier, characters transform to each other, not being present on screen simultaneously (much like Silmarils’ “Metal Mutant” of 1991). Of course game looks much and much better, the world is designed beautifully,
Game’s characters get experience from killing monsters and finding secrets, which can also contain unique items. Level-ups make them stronger in combat and platforming.
So if you are into mildly difficult puzzle-platformers with a bit of RPG elements, you should check this one out.

:SPOILERS CONTAINED:
Unfortunately the follow up to Wolfenstein: The New Order, The New Colossus, doesn't continue in the direction or encapsulate the appeal of what made first game so wonderful. Whether it's the low amount of gameplay material or new formulations in presentation and messaging (extreme politicizations) which are 'off point', it's far better that any one considering purchasing this game leave Wolfenstein to rest with their personal interpretations of the ending of TNO.
There are however a few points to the game which are positive: just as TNO and OB, the game is well optimized for PC players; the controls are a pinch wonky when compared to TNO, but that aside you should expect a smooth performance. I experienced some screen tearing in the first half of the game from time to time but it's incredibly difficult to say why - so, I'll take that as a personal oversight on my settings while playing.
The game follows a more direct formula in that you are running around in largely empty space, need to kill up to two 'commanders' and clear/evade rooms or prepare for some larger 'boss type' fight. This general flow of the game contrasts to what I experienced in both TNO and OB: in particular the first few stages of TNO with the variance and importance placed on stealthiness and objectives such as the path clear after saving Anya -- as well as density. Overall it's barely noticeable and not a significant flaw of the game, but it's subtle enough to unconsciously signal there may have been some rushing or lazy design.
But that's still far and away not enough for me to give the game a poor rating.
I'd also like to commend the game on a few 'moments' -- particularly the time you meet Hitler. That was a really well thought out piece, which takes a lot from history and expands upon it in a fictional setting. Sadly this isn't a game play moment, but one of what would have already been too many cinematic points in the game. I also thought the time after you've recently acquired a new body and met Anya in her room to be moving. As BJ, you ponder whether or not any of what you're experiencing is real. It's a poignant and timely demarcation for existential thought and serves as a kind of reflection for the player as to if what you're doing is just a dream or flashback when in consideration of the ending of TNO.
That brings me to the game's flaws in play material and presentation. Addressing the first problem: the game is basically just a movie. Perhaps you've read other reviews or watched a playthrough already - then you'd know The New Colossus seems like it is '50-50' play time versus cinematic. I only played once and on hard difficulty, but I kept getting to points in the game where I was like 'I've kind of been here before in other games -- I have a feeling this is really going to stretch out to an incredibly long playthrough.' Well, at least that's what I thought because of how many cinematics encountered.
Of the 13 hours I 'played', I left the game on for about an hour and a half while going out, had to redo the court room encounter about two dozen times (I'm no pro) and the final fight about ten times. The variety of enemies is about the same as TNO, although kills are not as satisfying as the soldiers and heavy-armored soldiers are one-two hit and the supersoldaten behemoth types are very vulnerable compared to their counterparts in TNO, taking only six or seven rifle hits to take down.
Of the boss fights - there aren't really more than two (of course that depends what you call 'boss' here). None of which of these (a large robot in Roswell/Southwest and the actual final fight) are in any way remarkable. The most interesting encounter or experience is definitely the court room, but nothing in this game compares to the final fight experience in TNO.
The 'apologists' for this would say 'well of course Engel shouldn't be like Deathshead.'. Yes, in fact, it's nothing at all except another cinematic. At this point while playing I thought I legitimately was at some kind of half way or three-fifths point in the game, hoping to finally encounter Hitler in manner like he 'imagined'. But no. The real 'boss fight' was a stream of soldiers, six or eight supersoldiers and two superbots (dead with three hits of your laser gun). A little more tedious than difficult or interesting. In what appears to be an alternate universe version of Jimmy Carter as a talk show host, you take control of the backstage command and projection room with the help of your surprisingly combat-adept pregant fiance/lover and friends, proceed to just walk on set, more or less, and axe the would-be-boss in the face.
It just feels at that point that I've been robbed out of a legitimately great gaming experience because of how little combat and play there is in the game up to that point. I think combined I spent more time watching cinematics and getting lost on the ship than playing the game.
Now - as far as the messaging goes there's a lot of parameters to take into account. What affects the mood and atmosphere in the game is what BJ says and how generally non-chalant the game becomes with Set, Anya and BJ after a point, despite the sincerity in TNO. BJ says things you would never think he'd even be inclined to think or say simply because of embelishments the developers wanted to put into their game. They radicalized their political commentary by putting their fascists in my god damn fascist game.
I could write too much more on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izations - the language and dialogue of course, not to mention the subtle changes with models becoming more or less attractive or the symbolisms of BJ losing his real body. I'll just say that in part because newer consumers like for 'their companies to take a stand on issues', the game takes on topics that have no place in the Wolfenstein universe - *as set by TNO*.
Why only now the outrage - why not in '92? Indeed. Personally, I won't be buying any more games from Bethesda because of their ignorance/lack of concern on discourse, perspectives and 1984. I wish I could refund, but it's just another lesson learned.

WARNING: If you have not played the trilogy yet, go away from this page right now. It is full of spoilers!!!!!
-------------
Style wise, Deponia Doomsday did not changed with respect to its previous instalements. The soundtrack is good as before. The puzzles are challenging as before (although I'm thinking they are a bit easier. But this might be that I improved on P&C games). And there is several jokes across the game. If you enjoyed playing the other Deponia games, you will enjoy this. Laso, on previous games I noticed small problems with lips syncing. On this one, I did not observed this.
Now, when I'm playing an adventure game, the main thing that matters for me is history. And as is well known, the ending on Goodbye Deponia were not very well received. And this game is the answer for those criticizing the game. The game starts acknowledging this and threaten the players with a "sharks and endings: don't tempt them". The Huzzah song finishes it by explicitly saying: There will be no happy endings. So, it is clear from the very beggining what the game is about: exploring alternative ways to save Rufus and Deponia to let the players conclude by themselves that the end in Goodbye Deponia is the best one. Did this worked? Nope! Actually, the effect was the opposite. There is always hope. That is the point. Time travel is just not the way to do it!
Still about the ending, it felt a bit artificial. The history flows in a natural way uintil near to the end. And the flow goes pointing in a possible happy end. But since that was not the writers' intention, he  forces things to go bad, so he can make his point. The positive thing is: at least this time, we have some closure. We know what happened to Goal, Rufus, Elysium and Deponia.
That said, this gives players the chance to see some background on the events of the first game. We see Elysium, it is hinted how was the relationship between Goal and her father, Goal and Cletus and Rufus and Toni. So it act as a kind of prequel for the series as well. We can see what happened after the end of Goodbye Deponia, at least the general shape of the facts. This was a thing very much needed.
Another thing that disapointed me a little: Looking at the soundtrack and achievements, I spoted just one Huzzah song! For me the Huzzah songs were the cherry in the cake for Deponia. It also worked as something that marked the beggining of a new chapter. I really missed them. Also, the new one is slight different. I persoanlly liked the old ones more.
Generally speaking, did I like this game? Hell yeah! Would I buy it again? In a blink of an eye! The general plot is brilliant as was the trillogy plot. Deponia universe still as one of the best universes I experienced in a long time (at side of Mass Effect and Portal). Despite my critiscism of the ending, it was an improvement compared to the trilogy ending. And i had already accepted Rufus death. But playing doomsday, gave me hope that in some way, Rufus can still be saved... somehow. After all, the main point of the game is that on the end, there is always hope, isn't it?

Oh my, this came out of the blue! I was completely thrilled when I saw this, although I was well-aware that my thrill might make me expect too much of the game. Sad to say, that's what happened - I was mildly dissapointed in this game (no sarcasm, btw, It wasn't too dissapointing), especially because I feel it had a bit of a different feel to it from the other Deponia games.
The other games often had comedy first, story second, yea? Well, in this case, it felt like it was the other way around. While that doesn't make this bad, it does mean that my expectation as a fan of this series was a bit misplaced. I expected to laugh a LOT. I expected to story to be mostly nonsense. Instead, I got only a few laughs, and a story of some depth. (It's not the deepest thing out there, but it had some depth to it)
Pro:
Most of the puzzles are sound and entertaining
You do get >some< funny moments out of this game
The game is long for a point-and-click game, and rarely lets up and becomes boring.
The game is a meta slap-to-the-face of the fans, and I love it! If you're a fan and starts playing this game, you'll know what I'm talking about.
Music is solid, writing is solid most of the time.
Art is great this time around, and it runs smoothly.
Cons:
One or two puzzles made no sense to me at all. I was stuck for hours.
The game is generally not as fun as I'd liked.
The time-travelling puzzle mechanic is incredibly annoying. ESPECIALLY when you find out it usually doesn't actually progress the puzzle.
The ending of this game came somewhat suddenly. Not only that, but they made your efforts in the game seem somewhat... Meaningless. "So if that other guy is solving all my problems, why am I even here?"
All in all, I'd say the game is decent, though I definitely preferred the original trilogy. If you've played that and miss Rufus, then go ahead, this game will be for you! Otherwise, play the first three games first before playing this.

An overlooked / underrated gem that is almost completely inaccessible. The game is split into a side A and a side B, and the theme is
style sci-fi sense of wonder. Side A is a fascinating first person puzzle that is a joy to solve, but only lasts for 30-45 minutes. Side B starts with you having to figure out how to fly your spaceship: the control panel itself is an unlabelled puzzle, and there is no tutorial. Once you solve that, a huge procedurally generated star cluster opens up. Each star has its own puzzle, and the goal is to solve a meta-puzzle that will reveal the location of the 'anomaly star'.
The procedurally genrated puzzles of side B aren't as good as side A, and they are generally small subsets of the big side A puzzle. Solving them becomes rote very quickly. So side B feels less like a puzzle game and more like a walking simulator, where the puzzles are an excuse to see the sights of all of the game's different stars. If your idea of fun is playing
for an hour followed by 9 or 10 hours of
and
, this is exactly your thing.
The soundtrack is worth mentioning too. It's brooding, static-laden ambient that suits the game perfectly.

Heilvetica.
The plot focuses on a society where memories are a commodity to be transferred, bought, sold and traded and uses this plot element very sparingly in gameplay - mostly a handful of sequences where you get to mess about trying to alter someone's memories. Some attacks and special powers are "explained" by using the ability to transfer and alter memories as a catch all, but it's a complete joke. In practice the takedowns and abilities have Jack and♥♥♥♥♥♥to do with memories, and Jack left town.
The plot appears to have been written by someone throwing things together in an attempt to get you moving about, as though he or she came up with a vague idea for Paris in the 2080s and then just kind of tried to give you a reason to go around beating up random people and mutants with weird weak points and jumping over things.
So, meh. It's not a bad game. It's not really a good one either. It's a pretty game (design-wise).

This game is quite a confusing one to review. The gameplay was quite boring. The biggest draw was the combat system, which wasn't even that great, and forced on the player at every instance of conflict (of which there were MANY). The climbing aspect of the game looked promising, especially considering the scenery, but it ended up being a very basic "you only have one path to climb" type of game (not like Assassin's Creed). The world of Neo-Paris is just fantastic. Everything from character design to architecture and vehicles just had me stopping to stare and enjoy the view. I think Hello Games was pressured (perhaps by Sony?) into hyping up No Man's Sky into something it wasn't. Prior to release, players were led to expect some ultra-ambitious space MMOFPS with a AAA budget and team - i.e., "Star Citizen Lite". Instead, what players got was more like Minecraft.
But, like Minecraft, No Man's Sky is incredibly fun on its own. Basically, you mine for resources in order to fuel & upgrade your ship to go explore the universe. What's rewarding is discovering a world with a beautiful array of plants and animals, beautiful planet-filled sky (all the more impressive with the knowledge you can actually travel to those worlds!), and watching the sunset over impressive landscapes. You can also build your own bases!
There are AI characters in this game. Aboard space stations or in small dwellings on planets you'll find characters you can trade with or hire. Sometimes space pirates will come attack you and you have to fight them off in a cool spaceship dogfight. Some planets have hostile life forms or robots too. Some planets are themselves hostile - extreme cold or radiation draining your life support system, which you'll need to recharge. Of course, there's plenty of opportunity to upgrade your suit & ship - or even purchase new ships. I haven't gotten that far, but I think you can even purchase your own giant freighter ships for extra storage space, which in turn can contain numerous smaller ships for exploring nearby solar systems. Overall, there are some pretty cool things to do in the game.
If you're the type of player who, like me, spent most of their time in Skyrim just wandering around and exploring stuff, you'll enjoy No Man's Sky. If you're the type of player who rushed through the quests and always used fast travel, it's likely you'll hate No Man's Sky because wandering around & exploring is what it's almost all about.
One more thing: this game is NOT worth the full price of $60. Get it on sale for $20 or $25 at most. This is not a AAA title. It really is closer to Minecraft or Kerbal Space Program than it is to Star Citizen, so don't pay more for this than you would for either of those.

The sequel of 12 Labours of Hercules brings more levels, increased challenge, and additional game mechanics to this enjoyable time management game. Sadly, it still couldn’t afford to have some form of story.
12 Labours of Hercules II: The Cretan Bull is the second instalment in a fairly successful line of time management games. Just like its predecessor, this one has no actual story or any real connection to the mythical jobs of Heracles, the title is just an excuse for the pleasant visual theme.
The core game mechanics are the same as before: you have a set of servants who are used to gather resources in order to remove road blocks to the next level. There are more instances where you need to call upon the help of Hercules himself or one of his mythological friends, but the bulk of the work still falls on the never-tiring servants.
Since a sequel needs some new gameplay elements, there are also a number of changes. Storage space is unlimited, but farms have to be harvested manually, before thieves steal the resources. You now start with at least two servants and most levels offer some form of achievable bonus to boost their efficiency; but you need to be a lot more careful and faster to clear the increased amount of obstacles to reach the bonus time limits.
The result is a sequel that is a little easier for casual players but a lot harder for those who want to get every award, which is probably the best outcome both sides could hope for.

There are certain games that leaves a horrific scar, be it for bad or for worse; and there are games which leaves an emotional scar, making the experience sweeter and satisfying. Do not let the RPG Maker tag deceive you -- To The Moon isn't an RPG: if anything, it's on the far-end of the spectrum, simply because the game has no combat mechanics of that sort. Instead, it relies on something triple-A games sorely lack and aspire to achieve: a player-invested story built upon multiple layers. And the game wears it like a proud dogtag.
What should be the focal point is always the story. About two "doctors" that help a man relieve his dreams again, eventually finding out the entire cause of it, and granting his wish of making it To The Moon. The game straddles the line between hope and despairity; loss and gain; tragedy and happiness -- all in under five hours (counting the 2 minisodes which are absolutely must-plays).
To The Moon is an all-round experience that leaves you wanting more, and hopes that after you've gone through all the sobbing tissues right by your side, that you still have a bottle of scotch waiting for you once the game ends. Because trust me: you'll need it. Brilliant story, brilliant soundtrack -- To The Moon is one of the best gaming experiences of all-time.

I have recommended this game, however it should be noted that it is a game that not everyone will 'get'/enjoy.
The premise of Hellblade is that you are Senua, a girl of about 20-30 from the Picts, on a quest to Hel to save the soul of your lover Dillion. The twist however, is that Senua is suffering from some sort of mental health issue that makes you wonder if she is traversing the lands of Hel or simply hallucinating due to her health issues. The game sees you visit several locations of various Viking design each of which tends to have a central theme regarding Senua's past.
The game's two strongest selling points are its story, though while a tad difficult to decipher remains strong and leaves you wanting more, and its dealing with Senua's mental health. While playing you will be bombarded with different voices in Senua's head which, if you are wearing a headset, are designed to assail you from all around and will sometimes call out to you in combat.
One thing that should be said is, while the game developers have sunk a good deal of time into studying people with mental health issues and taking their views into account, the game does focus largely on the extreme negatives of mental health. It creates the idea that people with mental health are constantly terrified and their heads full of screaming which might be over selling things a tad. The game also comes with an option called “Hellblade Feature” that talks about the making of the game and explores various questions regarding mental health.
The combat is quite well done but is not the key focus of the game so lacks too much variety, however still provides a healthy dose of entertainment. Impressively on occasion one of the voices tormenting Senua will speak up off behind you to the left will shout "Watch out!" and sure enough behind you and to the left a man with a sword will be trying to cut your head off.
The game’s biggest downfall I feel are its puzzles. The puzzles aren’t terribly difficult thankfully but often pull you out of the story or the action so sharply that it is almost frustrating.
One particular type of puzzle that comes up frequently in the game has you looking for shapes that resemble Viking Runes. Initially this is not terribly difficult but as the game goes on these shapes become increasingly difficult to find and sometimes you’ll stumble upon the solution accidentally and find yourself saying “That looks nothing like the shape.” Sometimes you’ll be told to find a rune that looks like the letter P. Sometimes this is easy as you’ll see a stone that juts upwards in a straight line and a few meters behind it is a small wooden beam shaped like the rest of the P and you’ll think “Bang, there it is.” Job done. Other times you’ll be stumbling around a rather dark cave for half an hour trying to line something up until you accidentally do it only to discover the solution was so vague that it wasn’t there at all.
The puzzles are a pretty frequent occurrence which makes what might have been a minor annoyance a major pain. Coupled with the games relatively short play time (I got through it in five hours without particularly rushing) that doesn’t seem to match up with a £25 price tag it brings what should be a very good game down to a passable play experience for me not to mention it does not feel like the kind of game you would play again, lacking any particular segment you’d want to go back in play.
All in all the game is playable, the story is good, it provides an interesting perspective on mental health issues and clearly the team has put in a lot of effort put into the game, but the puzzles and short playtime vs price issue twined with the lack of replay-ability really deflate the games worth for me.

I was very happy from start to finish playing Trine.
Trine is a relatively short platformer that uses 3 distinct characters with unique skills to help you progress and collect all the experience bottles throughout each level. You can change characters on the fly just by pressing 1, 2 or 3.
The visuals are stunning and I was constantly just looking at the scenery. The sound is equally good, with fantastic music that suited each level. It's worth noting the sound effects were all great and of very high quality.
There are several different enemies and "bosses" throughout the game. However, the enemies lack variety and will constantly repeat over and over. I put bosses in quotes because they are actually quite easy. Maybe mini-bosses is a better term.
Trine is a very forgiving game (played on the default difficulty). It's easy to pick up and play a level. It never gets very difficult and has a very generous checkpoint/revival system.
The story is as good as it can be for a game like this. There's not much too it, but it’s conveyed well to the player through a fantastic narrator.
The controls are ok. Sometimes I got frustrated with my character motion and jumping onto ledges. But it is a minor gripe.
+I ran an uncapped fps and left it to vsync to run at 60fps. This caused stuttering every couple of seconds. I fixed this by telling Trine in the options to run at a capped 60fps. Completely smooth after that
+Another easy fix. My mouse input lag was pretty bad. Trine has an option to reduce lag. You'll want to put a check mark in that box
+Beautifully styled graphics.
+Sound design is solid.
+Overall platforming is fun.
+Game rewards you (with experience) for exploring corners and trying to find the secret chests.
+Smooth 60fps
+Stable. Never crashed on my Windows 8.1 machine
+Great narrator voice acting.
+Fun puzzles and having to think how to progress further
+Not much to the story.
+At times I fought with the controls
+Default difficulty could be a little more challenging
+Only a few useful power-ups. A lot of them don't affect the characters much. (This may change when played on a harder difficulty)
+Very few unique enemies.
Very good
I would absolutely recommend Trine. The regular price of $14.99 seems a little much. I would not pass this up if it goes on sale. I got the Trine collections for $2.49 during the 2014 Summer Sale.

This game didn't scare me at all. Not even once.
I tried it just so that I could brag about it. Not that it's something to brag about, not absolutely, but in relation to other people who get scared by it, I guess so.
Before even playing the game, I knew I wouldn't be scared at all.
They say: Know yourself and you know the universe. Yeah, been there, done that.
I wrote these lines before I played the game.
Game tells me to press Enter. I press Space and get to the main menu. This game is not suitable for Sheldon Coopers.
Game completely screws up my window setup due to low res and crappy implementation. ... Who didn't see that coming? But no other game before managed to do it with all windows, even the ones that stayed minimized all the time.
Game has no mouse sensitivity setting. Speed is acceptable, but a bit bothersome.
This game literally redefines the genre of jumpscare games. It's like: You think you know jump scares? Well, I think ...THIS is jump scares, not what you know them as.
At the first cardboard popup I flinched a bit, because I got so bored from running through repetitive rooms that when I noticed something that looked like something finally happening, I jumped right at the opportunity for some action, afraid that I might miss it. So now you know what jump scares are.
Room 101: Yay, new wall textures! We're getting somewhere here.
Room 151: Yay, new wall textures! We're finally getting somewhere here.
Really wishing for another hostile creature trying to kill me. This is so boring. Had I known before, I wouldn't have continued playing after the first creature killed me because I wasn't in the mood for running. (The irony! But as I said, finally something interesting - why run away from it?)
Room 201: New wall textures AGAIN. So predictable. This is really getting boring.
Apparently I am being violently approached by another creature. I get hit twice while writing notes for this review. I run along a little.
Room 204: I got killed by an abomination. (This game.) And when I say "I", I mean my motivation.
Creature says "Come here" and I decide to do just that. Game over. Finally! I made it!
I tagged this game as "running simulator". It's not a walking simulator, because walking would bore you to death. I mean quicker than running. (This might be the only case where walking gets you somewhere quicker than running does.)
There will probably be people now being like: "Oh, you really should have played to room 205. That's when things get interesting."

This game is somewhat of a letdown. After the fun start with new order I had high hopes for the series, but sadly this installment continues the downward trend first spotted in old blood.
Level design feels lacking, and is nowhere near as well suited for stealth play as those from new order. This is strange, because the commanders system encourages sneaking. Going in guns blazing will cause these commanders raising the alarm, and calling for backup. this results in far more enemies to deal with.
The sneak system is also frankly a tad dodgy. Half the time the constrictor doesn't trigger, or in a silly way having you crawling around on the floor under a corner of something. This usually means having to wiggle back and forth a few times before the constrictor lets you enter a duct etc.
The shooting is also not very impressive. The only weapons that feel powerful are fully upgraded pistols, and charge shots from your laser. Even with all upgrades the other weapons feel sub par. Headshots for example are way easier on your pistol than your assault rifle in sniper mode with armour piercing rounds.
Level design is another problem. The vast majority of my playtime involved being lost. Either trying to find a collectible the map said was right in front of me, or just trying to figure out what I had to do next, and how on earth to get there.
The log is also just bad. At present I have accepted several optional side quests, but only one of them shows in the actual log. Because of the poorly made war table I frankly have no idea where I need to go next for these quests. What is the point of making a log with a specific section for side quests if it doesn't track bloody side quests?
On a story and writing level I also can't give this title a pass. To me it came across as alternating between being needlessly crude, crass, purile or graphically violent for the sake of shock value.
It also first plays with the horrors of a nuclear attack, only to be perfectly happy to detonate several of those very same nukes in the US because well it will kill nazis, or wedge lose our.. boat. (Seriously? You shoot a nuke into a city with people to wedge lose your bloody BOAT?)
The alternate history is also quite lackluster, and feeds into this strange notion that the Americans won WW2. (No honest, there were other countries, they also did things. Quite a few of them for a lot longer than the USA)
There are also a slew of technical issues: The first 2 patches outright broke the game for me, and I couldn't run it at all. Ironic since the release version ran just fine here.
Even now the moment any pop up comes in it will lock the game on my machine. So I can't leave open say a mail client, chat app etc. Alt tabbing out of wolfenstein 2 will also hard lock the program requiring me to kill it via task manager. (And yes, I have all overlays disabled.)
Putting driver version checks in your patches that will simply not let a game run on older driver versions anymore is also just not above board. Put up a warning, sure, but don't keep poeple from playing your game when it ran just fine before. Especially for people with older hardware, or on an older os this is just not acceptable. If it doesn't work well on these setups that's another matter, but now you are just locking these people out for no good reason what so ever.
Do yourself a favour and run the demo before you even consider buying this game. Even so this might be one of those games you should pick up in a sale for a tenner or less, because it probably isn't worth more. On that same note: If you have the base game play the zero mission before you get the season pass. I was foolsih enough to get the season pass right away, and very much regret that purchase.

I never write reviews for games, but I definitely feel as though I need to write one. From a technical aspect, the game is a mess on launch. Fortunately, my pc has been running the game flawlessly. Because of this, I have been playing a game that has grabbed me by the balls and hasn't let go. This game is everything I wanted and more. The gunplay is fast and fluid, challenging, but still fair enough that the game won't give you any issues. Weapons are impactful, tearing chunks out of Nazis left, right and center. Once again, the story will be a love it/hate it deal. Cinematics are frequent, yet polished and never feel as though they drag on. The writing is very pulpy, and at times cliched. Yet the characters are still as likeable as ever, especially B.J. His voice actor does a fantastic job with the material and delivers an incredibly touching performance at times. The story itself is as nonsensical and batshit as ever, with crazy technology being thrown around as if it were nothing. I love it, but I can see why many would take issue with it. It's very hammy, with plently of tonely jarring scenes that may leave many put off. At the end of the day, Wolfenstein 2 is everything I wanted in this sequel. If you can run this game, you're in for the most insane ride of this year. I don't hesitate when I say that this is my potential game of the year.

Remember Me is one of the best games ever made. It's top notch story, artwork and graphics that will leave you stunned, and great musical score makes this game something you 'll never want to forget. The only downside is the first few levels leave the combat a little meh(~2 Hours).
The Story:
Without spoiling anything Remember Me is a game where you think you know what's going to happen. When you finally play it you'll see that there is even more then you thought. The story in this game is one of the best stories ever told in a Big Budget released titles. The world feels real and the story plays off this amazingly constructed world perfectly. It may even make you rethink how you view your own memories.
The Graphic/Artwork:
The detail in this game is above any other I've seen. Little robot float by with signs showing you the specials of places to eat or shops. The floating text  of the signs are at the perfect depth in order to feel as if they are realistically placed. Dirty places feel dirty and not over done just like clean places feel just the right amount of clean. Nothing is over done and the detail is so perfect it's insane to think about. You really feel as if you are part of the world. The 3D is also very good.
The Sound/Music:
The Musical score in this game is perfect as well. It combines classic big orchestra sound with corrupt technology sounds in the perfect manner. Sound is one of my favorite things in a game so even if this styles sounds crazy even at first I didn't believe how well it sounded.
The voice acting in the game is great only maybe 3 lines in the game feel out of place. Each actor adds emotion to their character and draws you into the story and scene. The combat sounds can get a little repetitive though because the enemy are always saying the same one liner all the time. Nothing that can't be over look.
The combat noises and ambient sounds are also really well done. You heard ADs over a PA system about a product in the world or what just happened in the news. Robots talk about protocol for the area or you just hear people talking in the streets.  You can hear the distant sounds of computers running around a corner or a leaper hiding the shadows. The combat noise of punches landing and other abilities hitting are fine as well. Things sound satisfying when they land and never out of place.
The Gameplay:
The gameplay is one of the weakest parts of Remember Me at the start of the game. You don't have many abilities, pressens, or combos and it can feel as if you are just spamming the one or two combos you do have in order to just get through. When you finally unlock everything the style of combat you do is almost an art of itself. It flows so well and looks very good. At the beginning of the game it can seem that the combat is down right bad but give it time it gets really fun.
The platforming in Remember Me in very linear as the game is pretty much 95% linear. There are a few places you can go in order to find collectibles but other then that it's pretty much follow this path. The platforming is pretty easy and really just something you do in order to find the solutions to puzzle as it's pretty hard to fail these sections. Overall the platforming is neither good nor bad it's pretty ok.
All in all if you are looking to pick up Remember Me I strongly suggest you do. I played it the whole way through in Nvidia 3D and it was great. I recommend using a controller so you can lean back and enjoy this amazing game.

It's more like "remember parts of me" than "remember me" really since Remember Me is a pretty decent game as a whole but certain parts stand out while others fade into the background which to me either showed a lack of consistency within the game and maybe a lack of communication between the design team.
BUT anyway Remember Me is one of those titles that comes along once and a while and wows you with it's ideas and mainly it's ideas -  the game's main concept memory storage and distribution is a great concept and weaves the story together well making you question both your character (Nilin) and the other character's own memory as you try and get to the end buuuuuut it does kind of fall apart near the end and the amount of lore the game expects you to take in first time around is obnoxious to say the least. Yet like I stated before this is a game of inconsistency, even if the concepts are great the characters aren't as well done, yeah you may question them but it's not like their memorable. In contrast to this the world and environment design is top-notch and refreshingly makes the future an actual okay place to live in as it's littered with cafes and clothing shops making it feel like that the human race has actually progressed into this state. Another great visual aspect is the effects design as some of them are superb and fit into this sci-fi world so neatly that they are a joy to watch, blasting the memories out of a guy's head has never looked better :D. The most stand-out concept of the game is the fact that you can fiddle with people's memories, change them and therefore changing their life experiences forming them into a different person, it's a great story narrative device and probably could have had a whole game for itself from how enjoyable it was but I wish it was used more...
The combat system is a refreshing take on the usual beat em up, gone are the heavy  attack, light attack, dodge ceremonial dance that is worshipped by previous games and instead you create your own comboes with their own benefits, mixing up kicks and punches as you go - roundhouse kicking foes to give me health is just so sweet plus someone decided that you can dodge and carry on your combo which is a awesome touch yet the combat can get really clustered when fighting multiple foes and you can never seem to pull off your best comboes because you get blind sided by a dude lightly stroking your hair. On that note the humanoid enemy designs (the robots are pretty cool) and character designs (excluding a few characters) are really bland and take the life out of the world as the humoids all look like splicers that didn't make the cut to be in Bioshock. The boss battles excluding the last one felt really tedious to me, or in fact pointless, same goes for the stealth sections. There is a hell of a lot of climbing to do but Nilin moves so slowly that it makes it more of a chore to do it. The game time isn't that long with no replayablility at all and is pretty linear however the linear parts don't make it exactly bad as it does allow you to focus on the story.
Even though it does have it's faults and can be annoying at times Remember Me was pretty enjoyable for most of it, if your looking for a "different" type of beat em up I'd reccomend this.
+ Combat is refreshing and new
+ World, Special Effect and Environment design are superb
+ Memory remixing is a great gameplay mechanic
+ Story has it's moments
- Drab enemy and character designs
- Climbing and stealth are pretty boring
- Boss battles are annoying
- Short (but compact)

Oh for a neutral button for these reviews.......
This game is different - very different.
CONS:
Honestly, if I hadn't looked at some Youtube videos and discussion boards, I'd probably still be sitting on the first planet getting read to throw my computer out of the window.  There is no tutorial and absolutely no hints whatsoever to get you going in the game.  I have only gotten as far as I have by basically cheating (i.e. the aforementioned discussion boards) and that is not something you should have to do.
Same thing goes for the cockpit - again, if I had not cheated, I'd probably still be staring at the stupid thing mashing buttons and what not.
I'm still not sure EXACTLY what you are supposed to do, even though I have some ideas that, once again, come from the community for the game.  After about five or six planets, I started getting bored with trying to figure out each "puzzle".  Supposedly you are supposed to find something called the "anomaly" (I think), but I'll be darned if I know how to find it.  Supposedly the stars you see in the sky while on a planet are to be used on your ship for navigation.  I'm sorry, I'm not a junior astronomer and have no idea how to do that.  Supposedly there is a way to mark constellations (or something) to make it easier, but once again I have no clue how to do that.  It's nerve racking.
PROS:
The game is different and I like that.  The game has an interesting visual approach and the gameplay is also a bit different when compared to the average first person game.  As much as the game has been frustrating me, I still find myeslf drawn back to it and that is a good thing - not many games can do that to me.  I'm determined to figure out what makes it tick, even if I have to end up cheating to do so by getting answers via discussion boards, videos, etc.
The only helpful advice I would give would be to pick it up on sale like I did, that may help offset the awkwardness of the game.  Do not buy this game if you're looking for a traditional FPS type game, it's nothing like that.  There really isn't much to do other than walk around on the planets doing the puzzles (which after you do a couple of them become stupid easy and tedious after a while).  I would call this something like a minimalist/surrealist sci-fi type exploration/puzzle game that definitely isn't everyone's cup 'o tea.
Maybe this was meant for MENSA members only, who knows?  But I still find myself drawn back to the game which makes me like it for that reason if nothing else.  With that said, I still wouldn't recommend this to the average gamer unless you are looking for something a bit off the wall.  If you want to fly around space shooting stuff, this definitely isn't the game for you ;)

Even Pluto, now demoted to a dwarf planet, isn't that small and featureless. The planets all look alike except for the colour palette and some minimal debris here and there. Once you've seen one planet, you've really seen them all. There are puzzles on each planet (actually it seems to be the same puzzle over and over again), but I don't want a puzzle game, I want a game about exploration. I want to see beautiful vistas, meet strange animals, find crumbled old ruins, things like that. If you're looking for something similar to Noctis, skip this game. It's an abstract puzzle game that's only posing as a space exploration game.

I've bought this game on two different platforms (Playstation 4 and PC/Steam). I've got the platinum on this game for PS4 and intend on doing the same on PC within a few months. I
that there were a significant amount of promises that just weren't kept at the launch of this game - it's left a horrible aftertasted in everyone's mouth when it came down to Hello Games and "No Man's Sky". HG has attempted to push to make NMS
presentable, post-launch. I realize there was a large period lacking communication, no updates, and radio silence from Hello Games in general. After a while, this eased up and we got both the "Foundation Update" and "Path Finder Update" - not at once, but after the silence was over they kicked development up into high gear.
Aside from the marketing (and misleading statements [sic]), No Man's Sky is a pretty fun game if you go into it with a reasonable
-driven expectation. When I bought this for PS4 at $59.99 - I only wanted an exploration/mining game that took place in space. Multiplayer in a game like this, for me, would be an annoyance (if HG ever does implement "full" multiplayer, please make sure it's in another mode outside of survival or regular). I didn't want to run around with friends, nor get shot at by someone random that's flying through space. I've played 500+ hours of EVE Online - that's more than enough experience with getting salty over a game that should be "chill".
There's a little bit of everything in No Man's Sky - you can get creative in creative mode, you can test how long you can survive in survival, and so on. I enjoyed the main campaign - the hunt to keep yourself alive, while mining and crafting upgrades along the way, and trying to get to the center of the universe. Now that people know what's at the end of the universe, there's not many who's interested in such a thing - but they still exist (like myself). The point is - you can hate the game, you can like it, or you can find that it being on sale actually raises the dollar to value ratio for you.. whatever the case, you're free to believe what you will. You're free to meander around worlds or never buy this game.
Personally, I recommend it to those who simply want to explore or create. Exploration can be tricky, at times, but worthwhile if you're lucky enough to be on a resource-heavy planet. If you want to create, creative mode does allow some liberty and doesn't throw you into the deep end.

Surprisingly good! Nice little shooty monster-playing arcade game. That's how I'd say it. It feels pretty arcadey, like a 1980s arcade game made love with a first person shooter, but if you like that then it's actually really fun.
The mechanics aren't obvious or intuitive though, and the entire interface just feels a little alpha-ey to me, like it was made by someone's teenage kid who was still learning Photoshop at the time. But the game itself is actually pretty okay once you get the hang of it.
Underwater games that are more than a mere theater/aquarium experience are rare, and they usually look like butts and don't give that underwater feeling. This feels like you're actually in water instead of just a Unity level with a dark blue background. ;p
The action is pretty intense in a pleasurable way so long as you're not getting scared or frustrated. If you are, ask yourself if you understood the goals of each side, because it's a deceptively simple and easy game to play.
Expect to play it in little 5-minute squirts like Rocket League though, because the no-nonsense gameplay and the lopsided teams mean you're there to dash and shoot, not to meet people or polish your character's loadout.
For the $5 it costs now I'd say "definite yes". For $10 or even more at other times, I'd say "are you crazy?!" There's not enough depth to warrant a price *that* high, but if you look at it as a $5 timewaster it's pretty nice.

12 Labours of Hercules: Cretan Bull is the second installment of its' series developed by JetDogs Studios and Zoomout Games. Previous installment: 12 Labours of Hercules.
Note: There is a storyline for the game but it isn't much to it nor its' rememberable. Gameplay formula is pretty much the same as the first one.
This is a time management game, where careful planning is required, limited amount of resources that are available throughout the game; henced the word management.
This game has the total of four episodes with 11 levels each; totaling out 44 levels altogether. There twenty-two different achievements but each of them come with a requirement.  There are also puzzle pieces to find throughout the game. The four bonus levels can be unlock when the jigsaw puzzle is completed.
There are three modes, relaxed; casual and expert, the difference between them is the timer speed and scoring. In relaxed mode, no timer and no scoring. In casual mode, the timer drain a slowly and the scoring is moderately low. In expert mode, the timer drain much quicker and the scoring is much higher.
The stars that are earned from completing the level depends upon on how much time is left on the timer. This only applies to the causal and expert modes
Three Gold star is when the time has not gone pass the arrow. Two Silver star is when the time has gone pass the arrow. One Bronze star is when the timer is completely empty.
Replaying any of the levels will improve the game score and the amount star.
There are few special bonuses: Freeze Time, Worker Movement/Work Speed, Additional Worker and Increases Resources. All of these special bonuses has a certain time limit but they can be used again once the bar fills-up. These special bonuses are very useful when the game is being played on expert mode.
I don't think that this game much of replay value to it. If you're into time management games then you might find this game somewhat enjoyable to certain extent.

The story is, definitely, the strongest point. You play as two cientists working for a corporation that alters a dying person memories in order to artificially grant their last wish; in this case, Johnny, that wants to go to the moon. The way the story is told is amazing; you go from recent memories to more distant ones, and this creates mistery upon mistery that gets solved the deeper you go. You'll also find out more about the relationship between Johnny and his wife, River, and how much his life changed because of it, as well how their plans and dreams turned out in the future.
You will always want to know more because the misteries keep piling up, and feel touched and conected with the characters and their problems - both very real and well developed. The amazing and sentimental soundtrack helps to create this atmosphere.
Sadly, those are the only good points.
The gameplay is awful. Starting from the menu screen: you can't alter the resolution. Yup, this only runs on a ridiculous 640x400 resolution, and on full screen there's these huge black borders (it was released in November 2011; there's no excuse). Yuck.
To make it worse, the graphics are way outdated. It was supposed to be that "pixelated old school" look, but they are horrible and bad looking, with a tiny and way too bright color scheme.
To top it off, you'll hit invisible walls constantly. Sometimes you can go through bushes, chairs, logs and narrow paths, other times you can't. And there's no way to know until you try.
To proceed further in the memories, you have to solve some "turning titles" mini game that has no reason to be there. Oh, and even though it says it has controller support, it doesn't.
To The Moon has an excelent story, told in an original and intriguing way, with unique and believable characteres, but the gameplay and graphics are so horrible that you end up getting frustrated as you play (I couldn't play more than 30 minutes at a time), compromising the beautifull story.

I have previously written a review for this game but I think it's time to make a new one. My goal is to make this easy to understand at a glance.
This one is super opinion heavy and it's best to just judge for yourself.
+
- The characters are all well drawn and stand out from everything on the screen. There are a ton of colors to choose from (over 20 per character) and many are references to other characters. The fanservice in this game can be seen as excessive, but I don't care about it or notice it much.
+
- The stages, for the most part, look great. The stages are somewhat 3D (which can be changed in the options) but it isn't super noticeable. They all look like they were designed with a purpose; they don't look like they were just thrown in. Another good thing about the stages is that they never distract me from the game.
+
- Everything is super well animated in this game. The attacks always look smooth and there are no animation-hitbox oddities such as the super large Street Fighter II Shoryuken hitbox.
+
- Skullgirls allows you to select the number of characters are on your team. Single character teams are viable in this game because each character in a multiple character team is weakened based on the team size.
+
- Everything in this game feels crisp and responsive. This is personal opinion, but it is one of the best feeling fighting games I've ever played.
+
- This game has a mechanic where it detects when the opponent is doing an infinite combo and allows the other player to break free. Because of this, one combo doesn't mean a immediate loss.
+
- When selecting your characters, you can input normals and specials as assist moves. Since these aren't new moves, you will immediately know how they work. It also provides for options that are fun to test out.
+
- The tutorial teaches you mechanics that are used in many other fighting games. There is also a section that teaches about each character individually.
+
- You don't have to learn more than one character to start playing this game.
+
- Things like slow motion and showing hitboxes make it easy to understand the game's mechanics.
+
- When doing a 360 motion, the game will prevent you from jumping during it.
This is one of the best fighting games I have ever played. I know that it won't be to everyone's tastes, but I find it very hard to think of places where this game is lacking. Many of the problems that people had were ironed out by the developers who continue to work on this game.  If you like games such as Marvel vs Capcom you are going to want to check this one out.
Just keep your expections high because this game is sure to surpass them.

This game ticks all the boxes for me.
Hellblade is one of those rare breed of games that can act as a cinematic masterpiece while also providing an enjoyable gameplay experience. The first act of the game is a bit slow to start since it is mostly a puzzle game at that point, but the final act was probably one of the best gaming experiences I've seen in recent memory.

But there isn't a lot of combat in the game, so you spend more time experiencing the good parts of the game than the combat. There are some bugs i experiences throughout the game, most were ignorable but the biggest one was in the final battle where my sword went invisible until the ending cutscene happened. Good game, worth the experience.

At no point does this game hold your hand, so if you're not a fast thinker you might die a couple of times before realizing what you are doing wrong, and you can only die a certain number of times, so be warned.
However, I can understand that some people disliked the game as it is a bit repetitive in the sense that the puzzles and combat are similar during the experience. But, because of the story and setting, the puzzles did not bother me at all and as for the combat, it gets more challenging as you progress further in the story.
So far, this is my favorite game of 2017.

This game is somewhat of a letdown. After the fun start with new order I had high hopes for the series, but sadly this installment continues the downward trend first spotted in old blood.
Level design feels lacking, and is nowhere near as well suited for stealth play as those from new order. This is strange, because the commanders system encourages sneaking. Going in guns blazing will cause these commanders raising the alarm, and calling for backup. this results in far more enemies to deal with.
The sneak system is also frankly a tad dodgy. Half the time the constrictor doesn't trigger, or in a silly way having you crawling around on the floor under a corner of something. This usually means having to wiggle back and forth a few times before the constrictor lets you enter a duct etc.
The shooting is also not very impressive. The only weapons that feel powerful are fully upgraded pistols, and charge shots from your laser. Even with all upgrades the other weapons feel sub par. Headshots for example are way easier on your pistol than your assault rifle in sniper mode with armour piercing rounds.
Level design is another problem. The vast majority of my playtime involved being lost. Either trying to find a collectible the map said was right in front of me, or just trying to figure out what I had to do next, and how on earth to get there.
The log is also just bad. At present I have accepted several optional side quests, but only one of them shows in the actual log. Because of the poorly made war table I frankly have no idea where I need to go next for these quests. What is the point of making a log with a specific section for side quests if it doesn't track bloody side quests?
On a story and writing level I also can't give this title a pass. To me it came across as alternating between being needlessly crude, crass, purile or graphically violent for the sake of shock value.
It also first plays with the horrors of a nuclear attack, only to be perfectly happy to detonate several of those very same nukes in the US because well it will kill nazis, or wedge lose our.. boat. (Seriously? You shoot a nuke into a city with people to wedge lose your bloody BOAT?)
The alternate history is also quite lackluster, and feeds into this strange notion that the Americans won WW2. (No honest, there were other countries, they also did things. Quite a few of them for a lot longer than the USA)
There are also a slew of technical issues: The first 2 patches outright broke the game for me, and I couldn't run it at all. Ironic since the release version ran just fine here.
Even now the moment any pop up comes in it will lock the game on my machine. So I can't leave open say a mail client, chat app etc. Alt tabbing out of wolfenstein 2 will also hard lock the program requiring me to kill it via task manager. (And yes, I have all overlays disabled.)
Putting driver version checks in your patches that will simply not let a game run on older driver versions anymore is also just not above board. Put up a warning, sure, but don't keep poeple from playing your game when it ran just fine before. Especially for people with older hardware, or on an older os this is just not acceptable. If it doesn't work well on these setups that's another matter, but now you are just locking these people out for no good reason what so ever.
Do yourself a favour and run the demo before you even consider buying this game. Even so this might be one of those games you should pick up in a sale for a tenner or less, because it probably isn't worth more. On that same note: If you have the base game play the zero mission before you get the season pass. I was foolsih enough to get the season pass right away, and very much regret that purchase.

I never write reviews for games, but I definitely feel as though I need to write one. From a technical aspect, the game is a mess on launch. Fortunately, my pc has been running the game flawlessly. Because of this, I have been playing a game that has grabbed me by the balls and hasn't let go. This game is everything I wanted and more. Once again, the story will be a love it/hate it deal. Cinematics are frequent, yet polished and never feel as though they drag on. The writing is very pulpy, and at times cliched. Yet the characters are still as likeable as ever, especially B.J. His voice actor does a fantastic job with the material and delivers an incredibly touching performance at times. The story itself is as nonsensical and batshit as ever, with crazy technology being thrown around as if it were nothing. I love it, but I can see why many would take issue with it. It's very hammy, with plently of tonely jarring scenes that may leave many put off. At the end of the day, Wolfenstein 2 is everything I wanted in this sequel. If you can run this game, you're in for the most insane ride of this year. I don't hesitate when I say that this is my potential game of the year.

It's more like "remember parts of me" than "remember me" really since Remember Me is a pretty decent game as a whole but certain parts stand out while others fade into the background which to me either showed a lack of consistency within the game and maybe a lack of communication between the design team.
BUT anyway Remember Me is one of those titles that comes along once and a while and wows you with it's ideas and mainly it's ideas -  the game's main concept memory storage and distribution is a great concept and weaves the story together well making you question both your character (Nilin) and the other character's own memory as you try and get to the end buuuuuut it does kind of fall apart near the end and the amount of lore the game expects you to take in first time around is obnoxious to say the least. Yet like I stated before this is a game of inconsistency, even if the concepts are great the characters aren't as well done, yeah you may question them but it's not like their memorable. In contrast to this the world and environment design is top-notch and refreshingly makes the future an actual okay place to live in as it's littered with cafes and clothing shops making it feel like that the human race has actually progressed into this state. Another great visual aspect is the effects design as some of them are superb and fit into this sci-fi world so neatly that they are a joy to watch, blasting the memories out of a guy's head has never looked better :D. The most stand-out concept of the game is the fact that you can fiddle with people's memories, change them and therefore changing their life experiences forming them into a different person, it's a great story narrative device and probably could have had a whole game for itself from how enjoyable it was but I wish it was used more...
The combat system is a refreshing take on the usual beat em up, gone are the heavy  attack, light attack, dodge ceremonial dance that is worshipped by previous games and instead you create your own comboes with their own benefits, mixing up kicks and punches as you go - roundhouse kicking foes to give me health is just so sweet plus someone decided that you can dodge and carry on your combo which is a awesome touch yet the combat can get really clustered when fighting multiple foes and you can never seem to pull off your best comboes because you get blind sided by a dude lightly stroking your hair. On that note the humanoid enemy designs (the robots are pretty cool) and character designs (excluding a few characters) are really bland and take the life out of the world as the humoids all look like splicers that didn't make the cut to be in Bioshock. The boss battles excluding the last one felt really tedious to me, or in fact pointless, same goes for the stealth sections. There is a hell of a lot of climbing to do but Nilin moves so slowly that it makes it more of a chore to do it. The game time isn't that long with no replayablility at all and is pretty linear however the linear parts don't make it exactly bad as it does allow you to focus on the story.
Even though it does have it's faults and can be annoying at times Remember Me was pretty enjoyable for most of it, if your looking for a "different" type of beat em up I'd reccomend this.
+ Combat is refreshing and new
+ World, Special Effect and Environment design are superb
+ Memory remixing is a great gameplay mechanic
+ Story has it's moments
- Drab enemy and character designs
- Climbing and stealth are pretty boring
- Boss battles are annoying
- Short (but compact)
7/10

It is amazing how a few poorly thought out design choices can make an excellent game into merely "decent".
There are many excellent things about this game.  The graphics are amazing (if your rig can handle it), the combat smooth but challenging (think The Witcher 1), the level designs reminiscent of Mirror's Edge, the story line charged with lots of fun ethical and moral debate, the voice acting is excellent, and there's a well developed world style and backgroud.  Generally it's a great ride for about 10-15 hours of play.
However, the downsides are also many.  The world is a railroad platformer where the only side-tracks are for hidden items.  These (and achievement hunting) are an exercise in frustration; there is no capability to skip cutscenes and/or jump ahead in a level you've already completed.  The play can also be rather sketchy on a keyboard and I really recommend using a gamepad.  The late game story also takes some "twists" that are really kinda forced or unnecessary.  I also ran into several targeting and other bugs that required restarting the game.
I suspect that many of these issues are because this is DONTNOD's first production.  There's a lot of talent there that just needs a bit more polish.  I look forward to seeing future works from this group.

Remember Me is not a good game. Set in a future Neo-Paris, a technology called Sensen allows people to store and share memories. You play Nilin, a memory hunter who can remix memories. The concept would have been cooler and would have been more interesting if this wasn't such a warn path in film and television. I can personally recommend Joss Whedon's Dollhouse as it also has a strong female protagonist, but also a much better story and pushes the concept of altering memories much further than anything that Remember Me even eludes to. And I think this is a big sticking point with the game as it just isn't very interesting.
Graphically Remember Me is very nice, but as a third person adventure game it is very linear, the combat is boring on the side of being way too long and repetitive, the platforming is easy as all the jump spots have floating arrows next to them to tell you where to jump to. The reason why the floating arrows are there is probably because because the environments are so nice, it is almost impossible to navigate all of the invisible walls and climbing dead ends without them, especially since there is no Assassins Creed type procedural climbing engine at play.
A few reviewers have mentioned that the four brief remix sequences where you get to edit someone's memory is cool, but these are just trial and error puzzles that require very little skill and aren't particularly interesting. But if you like the idea then I can recommend the film Inception, as it is very similar in concept, but pushes the idea much further than Remember Me. If Remember Me had of taken the whole memory storing, sharing and remixing further than you playing a character who can't remember anything and needing to steal the memory of a keypad door code from some guy, I would have enjoyed this more, but it didn't.
For other memory altering films I can recommend, The Final Cut with Robin Williams, Dark City, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, Total Recall, 50 First Dates and Paycheck as they all take the concept much further than Remember Me or does it in a much more interesting way.
Remember Me is a missed opportunity. 2/5

This is a very pretty experience, but if you were expecting a game you'll end up disappointed.
You are basically guiding a beautiful, motion-captured woman through a beautiful city with well lit, realistic textures often scanned from real life. Depending on the scene, you get to walk, you may or may not get to jump, move faster, or orient the camera. If the scene is scripted as a combat scene you get to run through combos by alternating mouse buttons at the right intervals, and if it is scripted as a platform scene, you get to jump between tagged areas. The controls are modal, with the jump key used to trigger context-dependent scripted actions (a small jump that doesn't allow you to reach or jump over anything, a dodge, and the aforementioned ledge functionality).
Your next action is almost always highlighted with orange signage, and if you loiter even briefly some scenes will prompt you to look in  the right direction. Aside from the preset path and a few orange collectibles, areas aren't meant to be explored; your jumping ability becomes blocked by invisible walls, you can't crouch, you can't reach platforms or ledges that aren't tagged with the magic orange arrows. Aside from maybe combat, which is probably easier with an analog stick than with a keyboard, none of what you do feels earned or challenging.
All this to say that, while Remember Me is about as pretty as a movie, it's not much more interactive.

*note* Pay no attention to the time as i got this game when it was on indieDB and got pretty far before letting it collect dust while pursuing other games (and the fact i got as far as worth proceeding in version 1.2).
Now for the review.
I'm not really a person who could judge what is considered "cute". i guess the cardboard cutouts are a bit amusing. that said those same cutouts are made me jump more than once when they appear after just barely escaping an enemy that doesn't need to follow the path to catch you. So in that regard i guess you could call them scary too. i also like that it seems that the devs stopped throwing a cutout at you every other room (like how they were in the indieDB version i played).
But outside of those "enemies", the actual enemies are terrifying and will definitely get your heart racing. on top of that if it's your first time playing they can catch you off guard as there's no rhyme or reason for some of their appearances. What i mean is that unlike other horror games (good ones that is) there is a build up to an enemies appearance and on some occasions the "rules" to win against said enemies are laid out. take for example the first resident evil, the first zombie encounter is built up using sound effects to create an uneasy feeling of not knowing what's in the room with you. following up on that the rules for winning are laid out as if you try to fight the first zombie A) you'll notice you use up almost all your ammo and B) that you'll take damage whereas avoiding it you'll notice things like you are faster and more agile than the zombies (well agile while using tank controls) so evasion is a preferred option when you can.
That's not to say that how the enemies appear in SPHJ is bad in fact the opposite. the fact you don't know when you'll encounter a type of enemy or how to beat it without trying a few times against a new enemy adds it's own eeriness as you don't know what the next room holds for you. You have to constantly think on the fly and adapt even quicker.
However this brings up an issue i have with the game, there's way too much luck involved. i'll give a good example, the first enemy you meet is pretty easy to figure out, just run. but that strategy will bite you in the rear when you come to the first "catwalk" room (that's what i call it at least, the room with the narrow walkways that split in multiple directions). If you just dead sprint you have a 50/50 chance of taking the wrong path and getting cornered and that enemy takes you out in 3 hits.
There are other points like this as there's an enemy i saw in markipliers playthrough i've yet to encounter that seems to appear at random with no way to figure out what you did wrong (or right in my case as, again, i haven't encountered the red face enemy in any of my playthroughs). so like i said, this game takes alot of luck if you're going to get far (or just alot of patience till you get that lucky run).
the other issue i have i'm not sure if it's an aesthetic choice to encourage players to keep calm or if it's just how the game happened to be made. the issue is that you have to press forward every time you enter a room. what i mean is that you can't just hold down the W key and keep moving as soon as you enter the next room. No, in each room you have to release the key and press it again to move. this is really annoying against the aforementioned first enemy as if you forget this you won't move (and take damage) till you remember to release the forward key and press it again. Like i said i'm not sure if it's intentional or not, if it's not then i hope the devs will work on this as it's basically a cheap beginner's trap.
But other than those two issues i do really think this is a good horror game and can't wait to see what the full release is like.

I never write reviews, but the fact that this game has so many negative reviews makes me feel like I have to stand up for it.
For me this game is a complete delight.  I played this game for about an hour and became confused and kind of bored after the tutorial planet, but over the next few days I kept thinking about it.  Everything about the game is ethereal and inviting in an alien kind of way.  I kept coming back knowing that I would see something new and beautiful if I kept looking.  It's like chasing a mystery with absolutely no idea what you will find or if you will find anything at all, and to me that is the truest form of exploration.  It really makes you feel like you are alone in space searching for who knows what.  A lot of the negative reviews state that the worlds are monochromatic and difficult to navigate but I think it adds rather than detracts from the experience.
If you are looking for a game that has clear objectives and goals LOOK ELSEWHERE because this game is NOT for you.  If, however, you are looking for a beautiful and immersive experience that at times surprises and delights you with tiny snippets of a larger mystery, then play this now.  Keep playing it.  Find new things.  Feel like you have no idea where you are or what you are doing.  Feel discouraged.  Then find something new that begins connecting everything else.  And keep looking for more.  Rinse, repeat.  Lovely!
