I'm not usually a huge fan of platformers, but this is my absolute favourite kind, fast paced and filled with puzzles to solve! Ori and the Blind Forest is part of the Metroidvania subgenre, so if you love finding secrets and exploring a vast interconnected map full of things to find, this one is for you!
The controls are just perfect, they feel incredibly natural and responsive - it is a whole heap of fun to catapault Ori around the world. However, please be aware that this can get very challenging at times - the escape sequences were literally the most intense platforming experience I've ever had, and the game has me clocked at somewhere around 500 deaths in total. However, the fact that I never really minded dying 6 times in a row is a testament to the strength of this game. Even during the challenging parts, I always felt like I was progressing forwards at all times!
Some of the puzzles and world themes seemed almost Zelda-esqe, which I adored. I also love the fact that you control the savepoints, so you can tailor your saves to where you are finding things the most challenging.
Highly recommend this beautiful little game!

Modern breakout game for casual joy and relaxation. A Review by
The gameplay differs in no way from the usual breakout game, but since Breakout is a derivate of Pong, the multiplayer mode (player vs. player or player vs. [a very lethargic] AI) is literally just Pong, no bricks to smash.
The controls are very simple, you'll just need to move your mouse up and down to control the paddle. The only case where you need a keyboard is the multiplayer mode. Control keys are not changeable, which means that non-latin keyboards might need their virtual keyboard layout to be changed, in order to play with a friend.
When launching the game, you'll immediately be greeted with an epillepsy notice. At this point you'll notice that the user interface is not as well designed, as you might have expected it. Menu buttons are just a clickable piece of text, so it takes some time to figure out the difference between a button and e.g. the score display.
CRACKHEAD appears with bright graphics and "slow" electronic music. Playing this game is similar to a relaxing rave party, you don't know what you're doing and for how long you already smash bricks, but it likely won't stress you out.
CRACKHEAD is not worth the price of $3.99, but is availible in alternative shops for much less, due to being given away massively for free sometimes. At the current state, there are no features which justify buying it at this high price, but we do recommend giving it a try in case you already got this game in your library.

I have previously written a review for this game but I think it's time to make a new one. My goal is to make this easy to understand at a glance.
This one is super opinion heavy and it's best to just judge for yourself.
+
- The characters are all well drawn and stand out from everything on the screen. There are a ton of colors to choose from (over 20 per character) and many are references to other characters. The fanservice in this game can be seen as excessive, but I don't care about it or notice it much.
+
- The stages, for the most part, look great. The stages are somewhat 3D (which can be changed in the options) but it isn't super noticeable. They all look like they were designed with a purpose; they don't look like they were just thrown in. Another good thing about the stages is that they never distract me from the game.
+
- Everything is super well animated in this game. The attacks always look smooth and there are no animation-hitbox oddities such as the super large Street Fighter II Shoryuken hitbox.
+
- Skullgirls allows you to select the number of characters are on your team. Single character teams are viable in this game because each character in a multiple character team is weakened based on the team size.
+
- Everything in this game feels crisp and responsive. This is personal opinion, but it is one of the best feeling fighting games I've ever played.
+
- This game has a mechanic where it detects when the opponent is doing an infinite combo and allows the other player to break free. Because of this, one combo doesn't mean a immediate loss.
+
- When selecting your characters, you can input normals and specials as assist moves. Since these aren't new moves, you will immediately know how they work. It also provides for options that are fun to test out.
+
- The tutorial teaches you mechanics that are used in many other fighting games. There is also a section that teaches about each character individually.
+
- You don't have to learn more than one character to start playing this game.
+
- Things like slow motion and showing hitboxes make it easy to understand the game's mechanics.
+
- When doing a 360 motion, the game will prevent you from jumping during it.
This is one of the best fighting games I have ever played. I know that it won't be to everyone's tastes, but I find it very hard to think of places where this game is lacking. Many of the problems that people had were ironed out by the developers who continue to work on this game.  If you like games such as Marvel vs Capcom you are going to want to check this one out.
Just keep your expections high because this game is sure to surpass them.

"Without question one of the most forward-thinking fighters in the genre right now. While keeping true to its 2D-fighting game roots, LabZero recognizes some of the flaws and annoyances from other fighting games and seeks to correct them.
Faulty netcode? Nope, we've got GGPO.
Unexplained mechanics? Nope, pretty much everything you could want is given to you in the tutorials. More than that, it's done in a way that will challenge newcomers without overwhelming them.
Unblockable setups? Handled.
Unbalanced metagame? Not here. Game design is lead by MikeZ, who has been a part of the fighting game scene for a long while now. In addition to that, balance testing is regularly handled in conjunction with the playerbase itself in the form of the Endless Beta.
The community is currently not too big, so the players you'll find on quick match are generally somewhat skilled and experienced. Because of this, the game might be difficult to get into for a newcomer. But it truly is worthwhile to keep practicing and improve your skills."
This quote is a review that hits on about all the points I would point out to someone interested in the game.
As a long-time gamer and lover of fighting games, Skullgirls is easily one of the best to try if you are interested in the genre. That is, if you enjoy the feel and artstyle. As someone who plays fighting games ranging from 3D, 2D, anime air-dashers, or even Smash Bros, I want to really highlight Lab Zero's dedication to their project, and their design philosophy as well.

Without getting too into it all, LabZero's lead design not only made sure to make the game as balanced as possible (Through constant updates and bugfixes with help from community feedback), but they also went through a period of time where they went completely unpaid for their work. That dedication for an end product that is meant to be a quality, competitive fighter is what makes this game demanding of a chance.

Okay, so wow right? A NEW Deponia game! After the ending of the third game I was pretty sure that was all there was going to be of the franchise. Anyway this isn't going to be a super indepth review, i'm just gonna state my feelings on this game and how it impacts the previous 3.
To start off, this is a good game. It's funny and strange like the other three. Its feels like the devs never even lost touch with how this series is supposed to be presented like or how to write for it.
Thats pretty much it for the review portion of this.
Now for how I feel about this game and its inclusion into the series.
Warning heavy spoilers below.
It doesn't need to exist. There never needed to be a fourth game. You just end up ending the story the same way again as the third game did. This game was pretty much just the writers way of addressing the complaints of the players on the ending of the third game, which to be honest I really liked it. I was happy with how the series ended with Rufus sacrificing himself in order to ensure everyone on deponia and elysium were able to live together in relative peace. I know of course the writer could have made the story to where Rufus never had to sacrifice himself but they didn't. I know the appeal of wanting a happy ending too, I mean anyone who is interested in buying this game would have played the previous ones. I really wanted Rufus and Goal to have a happy ending where they are able to be together and be happy, but I know that not every story has to have a happy ending.
While I really enjoyed this game and I do not regret buying it I don't think I could recommend it to fans of the original trilogy.
Finally Rufus is back! Back with a great graphics, hilarious jokes and with mission to save the world. The game is great!

LEGO Worlds has delivered an outstanding sandbox product which, after an admittedly slow start, ultimately becomes the title we enjoyed throughout early access... and more. By exploring planets containing a variety of biomes you acquire a plethora of building elements, animals, vehicles and more to use in creating your own towns and ecosystems. You do need to capture guys carrying around different types of LEGO pieces to add them to your arsenal, but catching them isn't complicated. However, if you do want all pieces available up-front, this could be a negative. (See the explanation of LEGO Digital Designer integration further down and you can bypass this... in a way.)
This title is much more streamlined than during early access, especially with regards to performance, which has been vastly improved. Additionally, each of the in-game utilities is well-explained and straightforward to use, providing optional but helpful tutorials. Whether you want to build something from scratch, modify the landscape, go on an underwater expedition or cause absolute chaos and destruction, intuitive controls and menus make it easy.
As an added bonus for those of you who use LEGO Digital Designer (LDD), LXFML files for in-game elements you choose to save using the Copy Tool can be imported into LDD software should you want to expand upon them outside of the game environment. Additionally, you can take anything you've created in LDD and import it into the game under the "Brick Build" category. All models that are active in your game will exist in the following directory: C:\Users\<USERNAME>\AppData\Roaming\Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment\LEGOWorlds\SAVEDGAMES\CONTENT\S1-SYSGLOBAL\MODS\MODELS. I should note I have had a couple issues with some colors failing to export to LDD, but this could be an isolated case based on my system configuration. Either way, the structure of the builds is intact, which is the important part if you wish to have LDD generate instructions for you to build things in reality.
Overall, relaxing and enjoyable. The only limitation is your creativity.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a 2d action platformer in the Metroidvania style. At least, that's what I've heard, since I've never played the 2d Metroid games or the Castlevania games. All I know is that this game is an exemplary example of a smart control scheme and a well executed plan.
For gameplay, you start off with a little spirit called Sein who has the ability to shoot a Spirit Flame. Your job is to platform your way to victory, avoiding monsters that can be annoying but are neither difficult nor unfair, as well as environmental hazards (apparently the world consists of about 70% thorn bushes, in every climate. Who knew?), while progressively getting more skills that mostly have a dual purpose of unlocking more creative ways to platform as well as to kill the enemies that keep popping up. These start with an ability to hop up the side of a wall and go to things such as Bash, which is an interaction with either a projectile or enemy that swaps places with it and forcibly flings both the enemy/projectile and Ori in opposite directions. There are a myriad of other abilities, but they do not become so numerous that the sheer list is cumbersome, nor are they just gimmicks where you have to use them for a single area and then you're done with them forever. Some do become obsolete (e.g. wall hop, double jump in favor of wall climb and triple jump), but they are all useful in their own right, and offer quite a few ways to deal with progressing through the game.
As it is a Metroidvania style game, the platforming can be extremely unforgiving. Ori has relatively low HP and mana pools, which can be supplemented by finding Life and Energy Cells respectively that are hidden away throughout the game (most seem to become available when you get your last ability, but that may just be because that was when I unlocked the abilities to locate the secrets on the map). The game can occasionally be confusing as to where you need to go, but just like with any puzzle, careful exploration/manipulation (and a few dozen deaths or so) will generally allow you to figure out the mechanics of the area enough to follow the right path. Probably the most frustrating thing is that a lot of stuff can just instantly kill you, and you have a very minimal window to react in order to avoid getting plastered to the floor, skewered by a massive thorn bush, or deep fried in lava. I ended the game with about ~370 deaths, which feels absurd to me, but all of the frustration is definitely worth it as it makes it feel so much more rewarding when you finally break through and are able to hit that double jump into triple bash into rapid fire glide manipulation in order to navigate an extremely narrow corridor where one misstep just instantly kills you, even if you have a full 15 health with the damage reduction perk.
An interesting little tidbit in this game is the ability tree. There are three different paths to choose from: (from right to left) survival, exploration, and offense. All three are linear and exclusive (though you can level up each of the three, if you want a particular ability you're going to have to commit to one for a good chunk of the game), and while many of the abilities don't seem that great, they actually do make a difference over the course of the game. Half cost on soul links (which are the player's way of saving the game) as well as being able to heal 2 health per cast can be extremely useful when going through a particularly hazardous area where you really don't want to do the entire sequence 5 bazillion times. It is also extremely useful for those of us who would like to 100% the game but don't want to spend 15 hours testing every patch of wall to figure out whether there is a secret passage behind it or not.
For presentation, this game has that in spades. The game itself is gorgeous. I'm hard pressed to think of a single game with a better aesthetic, and there is always something going on in the background that lends itself to the current tempo of the game while not distracting the player overmuch. When all hell breaks loose, the game will let you know just how much trouble you are in, whether its having water pour in from half the screen, or having a lava tidal wave barrel down at you. And you'll get to experience it over and over again as you fail at least 10 times per epic escape due to having to run at 100 miles per hour while hitting precise jumps but also stopping because an instant kill beam is about to spew out of the wall but a chunk of the ceiling is coming down and you're gliding so you can't move horizontally very fast but you also have a monster spitting stuff at you that you have to Bash to get to hit the wall so that you can progress through that area and then another massive chunk of the ceiling comes crashing down where you have the space of about 1.5x the size of your character to squeeze in and then you have to navigate a little U bend with thorns which is no problem... Except you just flew straight into a steam geyser that is an instakill because it was hiding in the thorns just for you and gave you about a half second to react, while giving an extremely small window between 2 geysers and the thorns that you have to spam glide/stop in order to not fly too high or drop too low. Point being, the whole presentation of the game is absolutely fantastic, but there is a small problem in that it can be hard to identify exactly what can and can't kill you as some things can be blended into the background, but you have a knee jerk reaction to avoid that falling rock... Except it's falling in the background, not in the actual game. It is a small thing, but it can be quite frustrating when you're already frantically trying to escape a tree that is imploding upon itself.
As for the story... I really don't want to spoil any of it at all. Suffice to say, all of those reviews say that it is a tearjerker are true. The developers did a fantastic job of getting you to care for the characters in the game, and the progression of the story continues in that arc. It's even more impressive to me since it all comes about by the actions and interactions of the characters, not by dialogue. There is a narrator that chimes in now and then (I think its the same language as the opening to Circle of Life from the Lion King, so you'll have to read the narration) to guide the character and fill in knowledge of the lore, but is altogether unobtrusive. I love to play video games and read books for their stories, and it has been a very long time since I have experienced a story that made me care about the characters this much.
I found this game to be an absolutely fantastic experience, and will most likely play it every now and then down the road. It's just one of those games that is not only a great experience with a good story, but also has fun, fulfilling gameplay, and the icing on the cake is that it is just absolutely beautiful. I give this game a 9.5/10 and wholeheartedly recommend this game to anybody and everybody. It is definitely more difficult than most games I have played, but the gameplay is altogether not terribly unfair and is extremely rewarding to play through.

The first level of this game is amazing.
I cannot overstate that the first puzzle of this game is one of the most pure "Oh...Oh!....OHHHH!" momnts I've ever had as a gamer. When you organicaly stumble upon the mechanics of the game, and by extension the solution of the puzzle, after being lost and confused.
If that first level was a free demo I would recommend it to everyone I know.
After that level you're thrown into your ship and have to figure out how it works. You assume it's by trial and error, but there's so many bloody buttons and functions that you're never sure you're doing it right. There is absolutely 0 player feedback or explanation about what you're doing. I don't mean that in the sense of "Why am I exploring these planets, what's the story here?" I mean more in the sense of "Okay, that turned everything blue for a while....is that good? Bad?" If the developers were trying to achieve a sense of being in an alien craft and having to figure out how to make it go, then they succeeded I guess. But that is a huge barrier of entry to anyone who wants to see the rest of the game. I imagine most might only keep at it so as to justify the $10 they just spent on this.
At times though it feels like the game is obtuse purely for the sake of being obtuse in it's design choices, like the controls. You can't look arround, or at least not on the Y axis, and you're X axis movement is restricted to WASD, like an old DOS game. Until you figure out how the mouse comes into play it can feel very off putting. Mix that with the monochromatic landscapes, the bright garish colors, and a soundtrack that sounds like Risk of Rain slowed to a crawl and this game made me feel dizzy and even sick at times, someting I can't say a game has ever done to me.
Worst of all there's no drive to solve the obtuse puzzles of the game. You get one flash of a very vague story at the start and then are plopped into the game with little else to motivate you beyond "Solve the puzzle". And since all the worlds you land on have randomly generated puzzles they're often times never as complex as a handcrafted puzzle like the first level was. Of course you'll never see any of these puzzles if you can't figure out how to get your ship to work. You could look up the answer like I did, but that both defeats the purpose and leaves you with nothing to do but go to planet after boring planet.
So, final verdict? Even if everything I've described here sounds like your cup of tea I'd still recommend looking up gameplay so to better understand what you're getting yourself into. Like I said the first level is amazing, but not worth $9.99 they're asking for. This game is clearly targeted at an extremely niche set of gamers, who should still wait for this to be at least %50 before even thinking of purchasing. There's not enough enjoyable content, or good gameplay experiences in this to justify $9.99.

I consider this experience to be a very pleasant distraction. This is the type of game that I'd play during a study break, or while I'm waiting for a plane. It asks for very little from you in terms of brain capacity or effort, and offers a pleasing, casual adventure in return.
The gameplay consists of you the player directing multiple workers to remove obstacles, collect resources, and construct buildings for additional resources in order to complete the level's goal. You control your workers by simply clicking on the tiles where you would like for them to go. Strategery comes into play when considering which resources to collect first, when to build farms and workshops for additional resources, and when to activate other abilities to increase the productivity of your workers. This is most likely a game that will only take a couple levels to get used to (No more than 15 minutes), and the only control you need to know is the click of your mouse!
I got the most out of my experience when I decided to strategize before each level and optimized my pathing. Believe when I say that there
a best way to complete a level, and if you want to beat any developers scores you
have to put in the extra effort.
The negatives regarding this game don't have anything to do with the core gameplay (for the most part). The story is incredibly bareboned and the musical score is pretty forgettable (I turned it off after a few levels). The only problem with the gameplay was level 3.8, in which I discovered a game breaking issue that took me a few minutes spooling through forums to resolve. You can only hold 99 of a resource at a time, and this is a level where it is very easy to collect more than 99, meaning you can collect resources from the map without gaining resources in your inventory, so choose your routing carefully!
In conclusion, for the 99 cents I paid, there's not much complaining I can do. It gave me a solid 9 hours of easy gaming, it was nice to look at, and there is some replay to be had if you want to collect hidden puzzle pieces in the levels, tackle harder difficulties, or maximize your scores, not to mention achievements and trading cards.

EDIT: I've finished the game, so I can now write a full review for it. I'll leave my original first impression at the bottom.
Naturally, the game's art and voice acting are still of the same high level they were before. The humour feels like it got slightly tamer, but I actually think that's a good thing because the previous games veered into "dude, not funny" territory a few times (especially the third one). In sheer playing time, this game also took me the longest of them all. I think this might be because the puzzles are just a bit more obvious this time, which means I never got stuck for so long that I opened a guide but rather spent more time thinking about puzzles myself. (To be fair, after 3 games you have a very good idea of the kinds of solutions Deponia typically requires, so that might also be why the puzzles are more obvious.)
What I didn't like so much are the timed parts, because if you fail them you have to time loop and waste a lot of time and effort retracing your steps. The game's final section is especially guilty of this, and by far the most frustrating part of the game because of that.
Speaking of the final section, it's also where I started to lose track of the story. It becomes a big complicated mess of timelines and copies of characters. I guess the idea is to show what happens when you unleash Rufus' chaos onto time travel but it did make it a bit hard to figure out what was happening.
Overall, I don't think this game is as good as the rest of the series. I understand the point the devs tried to make with this fourth game, and I enjoyed the additional characters, character development, story, context and insight in Elysium, but I feel it misses the direction and urgency that the original trilogy had. It's an "extra" game that's not really part of the main storyline of the original series, and feels more like a bunch of ideas the devs couldn't put in the other games that were linked together with timetravel.
In conclusion: I recommend it, but only if you enjoyed the first three games and realize that what you're about to play is basically just extra stuff and more Rufus-ing around.
ORIGINAL REVIEW BASED ON FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
Please note that this review is based just on my first impressions of the game. I'll probably update it once I finish playing, but for now I wanted to share my thoughts with people who are also fans of the series and don't really know what to expect.
Those first impressions are very positive. The game's humour, puzzles, art and voice acting all remain of the same high level as before, although the fourth wall has rusted all the way down this time. Storywise, the game takes a very interesting turn. The narration itself opens by more or less saying "oh? you didn't like the ending to the third game? you want a different ending? well be careful what you wish for", which gives me confidence that, rather than a quick attempt to 'fix' the ending that so many people didn't like, this will be more like a deconstruction of that idea.
My recommendation right now? If you're a fan of Deponia, get it. If you've never played a Deponia game before, go play the first one, because obviously this one contains HUGE spoilers, right in the opening animation. If you're still in doubt, wait a few days for the full reviews to drop in. But I expect them to be positive as well.

- QUICKSAVES!
What I did not like:

Verdict:

Killing sh*tload of nazis is great fun, weapons really feel powerfull and every time I started shooting, I prayed that nazi waves wouldn't stop coming. Compared to TNO, I can definitely say that gameplay was slightly improved, but I liked TNO cutscenes a lot more, since they were shorter and every dialogue had it purpose, which sadly wasn't the case in TNC. And that ending... oh how could they not repeat that awesomeness from TNO? Final mission in TNC feels like just another mission, and then it suddenly ends. The gradation simply wasn't there at all... BUT it still easily is the best FPS game of the year (well it's basically just a one-eyed king), and I am sure that I will not stop at just one completed playthrough.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is hard game to explain because it does a lot of different things while still being narrow in its scope. It's not a "walking simulator" even though there is a lot of walking at a pace that can be seen infuriating by some. It's not a horror game, but there were moments when I was scared and stressed out to a degree where I didn't want to continue. It's not an action game, but at points I felt like the torrent of enemies would never stop. It's not a puzzle game either, but you will spend considerable time walking around trying to figure out environmental puzzles.
While the combat and puzzle mechanics are quite simple, the game isn't long enough for this to become a problem, clocking in at manageable 6-10 hours.
The games biggest strenght is the story telling, the uneasy atmosphere it creates, and the soundtrack which ties the two together perfectly.
Hellblade does a little bit of everything and manages to do so without it feeling like clash of genres. The end product is something that is not for everyone, but something everyone should try.

Amazing visuals and animation, paired with a deep but accessible combo system, and featuring the best tutorial ever in any fighting game. This is a must own title if you even have a passing interest in learning why you are terrible at fighting games.
My full review

Probably one of the most original fighting game to debut in the last decade or so,
is fast and super fun that is almost a must play for anyone with a even a remote interest in fighting games, made by a passionate team of individuals who really put their effort into making the best game possible.
has team-based fighting, similar to the Marvel VS Capcom series of fighting games, where you tag in up to three different fighters. Players can pick between fighting with one, two or three characters, giving the players a lot of different options to play with. The combat is fast and free flowing, which keeps the game very intense and fun. The free-flowing gameplay makes it really fun to experiment with different comobs. The gameplay is very technical for fighting game veterans to master, but can be picked up and played by anyone, so its good for both newcomers to fighting games and veterans. Furthermore, the tutorial is one of the best tutorials I have seen in any game of any genre. It literally goes over every aspect of the game in great detail so if you don't understand fighting games you can understand the more complicated mechanics with ease. There are also tutorials for every individual character giving guidelines on how to play and teaches you their special moves, which is great for helping choose which characters to main.
The artwork is amazing and beautiful to look at, as well as incredibly detailed, everything from the fluid character animations to the backgrounds is truly stunning, even breathtaking at moments. The soundtrack also fits the world and the fighting very well with some very cool theme stages.
Skulgirls probably has one of the strongest storymodes of any fighting game. The storyline is very engaging, the dialgoue is executed perfectly by the voice actors and the characters are all unique and interesting. What really makes the game stand out is the sense of humour, this game is one of the funniest games I've played, with very funny dialogue, even the announcers are memorable and produce some great lines. On the downside, the storymode is a little on the short side. Some people would complain about a lack of characters, since there were only eight on launch, however, they have since added six new player characters to the game and all the characters are unique and interesting and I would much rather have a small cast of characters that are all unique instead of a large cast with some duplicates and less interesting or fun characters.
Multiplayer in this game works very well, especially compared to some other PC fighting games' netplay *cough* Accent Core *cough*, you can almost always have a great match with little to no input delay. One of its faults is that there isn't a challenge mode or many extra modes like in other fighting games.

Games like these are an effective test of my capacity to review a game.
MirrorMoon EP, in short, is an art game, about discovery.
Because of this, it goes out of its way to obfuscate the controls and user interface in an artistic way, which I personally understand but find both intriguing and irritating. From what I can tell, the game is designed to be an open-ended experience to
from time to time, instead of accomplishing it in any definite or predictable way.
If you're up for that sort of thing, then you might have a great time here. I really enjoyed the visual aesthetics of MMEP as someone who likes rather minimalistic art from time to time.
I'd definitely say part of the experience is figuring out how the hell to do anything in the game, however. Feel free to take that as either a challenge or a warning.
I can easily see why some would be annoyed, and although there are a couple of Community Guides already there's definitely a part of me which is intimidated by the concept of an exploration game which forces you to understand a skeuomorphic user interface for both the ship and environment. Thing is, outside of procedurally-generated planetary exploration that's basically the point of the game to me, so I can't really be that upset about it.
I'd recommend it for an experience unlike most others, especially the ship's interface with all of its buttons and gizmos, but the game definitely defies what I consider conventional game design so if you're looking for that you're out of luck, I'm afraid.
Overall, I'd recommend it, especially at its current price point (during a Humble Store sale) of 2 bucks.

Over seventy constellations with lots of stars, each containing some kind of a puzzle, be it as simple as "find an orb", or as complicated as "find several, tools, activate pillars, change illumination of the star to activate certain areas, and finally unlock and find orb on the star".
Regular stars can be named, part of them have unique names [undiscovered but named], there are 2 special stars in each constellation, players all start in different parts and uncover and name different stars, everyone travel between them by operating a cockpit, from which you can adjust travelling speed at expense of the  fuel usage. Every travel takes a bit of it, and it restores over time of the ship not moving.
Travelling takes real time, so it's best to play windowed and have some book/tv around or other things open in the background.
It's an unique game, its mechanics are very limited, but as a whole concept - it's a completitionist's paradise. You can roam freely, solve puzzles, and be rewarded with a possibility to "mark" your territory, and help everyone uncover the whole constellation in the grander scale.
It's major downside are the controls, they're extremely limited to force player use the unconventional methods of orientation prepared for the game, another thing being the repetition, you will find yourself doing pretty much the same things all the time you play.
I however find it fair, it's a rather bland and simply bad game, but it's amazingly good background game, it's something that you don't focus too much on, but invest bits of your time.
Kind of like playing sudoku in the free time, you play it puzzle by puzzle to reach another milestone, that is what MirrorMoon EP is like, and I think I like it.

This game is for very specific kinds of people, very specifically me. This is a complex dimensional puzzle game in which the objective is to figure out the objective.
With the exception of keyboard controls (which is pretty much the only in game text you will see), all aspects of the game are learned by doing, entirely at your own pace in a perfectly serene (or maybe ominous) environment.
In Mirrormoon EP, you explore planets with navigational help from a moon that mirrors the planet's surface. The reward for exploring isn't so much what you find, but the very experience of exploring itself and immersing yourself in the game's beautiful abstract world and atmosphere. And perhaps the satisfaction of naming your very own planet for other players to see and explore.
A huge contributor is the game's audio, which (after having played Fotonica) seems pretty characteristic of this developer. Much of the game's beauty and texture exists in the deep and impressive sound rather than visuals. A great refresher from playing games in a time when graphics and visuals are usually seen as a video game's most central attributes, with sound a distant secondary.
I wouldn't recommend Mirrormoon EP to just anyone, but those who I would recommend it to will not have a moment free of my pestering to play this damn great game.

This game isn't for everyone. It isn't even for the majority... It's for a small dedicated group of people.
I have a problem with procedurally generated. games.  Occasionally the random variables all conspire to put a wall across the exit corridor, or make a 6-way symmetric equation solvable only by hours of trial and error...  Sometimes you just don't know if you're being dense, or the game's given you an impossible level.  When you play a human-crafted game, you know it's solvable.  Not so with random games.   Mirrormoon doesn't seem to have this problem because the 'randomness' is tightly controlled.   It works like this: "If thing A is here, then puzzle B must need to be solved", and vice versa.   Because every 'planet' is self-contained, the randomness is between planets...
So, it becomes clear that every sphere is basically a collection of the same puzzles, in slightly different configurations: You just randomly stumble about, trying to use the "mirror moon" as a map and do the exact same four or five 'puzzles', over and over again.  Oh, the colours changed, and the placement of the puzzles changes.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is hard game to explain because it does a lot of different things while still being narrow in its scope. It's not a "walking simulator" even though there is a lot of walking at a pace that can be seen infuriating by some. It's not a horror game, but there were moments when I was scared and stressed out to a degree where I didn't want to continue. It's not an action game, but at points I felt like the torrent of enemies would never stop. It's not a puzzle game either, but you will spend considerable time walking around trying to figure out environmental puzzles.
While the combat and puzzle mechanics are quite simple, the game isn't long enough for this to become a problem, clocking in at manageable 6-10 hours.
The games biggest strenght is the story telling, the uneasy atmosphere it creates, and the soundtrack which ties the two together perfectly.
Hellblade does a little bit of everything and manages to do so without it feeling like clash of genres. The end product is something that is not for everyone, but something everyone should try.

Let me explain.
Yes, No Man's Sky had an awful launch, besides the obvious lack of some promised features, the game wasn't as visually stunning as the demo footage had been, even up 'til release day. Also, it was plagued with performance issues.
Now, with my GTX 970 i7 4790k @ 4Ghz 16GB ram Win 8.1 system, I can run this game in 1080p with a 98% uptime of 60FPS, with the settings pretty much on max. How?
Fortunately for me, there is a rather awesome guide here on Steam written by a 970 owner, detailing how to get better and constant frame rates. I'll link it here in an edit.
One major issue with NMS is the repetitive grind of the core gameplay loop. But I have a suggestion for that:
Bear with me. The Sandbox mode is all well and good, but from what I can tell the story is then null and void (and there is a story, as such) and you kind of miss the point of the entire experience. But the "proper" modes, Normal, Survival and Permadeath, are just too much of a mind numbing drain of your soul.
This is where something like Cheat Engine comes in. There are a couple of tables out there (I will link the one I use in an edit) that work as of the current update (Pathfinder), and are VERY diverse in their options. Think less of it as cheating, and think more of it as a custom difficulty application, like Kerbal Space Program with mods.
While, yes, you
just turn everything on and be a God inside a
, but it is far, far better to just curate your own experience.
Maybe change the mining yields to 10 times, or even 50 times that of normal. That will ease the grind, right? Or maybe give yourself infinite resources, and instead focus on building up your pile of credits, your suit/tool/ship enhancements, and your standing with the three native species. Or max out your equipment but still rely on the mundane gathering of precious carbon and such like.
Ironically, I honestly feel this is how the game is meant to be played. Cater the game to your needs, not the other way round, and play the experience that you want to play. There are still things to do, those that follow the Atlas Path will still need to accomplish milestones to proceed. If you want to stake your claim on the Universe you'll want to chart every planet, and record every indigenous animal life, in all of their RNG glory.
The animals of No Man's Sky do take a lot of flak, and rightly so. The amount of times I've seen a neon green dinosaur like lizard with a acorn for a head is getting on the ridiculous side, but then even on the same planet you could find a species that actually looks rather realistic and beautiful, in its own cartoony cell shaded way. The first time I saw birds my jaw dropped, elegant Condor like creatures about the size of a dragon. It was incredible.
And that therein lies the fun of No Man's Sky. Take away the grind, or at least ease it, via the use of Cheat Engine. Go out and explore, find stuff, make a base, 100% your home planet, earn all the tech upgrades. While NMS cannot come close to offering an experience such as Elite Dangerous, Dual Universe or Star Citizen, there is actually a game under all that grind. It may not be the one that people expected, but there is still beauty in No Man's Sky, and if you have an interest in Sci-Fi games like this, it is well worth a pick up when on sale.
EDIT: 1.3 update very disappointing. Performance is downgraded, any previous progress pretty much nulled out (I dont mind that, was starting over anyway), again the build up has led to rather an anticlimax.
There are a couple of good new features, but overall, pretty irrelevant. Lowered my rating from "tentative thumbs up" to "only just a thumbs up". Like, borderline. Many people got caught up with Waking Titan, and to be honest, that in general was a better experience.

This is a great game with what for some - myself included - will be a fatal flaw. No spoilers...but about a third of the way through the game, after it has presented very little challenge along the way, you are hit with a platforming section that is borderline impossible. You need to make 15 - 20 perfect jumps in very quick succession. These aren't even 'normal' jumps; you have to riccochet off of enemy projectiles among other things. And there's no checkpoint during this entire sequence.
I've always been competent at platformers, and I can't remember the last game that I wanted to finish that I didn't, but after putting 3+ hours into the same exact spot, over multiple sittings, and still not getting past it, I'm done.
It's a shame, too, because the rest of the game (at least that I saw) was excellent. This whole section is just so out of place difficulty-wise that it can easily become a brick wall. I don't mind difficult games - but this went from having average or below average difficulty to the most difficult platform sequence I remember in 30 years of gaming. One simple checkpoint would have made a world of difference.

Thanks for those who took many efforts to make this game, I will treasure it.

I picked this game up on sale for $0.98... and it was worth every penny.  Heck, I'd have been happy paying as many as $3 for this game!!!
Seriously, 12 Labours is a silly little resource management game.  Essentially, it's like doing base management in an RTS game (Starcraft, Age of Empires, etc.), but without the whole "going to war" part.  You give orders to servents to farm, gather resources, clear obstacles, etc., and then try to hit the goals of the map before the timer expires.
It's not a deep game by any stretch, but it's fun enough.  Their isn't much plot, but the game does have a good sense of humor.  And if you decide that you really like it, there are a number of easter eggs to unlock... if you want to put in the time and effort.
Personally, I was happy to play through each of the maps just once; but like I said, that got me a few hours of enjoyment.  What more do you want for $0.98?

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is not only an incredible game, it's an important one. Dealing with a topic that for whatever reason is taboo, the game attempts to mimic many of the symptoms of severe mental illness. I loved the use of sound, you simply have to play this game with either a really good surround system, or some great headphones. Doing otherwise would be doing yourself a great disservice. Gameplay is a mix of puzzle elements, and sword fighting. To be fair, neither rewrite the book on these somewhat cliche video game attributes, but on the flip side, I found both well executed. I even found myself stumped on more than one occassion, which can take this game up to the 9-10 hour completion level depending on skill. But it's the world, the characters, the voice acting, the incredible soundtrack, and the downright feels this game evokes that makes it worth your time. When I wasn't drying the sweat from my palms, I was wiping the tears from my eyes from this incredible game. If you play one game the remainder of this year, make it Hellblade.

You have to plan out what kind of character you want to make allowing you to be different from other players characters. This also adds to the replayability to try new combos.
After you beat the game you can play 2 other modes that extend the lifespan of a single character, trying to make them the perfect hunter, by playing these gamemodes you get to find better loot and get points to further increase their stats. The max level is 30, I use to think this was bad but as I played it fit perfectly for the content available and with the glory point system in the other game modes you can still make them better.
The puzzles and side quests are also a lot of fun since it keeps things interesting.
The powerup abilities for your skills also adds depth to how you use your abilities.
Now for some negetive points, once in awhile buildings got in my way from seeing what was happening (they wouldn't go transparent) though this was only in a few places it still should happen. Some of the enemy champions (elites) have unfair abilities, the wall is fine since you can shoot it, the drain is fine since you can run away from it, most of them are fine except for 2, grapple is annoying and unfair, it grabs you from so far away, cant be dodged (haven't seen it miss), it stuns you as it pulls you to them, they can all cast it sametime increasing the stun effect. It has gotten me killed on multiple accounts. the other is the skeleton hand that cages you, you have to attack the hand to break free however you cant move and it works the same way as the grapple, it doesn't miss (haven't seen it miss) but these are from my experience there might be a way.
The lack of map variety, to what I see the maps are static, not randomized each time.
The game has some strange difficulty spikes, one moment its simple and easy, next moment you are running spamming pots cause the mobs are no joke anymore but overall it doesn't happen often.
If you accidently forget to complete a quest, the journal doesn't tell you which area the quest is for, so you have to do quite a bit of backtracking to find out which can be a pain.
Loading screens, it's not that bad but it would be nice if it was faster, it intrupts the flow of the game.
The music is good and the sound effects are pleasing. The graphics are great and the game runs very smooth. The variety of loot, enchanting, using essences, the dialogue, voice acting are all good. the game was lots of fun to play and got my monies worth.
I give the game a 8.5/10 for being what its suppose to be, to offer some unique features and have a good pace. But for the lack of replayability because of repeating exactly what you did before and the loading screens with not that great backtracking method, no randomized maps and some inconsistency. It's worth buying and offers enough and some for what you pay for.
